Headline: Exit polls show Merz’s party suffering heavy losses in 2 German state elections
Body: Exit polls showed Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s party suffering heavy losses in two German state elections on Sunday.Merz’s centre-right Christian Democratic Union is projected to fall to 5.5% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a largely rural state in Germany’s formerly communist east. That would be its worst result there since World War II.In Berlin, the CDU is projected to finish second with 20% of the vote, trailing the Left Party at 24.5%, according to an exit poll by the public broadcaster ARD.The Alternative for Germany (AfD) made significant gains in Sunday's regional elections. The vote came two weeks after the AfD finished just short of an absolute majority in the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, marking its best chance yet of forming the country’s first far-right regional government since the Second World War.Chancellor Friedrich Merz, 70, assumed leadership of Germany 16 months ago, pledging to revitalise an economy that has stalled for years. However, he has failed to lift a sullen national mood and has seen his personal popularity plunge.The AfD's strong showing in Saxony-Anhalt has further damaged the chancellor's standing nationally, sparking calls from within his own party over the past fortnight to replace him. Although no top-level allies have publicly demanded his resignation, many have warned against opening divisive internal personnel debates.Apparently anticipating a challenging post-election period, Merz abandoned a planned trip to New York next week to attend the UN General Assembly.Speaking after the publication of the exit polls, Merz stated that he intends to remain leader of the CDU and chancellor until the end of his term."The reforms have to come," 70-year-old Merz said. "I am taking on this responsibility because I want to move our country forward."

Headline: Meloni announces ban on burqa and niqab in Italian schools, cap on foreign students
Body: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has announced that the government is preparing a bill that would ban burqas and niqabs in schools and introduce a limit on the number of foreign pupils in each class.Several European countries, including France and Belgium, already ban face coverings in public places. Austria has also introduced restrictions in schools. Elsewhere, including Spain and Poland, freedom of conscience and religion is protected by the constitution.Meloni said a package of measures will soon go before the Italian cabinet, including a ban on burqas and niqabs in schools, a requirement for parents of pupils facing “serious difficulties integrating” into the national school system to learn Italian, and a limit on places for foreign pupils.Italy heads to the polls next year, with competition intensifying to the right of Meloni’s party following the entry of retired general Roberto Vannacci, who has called for even tougher measures. Migration is a highly political and divisive issue in Italy.“It is unacceptable that in an Italian classroom the children who end up feeling pushed into a corner are Italian children because they have become the minority. That cannot be allowed,” she said during a rally organised by Gioventù Nazionale, the youth wing of her Brothers of Italy party.“Calling all this integration is yet another lie, a convenient lie for those who live off ideology, for those who preach to us from their living rooms and then send their own children to schools where this problem does not exist.”Previous initiatives and legislative proposalsMeloni’s announcement comes after several related initiatives in recent months.In early August, Education and Merit Minister Giuseppe Valditara proposed action on the full-face veil through an amendment to the security bill.At the end of July, Futuro Nazionale — the party founded by far-right MEP Roberto Vannacci, who has backed Meloni’s proposal — tabled a resolution against the full-face veil in the Chamber of Deputies’ Culture Committee. It was approved with centre-right votes after being redrafted at the government’s request.In March, the League introduced a bill in the Senate to amend Article 5 of the 1975 Reale law, which was introduced by then-Justice Minister Oronzo Reale during the Years of Lead to ban face coverings in public places.The proposed amendment would create a new offence of forcing someone to conceal their face, punishable by one to two years in prison and fines of between €10,000 and €30,000. It would also bar those convicted from obtaining Italian citizenship.Full-face veils in EuropeMeloni referred specifically to a ban on burqas and niqabs. A burqa traditionally covers the entire body and includes a mesh over the eyes, while a niqab covers the face, leaving only the eyes visible. A hijab, by contrast, covers the hair and neck but leaves the face uncovered.Several European countries have introduced restrictions on face coverings in public spaces.France imposed a nationwide ban on concealing the face in public places in April 2011, a measure later upheld by the European Court of Human Rights.Belgium approved a nationwide ban in July 2011, with fines and prison sentences for violations. Bulgaria has prohibited full-face veils in state, administrative and educational institutions since September 2016.Austria passed an anti-mask law in October 2017 requiring faces to remain visible in public spaces. From September 2026, girls up to the age of 14 will also be prohibited from wearing at school any veil that “covers the head according to Islamic traditions”.Denmark introduced a nationwide ban in August 2018, with financial penalties increasing for repeat offences. The Netherlands introduced a partial ban in August 2019 covering schools, hospitals, government offices and public transport.Switzerland introduced a federal ban on face coverings in public spaces following a national referendum, with the implementing legislation coming into force in 2023. Portugal completed its legislative process in August 2026 with a law banning face coverings in public spaces and imposing financial penalties.Germany has no nationwide ban, but federal legislation prohibits public employees, judges, members of the armed forces and motorists from covering their faces while driving. Several Länder also restrict full-face veils in schools and universities for students and teachers.Foreign pupils in the classroomIf Italy introduces a statutory maximum for foreign pupils in each class, it would become the first European country to adopt such a rule, according to the proposal.Italy already has a 30% limit on non-Italian pupils, set out in a 2010 ministerial circular issued by then-Education Minister Mariastella Gelmini. The limit has often gone unenforced because of local demographic conditions and a lack of flexibility, particularly in urban outskirts.Other European countries use different approaches.Denmark has some of the most restrictive policies. The government has allowed upper secondary schools to introduce caps of up to 50% for pupils of “non-Western origin” or from disadvantaged neighbourhoods. Schools can also organise classes based on parents’ income, with the aim of encouraging social and ethnic mixing — a model the Italian government is watching with interest.In France, quotas based on origin would be unconstitutional because the state does not collect statistics based on ethnic or religious identity. Instead, authorities use “zoning” to redesign school catchment areas, linking working-class and wealthier neighbourhoods. In areas with high concentrations of migrants, the state also reduces the number of pupils per class.Criticism of Meloni’s proposalMeloni’s announcement has received support from members of the governing coalition but has also drawn criticism from the opposition and legal experts.Speaking to ANSA, Salvatore Curreri, a professor of constitutional law at the University of Enna, pointed to Article 34 of the Constitution, which states that “school is open to everyone”, including foreign children.“If the measure were so restrictive as to uproot minors and their families to other areas, far from where they live, it could prove excessive precisely because it conflicts with the overriding functional aim of integration, with the risk of infringing a right recognised by the constitution,” Curreri said.Angelo Bonelli, an MP for the Green and Left Alliance (AVS) and co-spokesperson for Green Europe, also criticised the proposal.“Yet again, instead of dealing with schools, she is chasing the neo-fascist right of AfD and Vannacci, who has proposed separate classes for students with disabilities,” he said. “The truth is that the prime minister is not at all interested in how schools work. Our teachers’ salaries are among the lowest in Europe.”

Headline: Climate Week warns of challenges in delivering the energy transition
Body: A Climate Week (source in Portuguese) began in New York this Sunday, with a series of events across the city, and runs until the 27th. Over the coming days, business and political leaders from around the world will discuss solutions for a more sustainable society with lower carbon emissions.The event is an initiative of the non-governmental organisation Climate Group (source in Portuguese), organised in coordination with the United Nations General Assembly, which takes place at the same time in the same city.The first day, Monday, features contributions from the Prime Minister of Australia, Anthony Albanese, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Milliband, and the Icelandic prime minister Kristún Frostadóttir.This is the largest event in the world dedicated to climate change. It includes more than a thousand events at various locations in New York, bringing together on average more than one hundred thousand people.This year's debates will focus on three aspects:Energy and the changes taking place in this field,The impact those changes are having,The joint action that is needed.This series of debates comes at a time when the impact of climate change is highly visible, with tragedies such as the one that recently hit Nepal and the heatwaves that have been battering many parts of the world in recent weeks.Climate Group has been in existence for around 20 years and aims to help create a world with zero carbon emissions by 2050.According to the description Climate Group gives on the event website, "the context is changing rapidly. Energy systems are being redesigned, supply chains are under pressure and demand for electricity is rising, driven by electrification, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital infrastructure. At the same time, the transition is opening up new sources of long-term growth, investment and competitiveness."The organisers also say that "the current challenge is not ambition but implementation". "Progress is being held back by outdated regulation, infrastructure constraints and misaligned markets. The priority is to remove these barriers and deliver change quickly and at scale. Climate Week exists to accelerate that progress," they add.This year's conference is taking place against a backdrop of the rapid expansion of AI and the revolution that implies, but also of the strongly climate-sceptic actions and policies pursued by the Trump administration.The last global climate summit, COP30, held in Belém do Pará, Brazil, ultimately delivered results that fell short of expectations. While a plan was agreed to help the countries most affected by the climate crisis, no precise timetable was set for the phase-out of fossil fuels.

Headline: Russians vote in final day of parliamentary elections
Body: Russians are casting their ballots on Sunday in the final day of voting in parliamentary elections, with the pro-Putin United Russia party widely expected to emerge victorious.United Russia has won every parliamentary election in the country since 2003.The 2026 vote marks the first since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, meaning it could offer a slight hint at public sentiment towards the conflict, which has been increasingly impacting Russians at home.However, in August, Russia's Supreme Court ordered the only party opposing the war - the Yabloko party - to be struck from the ballot. Its candidates are reportedly still able to run for individual seats in some districts.In a statement at the time, Yabloko cofounder Grigory Yavlinsky hit out at the decision and said they would appeal."Barring Yabloko from the elections means refusing to engage in dialogue with people who ask questions that are uncomfortable for the authorities," he said. "We stand for a ceasefire, diplomacy and peace, for the prevention of nuclear war".On Saturday, the party reported that one of its election observers had "lost consciousness" while being "subjected to force" by police in St. Petersburg. It also complained that party observers were being "denied access to polling stations" and that their movement was being "restricted."Russia reports cyberattacksElla Pamfilova, the chair of Russia's Central Election Commission, said on Sunday that Russia had recorded more than 1,000 waves of distributed denial-of-service attacks (DDoS) on election infrastructure over the last few days, per the Interfax news agency."The level of impact is assessed as very high," she said, adding that the attacks appeared to have been "carried out by highly professional, well-coordinated groups using artificial intelligence tools."A DDoS attack involves hackers attempting to disrupt a targeted network, server, or service by attempting to overwhelm the system with a large volume of traffic.Moscow hit by 'largest-scale attack'The vote comes as the Russian capital was hit by what its governor described as the "largest-scale attack" on the city since the war in Ukraine began.Sergey Sobyanin reported that Russian air defences had shot down more than 1,600 drones across the country since Saturday, 450 of which he said had been heading towards the capital."Several drones reached the territory of the Moscow refinery, and one struck a residential building. There were no fatalities," he wrote. Moscow Oblast governor Andrey Vorobyov said two people had been killed in attacks across the wider region.Sobyanin also accused Ukraine of attempting to "disrupt" Russia's elections - which will determine the makeup of the 450-seat state Duma - with the attacks.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine had targeted the Moscow region overnight, saying a "key" oil industry facility as well as a logistics facility were hit."Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night," he wrote in a post on X, adding that Russia had launched over 2,000 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 19 missiles against Ukraine this week.

Headline: 'Situation in Gaza is unjustifiable,' says Ed Sheeran as he addresses Macklemore 'Free Palestine' controversy
Body: Ed Sheeran opened a concert on Saturday with comments about Gaza after controversy swirled around his tour and supporting acts withdrew in solidarity with opener Macklemore, who was dropped after making pro-Palestinian comments onstage at an earlier show.Sheeran began the concert alone on stage with no opener, but was joined by other musicians later in the show.Sheeran said he wants his music and shows to be about unity and humanity, not politics. But he said that while the attacks in Israel of 7 October, 2023, were horrific, what is happening in Gaza “catastrophic and unjustifiable” and slammed it as “disproportionate”.“I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet,” said Sheeran during his performance at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia.The comments before a nearly full stadium came after a tumultuous week that began with rapper Macklemore, Sheeran's original US opener, being dropped in response to saying “Free Palestine” during a 5 September tour stop in New Jersey.Sheeran has said he was not responsible for the decision, which came at the urging of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. His company owns a stadium where Sheeran’s tour was scheduled to play on Friday. Within hours of Sheeran’s statement Tuesday, his supporting acts withdrew.Sheeran has performed many songs solo during his Loop Tour concerts, but was joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga before they dropped out in support of Macklemore.Macklemore was replaced by Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe before they backed out, and Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out this week.Before Saturday's show, a small group of pro-Palestinian demonstrators convened outside the stadium.Hillary Steinberg, 34, said she got concert tickets a year ago but wound up getting a refund and attended the demonstration instead, after she was disappointed that Sheeran refused to take a stand to defend Macklemore or empathise with the plight of the Palestinian people.“I was, until this week, a big Ed Sheeran fan,” Steinberg said. “I think all art is political, and all music is political, and so this choice — even though he was saying that he wasn’t complicit — is a political choice.”Diane Savitz, a 53-year-old from Stroudsburg, Pennsylvania, got tickets months ago and attended. She said she is a big Sheeran fan, doesn't think he did anything wrong and a concert is not the place for politics.“A concert should be for people enjoying the music. Music should bring people together,” Savitz said. “Everyone has their right to freedom of speech, but not every platform is the place for it.”The Grammy winning artist was adamant earlier this week that he wouldn't be drawn into discussion of the war in Gaza, arguing that his fans don’t come to his shows to hear about these issues. But, as the controversy grew, and ticket prices and sales declined, he decided to address the issue head on.Sheeran told the crowd in Philadelphia that everyone is welcome at his concerts, and they can have opposing points of view while still singing his songs, which are about “love, hope and unity.”He also told fans he worries about venues pre-approving performances.“This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world,” Sheeran said.

Headline: Germans head to the polls in state elections as pressure mounts on Merz
Body: Germans are heading to the polls on Sunday in two state elections that could prove decisive for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's future.In Berlin, Merz's ruling Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is facing a close fight against Die Linke, which has strong support among young people and has pledged measures to tackle the housing crisis.In the coastal state of Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania in northeastern Germany, the main race is between the Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the hard-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD).The AfD comes into Sunday's vote fresh off the back of its election success in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month and will be hoping for further gains.However, the party faces a sterner test in "MeckPomm," where it will come up against the SPD's Manuela Schwesig, who has served as minister-president of the state since 2017.The latest polling figures show Die Linke edging ahead of the CDU in the city-state of Berlin, while the AfD leads the SPD in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania - with the CDU flirting with the 5% hurdle required to remain in state parliament.Gains for the far-right or far-left would heap pressure on Merz, who became chancellor in May 2025 and has seen his popularity continue to decline.Moritz Lembke-Oezer, 43, summed up that feeling while speaking to the AFP news agency outside a polling station to the south of Berlin, saying that while he feared the vote could benefit the AfD, he hoped it would see the CDU "punished.""Maybe then Friedrich Merz will be gone," he said, adding that he planned to vote for Die Linke because of the far-left party's vows to address the housing issue.Speaking to AFP outside a polling station in Schwerin, the state capital of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, pensioner Peter Sommer added: "I'd be in favour of the AfD winning, because then they'll have to prove themselves: either something will happen, or it'll be the last time they get any votes."

Headline: North Korea launches 'suspected ballistic missile' into East Sea
Body: North Korea on Sunday carried out a launch of a "suspected ballistic missile," the Japanese Prime Minister's office said, while South Korea's military reported that Pyongyang had fired an "unidentified projectile" into the East Sea.In an update later in the day, Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said North Korea had launched "at least one ballistic missile from near its eastern coast towards the northeast" at around 3 pm local time."We estimate that the ballistic missile reached a maximum altitude of approximately 60 km, flew a distance of approximately 440 km, and fell outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ)," he said.It comes after North Korea this week rejected a resolution by the UN nuclear watchdog against its nuclear programme.A spokesperson for the country's Foreign Ministry said the International Atomic Energy Agency's resolution had "no effect on the DPRK's position as a nuclear weapons state."In August, Trump told reporters that North Korean leader Kim Jong-un had "57 very powerful nuclear weapons" as he once again touted the pair's relationship."You know what, the fact that I get along with him, that's a good thing not a bad thing," Trump said, adding that Pyongyang's nuclear arsenal should "never" have been allowed to happen.Trump announced at the time that he also intended to meet with Kim later this year, although he gave no further details on the plan - which would be their first meeting since Trump's first term in the White House.On Friday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said he was "urging" Trump to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang, adding that Seoul was working to facilitate talks between the North and the US."I cannot say for certain how likely it is, but it is also clear that we must make every possible effort to turn that possibility into reality," he said of the potential for a meeting between US and North Korean officials.However, hopes for an imminent meeting may have been doused slightly after Kim's powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong, criticised recent military drills in the Western Pacific, which she labelled a "US-led war rehearsal."The US, South Korea and Japan wrapped up Exercise Freedom Edge 26, which US Pacific Command said advanced "trilateral readiness across the Indo-Pacific," on 11 September."Our will to defend our sovereignty will be expressed in clearer action and there will be never ever change in the course of intensifying the nuclear war deterrence," Kim Yo Jong added in a statement shared by North Korea's KCNA state news agency on Friday.

Headline: Moscow hit by 'largest-scale attack' on capital so far, mayor says
Body: Ukrainian forces launched their "largest-scale attack" on Moscow since the war in Ukraine began, the city's mayor said on Sunday.In a post on Telegram, Sergey Sobyanin reported that Russian air defences had shot down more than 1,600 drones across the country since Saturday, 450 of which he said had been heading towards the capital."Several drones reached the territory of the Moscow refinery, and one struck a residential building. There were no fatalities," he wrote. Moscow Oblast governor Andrey Vorobyov said two people had been killed in attacks across the wider region.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that Ukraine had targeted the Moscow region overnight, saying a "key" oil industry facility as well as a logistics facility were hit."Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night," he wrote in a post on X, adding that the attacks had involved FP-1 attack drones and Palianytsia missiles, among other munitions."Moscow must end its brutal war and choose peace instead of building layered rings of air defense at the expense of other regions," Zelenskyy continued, while also sharing video footage appearing to show the aftermath of the strikes.Russian attacks on UkraineIt comes as Ukrainian authorities reported that a child had died following a Russian strike on the Kyiv region, bringing the death toll from the attack to four.Timur Tkachenko, the head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration, said on Sunday that the child died in hospital after having been injured in an attack on the Vyshhorod district."The Kyiv region has endured more than a day of enemy attacks," Tkachenko said in an update, adding that 31 structures had been damaged across five districts.In the southern Kherson region, a 71-year-old priest was also killed in a drone attack on a monastery in the village of Chervonyi Mayak on Saturday, per local authorities. Four others were reportedly injured in the incident.According to Zelenskyy, who has been calling for further sanctions against Moscow, Russia launched over 2,000 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 19 missiles against Ukraine this week.

Headline: Newsletter: Carney is right on EU associate membership — the name is irrelevant, the politics aren’t
Body: Welcome back to this newsletter, written en route from Strasbourg to Brussels, after a week of parliamentary coverage. In case you missed it, Mark Carney stole the show and Canada is our new associate BFF, whatever that means.It's easy to be cynical about the Canadian Prime Minister, but anyone who makes an intellectual effort citing Goethe on a Thursday morning gets my attention amid the sea of poor orators that populate the annual State of the Union (the EU's, to be clear).Carney chose his references deliberately, reaching for Faust right off the bat. One can only hope the MEPs — including the gentleman who shouted "USA! USA!" as he took the stand — appreciated the reference. Goethe argued that freedom is neither a condition nor a possession: it must be conquered. Nor can it be taken for granted, as freedom is as fragile as it is precious.Carney evoked that spirit from the get-go of his six-page address, taking the hemicycle on a journey through the forest of Ettersberg. Nur der verdient sich Freiheit wie das Leben, der täglich sie erobern muß (Only those who strive for freedom every day are deserving of it). Canada and the EU share that spirit, he told the European Parliament — and both are being tested on their ability to forge their own paths.His pitch? A new alliance between two sovereign blocs that looks beyond zero-sum geopolitics and builds on their complementary strengths and dependencies. A single tree, he said, can fall in a storm; a forest will not. For Europe, as for Canada, the storm has three names: Trump, Xi, Putin.Still, lumping them together would be intellectually lazy. The US doesn't threaten Europe's security architecture the way Russia does — NATO is still largely bankrolled by American taxpayers. Nor is China's economic predation on the European industry the result of Trump's economic agenda.But together, they have upended the status quo on both sides of the Atlantic and left Europeans feeling defeated, orphaned from a political offer that stands up to bullies. Carney is now their patron saint and newfound maple hero. You could say this is simply a rerun of speeches we've heard before.Carney himself said as much in Davos at the start of the year, calling for an alliance of middle powers to stabilise a world increasingly governed by brute force. In 2023, cameras caught China's Xi telling Putin that the world was witnessing changes not seen in a century. He was right. The question is whether nations can still decide their own paths, seal their own alliances, and resist the pull of the tide.Carney is playing politics — that's true. He owes his political success to Donald Trump: going elbows-up on the US, walking away from lopsided trade talks, and putting sovereignty above all else has resonated with Canadians — a country whose sole raison d'être is not being America.Carney, a product of the establishment and elite education, would never have been elected had it not been for Trump's provocations, and yet he is now the most popular Canadian PM; every dust-up adds points.His political calculus is very different to that of the EU, which desperately sought to cool down tensions and had the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, inking a deal on American terms. And that stings. Large swathes of the European electorate are hungry for political courage — courage von der Leyen lacks, and would struggle to project even if she had it, since doing politics has never been her strength. In Carney, Europeans see an alternative.Von der Leyen has amassed enormous power. She could have been a transformative Commission President; instead, she plays it safe. Let's be honest: Carney saved her State of the Union address — without him, she would have had little new to say. Too afraid to raise the question of joint debt and European financing, her "independence" moment comes without financial muscle. Mario Draghi put a number on the cost of an independent Europe: €800 billion a year. You cannot implement the Draghi report without addressing the elephant in the room — but she won't touch it. You can argue her institutional neutrality doesn't allow for it, but her peer Christine Lagarde has no problem saying Europe should at least debate joint borrowing. Plenty can be said about the tribulations and hurdles ahead for a transatlantic partnership meant to deepen trade, cultural, political and educational ties.CETA is proof enough: the Canada-EU trade deal, still unratified in countries like France, was painful to negotiate and remains unpopular in sectors like agriculture (and farmers are untouchable in Europe). Most MEPs we spoke to on the floor told us they didn't quite understand what an associate member would look like, but welcomed the move. The head of the European Parliament, Roberta Metsola, went a step further, telling Euronews in an exclusive interview that Canada could pave the way for other countries "with so much in common," like New Zealand and Australia. My colleague Vincenzo Genovese overheard a group of Renew MEPs debating the interview over lunch — that's zeitgeist for you.It’s tempting to write this pairing off as bluff — I mean, they can’t even agree on a name: an alliance for the future, or associate membership? But dismiss it at your peril, because Carney is right: at this point, the nomenclature is irrelevant.What matters is the political signal, and it's not a futile one — just ask the US president, who has already threatened tariffs if the two turn hostile to American interests. As you know, in MAGA world, you either align or you get punished. And yes, the US already has a deal in place with the EU which cut tariffs on American products.Before I go, I want to thank our team of reporters, correspondents, producers and cameramen for two marathon days in which Euronews brought you 16 interviews, an exclusive sit-down with the Parliament's President, the Commissioners that mattered on the day, and non-stop coverage. It's long hours and it's not easy. I had cold chicken nuggets for dinner each night, and believe me, you don't want that.But we take pride in what we do, and Euronews is Europe's newsroom — time to consider an antenna in Ottawa.Thank you for reading Off The Record make sure to subscribe here. Before you go, Europe Today, Euronews' flagship morning show, is live weekdays at 8am CET.

Headline: Macron touts relationship with Canada in visit to Saint Pierre and Miquelon
Body: French President Emmanuel Macron hailed France's relationship with Canada during a trip to Saint Pierre and Miquelon this weekend.Macron is visiting the French overseas collectivity from 19 to 21 September and is due to meet with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney there on Sunday.Speaking to reporters from the archipelago, which sits just off the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador, Macron said the goal of the visit was to help the territory "turn a new page" and gently pushed back on suggestions that the trip was intended to make a statement."We shouldn't be so obsessed with sending messages," he said, adding that France had "close friends" including Canada in the region.On the planned meeting with Carney, Macron said he saw it as "a very strong gesture of friendship" and pointed to the Canadian leader's blossoming relationship with Brussels.He also noted Canada's substantial reserves of critical raw materials and rare earth elements, as well as its liquefied natural gas production. He said France and the EU would be seeking contracts and arrangements to secure supplies of strategic minerals and LNG for Europe.It comes after US President Donald Trump hit out at Ottawa and the EU following European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's announcement that Canada could become the bloc's first "associate member."Trump called the idea "laughable" but warned that if the move went ahead and he considered it "at all a hostile act," then he would put "very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things."Earlier this month, Trump also posted an image on his Truth Social account showing a map of North America, including Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Greenland, marked with the US flag.The US and Denmark announced on Friday that they had reached an agreement over Greenland, with Trump saying the deal would give Washington "permanent control" of the island's security.CarneyCarney is due to arrive in Saint Pierre and Miquelon at around 12:30 pm local time, according to his office.He will then attend a "working lunch" with Macron before the pair take part in a wreath-laying ceremony. They will later deliver a joint statement before Carney heads to Ottawa.Macron is due to travel on to New York for the UN General Assembly next week - where Trump's Greenland security deal is also expected to be signed.In a post on X on Saturday, Macron said he was "very proud and happy" to be in Saint Pierre and Miquelon."The ocean separates us, but what truly unites us are our values, a shared destiny, and the Republic," he wrote.

Headline: From F1 to FIBA: Qatar unveils packed calendar of global events
Body: From Formula 1 and the FIBA Basketball World Cup to concerts and food festivals, Qatar has unveiled a calendar of more than 560 events stretching through 2027.The programme comes as the Gulf country looks to build on record visitor numbers following a period of regional uncertainty.Qatar welcomed 5.1 million visitors last year, according to Visit Qatar. Jassim Al Mahmoud, Director of PR and Communications at Visit Qatar, said another 2.9 million arrived in the first half of this year.“The biggest number of visitors arrived to Qatar last year, so this is something that drives us to have such a rich calendar in order to enhance their experience, to have more options, more variety, to bring more visitors to Qatar,” Al Mahmoud said.The Qatar Calendar brings events across sport, culture, entertainment and food together on a single platform, allowing residents and visitors to see what is happening and plan ahead.A busy roster of eventsSport features heavily, with several major international competitions on the schedule.The FIFA U-17 World Cup Qatar 2026 will run from 19 November to 13 December, while MotoGP returns to the Lusail International Circuit from 6 to 8 November.The Qatar T100 Triathlon World Championship Final follows from 10 to 12 December, with the Doha Marathon on 15 January 2027.Top-tier tennis returns in February with the Qatar TotalEnergies Open, scheduled from 8 to 15 February.Later in the year, Doha will host the FIBA Basketball World Cup from 27 August to 12 September 2027.Formula 1 is also set to return to Lusail in 2027, with the Qatar Grand Prix scheduled from 3 to 5 December.Beyond sport, the calendar also includes concerts, festivals, food and cultural events.Oscar-winning composer Hans Zimmer is among the international artists highlighted, alongside performances by Angham and Saint Levant. A Harry Potter film music concert is also on the programme.Other events include the Qatar International Food Festival, Art Basel and the Al Ruwais Festival.The idea is to give visitors a mix of experiences throughout the year rather than focusing solely on major sporting events, with shopping, food, culture and entertainment included alongside them.Steve Harvey returns with more eventsOne familiar face at the launch was US TV host and comedian Steve Harvey, who has already hosted several events in Qatar.Harvey said his previous experiences in the country helped bring him back.“When it comes to beauty and architecture and landscape and the people, it’s just a great place to come,” Harvey said.“I travel the world. And so this is a great place to come and do business and share the culture.”Harvey said he had signed a multi-year deal to bring more entertainment events to Qatar, including the return of FuelFest, a new comedy series and Family Feud.He also outlined plans to eventually stage what he called a Family Feud World Cup, bringing families from different countries to Qatar to compete in the game show.Building the tourism sectorThe calendar is also part of Qatar’s longer-term tourism strategy.Doha has set a target of increasing tourism’s contribution to GDP to 12% by 2030, according to material released alongside the calendar launch.Al Mahmoud said the range of events was intended to give visitors more options during their stays, spanning sport, culture, shopping and food.“We believe that we have the offering,” he said. “We have lots of options, a lot of variety.”He said the launch was also intended to signal continuity in Qatar’s events programme.“By revealing the calendar, we are saying to the world that we are ready, we are open, we have a rich calendar,” Al Mahmoud said.“Qatar remains fully operational.”

Headline: CNN, MS NOW, POLITICO journalists denied access to the White House after Trump said he'd bar them
Body: Reporters from three major news organisations were denied access to the White House on Saturday, a day after US President Donald Trump said he was barring them because of reporting he found to be “fake news.”The media outlets, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, have previously been targeted by the Republican president, particularly CNN, who Trump kicks his antics up a notch, regularly mocking their reporters and lambasting their authenticity.The actions were a clear escalation of Trump’s long-running efforts — in the courts and through administrative action — to restrict news coverage by journalists he finds objectionable, and the latest test of First Amendment protections in the United States.Trump said on Friday that he would ban all three outlets because of coverage he disliked.White House reporters from the two cable networks — Betsy Klein of CNN and Akayla Gardner of MS NOW — both went live to report they’d been turned away, their press badges deactivated, when arriving for their jobs at the White House.Soon after, Politico said its White House reporter Cheyenne Haslett was also denied entry and had her badge confiscated. All three news outlets hinted at legal action.“We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights,” Politico Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger said in a statement to the Politico newsroom. A CNN statement said the network “will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account."And MS NOW said it “intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.”In his second term, Trump and his administration have routinely punished certain media outlets, both in the courtroom and through regulatory action.Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms — insulting them in briefings, or in his recent speech at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner, where he called CNN’s Kailtan Collins “very dumb and unhappy”.The White House Correspondents’ Association President Jacqui Heinrich called on the administration to immediately restore the three outlets' access.“The implications extend beyond these organisations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future,” she said.“The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinise those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favourably.”The move follows the president’s decision last year to bar Associated Press reporters from the Oval Office, Air Force One and other events in retaliation for the news outlet’s decision not to follow his lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico.The AP said that it would note, when appropriate, that Trump had ordered the water body, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters, renamed the “Gulf of America.”The US news agency filed a lawsuit against their barring, and the case remains ongoing.Since returning to office, Trump has pursued other legal action against a variety of different outlets, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the BBC.His administration is also involved in a long-simmering confrontation involving ABC over renewal of its broadcast licenses.The AP said on Saturday it supported the news organizations banned this week. In a statement, the news cooperative said: “No news organisation — or person — should be retaliated against by the government over the words they use.”

Headline: US military says four killed in strike on suspected drug-trafficking boat in Caribbean
Body: The US military said its forces struck a suspected drug-smuggling boat in the Caribbean on Saturday, killing four people."Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean," US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said in a statement shared on social media.It added that "confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking."The post also contained video footage of what appeared to be the strike, showing a moving boat followed by a large explosion.The US has moved to clamp down on drug-smuggling routes under US President Donald Trump, who has pledged to "wage war" against drug cartels. The president says cartels threaten the US' national security and foreign policy and bring "devastating consequences" to communities across the country.As part of this push, the US launched operation "Southern Spear," which aims to "disrupt the flow of narcotics in the Western Hemisphere" through a campaign of air strikes on suspected drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific.Trump has also spearheaded a new security coalition including nations from across Central and South America - dubbed the "Shield of the Americas" - in a bid to combat cartels.

Headline: US embassies issue security alerts over Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
Body: US embassies across the Middle East have issued security alerts warning Americans to maintain "heightened vigilance" following attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia.Embassies in Bahrain, Israel, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE said the "military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly" and that the security environment remained "complex."The alerts also advised people to "be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions."It comes after the Houthi rebels on Saturday said they had carried out two operations using ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones to target Saudi Arabia in response to Saudi attacks."The first targeted sensitive sites in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu," the group claimed.A spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition forces - which were formed in 2015 to back Yemen's internationally recognised government - later confirmed that the Royal Saudi Air Defense Forces had intercepted a ballistic missile fired towards Riyadh. The spokesperson added that the group had also targeted the cities of Baish, Taif, Farasan, and Yanbu.On Saturday, residents of Riyadh reported seeing flames and smoke at the capital's King Khalid International Airport.Video footage circulating on social media appeared to show a towering column of smoke rising from the airport, which flight tracking site Flightradar24 had said was experiencing "major problems."Yemen's Houthi rebels, who declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in July, have been launching increasing attacks on Saudi cities and shipping, further heightening tensions in the Middle East.Saudi Arabia has hit back with its own strikes on the group - which has seized vast stretches of territory in Yemen this month in a lightning offensive - but has failed to stop its advance.In a press briefing on Friday, Stéphane Dujarric, a spokesperson for the UN Secretary-General, addressed the situation in Yemen."Since hostilities escalated in August, the Human Rights office has documented 110 civilian casualties in 31 incidents, including 28 killed and 82 injured, across Taizz, Al Hudaydah and Marib. Insecurity and access constraints continue to hamper our ability to verify the actual number as you can imagine is very likely higher," Dujarric said, according to a transcript shared by the UN."We urge all parties, and those with influence over them, to act immediately to de-escalate, protect civilians and facilitate humanitarian access. Every effort must be made to prevent further loss of life," he added.

Headline: Argentina’s first solar train runs on batteries charged by the Andean sun
Body: Sunshine is never in short supply in the high-altitude deserts of northern Argentina. In Jujuy province, all that abundant solar energy is now being put to an unusual use.Locomotion.The Tren Solar de la Quebrada is Latin America’s first solar-powered railway, running 42 kilometres through the Andes on state-of-the-art technology and batteries charged with locally generated solar energy.The train connects six towns in Quebrada de Humahuaca, a UNESCO World Heritage-listed valley that has served as a route through the Andes for thousands of years. Launched in 2024, it was designed in part to bring tourists to communities along the valley – and more significantly, without adding the emissions of a diesel train.How does Argentina’s solar train work?Despite its name, the Tren Solar does not generate electricity from  photovoltaic (PV) panels mounted on its roof.The two-car train is instead powered by six lithium batteries, which are charged using solar power generated in Jujuy. When it brakes, some of the motion is also converted back into electricity and stored in the batteries for later use.According to the operator, the batteries give the train a range of between 100 and 120 kilometres – more than twice the length of its current route.Two fast-charging points at Volcán and Purmamarca allow operators to recharge along the way. A third is planned for the northern terminus at Tilcara too.This battery-powered system allows the train to run without diesel – or even the overhead electrical lines typically used by electric railways.So far, the new service has been a hit.When it launched in June 2024, the Tren Solar brought passenger rail back to Quebrada de Humahuaca for the first time in 30 years. Since then, more than 90,000 people have taken the train, according to the Jujuy government.Europe is also electrifying its railwaysSouth America isn’t the only region upgrading its rail services and weaning them off fossil fuels.Almost 58 per cent of the EU’s railway network was electrified in 2024, according to Eurostat, the bloc’s’s statistical office.Since 2017, Dutch rail operator NS has bought enough renewable electricity to match the amount used by its trains each year. Since 2025, the mix of renewables has included both wind and solar power.In Switzerland, meanwhile, start-up Sun-Ways installed 48 solar panels between the rails on a 100-metre stretch of active track in Buttes in 2025. The pilot project generated around 16,000 kWh during its first year, roughly enough electricity to power four or five European homes for a year.Sun-Ways has also signed an agreement with Italian railway infrastructure company GCF to explore installing the system in Italy.For railways that can’t plug into an existing electric network like they can in Europe, however, Argentina’s tourist train could offer a promising alternative. In places graced with abundant sunshine, the power to leave diesel behind may already be there.

Headline: The cost of having a baby in Europe: Where are essentials cheapest?
Body: Most parents describe welcoming a baby as one of the happiest moments in life, but it also comes with a cost. From nappies and feeding to pushchairs and clothes, there is a long shopping list of baby essentials. The bill can be higher than many parents expect.The cost of baby essentials varies significantly across Europe. But how much do parents actually spend? Which countries are the most expensive for baby essentials, and where are they most affordable relative to average wages?Remitly calculated the annual cost of baby essentials during the first year of a baby’s life, based on prices as of July 2026. It includes 14 staple items across six categories:Nappy changes (nappies, wet wipes, rash cream), Bottles (bottle with caps), Baby formula Sleep (crib, carrycot, or moses basket, crib mattress, fitted sheets, blankets), Transport (infant car seat, stroller), Clothing (bodysuits or onesies, babygrow or pants, socks).Across 38 European countries, the estimated cost of baby essentials in the first year ranges from €2,813 in the UK to €6,294 in Spain, with a European average of €4,727.In addition to Spain, first-year baby essentials cost more than €6,000 in the Netherlands (€6,140), Finland (€6,066), Sweden (€6,025) and Switzerland (€6,018).Costs fall between €5,000 and €6,000 in Luxembourg (€5,665), Italy (€5,609), Lithuania (€5,563), Albania (€5,532), Serbia (€5,509), Montenegro (€5,500), Portugal (€5,337), Slovakia (€5,221), Norway (€5,079) and Iceland (€5,004).Among the five largest economies, Spain has the highest costs, while the UK has the lowest, at €2,813. Germany (€4,701) and France (€4,393) fall closer to the European average.Parents in Czechia (€3,211), Romania (€3,385), Latvia (€3,392), Croatia (€3,661), Bulgaria (€3,804) and Bosnia and Herzegovina (€3,844) face some of the lowest baby costs in nominal terms, with all six below €4,000.Turkey (€4,023), Belgium (€4,084), Malta (€4,118) and Greece (€4,158) are also close to the €4,000 mark, but slightly above it.Highest spending on clothing, baby formula and nappiesThe distribution of costs across the six categories varies widely across Europe. On average, clothing (30.3%), baby formula (25.7%) and nappies (24.5%) account for the largest shares, making up 81% of total first-year costs.Across the 38 countries, parents spend an average of €1,465 on clothing, €1,187 on baby formula and €1,152 on nappies, bringing the combined cost to €3,804.The breakdown varies significantly from country to country. Clothing accounts for just 16% of costs in Denmark, compared with 52.5% in Sweden. Its share is also above 45% in the Netherlands, Finland and Ireland.Baby formula makes up 10.8% of costs in Sweden but 41.3% in Latvia. Its share is also high in Turkey, Denmark and Hungary, where it exceeds 35%.Nappies account for 12.4% of costs in Turkey, compared with more than 36% in Switzerland and Belgium.The chart below breaks down how much parents spend on each category during their baby’s first year.Baby costs as a share of the average wageOf course, income levels matter when comparing countries, given the wide differences in wages across Europe. So, how much of the average annual wage is spent on baby essentials during the first year?Remitly’s research compared the cost of baby essentials with average wages in each country. It used the International Labour Organization’s average monthly earnings of employees, adjusted for inflation.Affordability can also depend on whether both parents work, as well as taxes and family benefits. These can make a big difference as the Euronews article shows.Across the 36 countries, baby essentials account for an average of 20.9% of annual wages. The share ranges from 5.4% in Belgium to 88.8% in Moldova.Parents in Albania (66%), Turkey (45.1%), Montenegro (45%), Serbia (41.4%), Bosnia and Herzegovina (36.1%), Portugal (35.7%) and Hungary (34.7%) spend at least one-third of the average annual wage on baby essentials, according to this calculation.Baby essentials account for less than 10% of the average annual wage in Luxembourg (6%), Denmark (6.7%), the UK (7.5%), Norway (7.6%), Ireland (8%), Switzerland (8%), Germany (8.1%), Austria (8.2%), France (8.5%), Malta (8.9%) and the Netherlands (9.4%).What about nursery and creche?This research does not cover nursery and crèche costs, which can be a significant additional burden for parents across Europe.For example, in 2023, gross childcare fees for two children reached €64,211 in Switzerland, while the Netherlands had the highest figure in the EU, at €39,229, according to the OECD. In Germany, the figure was just €552.The figures cover centre-based care, meaning childcare provided outside the home in licensed facilities. This includes nurseries, day-care centres, crèches, playschools and parent-run groups, either full or part time.When net childcare costs for two children are considered, the figure is €10,200 for a single-earner family in Switzerland and €27,551 for a two-earner couple. However, government support can significantly reduce costs for families in some countries, with net costs falling below €5,000, as this Euronews article shows.

Headline: All the direct flight routes from Europe to Central and South America
Body: Last week, we looked at all the new airline routes connecting Europe to Canada. Now we thought it was time to look slightly further south – more specifically, at Central and South America.According to the World Tourism Barometer by UN Tourism, both regions saw growth in 2025, with South America up 7% and Central America up 5% year on year.Destinations in the Americas seeing a big uptick in visitors include Brazil, up a mega 37%, and Guyana, up 24%.While many airlines offer routes from Europe to these countries via the US, there are still some options for those looking to fly direct.The best connected airport for travelling to these regions is undoubtedly Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas Airport, with airlines flying from here including Iberia, Air Europa, LATAM and more.Here, we outline your options in order of the most-to-least visited countries.BrazilSouth America’s largest country had a record-breaking year in 2025, with some 9.3 million international tourists choosing Brazil for their vacation.It’s little wonder – whether you’re looking to explore the wildlife of the Amazon or party the night away at the Rio Carnival, Brazil has something for everyone.The country’s most populous city, São Paulo, is home to the best connected airport for those travelling from Europe. LATAM flies to São Paulo from Madrid, Barcelona, Lisbon, Paris, Amsterdam, Paris and London Heathrow, while TAP Portugal flies there from Porto and Lisbon.Lufthansa serves this route from Frankfurt and Munich; KLM from Amsterdam; British Airways from London; Air France from Paris; SWISS from Zurich; and Turkish Airlines from Istanbul. Air Europa and Iberia also fly from Madrid. For those looking to visit Rio de Janeiro, TAP Portugal flies from Lisbon and Porto; Iberia from Madrid; Air France from Paris; Lufthansa from Frankfurt; KLM from Amsterdam; ITA Airways from Rome and British Airways from London. Gol also flies from Lisbon.Colombia Known for its wildlife, beaches and colonial architecture (and its coffee), Colombia saw 6.2 million international visitors in 2025.The capital Bogotá will most likely be your main point of entry. There, you can make your way through the culinary wonders of Colombia, explore the street art scene and climb Cerro de Monserrate for spectacular views, or head out of the city to Chingaza National Park.Avianca flies to Bogotá from Madrid, Barcelona, Paris and London Heathrow; Air France from Paris; Lufthansa from Frankfurt; Edelweiss Air from Zurich; KLM from Amsterdam; and Turkish Airlines from Istanbul.Alternatively, Cartagena with its UNESCO-listed fortress and walled city is served by airlines including Plus Ultra and World2Fly, which both fly from Madrid; Neos from Rome and Milan; KLM from Amsterdam; and Edelweiss Air from Zurich.Chile Another country bursting with things to do, Chile is known for its dramatic Patagonian landscapes, its stargazing spots in the Atacama Desert, and its volcanoes, with six million tourists descending on its attractions last year.You can fly direct to the capital Santiago with Iberia from Madrid and Barcelona; from Paris with Air France; from London with British Airways; and with LATAM from Madrid.Argentina Last year, 5.7 million tourists headed to Chile’s next-door neighbour Argentina for its diverse landscapes and as a jumping off point for visits to Antarctica.You can fly to the capital Buenos Aires with Aerolineas from Madrid or Rome; with Lufthansa from Frankfurt; with Air France from Paris; with KLM from Amsterdam; and with ITA Airways from Rome. Air Europa, Iberia and Plus Ultra also fly there from Madrid.PeruA bucket list destination for many thanks to Machu Picchu, Peru offers lots for history lovers, with Inca, Chavín, Moche, and Nasca sites for you to discover alongside Spanish colonial architecture. Around 3.4 million tourists visited last year.You can reach the capital Lima with Iberia from Madrid and Barcelona; with Air France from Paris; and with KLM from Amsterdam. Air Europa, LATAM and Plus Ultra also fly from Madrid.El Salvador Some 3.4 million people chose to visit El Salvador last year, thanks to its archaeological sites, brilliant beaches and volcanoes.You can fly to San Salvador with Iberojet and Iberia from Madrid, and with Iberojet from Barcelona.Costa RicaAnother popular choice for wildlife lovers, Costa Rica is known for its national parks and protected areas, with the country containing some 5% of the world’s biodiversity. Around 2.9 million tourists arrived in 2025.You will most likely fly into the capital San José, which is served by Iberia and Iberojet from Madrid; Edelweiss Air from Zurich; Air France from Paris; Lufthansa from Frankfurt; KLM from Amsterdam; and British Airways from London.GuatemalaSome 2.5 million tourists headed to Guatemala last year in search of its Mayan archaeological sites, Lake Atitlán and colonial architecture.You can fly direct from Madrid to Guatemala City with Iberia. UruguayBoasting beautiful beaches and a quieter pace of life compared to its larger neighbours, 2.5 million people headed to Uruguay in 2025.You can reach the capital Montevideo from Madrid with Air Europa, Iberia or Plus Ultra, and from Barcelona with Iberia.Panama Beyond the Panama Canal, Panama offers beaches, snorkelling opportunities, spectacular waterfalls and awe-inspiring hikes, with some 2.3 million visitors discovering the country last year.You can fly direct to Panama City with Air Europa and Iberia from Madrid; Air France from Paris; KLM from Amsterdam; and Turkish Airlines from Istanbul.Paraguay More waterfalls await in Paraguay, along with UNESCO-listed Jesuit missions, and little chance of overtourism, with two million visitors in 2025.Your only option to fly direct is from Madrid with Air Europa.Ecuador Best known for the Galápagos Islands, where Charles Darwin came up with his theory of evolution, Ecuador offers wildlife in abundance for visitors (including the 1.3 million visitors who came here in 2025).From Madrid, Air Europa, Iberia and Euroairlines fly direct to the capital Quito, while KLM flies here from Amsterdam.Bolivia Around 1.1 million were drawn in by Bolivia’s attractions last year, such as the Salar de Uyuni, the world’s largest salt flat, the ruins of Tiwanaku and the UNESCO-listed city of Potosí.Both Air Europa and BoA (Boliviana de Aviación) fly direct from Madrid.HondurasGetting firmly into the underexplored part of the region, Honduras welcomed 920,000 international tourists in 2025 who came for the coral reefs, beaches, and archeological sites.Two cities have direct flights from Europe: Comayagua, which you can fly to with Iberojet from Madrid or Barcelona, and San Pedro Sula, which is served by Air Europa from Madrid.Guyana Just 290,000 people visited Guyana last year, but those who did make the journey were rewarded with Georgetown’s unique food scene and the spectacular Kaieteur Falls.KLM flies direct to Georgetown from Amsterdam.Suriname Just next door, Suriname offers jungle exploration for those who come here, including the 220,000 people who visited in 2025.You can fly direct from Amsterdam to Paramaribo with KLM or Surinam Airways.French Guiana Last but not least, just 70,000 international tourists made it to French Guiana last year. The overseas department of France is perhaps currently best known for being home to the Guiana Space Centre, the European Space Agency’s spaceport, but it also offers an opportunity to explore the country’s dark past at Devil's Island, a former penal colony.You can fly to Cayenne from Paris Charles de Gaulle with Air France, or from Paris Orly with Air Caraïbes.Top tips for planning your tripWhile many routes mentioned above are served daily, you can use websites like flightconnections.com to see which days of the week different airlines operate the flights on, and this website will also flag if a route is seasonal.If you’re planning on flying with Iberia, don’t forget the Spanish flag carrier offers a stopover programme that will allow you to spend up to 10 days in Madrid before or after your trip.Be sure to check travel advisories for the country you are planning to visit. Many countries are currently telling citizens to avoid trips to Venezuela, for example, but there are also alerts in place for parts of Ecuador, Colombia and others.

Headline: Yemen’s Houthis claim strikes on Riyadh and the port of Yanbu
Body: Yemen’s Houthis have claimed strikes on Riyadh and the Red Sea port of Yanbu after Saudi Arabia issued emergency alerts over what it called a “hostile aerial threat”, as black smoke rose at the city's King Khalid International Airport on Saturday, hours after the raid alert.After the explosion, the flight tracking site Flightradar24 said the airport was experiencing "major problems." A journalist for the AFP news agency also reported seeing firefighters working to extinguish a burning fuel truck close to the site.Saudi authorities said there were no casualties or damage and did not say what prompted the alerts, but the Saudi Civil Defence had been sending messages to residents in several parts of the country overnight, warning of potential danger and advising people to remain indoors and away from windows.The Houthis later claimed, without providing evidence, that they had targeted “sensitive sites” in Riyadh and facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in Yanbu. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said cruise and ballistic missiles, as well as drones, were used. He also claimed Saudi Arabia had attempted to target the Houthi-held capital Sanaa, without providing details.The claims could not be independently verified.A naval blockade has already been declared by the HouthisIt comes amid an uptick in attacks from Yemen's Houthi rebels, who declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia in July.The Houthis, whom the US has designated as a Foreign Terrorist Organisation, have since been increasingly targeting Saudi cities and shipping, further heightening tensions in the Middle East - which is already reeling under the effects of the Iran war and tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz.Saudi Arabia has hit back with its own strikes on the group - which has seized vast stretches of territory in Yemen this month in a lightning offensive - but has failed to stop its advance.“Developments around the Bab al-Mandab Strait underline the urgent need to prevent Yemen’s conflict from further threatening the security of the Red Sea and this vital international maritime route,” Khaled Khiari, the UN assistant secretary-general for the Middle East, Europe, the Americas, Asia and the Pacific, said earlier this week.“What is needed now is sustained engagement that reduces tensions, prevents further escalation and safeguards freedom of navigation," he added.

Headline: Dutch police clash with hundreds of far-right protesters at anti-immigration rally
Body: Dutch riot police clashed on Saturday with around 500 far-right protesters in the centre of The Hague, using baton charges, specialist dogs, and water cannon to disperse the crowd after violence erupted.Demonstrators pelted officers with fireworks and other projectiles, shouted anti-semitic chants, and performed Nazi salutes during the "We Are The People" rally, which was organised to protest government policies on immigration and asylum."We're losing our country. We're literally losing our country to mass migration," 31-year-old mechanic Thijs Jansen told news agencies at the scene.Protesters had intended to march through the city, but local authorities banned the procession and ordered the crowd to disperse after clashes broke out at the Malieveld, a central park where demonstrators had gathered. Mounted police made several arrests during the operation.Justice Minister David van Weel condemned the "disgusting scenes" on social media platform X, calling for an "extremely firm" response to violence against law enforcement and the use of hate speech."Thanks to all the police officers who are once again standing up for our democratic rule of law," van Weel wrote.Saturday’s unrest follows similar violence a year prior during a right-wing demonstration in the city, when rioters set a police car on fire and targeted the headquarters of the centrist D66 party, currently led by Prime Minister Rob Jetten.

Headline: Tense Berlin election finale: who is to emerge strongest in the capital?
Body: On Sunday, Berliners will vote to elect a new state parliament, the Abgeordnetenhaus, alongside the regional vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The race is wide open: the Left party and the CDU are neck and neck in the latest polls, both at around 20-23%, with the AfD at 18% and the Greens at 16% close behind. The SPD, with 10-12%, is now clearly below its 2023 result.That means it is also unclear what the political landscape will look like after the vote.According to recent surveys, the current black-red coalition of the CDU and SPD would no longer have a majority. The CDU’s campaign has also shifted: instead of incumbent Governing Mayor Kai Wegner, finance and culture senator Stefan Evers is running as lead candidate. Wegner announced in the summer, after months of criticism of his handling of the January power outage, that he would not run again as the party’s frontrunner.On policy, the CDU is focusing on law and order, a more capable state and economic growth. To that end, both the police and the judiciary are to be strengthened, approval procedures accelerated, and public administration digitised.Based on current polls, several coalition options are on the table, including a government of the Left, Greens, and SPD, or a CDU-Green-SPD alliance. Whether such constellations materialise will also depend on which parties ultimately make it into the Abgeordnetenhaus.In the latest ZDF projection (source in German) published on 11 September, the Left stands at 23%, the CDU at 21%, the AfD at 17%, the Greens at 16%, and the SPD at 10%. On that basis, both a Left-Green-SPD alliance and a CDU-Green-SPD coalition would have a numerical majority. The current BerlinTREND (source in German) survey by Infratest dimap paints a similar picture: the Left at 21%, CDU at 20%, AfD at 18%, Greens at 16%, and SPD at 12%.SPD fighting to stay in governmentThe Social Democrats have now slipped to between 10 and 12% in the polls. In 2023, they were still at 18.4%. Their lead candidate is Berlin SPD co-chair Steffen Krach from Lower Saxony, who is under investigation by the Hanover public prosecutor over allegations linked to a donation of 9,900 euros to the Berlin SPD. Krach rejects the accusations and is continuing his campaign under the slogan "Wieder Berlin" – "Berlin again" – despite them.Substantively, the SPD, like most other parties, is focusing on affordable housing, investment and a functioning infrastructure. In its manifesto, it promises 100,000 new homes over the next legislative period and aims to increase the share of social housing in new-build projects from 30% to 50%. It also plans to invest in roads and bridges, schools, hospitals, and public transport.Affordable housing is also a central campaign issue for the other parties. According to Berlin’s Senate Department for Urban Development, Building and Housing, more than 100,000 new homes are missing in the capital. On top of that comes demand for additional housing for the roughly 200,000 people expected to move to Berlin by 2040. This translates into an average need for around 20,000 new homes per year in the coming years.The CDU is relying above all on faster construction and more homeownership. The Greens place greater emphasis on housing oriented towards the common good. The Left, by contrast, is calling for large housing portfolios to be brought into public ownership. The AfD and FDP reject this approach and likewise want to prioritise private construction and less regulation.The Left eyes the Red Town HallThe Left has gained significant support since the 2023 election. At the time, it stood at 12.2%; in current polls, it is around 21-23% and is now one of the two strongest parties in the race.Lead candidate Elif Eralp is campaigning primarily on rents and social policy. The Left is calling, among other things, for the socialisation of large housing stocks and stronger tenant protections. In public transport, social benefits and climate policy, the party also wants the state to play a bigger role.The Berlin Left’s campaign is, however, overshadowed by a debate over how the party deals with antisemitism and the Middle East conflict. One trigger was a performance by rapper Dahabflex at a campaign event organised by the Neukölln district branch of the Left at the end of August, where he chanted "Yalla Yalla Intifada, Westbank, Palestine, Gaza" and "Death to the IDF" (death to the Israeli armed forces).CDU lead candidate Evers accused Eralp of not acting decisively enough against antisemitic tendencies in her party. Eralp rejects that and stresses her commitment to combating antisemitism and protecting Jewish life. The Berlin Left has also adopted its own guidelines on dealing with antisemitism and says it wants to protect Jewish life in the city. As T-Online reports, the party’s Berlin executive invited the Neukölln district spokespeople to an extraordinary meeting at which "a unanimous decision was taken that Dahabflex’s performance was a mistake and that we reject all forms of violence", according to Eralp.AfD also on course to double its vote in Berlin?The AfD has also made strong gains in Berlin. In the 2023 repeat election, it took 9.1%; it now stands at 17-18% in most polls. In the latest BerlinTREND survey by Infratest dimap, it reached 18%, making it the third-strongest force behind the Left and the CDU. Compared with 2023, it has almost doubled its share of the vote.The party is once again led by Kristin Brinker, who is running as the AfD's top candidate for the third time. As with the Greens, however, Brinker is not widely known. In the current Infratest dimap poll (source in German), around two-thirds of respondents say they do not know Brinker, or do not know her well enough to judge her. The picture is similar to the Greens’ Werner Graf.In the campaign, the AfD is focusing above all on migration and internal security. The party wants a halt to the admission of asylum seekers in Berlin and the "immediate deportation of all of the up to 20,000 people in Berlin who are required to leave the country".For subsidised and state-owned housing, the AfD wants to allocate it using a points system so that it primarily benefits Berliners who have lived in the city for a long time and work in "system-relevant professions" such as the police, fire service, health care, or refuse collection. Otherwise, building should be encouraged by scrapping the property transfer tax or speeding up planning approvals.Despite its high poll ratings, the party remains excluded from any role in government: CDU, SPD, Greens and Left all rule out forming a coalition with the AfD.Will the Greens be the kingmakers?The Greens are currently polling at around 165, clearly below their 2023 result of 18.4%. Nevertheless, they could play a crucial role in forming a government: both a Left-Green-SPD alliance and a CDU-Green-SPD coalition would have a mathematical majority in current projections.Lead candidate Werner Graf is trying to present the Greens in a less confrontational way during the campaign. He wants to avoid the major rows of recent years, such as the dispute over Friedrichstrasse. Graf himself told rbb that the Greens "have learned from that". Instead of sharply polarising demands, he is adopting a more pragmatic tone and presenting himself as someone who can bring different parties together.In the election arena, shortly before polling day, both the Left's lead candidate, Eralp, and the SPD frontrunner, Krach, explicitly courted cooperation with the Greens. Graf signalled openness to an alliance and called for a "progressive government". He rules out any cooperation with the AfD.Volt, FDP and BSW battling to enter parliamentAlongside the larger parties, Volt, the FDP and the BSW are also competing to enter the Abgeordnetenhaus. For all three, the five% threshold is the decisive hurdle. Volt is standing in a Berlin Abgeordnetenhaus election for the first time and is focusing above all on digitalisation, administrative reform and faster housing construction.The FDP wants to return to the state parliament with its lead candidate, Christoph Meyer, and is campaigning for less regulation, more private investment, and homeownership. In the final stretch, Meyer is also backed by party chairman Wolfgang Kubicki, who has appeared with him in Berlin on several occasions.The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) is polling at 3-4% and therefore has to fight to clear the threshold for the Abgeordnetenhaus. The party is running in a Berlin Abgeordnetenhaus election for the first time and is led by Alexander King and Michael Lüders.In this campaign, foreign and peace policies are playing an unusually prominent role for a state election. King is calling for an end to sanctions against Russia and for negotiations with Moscow. BSW also wants to improve relations with Russia and is targeting Russian-speaking Berliners. The party, moreover, wants to prevent the Russian House on Friedrichstrasse, operated by Russia, from being closed.Vandalism: campaign posters damagedDuring the current election campaign in Berlin, the police have recorded more than 1,300 incidents of damaged campaign posters between 2 August and 16 September.Posters belonging to the AfD are particularly frequently affected, according to Bild, which asked the Berlin police for figures: across the city, 801 cases of criminal damage to AfD posters have been recorded so far. Next come the CDU with 148 cases, independent candidates or lists with 102, the Left with 95, the SPD with 88, Alliance 90/The Greens with 37, the FDP with 30, BSW with 16, Volt with 13 and the ÖDP with two cases.

Headline: Germany's defence chief Carsten Breuer chosen to head NATO military committee
Body: General Carsten Breuer, Germany's chief of defence, was selected on Saturday as the next head of NATO's military committee, the alliance's supreme military authority and a primary advisory body to its political leadership.Military chiefs from the 32-nation alliance elected Breuer during a meeting in Copenhagen, the current chair, Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, announced in a post on X.Breuer will assume the role in July 2027, succeeding Dragone for a three-year term that aligns with NATO's strategic efforts to bolster deterrence against potential Russian aggression by 2029.Alongside the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), the chairman of the Military Committee is among the most influential figures in NATO. In this role, Breuer will serve as chief military advisor to Secretary-General Mark Rutte and act as the primary bridge conveying recommendations from alliance chiefs of staff to senior political decision-makers.German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius praised the appointment, stating that Breuer had demonstrated exceptional strategic foresight and played a pivotal role in restructuring the Bundeswehr."Now he will bring all his strength and experience to NATO, which faces major, historic challenges," Pistorius said, highlighting an escalating threat from Russia as European partners take greater responsibility for conventional deterrence while the United States broadens its strategic focus to other regions, according to German media.Breuer, Germany's highest-ranking soldier, has served as Inspector General of the Bundeswehr since March 2023. He previously led the Bundeswehr's Territorial Command, which he established, and gained national prominence directing the Federal Chancellery's COVID-19 crisis staff under Chancellor Olaf Scholz. An army air defence officer who enlisted in 1984, Breuer is married with three children.A successor to fill his current post as Inspector General has yet to be named.
