Headline: A ticking 'mercury bomb'? Ancient Nazi U-boat lies off Norway
Body: Around 150 metres below the water's surface, west of the Norwegian island of Fedje, a fragment of German wartime history lies on the seabed. A submarine called U-864 has been resting there for more than eight decades, broken into two parts, surrounded by sediment and a cargo that still poses an environmental problem today.U-864 is an exceptional case: according to historical records, large quantities of mercury were probably on board, with a Japanese order mentioning 1,867 containers.If the entire shipment had been loaded, that would correspond to between about 65 and 67 tonnes. However, the exact loading documents have not survived, so the actual quantity cannot be definitively established. The only certainty is that mercury is still stored in the wreck.A final voyage with a deadly endBy February 1945, the war was in its final phase. Even so, U-864 was still on a special mission. The German submarine was supposed to travel via Norway to Japan. On board, in addition to military and technical equipment, were specialists and material intended for Japan’s armaments industry. But the voyage ended off Fedje.The British submarine HMS Venturer had decrypted German radio transmissions and tracked down U-864. On 9 February 1945, Venturer fired a torpedo. It hit the German submarine and destroyed it. U-864 sank to a depth of around 150 metres. All 73 people on board were killed. The attack is considered the only known case in which one submerged submarine sank another.After that, the wreck was forgotten for decades.It was not found until 2003Only decades later did U-864 return to the spotlight: clues about the special cargo ultimately led to investigations off the Norwegian coast.In 2003, the wreck was located by the Norwegian naval vessel KNM Tyr. It became clear that the submarine had not remained intact on the seabed. The two parts of the wreck lie separated from each other at a depth of about 150 metres.The problem with the cargo is that mercury does not simply disappear. Mercury can remain in the environment for a very long time because, unlike many organic pollutants, it is not broken down biologically.How long mercury persists in the environment depends on its chemical form and the prevailing environmental conditions. In contaminated sediments, it can remain for decades, in some cases even for centuries. The US environmental agency EPA points out that mercury can be released from soils for potentially hundreds of years.Particularly problematic is the fact that micro-organisms can convert mercury into methylmercury. This especially toxic form accumulates in the food chain, especially in fish.New images from the depthsNew images released by the Norwegian Coastal Administration Kystverket (source in German) show what the wreck looks like today.In May 2025, Kystverket had the wreck examined using remotely operated underwater vehicles. Among other equipment, WROVs (remotely operated underwater vehicles connected to a ship by cable), 4K cameras, photogrammetry and acoustic measurement techniques were deployed. The recordings were also used to create a three-dimensional model of the wreck and the surrounding seabed.The submarine lies far below the surface of the water, partly embedded in sediment on the sea floor.Dangerous cargoMany of the presumed 1,867 containers are likely to have been damaged when the submarine sank.A recovery operation could remove some of the mercury from the wreck, but the work itself could also stir up contaminated sediments and release pollutants.This is exactly what the Norwegian authorities experienced during investigations and salvage work in 2026, when 22 containers were recovered from the wreck. Initial examinations showed that around 80% of the containers were damaged and leaking. Around half a tonne of mercury was brought ashore. At the same time, according to the Norwegian Coastal Administration, mercury was also released into the water from the working area.Recover it or seal it for good?Norway is therefore facing a dilemma. Should it try to retrieve the dangerous cargo from an 81-year-old wartime wreck lying at a depth of 150 metres? Or should the wreck and the contaminated seabed be permanently covered?This question has been fiercely debated for years. In 2026, after its experience with the operations, Kystverket again recommended covering the wreck. In the authority’s assessment, a large-scale recovery could ultimately release more pollutants than it would remove.Covering the wreck would not be a simple, final solution either: the cover would have to be monitored over the long term.The people of Fedje live with the knowledge that just a few kilometres off their coast lies a German submarine whose cargo still raises questions. And while decades later, technology can now look deep inside the wreck, the crucial question remains unresolved: what should be done with it?The Norwegian authorities have, incidentally, been analysing fish and shellfish from the region for years. So far, there appears to be no reason for undue concern: the tests have so far shown stable or low mercury levels.

Headline: Contrast in Tehran as unveiled women race marathon alongside regime military display
Body: Tehran saw two very different scenes unfold at the same time on Friday, as in one part of the city, many women raced a marathon without a headscarf, and in another part, a regime military display took place with thousands of women in hijab showing their loyalty with machine guns in their hands.The state-organised rally brought together 300,000 supporters of the Islamic Republic. The "Jan-Fada" (Self-Sacrificers) marched from Imam Hossein Square toward central Tehran. Among these, the image of a woman in a full chador with a baby wrapped in a keffiyeh perched behind a machine gun stood out as particularly striking.On the other hand, female runners joined a sporting event and competed in a track-and-field race. During the event, women whose clothing, according to published images, did not comply with Iran’s mandatory hijab rules were featured.The Tehran 10-kilometre marathon was held at Velayat Park, with men and women competing in separate divisions.According to the official schedule, the women’s race started at 5:30 AM, followed by the men’s at 7:00 AM. Published photos showed some female participants running without headscarves and wearing standard athletic gear, including long-sleeve tops and track pants.This event proceeded despite the cancellation of the "Mahan Run" in the city of Kerman just days earlier, which had been scheduled for 5km, 10km, and 21km distances.Kerman's seminary had demanded the cancellation, citing co-ed participation and concerns over "religious values", ultimately leading authorities to withhold a permit.Similarly, in December 2025, images of unveiled women running in a Kish Island marathon sparked widespread backlash from conservative figures and led to legal actions against the organisers.Meanwhile, the Tehran Prosecutor's Office has announced the opening of a judicial case against the organisers of the Tehran Marathon over what it described as a "failure to observe legal and religious standards," HRANA (Human Rights Activists News Agency) reported.Pro-regime rallyA short distance away, in a markedly different atmosphere, central Tehran hosted the "Jan-Fada-ye Iran" (Iran's Self-Sacrificers) drill. The event featured Basij forces, campaign volunteers, and several senior military and political figures, including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. State media claimed an attendance of 313,000 people.The procession moved from Imam Hossein Square toward the city centre, showcasing military hardware, drones, and organised Basij units."Jan-Fada-ye Iran" is a campaign launched following the outbreak of armed conflict. Islamic Republic officials initially claimed over 30 million enrollments, later updating the figure to around 32 million, and asserted that 32% of registrants are women and 68% are men.Given Iran's population of roughly 90 million, 32 million would represent nearly 35% of the country's total population.However, this statistic relies solely on the organiser's claims and cannot be independently verified.What is the law, and where is the contradiction?Under Iranian law, women are required to wear the hijab in public. However, four years after the start of the “Woman, Life, Freedom” movement, an increasing number of women have openly refused to comply with the rule.This trend has continued despite the two recent wars involving Iran against Israel and the US.A similar change has also been evident at pro-government rallies in recent weeks and months. Images from several events have shown women attending without headscarves or wearing them in ways that do not fully comply with the official dress code.At the same time, some voices within the Iranian establishment have argued that women who support the Islamic Republic should still be considered supporters of the system, even if they do not fully comply with the mandatory hijab rules.What defined Tehran on Friday morning was the juxtaposition of these two realities: on one side, thousands of mobilised forces gathered for a state military display focused on "comprehensive defence"; on the other, men and women took part in an athletic event that presented a distinctly different picture of women's presence in Iranian public life.These paradoxes play out against a heightened political and security backdrop inside Iran following the start of US and Israeli military strikes on February 28.Even as state rallies and pro-regime demonstrations fill the streets, reports indicate an ongoing crackdown marked by detentions of protesters and state executions.According to Human Rights Watch, the Islamic Republic executed at least 29 people between March 18 and the end of August who had been arrested in connection with the January protests.

Headline: The keg is tapped: Munich springs to life as Oktoberfest returns
Body: By late morning, it was clear: the Wiesn was back. Decorated horse-drawn carriages, brass bands and festival hosts made their way towards the Theresienwiese, while growing crowds gathered around the fairground. Munich had dressed up for the occasion, and apparently nobody intended to worry about details such as calories, footwear or the weather forecast – not least because Bavaria was enjoying glorious sunshine and temperatures just above 20 degrees Celsius.The Theresienwiese was already filling up earlier in the day. At around 10:35 a.m., the traditional procession of the Wiesn landlords got under way. Around 1,000 participants, including festival hosts, showmen, musicians and waiting staff, made their way through central Munich to the Theresienwiese in decorated carriages and horse-drawn wagons.Beer only after the keg is tappedThe festival tents had already opened at 9 a.m., initially serving non-alcoholic drinks and light snacks. Beer could only be served after the official tapping of the first keg. The fairground rides also started operating only afterwards.The big moment finally came at exactly noon in the Schottenhamel festival tent. Munich’s new mayor, Dominik Krause, took the mallet and, for the first time in his term of office, tapped the first keg. After the traditional “O’zapft is!” and the twelve cannon shots fired from the Bavaria, the monumental bronze statue and landmark of the Free State of Bavaria, it was clear: there was no turning back. The beer could flow.As the first one-litre stein made its way to Bavarian Minister-President Markus Söder, the most important question of the day on the Theresienwiese was probably already being asked: Where can we still find a seat?Millions of visitors expectedThe Wiesn is one of the largest folk festivals in the world and attracts millions of visitors from Germany and abroad every year. According to Bavarian public broadcaster BR, around 6.5 million people attended the last Oktoberfest.This year, a Maß of beer costs between €14.80 and €15.90, depending on the tent, meaning visitors once again have to dig a little deeper into their pockets. A large pretzel at the Wiesn costs around €5 to €6.For getting to the festival, the city recommends using public transport. The Theresienwiese can be reached via several U-Bahn and S-Bahn stations. Anyone travelling by car should be prepared for an extremely difficult search for a parking space around the fairground.

Headline: Thousands of migrants return to beaches in Ceuta after new port facility runs out of space
Body: More than 2,000 migrants in Ceuta had to return to the beaches after there was not enough space to accommodate them at a new facility located in the autonomous city's port.Thousands of migrants had been moved from the territory's Trampolín and Benítez beaches on Friday morning, escorted by officers from Spain's Civil Guard and National Police towards the new temporary reception centre, which is designed to accommodate 1,700 people.However, there were over 4,000 people coming from the beaches, meaning many had to return after the new camp filled up. According to government sources, around 3,000 migrants remain on the city’s streets in total.Police had struggled to maintain order on Friday as people fought to secure a spot at the new site after weeks of living on the beaches and streets, with officers firing warning shots into the air in an attempt to contain the crowd. No serious incidents were recorded, however, according to local authorities.The migrants' return meant a clean-up operation that had been planned for the beaches once they were cleared also had to be put on hold.As a result, Trampolín still looks much as it had in recent days, with makeshift tents and shacks strewn across the sand.The Ceuta migrant crisis began in late July when more than 70,000 people crossed into the Spanish exclave from Morocco.Kissy Chandiramani, a member of Ceuta's autonomous government, has described the port transfer as chaotic and said that neither the city government nor port authorities had been given advance warning.Chandiramani also called for procedures to return the migrants to be speeded up, warning that otherwise, Ceuta risked becoming "the great CETI of North Africa," in reference to the Temporary Immigrant Reception Centres.She noted that around one hundred migrant cases were being processed each day and that, with more resources, the process could be completed in 15 days.If the current pace continues, she warned, the situation "is going to drag on forever."

Headline: UN condemns 'shocking pattern' of sexual violence by Russian troops in Ukraine
Body: More than 1,000 cases of sexual violence recorded since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 involve victims as young as 4 and as old as 82 in a "shocking pattern of torture, intimidation and coercion," according to the report published on Friday by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights."I am deeply alarmed by the prevalence of these abhorrent acts documented in our report, and fear that they are almost certainly continuing amid the unceasing violence we are witnessing every day in Ukraine," said UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk.Both crimes were committed by Russian troops, who account for 89% of perpetrators in the 1,004 cases included in the report.While the majority of documented victims are men, particularly those held in places of detention, women and children have been most severely affected in occupied Ukrainian territory.Crimes against Ukrainian prisoners of war and detained medical workers include gang rape, genital mutilation and other acts of sexual humiliation.The most common single method recorded was the use of a Soviet-era military field telephone known as a "tapik" to administer electric shocks to the genitals: 155 cases, or 27% of the total, involved this form of abuse at least once, the report says.Individual survivor testimonies documented in the report include Ukrainian prisoners of war sexually assaulted with objects such as batons, cell door keys or shovel handles.A woman in Zaporizhzhia was raped several times a week for a month by a Russian soldier who promised better treatment for her detained husband. A woman in Kherson was assaulted nightly and repeatedly threatened with gang rape.In the Kyiv region, two Russian soldiers broke into a family home in 2022, shot and killed a woman's husband, then gang-raped her, threatening to shoot her in front of her four-year-old son if she resisted."Sexual violence is a grave feature of the full-scale armed attack against Ukraine. It must stop immediately, irrespective of the perpetrators," Türk said."Given the high prevalence of cases attributed to its forces, however, the Russian Federation in particular must take concrete and discernible steps to protect civilians and prisoners of war from all forms of torture, including sexual violence."The 20-page report covers the period from 24 February 2022 to the end of July 2026 and draws on confidential interviews with hundreds of victims, along with court documents and official records.Of the 11% of cases attributed to Ukrainian forces, nearly half involved threats of sexual violence against Russian prisoners of war and prisoners of war from third countries. The remainder included forced nudity, electric shocks and beatings to the genitals, sexually degrading treatment and two cases each of sexual assault and attempted rape.Conventions disregarded, withdrawn fromRussia was added to the UN Secretary-General's list of parties credibly suspected of committing sexual violence in conflict in May of this year — a list that includes Sudan, Somalia and Haiti as repeat offenders. The Kremlin rejected the findings as politically motivated.The UN Human Rights Council's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine has separately documented widespread use of torture by Russian authorities against Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war in occupied territory and inside Russia.Russia formally withdrew from the European Convention for the Prevention of Torture in September 2025 following its expulsion from the Council of Europe, ending visits by European monitors to Russian detention facilities.Russia remains a formal party to the UN Convention Against Torture and prohibits torture under its constitution and criminal code.The Ukrainian foreign ministry welcomed the report, saying it had "once again demonstrated the scale of systematic human rights violations committed by the Russian Federation."Rape and sexual violence were codified as war crimes and crimes against humanity under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, which entered into force in 2002.The use of systematic rape as a weapon of war was first formally prosecuted as a crime against humanity and an act of genocide by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s.

Headline: Russian attacks on Ukraine kill at least 11 and injure dozens over past 24 hours
Body: Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least 11 people and injured dozens more over the past day, according to local authorities.In Kharkiv Oblast in northeastern Ukraine, five people were killed and 15 were injured in Russian attacks, governor Oleh Syniehubov reported, adding that Russian forces had fired two missiles, five guided aerial bombs, and almost 60 drones at targets across the region.Strikes reportedly hit the villages of Lypkuvativka, Velykyi Burluk, and Slatyne, as well as the cities of Kharkiv and Balakliia, among other locations.Two people were also killed and five were wounded following a wave of drone attacks, air strikes, and artillery shelling across the Kherson region of southern Ukraine, per the Kherson Regional State Administration."Russian troops struck critical and social infrastructure, as well as residential neighborhoods in the region’s settlements, damaging, in particular, five high-rise buildings and seven private homes," it said in a statement posted on Telegram. "The occupiers also destroyed administrative buildings, stores, a cell tower, a utility building, a gas pipeline, and private vehicles".In Donetsk in the east of the country, one person was killed in the city of Kramatorsk while 13 people were injured across the wider region.A 51-year-old man and a 45-year-old woman were also killed after a guided missile struck a high-rise building in Sumy Oblast in the north, authorities said. A 32-year-old man also died following a drone attack in the region.The Sumy Regional Military Administration reported 50 attacks on 21 settlements from Friday to Saturday morning, with Russian forces said to have launched drones, mortars, artillery, and guided aerial bombs.It comes as the Ukrainian air force reported that Russia had fired two “Zircon” missiles from its Kursk region as well as 174 drones at Ukraine overnight."According to preliminary data, as of 8 am, air defence forces shot down or neutralized 141 targets," the force said, adding that strikes had been recorded at 15 locations.On Saturday, Poland's Armed Forces Operational Command said it had activated air defence measures and scrambled military aircraft in response to Russian drone attacks on Ukraine."These measures are preventive in nature and are aimed at securing and protecting Polish airspace, especially in regions adjacent to threatened areas," it said in a statement.

Headline: Shakira returns to Spain in fire, tears and 'Waka Waka'
Body: At 20:49 on Saturday 18 September, Spanish time, Shakira stepped onto the stage of the Madrid stadium that bears her name. The setlist of 25 songs spread over two hours opened with 'La fuerte', her collaboration with Bizarrap from her latest album, and continued with 'Girl like me' and a medley of 'Las de la intuición' and 'Estoy aquí', her first international hit."Good evening, Madrid, I can't believe I'm here", the artist said after the first few songs, before referring, without mincing her words, to her private life: "You'll be thinking, the face I left with and the face I've come back with." She added that "there is nothing like a she-wolf being reunited with her pack".To the reggaeton beat of her latest work came 'Te felicito' and 'TDG', with Rauw Alejandro and Karol G respectively, as well as 'Don't Bother' and 'Can't Remember to Forget You', her collaboration with Rihanna.Amid costume changes and images of water and fire projected onto the screen, the set also included 'Copa vacía', 'La bicicleta' and 'La tortura', along with 'Hips don't lie' and 'Chantaje', the latter coinciding with the end of the concert's first hour.The second half opened with 'Loca' and a personal confession from the singer: "When a family breaks apart, as mine did, you feel as if you have lost your compass, until you realise that you can get through it and start to see single life as an opportunity." Those words were followed by 'Soltera', performed beneath a giant S on stage.Songs such as 'Ojos así', 'Pies descalzos' and 'Antología' revisited her earliest years as an artist. "The most important years of my life I lived here, in Spain. It was here that I became a mother. You saw me arrive, fall, get back up and return. Thank you for walking with me for more than 30 years", she told the audience.Near the end, 'Waka, waka' rang out, now also turned into an anthem for the 2026 World Cup, and the concert closed with 'BZRP Music Sessions #53', amid confetti and fireworks.Macondo Park, a temporary city next to the concertThe concert venue, named Macondo Park in tribute to the town invented by Gabriel García Márquez in 'One Hundred Years of Solitude', opened its doors this Friday at around 17:00, albeit with an hour and a half delay. The space, carpeted with coloured artificial grass, comprises eight pavilions dedicated to different facets of Hispano-American culture under the Es Latina project.Before Shakira's performance, Guitarricadelafuente played on one of the venue's stages, alongside Maro, Virtual Diva and Santos Bravos, who all declared themselves admirers of the Colombian star.The album that lends its name to the tour, 'Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran' (2024), is the singer's twelfth studio record and, judging by its lyrics, deals with her break-up with former footballer Gerard Piqué. Macondo Park will close its doors on 11 October, after the last of the 12 concerts scheduled in Madrid.

Headline: Ed Sheeran backlash continues as radio station bans songs and Instagram fans unfollow
Body: Ed Sheeran has become a political lightning rod in a snowballing controversy which shows no signs of slowing down.The British singer's once-wholesome image has taken an almighty nosedive following the dismissal of Macklemore from his US tour after venues objected to the rapper's outspoken support for Palestine.After a very ill-advised PR statement - which did more damage to Sheeran's brand than anything else – and all of the singer's opening acts quitting in solidarity with Macklemore, Ed has faced a reputation-staining backlash. This includes calls for boycott and criticism from major figures in the music world and beyond.In a lengthy post on Instagram earlier this week, Sheeran responded to the backlash, saying it was "important that I set out some facts.""I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine. The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated," he wrote, adding that the decision to drop Macklemore was "the promoter's" and "not mine."Commentators have called the singer "spineless" and a "lowlife coward"; former Pink Floyd Roger Waters has dismissed him as a "prick"; and Massive Attack reminded Sheeran that "Neutrality’ in the face of the slaughter of more than 20,000 children can never be neutrality.” Then came New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who argued the controversy was bigger than either performer, framing it as an example of powerful interests allegedly being able to silence artists who speak on political issues. Still, she admitted to TMZ that she would switch radio stations if a Sheeran song came on... And one radio station won't be an issue in this regard...  One of Ireland’s biggest commercial radio networks has announced that it is pulling Sheeran's music from its playlists - just hours before he is due back on stage in Philadelphia for his first show since he was left without 'A Team'. Classic Hits Radio announced it would stop playing Sheeran's songs following feedback from listeners.“Our decision to remove Ed Sheeran’s music from the Classic Hits Radio playlist has been carefully considered,” Dave Kelly, group programme director at Bay Broadcasting, which runs the radio station, said in a statement. “It is not intended as a personal judgment on Ed Sheeran, and we acknowledge his own explanation of the circumstances surrounding recent events.”The station said it had also taken into account the decisions of Irish acts Aaron Rowe and Beoga, who withdrew from Sheeran's tour.“As an independent Irish-owned radio station, however, we believe it is important to listen to our audience and to stand alongside Irish artists who have made what is undoubtedly a significant professional decision based on their own convictions,” Kelly said.“Ultimately, our position is a simple one. We believe in peace, humanity and respect, and in the right of people and artists to express and act upon their sincerely held views."Although Sheeran was born and raised in England, he has strong Irish family connections through his father and grandparents and has spoken publicly about his Irish heritage.Previously, Rowe said that Sheeran had been a friend to him, “but as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation”.“I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children. I would lose all respect for myself to carry on as normal.”Beoga stated on Instagram that they would no longer be a part of Sheeran’s band “following the silencing of Macklemore by zionist lobbies”. They added that while they have been friends with Sheeran for over 10 years and will continue to be, “to play in venues that silence anyone advocating for Free Palestine is simply not an option for us”.The Israeli-American Council has also criticised Sheeran over the situation, telling the Jewish Telegraphic Agency that it was "time to take responsibility for giving a stage to antisemitic messaging."“This isn’t just ‘criticism of Israel.’ It’s a message that crosses the line between legitimate political criticism and antisemitism. This is Ed Sheeran’s stage, it’s the tour that carries his name — and so the responsibility for what happens on it is his too," it told the outlet.In a separate statement posted on Facebook, the Council also praised New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft for what it called his "moral leadership in expelling rapper Macklemore from the concert stage rather than allow him to promote antisemitism."Lisa Nandy, the UK's Culture Secretary, told LBC earlier this week that she had "enormous sympathy" for Sheeran and that he had been left in an "impossible situation.""I really feel for Ed Sheeran in all of this," she said. "He's got support acts who he wants to profile and platform. He's got promoters saying that they won't when politics is being introduced to the stadium."Elsewhere, the fallout has extended to Sheeran's social media accounts, as the singer's Instagram follower count is tumbling.According to social media analytics company Social Blade, Sheeran lost 149,636 followers on Instagram in the day following Macklemore’s dismissal, while the rapper gained 750,098 followers during the same period.In the space of three days, Sheeran has lost more than 260,000 followers, while Mackelmore and the artists have quit his tour have gained a combined 1.638 million.Sheeran is due to perform at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia on Saturday – which will be his first time back on stage since the controversy spiralled. As of writing, no news on whether Sheeran will have new opening acts or if he'll perform alone.

Headline: EU fuel prices hit records as ECB experts see diesel margins peak in October
Body: Filling up a car has never cost more on average across the European Union, according to European Commission data going back more than two decades. At the latest average prices, it costs about €103 to fill a 50-litre tank with petrol and €108 with diesel.Retail fuel prices have surged since the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East, adding to inflationary pressures. Eurozone energy inflation rose to 14.3% in August, up from 10.3% in July, according to the European Central Bank.A litre of petrol cost a weighted EU average of €2.063 as of 14 September, while diesel reached €2.159 per litre. Both were the highest readings in the Commission’s series, which begins in 2005. Petrol’s previous peak was recorded in 2022, while diesel last approached its current level in April this year.Prices varied considerably across the EU. Petrol was cheapest in Malta, at €1.34 per litre, and most expensive in Denmark, at €2.56. Diesel ranged from €1.21 per litre in Malta to €2.51 in Finland.The figures come from the European Commission’s latest Weekly Oil Bulletin, published on 17 September using prices reported for 14 September. They include taxes.Fuel prices have been rising for months since the war with Iran broke out at the end of February and disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz. International benchmark Brent crude prices rose above $126 at the height of the conflict and were trading at more than $104 a barrel for delivery the following month on Friday. Brent cost about $72 per barrel before the war broke out.European crude supplies face further disruption after Saudi Aramco told at least two European refiners that they would receive no oil under long-term contracts in October following an attack on the kingdom’s key pipeline to the Red Sea, Bloomberg reported, citing people informed of the decision who said it applied to all European buyers.What makes European fuel prices expensive?But international crude prices are not the only factor driving petrol and diesel prices higher. Refining costs and margins have also risen significantly, putting further pressure on prices at the pump.Refining margins reflect the difference between the cost of crude oil and the price of refined products such as petrol and diesel. While petrol margins appear to have peaked, ECB experts told Euronews Business that diesel margins are not expected to reach their highest point until October.“Looking ahead, based on refined diesel futures from LSEG on 16 September, the margin for diesel is expected to peak in October. Based on refined petrol futures from LSEG on 16 September, petrol margins peaked in August,” they said.Since the beginning of 2026, the weighted EU average petrol price has risen by about 29%, while diesel has surged by almost 40%.Higher crude prices have also fuelled energy inflation across both the eurozone and the wider EU. According to an ECB blog published in July, increases in crude-oil prices generally feed through fully to pre-tax pump prices within one or two months. Governments can temporarily cushion the impact through measures such as cuts to fuel duties.Crude oil accounted for less than a quarter of the euro-area pump price in the ECB blog’s July calculations. The remainder included refining and distribution costs and margins, excise duties and value added tax, helping to explain the significant differences between countries.The blog’s calculations indicated that excise duties and VAT together represented around 44% of the euro-area diesel price and 52% of the petrol price in July.ECB experts told Euronews Business that refining margins are now making a large contribution to diesel prices.“At the current juncture, we have estimated that in the third week of September refining margins have contributed €0.41 (19% of the pump price) and €0.17 (8%) per litre to the retail diesel and retail petrol prices in the euro area, respectively.”Could fuel prices rise further?The ECB’s monetary policy statement, published on 10 September, warned: “Renewed disruption of energy supplies could cause energy prices to rise further and for longer than currently expected.”ECB experts said an end to the Middle East conflict and the restoration of energy and refining flows would be central to bringing prices down.“For petrol and diesel prices to decline, the key factor would be a cessation of the war in the Middle East, a normalisation of flows through the Strait of Hormuz and a restoration of global refining activity to allow oil inventories to rebuild,” they said.Such a normalisation could quickly lower crude oil and retail fuel prices. However, disruptions to Russian refining capacity could keep margins elevated even if the Middle East conflict were resolved.

Headline: Ed Sheeran set to resume tour after Macklemore was controversially dropped for making pro-Palestine comments
Body: Ed Sheeran is set to resume his tour on Saturday, possibly solo, after all his supporting acts withdrew in solidarity with opening-act Macklemore, who was dropped after making pro-Palestinian comments on-stage.It remains to be seen how Sheeran will handle the performance at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field given the departure of his opening acts and supporting band.Sheeran has performed much of his Loop Tour concerts solo, but he had been joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga. Macklemore, Sheeran’s original US opener, had been replaced by Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe before they backed out.Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out earlier this week.Sheeran has not said anything publicly since losing the artists' support. As of Friday, tickets were still available for Saturday's show, and his website did not list any replacement acts. A coalition of pro-Palestinian organisations plan to protest outside the show on Saturday afternoon.The show comes after a tumultuous week that opened with Macklemore being dropped in response to exclaiming “Free Palestine” during a 5 September show in New Jersey.Sheeran has said he was not responsible for the decision, which came at the urging of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. His company owns a stadium where Sheeran’s tour was scheduled to play on Friday. Within hours of Sheeran's statement Tuesday, his supporting acts withdrew.Macklemore said on Wednesday he is donating $1 million (€871m) to support Palestinian relief efforts and called on Kraft to match the gift, a spokesperson for Kraft has said the billionaire and Sheeran have each agreed to donate $2 million (€1.74m) but have not specified where the money will be directed.Sheeran’s Loop Tour was the highest-grossing in the world, with an average box office gross of over $7 million (€6m) per city, Pollstar said in May. Through the end of 2025, Sheeran was the third-highest earning concert act since 2021.Sheeran has said the tour promoter was ultimately responsible for the decision to drop Macklemore.The Grammy winner was adamant in his Tuesday statement that he wouldn't be drawn into discussion of the war in Gaza, arguing that his fans don’t come to his shows to hear about these issues.He also said he “spoke with the venues at length all week to try to build a bridge” before Macklemore was dropped. He insisted he would never willingly let down his fans or abandon the touring crew and others who rely on him to make a living.While promoters and venues wield great power over concert tours, experts say an artist of Sheeran's magnitude generally has the final say about what happens concerning the shows.

Headline: What we know (and still don't) about Canada's 'associate membership'
Body: It's the head-turning, eye-popping announcement of the week: Ursula von der Leyen has invited Canada to make history by becoming the first-ever "associate member" of the European Union."We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible," the European Commission president said in her State of the Union speech.The following day, speaking from the same lectern in Strasbourg, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said his country "welcomes" the offer and hailed the dawn of an "alliance for the future"."Europe and Canada are stronger together," he said.The back-to-back speeches made international headlines, caused a political furore, inspired countless memes and even caught Donald Trump's attention. But they also left many burning questions unanswered.Here's what we know – and still don't know – about the splashy idea.There's just no precedentThe concept of "associate membership" is not envisioned in the EU treaties as such. And since it does not exist on paper, there is no precise playbook that Brussels can follow to make it reality.A similar dilemma emerged earlier this year when German Chancellor Friedrich Merz proposed making Ukraine an "associate member" of the bloc. This, he said, should grant observer status in the decision-making bodies, gradual access to some EU programmes and mutual assistance in the event of a future attack.Merz's surprise pitch received mixed reviews from capitals and was rebuffed by Kyiv, which worried the half-in, half-out rank would plunge it into accession limbo.Commission officials say von der Leyen's vision fundamentally differs from Merz's because it is designed for countries outside Europe's geographic sphere that wish to be politically and economically closer to the bloc.Brussels is confident the ground-breaking concept can be designed from scratch without the need to revise the EU treaties, a perilous avenue.Some have suggested that a possible way forward lies with Article 217 of the EU treaties, which holds that "The Union may conclude with one or more third countries or international organisations agreements establishing an association involving reciprocal rights and obligations, common action and special procedure."Carney, meanwhile, said the set-up should be "open enough that others can join".It's not enlargementOne thing Carney made sure to stress is that his country would not pursue the conventional full-time membership that Ukraine, Moldova and other candidates are seeking.According to the treaties, this process is available to "any European State", which means a nation on the other side of the Atlantic would not qualify."Canada is not in a position nor seeking to become a full member of the European Union. Therefore, it's a different framework," Carney said after his speech. "It's a framework that is relevant for a country that shares deep bonds with Europe."Accession is a notoriously cumbersome process that requires candidates to adopt thousands of EU laws and align themselves with the bloc's world-class standards. Each step is subject to unanimity, creating multiple opportunities for vetoes.Ottawa and Brussels want an arrangement that can be concluded much faster.But it seems curiosity has been piqued: ahead of Carney's trip to Strasbourg, a poll showed that a whopping 49% of Canadians supported full-fledged EU membership.The name is TBDThough the headlines that emerged from Strasbourg all honed in on the striking "associate member" title, Carney did not outright endorse it. Instead, he stuck to his "alliance for the future" moniker, which is less politically charged."President von der Leyen used both terms: alliance for the future and associate membership. The nomenclature, the precise nomenclature, is a question for Europe," he said. "What matters is the substance."For the Canadian premier, "associate membership" carries the connotation of ceding sovereignty to Brussels, something he vowed would not be the case under any circumstance."We are looking for partnerships that are complementary, that reinforce our sovereignty, and that's what is on offer here," he said. "Canadians are united that nobody is going to tell us what language we speak. No one is going to dictate our culture or with whom we can strike international agreements."EU officials have brushed off the semantic clash. For them, the "alliance for the future" is the immediate deliverable and "associate membership" the long-term prospect.It'll be put to a voteAfter von der Leyen extended her invitation, the conservative opposition in Canada criticised Carney for seeking deeper ties with the EU without an electoral mandate.In response, Carney cautioned the negotiations were still in early stages and committed to bringing the outcome to a final vote in the Canadian parliament."We will have a series of debates, I'm sure, in parliament (and) relevant committees. And ultimately, there will be a vote in the Canadian parliament for the final structure of the alliance that we're working on," he said. "It will all roll out transparently."On the European side, it remains to be seen how von der Leyen's team will advance the novel concept through the legislative cycle. The executive has not yet said which department will supervise the work, though the Secretariat-General and DG Trade appear the likeliest candidates to take the reins."We're talking about a very ambitious project here, so this is going to require many services across the Commission. It's going to be a whole-of-government approach if you want to call it that," Olof Gill, the Commission's deputy chief spokesperson, said.Gill insisted the talks would be carried out in close coordination with the member states, some of which were given a heads-up right before von der Leyen's speech."Big changes in the European Union only happen with the say-so of our member states, and that will always be the case," he said.Ireland, Spain and France are among those who have expressed support for exploring the original idea. A high-level discussion on the matter is not excluded when EU leaders gather in October for a busy two-day summit in Brussels.Later that month, von der Leyen and Carney will meet in Montreal, Quebec. This will be a chance for both to flesh out what exactly they have in mind.Economy comes firstStill, Strasbourg already gave us a pretty good idea of the areas that von der Leyen and Carney have set their sights on.Chief among them is commerce, building on the EU-Canada free trade deal, CETA, which still has to be ratified by 10 member states.Von der Leyen said the goal should be to establish a "common prosperity and economic security space" encompassing intelligent manufacturing, energy, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum, cyber, defence industry and the Arctic.Carney echoed these areas and added broadband connections, semiconductors, liquefied natural gas and hydrogen to the list.He also made sure to underscore Canada's position as a supplier of critical minerals, which Europe desperately wants to diversify to cut off Beijing's chokepoints."Canada has deposits of over 34 critical minerals, and we are among the top producers of the 10 most essential for the world's energy transition," he said."Our alliance can help fill Europe's need for reliable supply, Canada's need for advanced processing capabilities and our common objective to build complete value chains."Another way to deepen ties is for Canada to participate in EU programmes. Canada is already part of the Horizon research platform and the SAFE defence initiative and wants to join the popular Erasmus+ for students and the €90 billion loan for Ukraine.The four freedomsVon der Leyen's invitation has raised the question of whether Canada, a country more than 6,000 kilometres away from continental Europe, will one day benefit from the bloc's four freedoms of movement: goods, services, capital and people.The four freedoms are what make the single market seamless, borderless and effectively invisible. Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland are the only nations outside the EU that enjoy this unfettered access. In return, they have been asked to apply thousands of EU laws without having a direct say in their approval.Will Canada go as far?In his speech, Carney said the burgeoning alliance should aim to enable free movement for young people between the EU and Canada."We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic," he said.Carney also spoke of an "integrated market for financial services to broaden choice and reduce costs for our citizens, improve access to capital for our companies while maintaining our world-leading financial resilience".Von der Leyen, however, did not mention any of the four freedoms.The Commission has consistently said the four freedoms cannot be "cherry-picked". Earlier this year, Brussels reportedly rejected a post-Brexit overture from London to secure free movement of goods but not people.Asked if any of them would be available under the "associate membership", Gill, the spokesperson, neither confirmed nor denied."Let's see where these discussions go," he said. "Right now, we have a shared commitment between the European Union and Canada that we want to strengthen our relations for mutual benefit, in our own interests."

Headline: Macron heading to Saint Pierre and Miquelon to meet with Canadian PM Carney
Body: French President Emmanuel Macron is travelling to Saint Pierre and Miquelon this weekend to discuss the future of the archipelago, as well as France's geostrategic presence in the North Atlantic, maritime sovereignty and cooperation with Ottawa.The last French president to make a trip to the overseas collectivity, which is located some 20 kilometres off the Canadian province of Newfoundland and Labrador, was François Hollande back in December 2014.Eleven years on, Macron will be there on Sunday alongside Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister.Their meeting comes amid Carney's apparently blossoming relationship with Brussels and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's proposal to make Canada an associate member of the EU.An archipelago 'central to today's France'The key goal of the trip is to "deliver a message (...) about France's presence across five oceans," the French presidency said during a telephone briefing with the media, including Euronews. France has a presence in the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans, as well as "in the Arctic, through Saint Pierre and Miquelon" and in the Southern Ocean.Located at the gateway to the Arctic, Saint Pierre and Miquelon gives France a significant exclusive economic zone and allows it to maintain a military presence there.That presence is partly provided by the Fulmar, a navy patrol vessel and the only French military ship permanently based in the archipelago, which is due for replacement.Saint Pierre and Miquelon is not a peripheral outpost, the Élysée stresses, but "a territory, an archipelago that is central to today's France."During the presidential visit, questions of sovereignty will also be discussed in relation to digital cables and connections linking the archipelago and the European continent, as well as space-related activities, where further investment expected.Another item on the agenda will be regional cooperation. Paris wants to turn Saint Pierre and Miquelon into a "rear base for polar cooperation," working not only with Canada but also with Denmark and Greenland.The president is also expected to focus on the day-to-day difficulties faced by residents.Saint Pierre and Miquelon is grappling with economic and social problems similar to those seen in many isolated territories around the world while also experiencing the effects of climate change.The archipelago's population is also declining. The biggest blow came with the collapse of the fishing industry following years of a Canadian moratorium on cod fishing. France also saw its exclusive economic zone there reduced following a court ruling in 1992.Another threat facing the territory is rising sea levels. The village of Miquelon-Langlade, located on a narrow strip of sand just two metres above sea level, is being moved farther inland. It is the first relocation project carried out in France in response to the effects of global warming.Canada, a new energy partner?Paris supports closer ties between Brussels and Ottawa and has reiterated its willingness to work with all countries that "share our values and want to strengthen their ability to decide, produce and act for themselves."The practical details of this new partnership, however, have yet to be worked out.Energy could become one of its main areas of focus.France is looking to Canada to help secure European supplies of hydrocarbons, at a time when fuel prices are soaring due to global conflicts and tensions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz.This situation is already putting additional pressure on France's heavily indebted public finances, forcing the government to extend some existing measures and step up talks with partners, particularly in the Middle East.Macron and Carney are due to continue their talks next week in New York, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

Headline: Who deserves a transplant? AI's answer isn't the same as a human doctor's
Body: Would you get a transplant if AI were the one deciding? New study points to differences in decision-making and prioritising between artificial intelligence language models and human doctors. AI models show overconfidence, value different factors and oversimplify complex decisions when deciding which patient should receive a transplant, according to a new study. For their study, researchers from Penn State University in the United States gave Large Language Models (LLMs) hypothetical scenarios, based on existing datasets from published human research on kidney allocation, where real participants had already made these same choices. Each scenario involved two patients, Patient A and Patient B, both eligible for a single available kidney and characterised by age, health, and drinking habits. A decision maker must then choose which of the two patients should receive it.“We ran these comparisons in a few different ways,” Hosseini said. “Sometimes we isolated just one trait at a time, sometimes we mixed several traits together to see how AI weighed competing factors, and sometimes we added a flip-a-coin option to measure indecision, a key factor present in human moral judgment.” While human respondents tended to place greater importance on age — favouring younger over older patients — many models favoured lower alcohol consumption instead. Human decisions considered multiple factors and were more context-sensitive than those of LLMs, which often focused on a single attribute.“First, AI chatbots often diverge from human values in how they weigh a patient’s traits,” said Hadi Hosseini, lead of the study at Penn State University. “They fixate on a single factor, like drinking habits, rather than balancing multiple considerations the way people do.” The researchers also saw that AI did not struggle with indecision. While humans recognised there is no single objectively correct answer and decisions can rely on nuanced human moral judgements, the systems committed to a single option with little hesitation."When we allocate something scarce, whether it’s a kidney, a job or access to some other resource, there isn’t always a single objectively correct answer,” said John Dickerson, chief executive officer at Mozilla.ai, who collaborated in the study. “Humans recognize that ambiguity and codify it via open debate into the allocative process. AI models often don’t.” AI and ethical decisions Recent interactions with AI systems increasingly require them to go beyond factual information and make value judgments, the authors noted. Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into healthcare, supporting clinical workflows, diagnosis, treatment planning and timely utilisation of scarce medical resources. One of their applications involves decisions on allocating deceased-donor or living-donor kidneys to patients, which, according to the authors, depend on complex ethical and moral considerations.In such high-stakes scenarios, the researchers pointed out that decisions demand not only accuracy but also alignment with human values and moral judgement. According to the researchers, asking if AI can make moral decisions or whether they’re aligned with human values lies at the core of today’s wider debate on artificial intelligence. “The ethical stakes are high, and AI’s role in such life-altering decisions requires deep reflection,” said Hosseini. “Moral decisions in settings like organ allocation directly determine who lives and who dies, so getting AI's role in them right isn't optional.”“While we do not intend to encourage the use of AI as a substitute for professional judgment in medical decision-making or other high-stakes contexts, it's becoming essential to understand their behavior as individuals, organizations and firms more and more rely on AI to make decisions or receive recommendations,” he added

Headline: Bolivia slashes diesel subsidies as its Congress ratifies $1.9 billion IMF deal to ease deep economic crisis
Body: Bolivian lawmakers approved a $1.9 billion (€1.65bn) loan agreement with the International Monetary Fund on Friday, delivering the conservative government a key victory in its efforts to ease the country's deep economic crisis as unions threatened to renew protests.Just hours after Congress approved the loan, President Rodrigo Paz announced an immediate end to subsidies for the diesel powering Bolivia’s trucks, buses and tractors — a step towards meeting IMF demands.Gasoline, used mainly in private cars, would remain subsidised for now, though Paz had already scaled back that support in recent months.The Bolivian Senate ratified the IMF agreement a day after the lower house approved it, clearing the final legislative hurdle for the three-year financing programme aimed at replenishing dwindling foreign reserves and stabilising an ailing economy marked by high inflation and weak growth.The IMF first announced the staff-level agreement in July after months of negotiations with Paz’s market-friendly government, which took power last year after nearly two decades of socialist rule as part of a wave of new Latin American leaders allied with the Trump administration.The programme still requires approval from the IMF’s executive board before funds can be disbursed. Economy Minister Christian Morales told senators that the deal would give other lenders, including the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, greater confidence in the government and help it secure about $5 billion in additional financing.But the assistance is conditioned on tough economic measures, including the elimination of fuel subsidies, that threaten to reignite unrest in Bolivia, where weeks of road blockades in June and July paralysed much of the South American nation as protesters demanded Paz’s resignation.Congress on Thursday extended for another 90-days a state of emergency that Paz had declared to clear roads during the protests. It allows for military intervention and the suspension of some civil liberties to quell unrest.The Bolivian Workers’ Central, the country’s main labour federation, and other unions have voiced fierce opposition to the IMF loan, warning that the government spending cuts required under the deal would drive up living costs and deepen hardship for low-income and struggling families.Although Paz’s Christian Democratic Party lacks a majority in Congress, the centrist and right-wing lawmakers that dominate both chambers rallied behind the deal.The Movement Toward Socialism, the party that dominated Bolivian politics after the former coca growers’ union leader Evo Morales won the presidency in 2005, now holds just two of the 130 seats in the lower house and none in the 36-member Senate.Declining natural gas exports have deprived Bolivia of billions of dollars it had relied on previously to import gasoline and diesel, contributing to chronic fuel shortages that began in 2023 and have persisted under Paz.The Iran war dramatically surging global oil prices have made fuel subsidies even more burdensome and dug the country into a deeper financial hole.“No one can buy something expensive and sell it cheap,” Paz said in his late-night declaration that diesel in Bolivia would now be sold at international prices.To cushion the blow, he announced about $79 million (€68.8m) in cash assistance for approximately 2.9 million Bolivians, along with loans on preferential terms for truckers, small businesses and producers facing the new higher diesel costs.He pledged to redirect subsidy spending toward schools, hospitals and roads.Paz also promised the change would end the country’s persistent diesel shortages, which have disrupted harvests and delayed deliveries of imported goods.“With this measure, we guarantee supplies 24 hours a day, seven days a week,” he said.

Headline: Operations resume at Luxembourg airport after 'unauthorised' drones halt flights
Body: Flights were temporarily suspended at Luxembourg airport overnight due to "unauthorised" drone activity."Flight operations at Luxembourg Airport (ELLX) have resumed following the temporary suspension on the evening of Friday, 18 September 2026, due to the detection of unauthorised unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) in the vicinity of and subsequently over the aerodrome," a statement on the airport's website said.The airport - the main hub for Luxembourg's national airline Luxair and cargo airline Cargolux - did not provide any details on where the drones may have come from or who was operating them, but it said it was continuing to monitor the situation alongside relevant authorities, airlines, and air traffic services.It also warned of knock-on delays and disruption as airlines work to restore regular flight schedules."The temporary suspension of flight operations was implemented as a precautionary measure to ensure the safety of passengers, airline crews, airport personnel and aircraft," the airport added in its statement.

Headline: Trump signs into law sweeping Russia sanctions package aiming to choke off revenues funding the war in Ukraine
Body: US President Donald Trump signed into law a sweeping sanctions package targeting Russian officials and key pillars of its economy on Friday, that is meant to punish and pressure Moscow for its ongoing war against Ukraine.The measure was a final legacy item for the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a close ally and friend of the president who had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly died in July.In the works for more than a year, the bill passed with large bipartisan margins; 86-11 in the Senate and 262-159 in the House.It’s meant to starve Russian President Vladimir Putin of the resources Moscow needs to continue its war in Ukraine after invading its neighbour in February 2022.The bill, co-drafted by Senator Richard Blumenthal, sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers the Kremlin uses to evade existing Western sanctions and keep Russian energy moving.“I wish Lindsey were here to celebrate this historic day. I know he would be so proud. Lindsey believed this bill, which he worked on for well over a year, would help end the war through squeezing Putin economically and forcing his customers to re-evaluate their relationship with Russia,” said Senator Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham's sister, in a statement Friday.Darline Graham was appointed to complete her late brother's Senate term, set to end on the 3rd of January 2027.“If he were here today, he would be jubilant about our bill’s passage — and already thinking about the next one,” Blumenthal said of Graham after the House passed the legislation on Wednesday evening.“Putin is a thug who understands only force and strength, which is what we must show clearly and unequivocally,” Blumenthal added.The bill also enables Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.Despite overwhelming support on Capitol Hill, the legislation faced criticism from a vocal set of Democratic lawmakers, who favoured a tougher stance on Russia, but warned that Trump could use his new expanded tariff powers to impose fresh levies in the European Union and elsewhere.“Why in the world would this Congress or the People’s House give this president unfettered authority to visit more tariffs on the world that will have an adverse economic impact on the American people?” said Democrat lawmaker and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.Graham’s journey to getting Trump’s sign-off on the bill had been full of turbulence, as the White House had to be convinced that the president would be able to retain sufficient flexibility on sanctions.Eventually, Trump gave a final nod of approval to the bill after it included his push for a provision which would enable his administration to extend sanctions on Iran for another five-year period.

Headline: US and Denmark reach deal over Greenland's security
Body: The United States and Denmark have announced that they have come to an agreement over Greenland, with US President Donald Trump saying the deal would give Washington "permanent control" of the island's security."I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social account on Friday."From now on, no U.S. adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval," he added.Trump has repeatedly threatened to seize the Danish autonomous territory since his return to the White House in January 2025, arguing that it was an essential "national security" concern and that if Washington did not act, then China or Russia would do so.His rhetoric has sparked pushback from across Europe and prompted fresh funding pledges from Brussels and a renewed focus on Arctic security.In a statement on Friday, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen touted a "great agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, and the United States," while promising that it would recognise "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination.” "An agreement which strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic Area and therefore is great for NATO and Europe as well," she added.Greenland's prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, also welcomed the agreement with the US, saying it was "to the benefit of us all" and that it would "ensure and strengthen the security of the island.The deal is expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly in New York next week.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had visited Greenland earlier this month as part of EU efforts to counter Trump's Arctic ambitions, announcing a €200 million partnership with the territory during her visit - which is set to be invested this year and the next.Speaking at the World Economic Forum's annual meeting in Davos this year, von der Leyen had said the EU was working on a "massive European investment surge" in Greenland in a bid to ramp up Arctic security.The Commission has proposed allocating €530 million to Greenland under its budget for the 2028–2034 period, which it said reflected its "growing geostrategic importance in the Arctic."The US is reported to have had 17 military facilities and over 10,000 troops on Greenland at the height of the Cold War. It now operates just one base on the island, the Pituffik Space Base - the US Department of Defense's northernmost installation.Pituffik is used for missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance missions, per the US Space Force.

Headline: What happens if a solar farm catches fire? Europe’s biggest battery test centre is finding out
Body: Eastern Germany is home to some of the world’s most advanced ‘torture chambers’. Here, water, fire, high-voltage current and even dust are used to press and squeeze, twist and strike, shake and hammer the beating hearts of the technology we use every day, like electric vehicles. At Europe’s largest battery testing centre, they put batteries into every imaginable situation to see what happens. Whether they explode, survive or thrive, it’s better to find out here than in a consumer’s garage.Batteries are subjected to extreme temperatures and full-blown sandstormsI am standing beside a long row of garage-sized boxes inside the DEKRA facility in the small town of Klettwitz in Lusatia. Each box has its own unique purpose. Head of DEKRA, Thomas Hucke, is showing me around. Thermometers and warning lights surround me – what do they mean? “We’re testing how battery prototypes behave at very low temperatures, or at very high temperatures. From Siberia to the Sahara,” Hucke explains. “In other words, the classic environmental conditions that a battery like this experiences over its lifetime.” He then walks over to a control panel and, with grim determination, turns it all the way to the minus max level: “Right, minus 40 degrees Celsius – let’s take it right down to the limit…”Full-blown sandstorm? No problem for Hucke and his team. If a specialised battery is to survive use in the desert, its suitability must be certified before it can be marketed and sold. For that, the DEKRA team naturally have some particularly gruelling dust chambers.We cross an industrial road and enter a hall on the opposite side. A few staff members hurriedly push plastic crates in front of a prototype that has just been delivered to block the view. “Camera off!” they say. This is top secret.“We also test very large batteries,” says Hucke, explaining the enormous size of the test hall, “such as stationary energy storage systems, for example. “Over there,” Hucke points to another test chamber, “we carry out vibration tests. In vehicles, batteries are usually subjected to vibrations. What happens when a vehicle drives over a curb, or when it receives a mechanical impact?” All of this is tested, documented and reported to the manufacturer. Certification is only granted once the new battery model has met all stress parameters to Hucke’s complete satisfaction.Consumer safety is a top priority in the European Union. “The EU has drawn up a Battery Regulation which sets out the tests that must be carried out on batteries. It’s about sustainability, the value chain, and ultimately, always about safety.”Hucke elaborates: “The energy transition isn’t just about electric mobility. At the test centre, we naturally also test vehicle batteries. But beyond that, we are increasingly testing energy storage solutions for stationary applications. These are mostly intermediate storage systems for renewable energies, namely solar and wind. That is the future.”Batteries are crushed and burnt – to find out what happensHucke smiles as he leads us into the next fiery circle of battery hell.“What happens in the event of a fire? In an accident? Or if batteries are overcharged or discharged improperly? Batteries must remain safe even in these situations,” he says. “The energy transition [and the associated electrification] must function safely and sustainably. This requires testing service providers who ensure that certain rules and standards are adhered to.” Hucke nods towards the ‘fire hall’. There, they recently tried to set an entire battery container alight. This is not an unrealistic scenario: planet-heating fossil fuel emissions are leading to increasingly extreme temperatures. Europe experienced this first-hand in a scorching summer filled with devastating wildfires and drought.It cannot be ruled out that one day a major fire might also reach the buffer electricity storage facility at a solar or wind farm. Up to certain temperature levels, a large-scale battery storage facility must be able to withstand this.Opening a high-security airlock, Hucke leads me into a room with a cathedral-high ceiling. Massive metal blocks are firmly bolted to the floor. This is the bunker hall of the ‘crush bed’. “We’ve got an oversized vice here,” says Hucke, where batteries are clamped to be stress tested. “The battery is squeezed – and the regulations stipulate that absolutely nothing must happen.”But what if it does? What if the new prototype can’t take any more, after the water, dust, heat and cold tests? What if it really does crash and explode in the crushing bed between the jaws of the steel clamps?Hucke points to the special fixtures on the thick walls. “We have pressure relief flaps here – and outside the building, a complete flue gas scrubbing system that extracts the gases in an emergency.”Batteries are key to a safe and sustainable energy transitionWind and solar power are a rapidly growing source of energy in Europe. Grid constraints and the intermittent nature of these renewables means the need for flexible storage is rapidly increasing.Battery test centres are “a key component” of the energy transition, says Hucke, ensuring that this renewable power can be stored safely.“Standards and regulations have been in place in the automotive sector for some time now. And the same is now happening in the field of stationary battery storage solutions for renewable energies,” he tells me. “This requires state-of-the-art testing laboratories. We ensure that batteries entering service meet all safety requirements.”What about the test centre’s own sustainability? A huge, ultra-modern battery test centre like this requires a lot of energy. “We’re expanding our solar PV systems,” emphasises Hucke, “and using stationary battery storage to ensure we can recover energy”.The DEKRA Group also took a stand at the World Economic Forum (WEF) in Davos, joining the Alliance of CEO Climate Leaders. “In an increasingly disruptive global environment, in which the urgency and even the existence of the climate crisis is, in some quarters, being called into question once again, we emphasise the strategic importance of jointly combating climate change,” states the Group headquarters.The DEKRA Climate Impact Programme includes internal decarbonisation and support for external climate projects that make a measurable contribution to the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
