Headline: Drums, dancing and definitely no tears: Here’s why you need to experience Nepal’s Sa: Paru festival
Body: The sound I most associate with death is silence. Not just the obvious one, in that the dearly departed will never speak, never yell, never cry, never laugh again.Smaller silences, like post-funeral, when the last guest is gone and all you’re left with are your thoughts and an inordinate amount of food shared by well-wishers. Or when weeks have passed and you go to call or text them about your day before you stop yourself because you can’t do that any more.Even years later, it lingers in that awkward pause when you reveal someone close to you has passed away and the other person doesn’t quite know what to say in response.Drums and bells, it is not. Music, beyond the songs chosen for the service, feels incongruous. The loud, chaotic energy of a festival? Never.Yet that’s exactly what Sa: Paru, an annual festival honouring those that have died in the past year, is all about, as I discovered on my recent trip to Nepal’s Bhaktapur. Celebrated across the Kathmandu Valley by the Newar people, the festival turns the western idea of grieving on its head, giving the dead a joyous farewell as they head towards salvation.“When people pass away in western societies, people wear black. They grieve in silence – it's a very somber moment,” says Ajay Bahadur Pradhanang. “But in Nepal, everybody comes together and it's turned into this carnival, a real joyous moment of farewell.”A community coming togetherWhile the festival also takes place in other cities like Lalitpur as well as the capital Kathmandu, which is around 13 kilometres away, the celebration in Bhaktapur takes its own unique form.Prior to the festival’s main day, which takes place after the full moon during the 10th month of the country’s lunisolar calendar in August or September, neighbours – whether they’ve lost someone or not – gather to create taha: sa.The bamboo structures, which replaced the cows that would traditionally have been used as part of the procession, are wrapped before a painting of the sacred animal is placed at the top.It takes skill, and manpower, to complete the whole affair. After the cloth (generally red for women, and white for men) and cow portrait are added, various decorations follow, like a photograph of the deceased, depictions of Shiva, and, finally, an umbrella to shield them from sun and rain – a sign of respect.“For Sa: Paru, we have to have certain rituals, and these would be impossible if it was just me, or just my family, without the wider community to help us,” Ajay notes.It might take a village to raise a child, but the celebration in Bhaktapur goes to show that it takes a community to mark the other end of somebody’s life, too.I’m here at the invitation of The Nanee, a boutique hotel near the city’s centre. Ajay, the hotel’s chairman, lost his mother this year, which means I can see the work underway in the neighbouring courtyard, but any visitor to the city will easily be able to find taha: sa being constructed throughout the day.The festival starts early the following morning, with a steady stream of taha: sa passing through the streets accompanied by music, drums, bells and the sound of sticks clashing together as pairs take part in the Ghintang Ghisi dance.The procession follows a set route, and at the beginning, it seems each troupe is moving to its own beat – some rush, causing the structures to sway, giving the effect of a drunken cow passing by; others march slowly, pausing to dance together. It’s only as the streets begin to clog up and movement reaches a snail’s pace that they move as one.While some attendees don traditional wear, or modern interpretations of it, you’re just as likely to see people wearing football kits and Hawaiian shirts. Come as you are – you’re welcome to get involved in the festivities, provided you don’t mind crowds.After taking a pause to catch my breath, I get chatting to Mano Dhaubhadel, a Nepali living in the US who recently lost his younger brother and has returned for the festival.“This is something you don’t see anywhere else in the world,” he told me. “The culture here is just magnificent, and it’s there for everyone to enjoy, not just Newars. The best way to learn is to get involved.”Of course, you can also attend the festival with a guide. I’m joined by The Nanee’s curator, Peepul Subedi, a priest and PhD student who is more than happy to explain the meaning behind the festival’s various elements, and its importance."The whole city comes together for this festival, and every household who has a family member who has passed away in the past year will take out this sort of structure,” he tells me.“It represents the message that everyone has to die, and all of us are going through the same sort of sorrow – that's life. We're not celebrating death by dancing and singing, we are celebrating the fact that the departed soul is moving towards salvation.”Celebrations in most of the valley last just a single day – here in Bhaktapur, the festival continues on for eight, with different dance performances throughout the city.The exact origins of Sa: Paru, which is also known as Gai Jatra, aren’t precisely known, but historians believe that the tradition may have started in the 14th century.The name most commonly associated with the festival is King Pratap Malla, who is said to have expanded the festival to cheer up his wife following the death of their son Chakravartendra Malla with the inclusion of satirical elements, which today sees people don satirical masks of political figures like US president Donald Trump and Russian president Vladimir Putin.A reason to linger in BhaktapurTravel itineraries for tourists visiting Kathmandu often include a detour to Bhaktapur – but they typically only mention a visit to the Durbar Square, with its various temples and the 55 Window Palace.Similar to the cruise ship tourists who swarm cities in Europe for a few hours in the summer months, climbing back on board having contributed nothing to the local economy beyond the cost of an ice cream and a fridge magnet, these visitors will spend an hour or two in town before heading back to the capital.It’s a real shame – not just for the locals, who fail to see the financial benefit, but for the tourists themselves, who miss out on the best Bhaktapur has to offer.Life is slower here, and the city is best experienced in the early mornings, when you’ll see folks milling about, praying at the Hindu and Buddhist temples, or buying produce at the market.Aside from the Durbar Square, you can see ceramics drying under the sun at Pottery Square, give pottery a go yourself at one of the workshops, or pick out some pieces to add to your homeware collection.The Peacock Shop is another must visit, where the chatty owner is more than happy to talk, and walk you through the traditional Lokta paper making process.The Nanee was founded by Ajay and Shailaja Pradhanang with a view to encourage people to linger longer while enjoying the comforts of a luxury boutique hotel.“Bhaktapur is a living heritage site, and we wanted that to continue,” Ajay tells me.“With The Nanee, we offer guests a small oasis in the beautiful city of Bhaktapur while ensuring that the community, which has done so much to preserve and conserve its heritage, benefits from their stay.”Experiences offered by the hotel are in partnership with locals, like the morning walk with a housewife, or the evening dinner with an artisan.Aside from Sa: Paru, there are numerous festivals throughout the year, including the famed Bisket Jatra, celebrated for eight nights each April.A note on the recent floodsJust hours before landing in Kathmandu for the festival, a series of flash floods near the border with Tibet saw the loss of at least 1,369 lives, with some 5,000 people missing.Naturally, many people have cancelled or are thinking about cancelling their trips to Nepal as a result, which will have a serious impact on a tourism industry that is already dealing with the impact of the Iran war on flight routes to the country.Popular tourist spots like the Kathmandu Valley, as well as Mount Everest and other trekking trails, were unaffected by the tragedy, and your tourism dollars are more needed than ever. Dianne Apen-Sadler was hosted by The Nanee during the Sa: Paru festival. You can reach out to the hotel directly to enquire about your potential stay in order to align your trip with one of Bhaktapur’s many festivals. For more information about Bhaktapur, visit the official tourism board website.

Headline: Fear of AI job losses now outweighs hope of new jobs, study finds
Body: People’s view of a country and trust for its artificial intelligence (AI) regulation tend to be closely linked, Moira Fagan, senior researcher at the Pew Research Center and one of the authors of a new study on AI, told Euronews Next. According to the report, in Bangladesh, Malaysia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the West Bank and East Jerusalem, people trust China more than the United States (US) or the European Union (EU) with AI governance. And, taking into consideration the other seven middle-income countries where this question was asked, a median of 43% trust China to regulate AI, 35% trust the US and 34% trust the EU. “Favourable views of China tend to be quite high in middle-income countries – and opinion has risen in many places since last year, likely contributing to some of the high marks we see for trust in China on this particular dimension,” Fagan said. The report, which was built on a survey conducted between February and June 2026, polling over 50,000 people from 37 countries, also examines people’s opinions on AI’s impact on the job market. Specifically, more people expect AI to lead to fewer jobs than to job creation, according to the study. A good share of respondents, though, also report uncertainty about the impact AI will have on the number of job opportunities. The survey also shows that worries about job losses due to AI are particularly high in wealthier countries. For instance, in Australia, South Korea and the US, around seven-in-ten adults or more believe AI will result in job loss over the next 20 years. Similarly, richer countries are more concerned about AI increasing economic inequalities than middle-income ones, the report highlights.According to Fagan, these tendencies appear to be linked to other data, including people’s familiarity with the technological tool.“People in wealthier countries are more likely to say they have heard or read a lot about AI. And we also found that people with higher AI awareness are more likely to believe it will lead to job loss,” she told Euronews Next. However, some high-income and middle-income nations are brought together by a shared thread: young adults aged 18 to 34 are more concerned about AI-related job loss than older generations. And this is the case for countries like Canada, France, Singapore, Sweden, Indonesia, India and Malaysia, according to the survey. Opinion divides are less pronounced when it comes to the rise of AI in daily life. Across the 37 countries, a median of 37% are more concerned than excited, while 41% median are equally concerned and excited, the survey found. Although the survey was conducted in the first half of 2026, its publication arrives at a very crucial moment for AI. Leaders of major AI companies, including Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Dario Amodei, are increasingly concerned about the risks their AI creations pose to humanity and are calling for a slowdown in the pace of AI development. President of the European Commission, Ursula Von der Leyen, also backed the deceleration effort in her landmark State of the Union address to the European Parliament earlier this week. On this occasion, she also pledged closer safety cooperation with Canada, the UK, and other like-minded partners.

Headline: Russians leave before election ends, fearing mobilisation to follow
Body: Russians fearing a new military mobilisation are leaving the country in advance of possible restrictions on departure, according to the anti-war project Ark, after requests for emergency assistance and emigration advice from Russia have nearly octupled since the start of the summer.The surge coincides with Russia's State Duma elections, which began on Friday and run through Sunday.Kremlin critics and several Western governments have accused Moscow of planning to announce a new call-up to beef up its troops in its ongoing all-out war in Ukraine after the vote concludes, allowing an unpopular measure to avoid affecting the election.Russia's Vladimir Putin has dismissed mobilisation rumours as "utter nonsense," but independent Russian media have counted 17 official denials of an imminent draft since the summer.Jan Slovitsky, a human rights activist and coordinator of the Ark project, said the current wave was driven by lessons learned from 2022."Since mid-July a wave of panic has been rising in Russia, linked to the risk of mobilisation, fuel shortages and lack of internet access," he told Ark's network from Yerevan, where he is assisting new arrivals."People are leaving in advance because they have seen what happened during previous waves. And Armenia is facing a migration crisis, if we are not already in the thick of it."'How to leave' online search spikesThe number of daily requests for relocation assistance has risen from around 70 to 120 since July, according to organisations helping Russians move abroad.Yandex and Google searches for "how to leave" and "mobilisation" reached their highest level since early 2023 during the summer and the first ten days of September, according to independent Russian media analysis.Preparations for a possible call-up are already visible. Tens of thousands of people have received mobilisation notices setting out the steps required if called up, and an electronic register of summonses has been introduced under which an exit ban takes effect automatically when a notice is issued.In early September, passport control officers in Krasnodar detained a 24-year-old resident of Rostov region who had completed his military service in 2024 and served him with a notice banning him from leaving the country, the first such case reported at that crossing.Daniil Neonov, a former candidate for municipal deputy in the Moscow City Duma, described leaving at the last moment."If I had waited another day or two, they would most likely not have let me leave, because they would have blocked my exit," he said. "I received an electronic summons. But I still managed to get out."Fear of mobilisation has also spread to members of the elite and draft office staff, according to international media reports claiming officials have begun opening foreign bank accounts and moving assets abroad.In August, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned of the risk of mobilisation in Russia, citing intelligence data.Kyiv described a Kremlin plan to rapidly call up several hundred thousand Russians by the end of the year, with at least as many again the following year. Moscow has not commented on those claims.Neighbouring countries firstArrivals are heading primarily to visa-free destinations: Armenia, Georgia and Kazakhstan. Yerevan said in recent days it was ready to assist Russians arriving in the country.The exact scale of the current wave is unknown, but it is likely less intense than the exodus of 2022, when between 600,000 and 700,000 people left Russia within weeks of the partial mobilisation announcement, according to independent estimates.That mobilisation has never been formally cancelled, and those called up then have not been demobilised."It is very sad to leave Russia," said a 28-year-old marketing specialist, whose name was withheld for security reasons."My family lives here, my elderly grandparents live here. My girlfriend is here too, she is still in her medical residency, and it is very hard for me to leave her behind."Russia's Duma elections, running from 18 to 20 September, include only parties that back Moscow's war in Ukraine. Yabloko, whose platform called for an immediate ceasefire and peace talks, was barred from standing by the Supreme Court in August.

Headline: European leaders rush to counter looming diesel price surge as Saudi pipeline attacked
Body: European leaders are once again rushing to mitigate rising oil prices as Saudi cargoes are delayed or cancelled amid another conflict escalation in the Middle East, raising fears of soaring prices at the pump across many capitals.The latest shock is coming from Saudi Arabia, where Houthi and Iran-backed Iraqi militias' attacks have forced the temporary closure of the 1,200-kilometer East-West oil pipeline – a crucial route designed to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.The disruption threatens as much as 4% of global oil supply if it persists, this after Saudi crude output fell sharply in August to its lowest level in more than three decades. Meanwhile, Brent crude oil recently traded above $113 a barrel due to mounting supply risks.For France and Italy, both of which will hold crucial elections in 2027, high energy prices are a major domestic political issue, as voters are preparing to judge governments on purchasing power.Rising energy and fuel costs in France are already feeding into consumer anxiety, with inflation reaching 2.7% in August and energy among the main drivers. Italy faces a similar problem, with August inflation accelerating to 3.3%, driven heavily by energy, while petrol and diesel prices have climbed sharply. French diplomacyOn Wednesday evening, French President Emmanuel Macron ordered a "mobilisation" to tackle fuel prices, while saying France is working to secure oil supplies and reduce pressure on motorists.Macron has also linked energy security directly to diplomacy in the Middle East, arguing after talks with Iraq's prime minister this week that alternative routes around Hormuz and regional de-escalation are necessary to protect French consumers."The priority: restoring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital artery for oil transit, protecting the energy infrastructure of our partners, and securing production. It's essential to guarantee our supplies. We're working with our coalition partners to ensure freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz," Macron wrote on X.The French President added that ongoing work alongside "our coalition partners for freedom of navigation" through Hormuz aims to open alternative routes to reduce dependence on the vital waterway and secure supplies.Italy scraps car taxesMeanwhile, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced overnight the abolition of the stamp duty imposed on small and medium-powered cars, which she described as one of the taxes most hated by Italians."We have chosen to redirect a portion of the resources used so far to address rising fuel prices into a simple, structural measure designed especially for those who use cars and motorcycles every day to work, take their children, or get around," Meloni wrote on X.The Italian leader stressed that the car tax will remain beyond 2027, noting the measure is designed to be "structural and permanent". Meloni has also asked the European Commission to treat the energy crisis like a defence emergency and relax fiscal rules that member states must comply with.At the same time, Rome has already adopted measures to accelerate domestic oil and gas projects, explicitly presenting increased production as part of a broader energy-security response.Spain doubled its diesel tax cut to 20 cents a litre from September 1 after diesel prices jumped 15.7% in July, activating an automatic mechanism in the government's anti-crisis package. Spanish Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo is meeting with social partners in Madrid on Thursday to assess the war's impact on Spain.Germany coming soonChancellor Friedrich Merz said recently that Berlin will "soon" present measures to ease the impact of record fuel prices. Petrol and diesel prices stood at €2.45 per litre on Thursday, according to the General German Automobile Club.However, just like any other nation, Germany's exposure to imported energy means the government has little ability to control the underlying international price. After losing a tremendous number of seats in the latest regional election to the far-right Alternative for Germany, Merz’s Christian Democrats must strike a delicate balance to avoid alienating its electorate further.Merz also framed the problem as one requiring international coordination, warning that the expansion of Houthi control around the Bab el-Mandeb threatens Saudi and other regional oil exports and further tightens global energy markets.“The Houthis now control strategic positions around the Bab el-Mandab Strait and are attacking energy facilities in Saudi Arabia; this further exacerbates the situation in international energy markets,” Merz told a press conference on 14 September.Pricing issueAsked whether Europe is approaching a potential supply shock, a Commission spokesperson said pricing is the major crisis rather than diesel shortages, noting that no member state has so far raised any security of supply concerns."There is no supply problem in the EU at the present time," Commission Spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen told Euronews. "Demand for jet fuel and diesel in Europe continues to be met through higher EU refinery production, as well as alternative supplies from global markets."However, Itkonen acknowledged that the evolution of the conflict in the Middle East, as well as usual autumn and winter demand trends, could impact the coming weeks and months and further tighten markets."We're not yet in a situation where we'll be tapping strategic resources, and we keep monitoring the situation alongside member states and the industry," she added.Nonetheless, the Commission said that it has been encouraging EU countries to cushion prices through taxation, which plays a big role in determining energy prices, noting that it is beyond its power to influence global oil prices.Homayoun Falakshashi, head of crude oil analysis at the market intelligence firm Kpler, said the Saudi disruption – which runs as high as 5.5 million barrels per day – could be less bad than expected, as the Saudis have said work on the damaged pipeline has started."Up to 3.5-4 million barrels per day of exports are at risk, but also some 1.5 million barrels per day that feed western Saudi refineries, so it's also bullish for diesel," Falakshashi told Euronews, referring to a likely price increase regardless of supply.Nonetheless, Falakshashi said throughput should come back to 3-4 million barrels per day instead of 5.5."On the other hand, we are hearing that Yanbu loadings are continuing, but we cannot yet confirm if this is true. So the key question is how much can get loaded from the east coast (Ras Tanura) and if these volumes can escape the Persian Gulf."Momentum for windfall profit taxWith soaring prices and rising inflation, the call for a windfall profit tax is gaining traction, with several EU lawmakers and EU leaders mentioning it on the sidelines of Ursula von der Leyen's speech at the State of the Union on 16 September.During her address to the plenary in Strasbourg, the leader of the centre-left Socialists and Democrats group, Iratxe García Pérez, proposed introducing a windfall tax on energy companies to finance a social support scheme.“Trump and Netanyahu's war against Iran has strengthened the ayatollahs and sent the cost of living soaring,” she said. "Let's accelerate renewables. And let's get those who benefit from this crisis to contribute."García said the contribution would be used to help fragile households pay their electricity bills, fill their shopping carts, put petrol in their cars and heat their homes.Her remarks were echoed by those of her Green counterpart, Terry Reintke, who argued energy companies continue to profit from Europe’s extraordinary energy crisis, leaving the big bill for consumers to foot.In August, Germany, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Poland and Austria asked Ireland's EU Presidency to put an EU-wide windfall-profit mechanism on the agenda of the September finance ministers' meeting, which will be held during an informal gathering of finance ministers on the 18 and 19 of September.Esther Lynch, General Secretary at the European Trade Union Confederation representing millions of workers in the EU, said the introduction of windfall taxes is a "matter of justice" needed to stop price gouging and relieve the cost pressure on working people."It has been clear for some time now that energy companies are exploiting the geopolitical crisis to cash in at the expense of working people suffering a prolonged cost-of-living crisis," Lynch told Euronews.

Headline: Trump threatens to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House
Body: President Donald Trump has said he is banning three major news organisations, CNN, MS NOW and Politico, from the White House with immediate effect, accusing them of publishing “fake news”, “fiction” and “lies”.It is not yet clear what the ban will entail. Trump also warned that restrictions could be extended to other media outlets.In a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday, the president said the three outlets “constantly write or report fiction and lies” about his administration, although he provided no specific examples.The move is the latest test of First Amendment protections guaranteeing freedom of the press in the United States.It is also the latest move by Trump’s second administration to restrict press access. He has already tightened controls over which journalists can join the White House press pool, the small group of reporters who accompany the president into restricted spaces such as the Oval Office and aboard Air Force One.CNN is part of the traditional five-network television pool that travels with and covers the president. It is not yet clear whether the new ban will affect that arrangement.In 2025, Trump restricted Associated Press access to some presidential events after the news agency continued to use the name “Gulf of Mexico” rather than Trump’s preferred “Gulf of America”. AP subsequently launched legal action over the restrictions. The case remains ongoing.During Trump’s first term, CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins was barred from a White House Rose Garden event after officials said questions she asked the president earlier that day were "inappropriate" for the venue.While it is extremely rare for a US president to bar an entire news organisation from the White House, previous administrations have also imposed restrictions on individual outlets. President Richard Nixon restricted access for The Washington Post during the Watergate scandal in the 1970s.

Headline: Sweden's Social Democrat leader Andersson formally asked to assemble new government
Body: Sweden’s parliamentary speaker has formally asked Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson to try to form a government after her centre-left alliance won a narrow majority in Sunday’s election.In a post on Instagram, Andersson said she had accepted the task and that she wanted to "lead a government that realises the new direction that the Swedish people have voted for -- a direction that moves Sweden forward and keeps our country united,"Andersson has 28 days to assemble her cabinet and report back to the parliamentary speaker, Andreas Norlen. Earlier, Norlen held consultations with party leaders over coffee and a pound cake he baked himself, before announcing his decision to give the Social Democrats leader the go-ahead.She faces an uphill battle, with many tricky negotiations in the days ahead, with key differences between the four parties in the bloc - the Social Democrats, the Left Party, the Green Party and the Centre Party. In particular, the Left Party has said it would only give its support if it had ministers in the government, an idea the Centre Party has been staunchly opposed to.If they can find an agreement, it would see Andersson take over as prime minister in the coming weeks, after PM Ulf Kristersson resigned in the wake of the election. Andersson previously served as Sweden’s first female prime minister from 2021 to 2022.Her centre-left alliance holds a three seat majority in Sweden's 349-seat parliament.Resigning on Thursday, outgoing prime minister Kristersson called for "constructive openness" across parties to move forward."Discussions will need to be held with all parties to find ways around these deadlocks and create the conditions for a stable and effective government," he wrote.

Headline: As Russia strikes Kyiv and Kharkiv, Russian cooling tower hit by drone
Body: Russia has launched attacks on several areas of Ukraine, with two killed in Balakliia in Kharkiv and missiles launched at the capita, Kyiv.In a post on Telegram, the head of Balakliia's military administration Vitalii Karabanov gave an update on the damage and loss of life: "Sadly, the consequences of this attack are terrible. Early reports indicate that two people have been killed in the strike. I extend my deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed."There have been further attacks on the Kyiv on Friday evening. Ukrainian media reports the city has been hit by ballistic missiles.The Mayor of Kyiv, Vitali Klitschko, posted on Telegram at 19:32 local time (18:32 CEST) warning of the strikes, which read: "Air defense forces are working in the capital. Kyiv is under ballistic fire. Stay in shelters!"Meanwhile, there have been repeated attacks on central Odesa, with strikes twice in quick succession. The second hit during the rescue operation. Local media reports 10 people have been injured in the attacks.In Russia, a drone hit a cooling tower of the Kursk Nuclear Power Plant early on Thursday. The International Atomic Energy Agency reported Friday that it was aware of the strike on the Kursk plant, adding that the power station remained operational at the time, but that there was no fire and operations had continued.In the post, the Director General of the IAEA, Rafael Grossis warned against further attacks near nuclear infrastructure, and reiterated the need for "maximum military restraint to prevent the risk of a nuclear accident".

Headline: Irish Finance Minister says Hormuz closure, not Ukraine, causing energy crisis
Body: The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Trump's war with Iran are causes behind the turmoil in the energy markets, not Ukraine's attacks on Russian diesel refineries. That is the message Irish Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister (Tánaiste), Simon Harris, shared with Euronews in an exclusive interviewHarris pushed back against recent remarks made by US President Donald Trump, who blamed Ukraine's strikes on Russian diesel refineries for creating a shortage. Oil prices are hovering around $108 per barrel."The reason there's a major energy crisis in the world right now is because the Strait of Hormuz is closed," Harris said on Euronews' interview programme 12 Minutes With. "I always make the point, and I would make it again today, that the greatest economic intervention we could see is de-escalation in the Middle East," he added.He noted that this became evident during the summer, when there was a brief moment of respite in the conflict. "We saw a very rapid fall in the commodity markets and therefore a benefit at the pump."Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil and gas facilities are squeezing Moscow’s oil output and having an impact globally, as Russia is one of the world’s largest oil producers, but experts agree the current energy crisis is primarily caused by the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz – the transit route for 20% of the world's oil and gas supplies.The situation has escalated after Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline, also known as Petroline, following drone attacks earlier this month from Iran-backed allied Houthis and Iraq."From an economic perspective, I'm very concerned [after] what we've seen on oil markets in recent days," Harris said. "I'm also very concerned about the fact that we aren't seeing de-escalation; we're actually seeing an escalation and indeed more fronts in terms of complications opening up regarding energy."Windfall tax on the tableIt is against the backdrop of mounting energy costs that finance ministers from eurozone countries gathered in Dublin on Friday, rushing to mitigate the rising prices and discussing measures to mitigate the impact on citizens.One of the ideas circulating among EU ministers at the meeting is a windfall tax for firms profiting from energy price volatility, following calls from several member states to consider this measure."Some energy companies are making extraordinarily large profits on the back of this energy crisis," Harris said, noting that they are not doing so by "being innovative," but "because of the chaos that we're seeing in the energy markets as a result of the Strait of Hormuz being closed."Without pre-empting possible outcomes of the talks, Harris said he would be having an initial conversation on such a tax with ministers in Dublin. Ireland currently holds the rotating EU Council presidency, allowing it to set the work programme and Council meeting agenda."It's likely that we will ask the European Commission to further examine this and that we would formally discuss it in Brussels at the next formal [Economic and Finance Council] meeting in October."World 'cannot become numb to loss of life'Harris stressed that, aside from the economic importance of ending the Middle East conflict, the world can not turn a blind eye to the human toll either."I think while I'm obviously speaking in the capacity of a finance minister, we should never become numb to the loss of life in war, whether that's the loss of life in Ukraine, whether it's the horrific genocide we've seen in Gaza, whether it's a situation in the Middle East more broadly," he said. "We need to see a de-escalation of conflict more broadly in the world."On settler violence seen in the West Bank against Palestinians, the Tánaiste argued in favour of a tougher stance on Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law."I'm massively pro-European, but I think when it comes to Gaza, it's been disappointing, to put it mildly, that more hasn't been done at that coordinated level," Harris said.Several European countries, including Ireland and more recently the United Kingdom, have announced national bans on the import of all goods produced in illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank."Member states are listening to their public and are moving ahead, but we would always rather see action at an EU level because we think it's more impactful."The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, recently put forward an EU-wide ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements as a "principled stance" for the bloc, comparing illegal settlements in the West Bank to Russia’s occupation of Crimea.

Headline: Shakira opens her Madrid stadium with the first of 12 concerts
Body: Shakira kicks off in Madrid this Friday night a marathon of 12 concerts that will bring her world tour to a close and end an eight-year absence from Spanish stages.The Colombian singer, 49, will perform until 11 October in a temporary venue with capacity for 50,000 spectators, erected in the south of the capital and dubbed "Shakira stadium", according to Live Nation, the promoter of the shows.With no new European dates announced, Madrid’s authorities are expecting a major economic impact from her return to Spain. In May and June the city already hosted ten concerts by Bad Bunny, another of Latin music’s biggest stars.Shakira had not performed in Spain since 2018, several years before her separation from former Spanish footballer Gerard Piqué, a legendary Barcelona defender, became public in 2022.The artist embarked in February 2025 on a world tour to present "Las mujeres ya no lloran", an album inspired by her break-up with the former Barcelona player and which earned her a fourth Grammy Award.Over a career spanning several decades, Shakira has sold more than 95 million records worldwide and has performed at both the opening ceremony and the final of the 2026 football World Cup. "Waka Waka (This Time for Africa)" was also the official song of the 2010 World Cup, held in South Africa, the first ever staged on the African continent.Shakira’s return to Madrid also comes after, in November 2023, she paid a fine of 7.3 million euros as part of a settlement with the Spanish justice system. The singer pleaded guilty to avoid having to stand trial for tax fraud.In that high-profile case, Shakira also paid 17.45 million euros to the Spanish tax authorities to regularise her tax affairs in the country.

Headline: Three dead and eight injured in Philippines school shooting
Body: Three people are dead after a school shooting in the southern Philippines, including two 14-year-old students and the 16-year-old gunman. At least eight others are reported to be injured.Authorities say the gunman, a student at Banga National High School in South Cotabato, opened fire on students in a neighbouring classroom.The school is located in the town of Banga, which is on the island of Mindanao.This is the third school shooting incident in the Philippines since June.The Governor of South Cotabato, Reynaldo Tamayo, said the two students killed were a boy and a girl. He added the gunman, also shot himself and died.Officials say the teenager had warned friends after lunch that he was “going to do something” and told them to go home, but they thought he was joking.The weapon used in the attack, believed to be a 9mm gun, reportedly belonged to the shooter’s father, a Department of Education employee, and had been stored in a locked vault.The Mayor of Banga, Albert Palencia, told local media that police found posts made by the shooter in an online community, where young people involved in school shootings are "idolized". Quoting the boy's school adviser, Palencia said the mother of the boy wanted to bring him to a psychiatrist.

Headline: Three parties to attempt to form new cabinet following Romanian election
Body: Romania’s nominee for prime minister, Siegfried Muresan, has said he will attempt to form a government with a coalition involving three parties.The country's president Nicusor Dan nominated Muresan after consultations with political parties. Muresan now has 10 days to present a cabinet to parliament and seek a vote of confidence.Muresan, who is a member of the centre-right National Liberal Party (PNL) and the European Parliament, says he will try to form a government with the PNL, the Save Romania Union (USR) and the ethnic Hungarian UDMR party.These three parties do not currently have a parliamentary majority, meaning Muresan will need support from other politicians for his proposed government to pass.He told reporters at a news conference that his coalition would pursue a “pro-European and forward-looking” programme.Under Romania’s constitution, the president can dissolve parliament if it rejects two proposed governments within 60 days of the first rejection, which could trigger fresh elections.The previous government, led by Ilie Bolojan, collapsed after a no-confidence vote following tensions over austerity measures and efforts to reduce Romania’s large budget deficit.

Headline: easyJet cabin crew in Portugal plan October and December strikes
Body: easyJet cabin crew in Portugal are set to stage two strikes, the first from 2 to 6 October and the second from 19 to 23 December, with the action expected to affect the airline's operations at Lisbon, Porto and Faro airports.According to the National Union of Civil Aviation Flight Personnel (SNPVAC), around 500 scheduled flights could be grounded during the October strike, excluding any minimum services imposed by the authorities.The walkout in December could have an even greater impact on the low-cost carrier's operations, as it coincides with the busy Christmas travel period.easyJet cabin crew held an emergency general meeting this week to discuss working conditions at the airline and decide on further action.In a statement, SNPVAC said the decision to call the strikes was approved unanimously by the 188 easyJet employees who took part in the meeting. It followed "numerous attempts made by easyJet cabin crew to resolve labour and pay issues, which the company has ignored", the union said.Among the grievances raised are frequent changes to duty rosters, the alleged breach of the collective labour agreement, unequal treatment of cabin crew and pilots, problems with operational planning and pressure to work overtime because of staff shortages.The union accuses easyJet of keeping Portuguese crew on "wages below those paid by other airlines operating in Portugal and below those paid by easyJet itself in other countries in the network", where it said salaries fairly reflect the cost of living and the national minimum wage.SNPVAC also speaks of a "climate of tension and dissatisfaction caused by the long and intolerable deadlock over the various labour disputes" which, it stresses, "has worsened", leading the union to conclude "that easyJet's ultimate aim is to prolong indefinitely the position it has adopted".In the same statement, the union claims that easyJet "has repeatedly resorted to replacing striking crew members with managers and colleagues from other countries in the network", allowing it to operate flights that would otherwise be cancelled and, according to SNPVAC, effectively undermining the right to strike.The October strike coincides with the long weekend around Portugal’s Republic Day public holiday on 5 October, which falls on a Monday this year. The December stoppage runs until two days before Christmas, when many people travel for leisure or return home for the festive season.

Headline: What to expect from the Trump-Xi summit, from tariffs to a possible $30 billion deal
Body: This is the return leg.US President Donald Trump went to Beijing in May, and Chinese President Xi Jinping is now expected to come to him, scheduled to arrive next Wednesday and depart on Friday with his wife, Peng Liyuan, skipping the UN General Assembly entirely.Beijing has not yet given the final confirmation, pending the meeting between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng this weekend.The expected visit to Washington is Xi's first since 2015, and two US- China state visits within five months are highly unusual. However, expectations are modest by design."The visit is the message," said Edgard Kagan, senior adviser in China studies at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS)."There's been a surprising lack of signalling by either the White House or the PRC on major goals for the visit," Kagan added.What is actually on the tableThe commercial substance starts before either leader speaks.Bessent meets Lifeng this weekend as the pair have conducted most of the practical negotiations, and their job is to have deliverables ready.The central one is the truce struck in Busan on 30 October 2025, which suspended Washington's Affiliates Rule in exchange for continued Chinese exports of rare earths and critical minerals.It runs for one year and is due to expire roughly five weeks after the summit. Both sides want it extended, but not by the same amount."The Chinese have wanted an agreement to extend the trade ceasefire through the end of the Trump administration," said Scott Kennedy, trustee chair in Chinese business and economics at CSIS."The Trump administration just wants to extend it for a few months to maintain leverage on China. I think they'll end up somewhere in the middle, probably at about a year," Kennedy estimated.Beijing expects more than a rollover.According to Kagan, the Chinese anticipate an announcement of around $30 billion (€26bn) in duty-free or low-tariff imports in return for fulfilling the purchase commitments they made in May, while Washington believes it will extract further purchases in return.Deals on agriculture and aircraft are likely, possibly with signing ceremonies attached, and Trump has previously hinted that Boeing could feature.Two economies under strainTrump faces midterms in November that will be fought on the cost of living, with diesel above $6 a gallon and inflation stuck at 3.4%. He needs wins that show up in prices.However, Xi's problem is deeper.Retail sales grew just 0.4% in August, while fixed-asset investment contracted by 7.2% in the first eight months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025. Beijing has also injected 360 billion yuan (€46bn) into state banks and insurers to keep credit flowing.The official growth target of 4.5% to 5% for China is the lowest in decades, and Kennedy suggests even that flatters the reality."China's got a bunch of challenges," he said, adding that "it's growing very, very slowly, not 5% or anywhere close to it. It's got a massive debt problem, unemployment is growing not just for young people, but for others."Nonetheless, Kennedy argues the summit framework favours Beijing, describing the US strategy as having failed to constrain China in any meaningful way.Business leaders on both sidesThe state dinner, held under a tent on the White House lawn because the new ballroom is unfinished, will seat an unusual guest list.Sam Altman of OpenAI, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, Qualcomm's Cristiano Amon and Apple chairman Tim Cook are all expected, according to Politico, which cited four people familiar with the arrangements.They arrive amid an argument the AI industry is having with itself.Anthropic's Dario Amodei published an essay this month urging labs to slow frontier development, a position Altman and Elon Musk both endorsed. Trump rejected it flatly, saying that "whoever wins AI wins".Huang has dismissed catastrophic scenarios as hysterical while arguing that companies should police their own pace by stating that "if it's not ready, just hold it back. You should go as fast as you can, but no faster than that."Anthropic declined to say whether it had been invited. Altman, for his part, has suggested Trump and Xi could earn a Nobel Peace Prize if they reach an agreement on AI, which gives some measure of how much the industry has riding on the meeting.Xi is reportedly bringing his own delegation, and Kennedy calls it one of the most interesting unknowns of the week, with BYD's leadership among the names rumoured.Whether those executives are given any platform, he notes, is among the few genuinely unclear elements of the visit.The geopolitics that could derail itOutside the economic and technology issues, the two leaders have different geopolitical priorities for the meeting.Iran is Trump's.Washington launched Operation Economic Outcast in August to sever Tehran from the global financial system, and China remains Iran's largest trading partner.Notably, Beijing has been buying more oil on the open market, which Kagan says reflects reduced purchases from Iran and could itself move prices.Taiwan is Xi's.A $14 billion (€12bn) arms package for Taiwan was pre-approved by the US Congress in January but has not been formally notified, a delay interpreted as an attempt to avoid a probable irritant before this summit and, previously, ahead of Trump's visit to China.Beijing certainly wants the freeze extended, and perhaps the decision reconsidered.

Headline: Russian man swims from Kaliningrad to Lithuania in failed asylum attempt
Body: A 68-year-old Russian man, who travelled from the Russian Baltic sea enclave of Kaliningrad to Lithuania by river was met by border guards on the riverbank on Thursday afternoon and was sent back without being granted asylum. “After the swim, he was provided with dry clothing,” Lithuania’s State Border Guard press service told Euronews. “More details about his journey, such as the exact distance covered, the route or how long he was in the water, cannot currently be provided.”The man allegedly told Lithuanian authorities that he was fleeing Russia because of persecution over his activity on social media, according to the Lrytas news portal.But after assessing the circumstances, "inconsistent" information provided by the man and “information concerning the threat posed by this person if he were to enter the EU”, Lithuanian authorities decided to return him, a spokesperson for Lithuania’s State Border Guard Service, Giedrius Mišutis, told Lrytas.It is unusual for people to attempt to enter Lithuania from Russia by swimming across the Nemunas. Nevertheless, Lithuanian border guards continuously monitor the section of the river using technical surveillance equipment, meaning such incidents can be detected and responded to immediately, the service said.The incident comes as the Baltic state is operating under heightened security pressure along the European Union's eastern frontier: Lithuania borders Belarus, a close Russian ally, as well as Russia’s heavily militarised Kaliningrad exclave.The country has recorded multiple drone incursions, with the latest being one on Monday, when a NATO fighter jet shot down a drone after it entered Lithuanian airspace from Belarus.Since 2021, Vilnius has also had to contend with what the EU has described as a weaponisation of migration by Belarus and Russia, after thousands of migrants were directed towards the bloc’s eastern borders. This has prompted Lithuania to reinforce surveillance, border infrastructure and staffing along its frontier.

Headline: Europe’s most popular castles and palaces revealed – according to traveller reviews
Body: As we ease into autumn, many European travellers say that culture and heritage are among their main travel motivations. When the weather starts to cool down in October and November, people are increasingly planning trips around these activities, according to the European Travel Commission.That research is backed up by data from travel company TUI Musement, too. Its findings show that 94% of people say they are interested – or very interested – in enjoying experiences related to history, culture and heritage during their next city break. Eight out of 10 respondents also say they have visited a monument or landmark close to where they live.With that in mind, TUI Musement has revealed a new ranking of the 30 most popular castles and palaces in Europe for 2026, using accumulated Google reviews to back it up.  Its analysis compared the volume of reviews recorded in 2023 and 2026 to show how the ranking of attractions has changed over the past few years.The list shows that Spain is the country with the greatest representation, with six of the 30 castles and palaces located in the country. Both the Alhambra in Granada and the Royal Palace of Madrid are in the top 10.Ever-popular Prague Castle manages to retain its first-place spot, while Schönbrunn Palace in Vienna enters the top three. Buda Castle in Budapest was the only new entry into the list,  thanks to a 65% increase in the number of accumulated Google reviews compared with 2023.These are the top 10 castles you may want to consider visiting this autumn. Top 10 shows a wide geographic spreadFew who have visited Prague Castle will be surprised to see it in the top spot. Boasting 199,000 reviews – 31% more than in 2023 – it’s one of the largest palace complexes in the world. A visit offers travellers the chance to discover centuries of history in one place, as a ticket includes the chance to see landmarks including St Vitus Cathedral, the Old Royal Palace and the picturesque Golden Lane.Next up on the list is Buckingham Palace, arguably London’s most famous monument. One of the three official residences of the British monarchy, it’s an enormously popular tourist attraction.Thousands of visitors annually watch the daily Changing of the Guard and, in the summer, they can opt to enter the building and tour its iconic state rooms. Climbing two places from its 2023 ranking to third is Schönbrunn Palace in Austria’s capital, Vienna.This year, it’s celebrating the 30th anniversary of its designation as a World Heritage Site, and offers a rich history and insight into the world of the imperial legacy that shaped centuries of Austrian history.In fourth place is the Palace of Versailles, an integral part of French history, and the former residence of the kings of France. The beautiful structure houses the Hall of Mirrors, royal apartments and extensive, manicured gardens. Here, you can explore everything from the absolutism of Louis XIV and the fall of the monarchy to the signing of the Treaty of Versailles that brought the First World War to an end.Although it’s dropped two places since 2023, Wawel Castle in Kraków still ranks fifth and remains one of Europe’s major cultural attractions. The former residence – and coronation site – of Poland’s kings also houses the famous Dragon’s Den statue at its foot, which remains one of the city’s best-known symbols.Castles in Spain take the sixth and seventh places in the ranking.Granada’s Alhambra is in sixth, and its complex of palaces, gardens and fortresses is nothing short of breathtaking. Once home to the Nasrid sultans and then the kings of Castile, the Nasrid Palaces, Generalife, Alcazaba and Palace of Charles V are among its most iconic spaces.In seventh spot is the Royal Palace of Madrid, which is up one position after increasing its number of accumulated Google reviews by 47% since 2023. The vast space actually continues to host receptions and official events of the royal household, but members of the public can visit highlights including the throne room, Gasparini room and royal chapel.For eighth place, it’s back to London and the iconic Tower of London. This ancient building saw events which shaped England’s destiny, including the execution of Anne Boleyn and the disappearance of brothers Prince Edward V and the Duke of York. Today, it’s home to the legendary Crown Jewels and is guarded by traditional Yeoman Warders as well as ravens, who some consider the guardians of the fortress.Neuschwanstein Castle, in the Bavarian Alps, has risen to ninth place in the ranking, thanks to a significant increase in reviews. The palace, which looks like something out of a fairy tale, invites visitors into the world of King Ludwig II of Bavaria, known as the “Mad King” or “Swan King”, and his fascination with art, architecture and medieval legends. Rounding out the top 10 is Bran Castle in Romania. Also known as “Dracula’s Castle”, it makes a visit to Transylvania a must for fans of all things spooky. Beyond the Dracula myth, it also lays bare centuries of Romanian history, from its role as a frontier fortress to its period as a royal residence.The top 10 most popular castles in Europe Prague Castle, CzechiaBuckingham Palace, United KingdomSchönbrunn Palace, AustriaPalace of Versailles, FranceWawel Castle, PolandThe Alhambra, SpainThe Royal Palace of Madrid, SpainThe Tower of London, United KingdomNeuschwanstein Castle, GermanyBran Castle, Romania

Headline: Macron to convene G7 on energy, warning of 'Russian aggression'
Body: Emmanuel Macron has condemned what he calls Russia's "intent" to "intimidate" and to "undermine efforts to support the Ukrainians". In his view, "the outcome will be the opposite".The French president was speaking after a confidential meeting at the Élysée with the main presidential candidates or their closest associates.Macron warned the "nature of Russian aggression and threats in Europe is changing".One example cited by Macron was the discovery of a drone loaded with explosives at Leipzig airport this summer. "We are not intimidated because we know that what is at stake in Ukraine is our security today and tomorrow", he said.Macron revealed that he has requested "a plan to protect our critical infrastructure" in the face of "Russian hybrid attacks".The French president also stressed the "need to keep sending messages to Russia" and to avoid "entering into a state of belligerence" with that country.Surge in fuel pricesThe sharp rise in fuel prices was an other issue raised by Emmanuel Macron during the meeting at the Élysée.According to the president's inner circle, public opinion tends to forget that the international situation is the root cause of the crisis. Emmanuel Macron aimed to remind the candidates for the 2027 presidential election of this.The rise in prices is "not the result of government decisions", he said.The blockages in the Strait of Hormuz, in the Gulf, and more recently in the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, in the Red Sea, "have direct consequences for our daily lives", Emmanuel Macron wrote on the social media platform, X.The French president is calling for the causes of rising petrol prices to be addressed "before spending large sums of money" which he warned would mean "either a bigger deficit or higher taxes".Macron announced his intention to convene a G7 meeting devoted to energy issues. The meeting, he says, should be held in the coming weeks and will aim in particular to "move towards better coordination on stock levels".

Headline: Burnham pledges 'further steps' to deepen ties with EU in meeting with Irish Taoiseach
Body: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham vowed to take "further steps" to deepen ties with the European Union during a meeting with Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin.The pair met in Manchester on Friday, with Martin becoming the first international leader to visit Burnham's No10 North, a new regional office established as part of the PM's devolution drive.During the talks, Burnham "underlined the UK's desire to work closely with Ireland during its presidency of the European Union as the UK seeks a closer relationship with Europe," a spokeswoman for Downing Street said.The two leaders, who also reaffirmed their commitment to upholding the Good Friday Agreement, had been expected to discuss further strengthening the UK and Ireland's relationship, focusing on several "shared objectives" including working with the EU, security, and ramping up trade."The relationship between the UK and Ireland matters so much on every single level," Burnham said from No10 North on Friday.He told reporters that the government was also "looking forward" to a long-awaited UK-EU summit later this year and that it was "wanting to take further steps to deepen the relationship with Europe."A summit had been scheduled to take place in July but was postponed following former Prime Minister Keir Starmer's resignation. The summit is expected to centre on key aspects of Starmer's "Brexit reset," including a potential youth mobility scheme.For his part, Martin said: "We look forward to discussing with you even stronger and closer relationships between the European Union and the United Kingdom, which will be of benefit to the European Union and indeed to Ireland, quite frankly."Burnham has previously called for the UK to rejoin the bloc, but he toned down those comments as he was campaigning for the Makerfield by-election in May."My view is that Brexit has been damaging," he said. "But I also believe the last thing we should do right now is rerun those arguments.His comments came as the UK's divisive 2016 vote to leave the EU came back under the spotlight in spring as Labour figures jostled for position amid party turmoil following disastrous local election results.Starmer had pledged to "put Britain at the heart of Europe" as his government slowly and carefully began to reforge closer ties with Brussels, but some senior Labour figures sought to go a step further as a leadership contest looked increasingly likely.Speaking at the time, Wes Streeting, now the UK's Defence Secretary, labelled the UK's decision to leave the bloc a "catastrophic mistake.""It's left us less wealthy, less powerful and less in control than at any point before the industrial revolution," he told an audience at the Labour Party's Progress conference in May."We ‌need a new special relationship with the EU, because Britain's future lies with Europe, and one day, one day, back in the European Union," he added.Kemi Badenoch, the leader of the main opposition Conservatives, called Labour's return to the issue "a sign of a Labour party that does not have a plan for the country."

Headline: The world's 20 best airlines for 2026 have been announced – with only six in Europe
Body: European airlines have been largely pushed down the pecking order in this year’s World Airline Awards, with Asian and Middle Eastern carriers dominating the top 10.Singapore Airlines took the overall title, followed by Qatar Airways and Cathay Pacific, while Turkish Airlines was the highest-ranked European carrier in fifth place. Just six European airlines made the top 20, with Air France, Lufthansa, Iberia, Virgin Atlantic and Swiss International Air Lines joining Turkish Airlines.The 2026 World Airline Awards were announced at a gala ceremony in London hosted by air transport rating organisation Skytrax. Known as “the Oscars of the aviation industry”, the awards have been running since 1999 and, according to Skytrax’s CEO Edward Plaisted, “highlights the level of product and service excellence they are providing to customers”.More than 300 airlines were assessed in the ranking and, although Europe’s operators didn’t blow the competition away in the main category, they did have a decent showing in others. European airlines triumph in some categories – and fall down in others Air France did particularly well, scooping awards for the world’s best first class, the world’s best first class lounge dining, and the world’s best first class comfort amenities, as well as being given the nod as the best airline in Western Europe.Spanish-headquartered Vueling won the award for the best low-cost airline in Europe, a category which also saw the inclusion of Germany’s Eurowings, Spain’s Iberia Express and Volotea and Dutch Transavia. Meanwhile, Turkish Airlines took a trio of awards, scooping gongs for the best airline in Europe, the world’s best business class catering and the best airline in Southern Europe. “Being recognised as ‘Europe’s best airline’ for the 11th time and ranking first in two other categories is a great source of pride for us as the Turkish Airlines family,” Murat Şeker, Turkish Airlines chairman of the board, said. In other categories, Iberia won the award for the best airline staff service in Europe, while LOT Polish Airlines received the award as the best airline in Central Europe. All European airlines were absent from the world’s best cabin crew category, which was topped by Cathay Pacific Airways, and only Greece’s Aegean Airlines made the top 10 of the world’s best regional airlines category, coming in fourth place. Qatar Airways loses its top spotIn the overall ranking, Qatar Airways, a nine-time winner of the world’s best airline title, dropped to second spot behind Singapore Airlines.Nevertheless, the Doha-based operator did manage to scoop four top awards, including the world’s best business class airline – the 13th time the airline has received this accolade – and the best airline in the Middle East. It also received the first-ever award for the World’s Best Onboard Wi-Fi. That category was introduced this year to recognise the importance of fast and free onboard connectivity for many modern travellers. The world’s top 20 airlines in 2026 1. Singapore Airlines2. Qatar Airways3. Cathay Pacific4. ANA All Nippon Airways5. Turkish Airlines6. Emirates7. Air France8. Hainan Airlines9. Japan Airlines10. Korean Air11. EVA Air12. Qantas Airways13. STARLUX Airlines14. Headline: Monet time: French Renaissance painter's rarely seen 'Iris' set to break sale record
Body: Between €22 and 30 million, the highest estimate ever placed on a painting sold in France. That is what a buyer could spend to obtain 'Iris' by Claude Monet.On 22 October, Sotheby's auction house will be offering the rarely seen work by the French Renaissance master for sale, alongside other works from the Schlumberger family's private collection.A monumental painting created by Monet at the end of his life, the canvas is, according to curators, in remarkable condition. "It has no varnish, it is on its original canvas and has never been restored. They are exactly as Monet painted them 100 years ago," explains Thomas Bompard, co-director of the Modern and Contemporary Department at Sotheby's France. Canvases preserved in the Schlumberger living roomEvery detail counts. Varnish alters the chromatic tones of a painting, according to art historian Marianne Mathieu.But restoration could damage the texture of the paint on the canvas. "Late Monet is a Monet who works the material. So to truly discover and understand him, that material has to be preserved. And we still have these thick impastos."Hung in a Schlumberger family sitting room for a century, 'Iris', like 'Weeping Willow', also up for sale and valued at between nine and ten million euros, has never been moved.Above all, it has never been seen in colour by the general public. It was acquired by Jeanne Schlumberger (1889-1983), "a brilliant art collector", from the painter's family through "the visionary gallerist" Katia Granoff, according to Thomas Bompard, without going through an auction room."Many people knew the story, or at least knew of the existence of this collection; people whispered that these were the finest Monets in Paris, but very few had actually seen them. That is also what is fuelling today's excitement," he notes.A collection valued at €40 millionAnother factor that has pushed prices higher is the centenary of the death of the Impressionist artist, who died on 5 December 1926. Two exhibitions on the painter's life open in Paris at the end of September: "Monet, Painting Time" and "Stories of Landscapes, from Monet to Hockney".In all, 28 works are up for auction at Sotheby's, in a sale expected to raise more than €40 million. Among them are four Monets, as well as a sculpture by Camille Claudel and several paintings by Gustave Moreau.Also being sold on this occasion is a wall composition of three works by Paul Cézanne. "La Ferme", the central painting, is "the largest work by the artist ever to be offered at auction" and is estimated at between €600,000 and €800,000.The three paintings have been designated as "national treasures", a measure intended to give the state 30 months in which to arrange a possible acquisition.

Headline: Portugal braces for rising temperatures and possible heatwave
Body: Portugal is set to see a gradual rise in temperatures from this Saturday. The Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (IPMA) has raised a yellow warning for nine districts (source in Portuguese).For this Saturday three districts are under a yellow warning: Coimbra, Leiria and Lisbon. On Sunday, the warning is extended to Setúbal, Santarém, Aveiro, Porto, Braga and Viana do Castelo. The alert will remain in force in these nine districts at least until eight o'clock on Monday evening.The yellow warning is the lowest level of risk on a scale that also includes orange and red alerts. According to the institute's website, it indicates a "situation of risk for certain activities".The IPMA says there is a likelihood of a heatwave:"This spell of hot weather will be defined mainly by its duration, with a high probability of meeting the criteria for a heatwave across much of the territory", the institute said in a statement (source in Portuguese).The document explains that a heatwave occurs when "over a period of six consecutive days, the maximum air temperature is 5 °C above the average value of the daily maximum temperatures".Temperatures are therefore expected to reach above 30 °C on the mainland. In some areas, such as Lisbon and the Tagus Valley, they could even approach 38 °C.Minimum temperatures will also rise, staying above 20 °C in some parts of Alto Alentejo, Beira Baixa, the Tagus Valley and the eastern Algarve."Although the forecast maximum temperatures are lower than those recorded in some episodes this summer, they will be substantially above the average values for the second half of September", the statement adds.The hot weather is due to "the influence of an anticyclone located to the north of the Azores, extending in a ridge as far as the Bay of Biscay". This will bring "a mass of air of continental origin (hot and dry) over the Iberian Peninsula".In July, Portugal had already experienced anomalous temperatures, with red warnings in most of the country and the government declaring an alert situation. That situation extended to the rest of continental Europe during July.A report by the non-profit organisation Climate Central concluded that the continent was "the most abnormally warm region on the planet". Almost nine in ten Europeans lived through an entire month of "dangerous heat".

Headline: Meet the beekeeper carrying on three generations of family tradition
Body: Beekeeping has been part of Sabir Mustafayev’s family for generations. With more than 40 years in the profession, he says the craft has changed significantly, with beekeepers adapting to new challenges including global warming. His family brought its farm to Kalbajar in 2021 and later opened a honey shop there, followed by a branch in Baku. The annual Honey Festival is putting Kalbajar’s beekeeping tradition in the spotlight, as producers look to bring the region’s honey to a global audience.

Headline: The world’s first laser fusion power station is being built in Germany
Body: The race to develop the energy source of the future is gathering pace. Who will win? The US and China? Or Europe? German start-up Focused Energy, based in Darmstadt, aims to become the global leader in the construction of commercial laser fusion power stations. The development of fusion energy is on top of the political high-tech agenda of Germany and the European Union. Fusion start-ups are being founded in great numbers around the planet, especially laser based fusion technology, which attracts huge amounts of risk capital. This spring, Focused Energy raised $240 million dollars alone – the largest figure ever raised in the first round of financing in the global fusion industry.After a tough security check, the gates of the Biblis power station open for Euronews. The site was used to be one of Germany’s largest nuclear fission power stations. Now it is where the new laser fusion facility will be built.Germany is getting serious about phasing out nuclear fission. All over the country, buildings are being decontaminated and cooling towers demolished. The giant reactor domes at Biblis, however, will remain in place. But in future, it will be nuclear fusion inside - rather than nuclear fission. RWE, one of Europe’s largest energy companies and the site’s owner, has invested €60 million in Focused Energy.The company rolls out an extremely ambitious roadmap. “In five years’ time, I want to have a first laser fusion demonstrator here in Biblis,” Ulrich Sigel, Focused Energy’s Vice President, tells Euronews. “In ten years’ time, we want to build the pilot power station there, and in 15 years’ time, the world’s first commercially competitive laser fusion power station.”Why Biblis? “The conditions here are simply superb”, explains Sigel while showing us around. “We can make use of the existing infrastructure – from the grid connection right through to buildings.” Sigel points to the main reactor dome of the decomissioned nuclear power station: “In the former Reactor Block A, our pilot laser fusion power station is to be built.”The fusion power station is set to produce almost one gigawatt of electricity, enough for two million households. Critics consider the technology to be not yet developped enough and too expensive. Focused Energy, on the other hand, believes that laser fusion will be competitive – even when compared with electricity generated from nuclear fission or renewables.However, the remaining technical challenges are enormous. There are unsolved problems linked to the fuel cycle and the scaling up of the first promising results incoming from the laboratories to be overcome.

Headline: Revolut weighs dual listing in New York and London for its long-awaited IPO
Body: Britain's most valuable private company has clarified where it intends to sell its shares.Nik Storonsky, Revolut's founder and CEO, told French newspaper Les Echos on Thursday that the group is weighing a dual listing across the London Stock Exchange and the Nasdaq, confirming earlier media reports.A spokesperson for Revolut confirmed the report to Euronews.The US remains Storonsky's preference, and he was candid about why, stating that "it's a larger market. It includes institutional investors, hedge funds, fund managers and a considerable number of individual investors.""So we have the choice between selling in a small market with few buyers, or in a gigantic market with a huge number of buyers who will compete fiercely for our shares," Storonsky added.The comments mark a softening in rethoric.The Revolut CEO argued in 2024 that the London Stock Exchange simply could not compete with American venues, citing thin liquidity and the UK's 0.5% stamp duty on share purchases, and had appeared to rule out listing at home altogether.The London exchange has endured a prolonged drought of new listings, with companies either staying private or heading west. For instance, payments group Wise moved its primary listing to New York this year, and AstraZeneca has also expanded its presence in the US.Revolut going public at anything near its current valuation would make it one of Britain's largest listed companies, potentially worth more than Barclays or NatWest.A secondary share sale in July valued the business at roughly $115 billion (€100bn), up from $75 billion (€65bn) in November.No date for the IPO yetWhen asked by Euronews about internal discussions regarding a timeline for the IPO, the spokesperson refused to comment, but pointed to a previous interview with Bloomberg in April of this year where the Revolut CEO stated "in two years time, but it depends on how good the market is."Progress as certainly been made as the company has spent this year assembling the regulatory foundations a listing will require.It secured a full UK banking licence in March after a long wait that Storonsky has publicly blamed on British regulators, obtained a French licence in August, received conditional approval for a US national bank charter this month, and announced on Wednesday that it had applied for a Swiss licence alongside plans to invest more than 150 million Swiss francs (€158m) there.Revolut has not stated which venue would host the primary listing, whether the two would happen simultaneously, or when formal preparations might begin.

Headline: EU weighs windfall taxes on energy firms amid growing economic strain
Body: A windfall tax for firms profiting from energy price volatility is one of the ideas circulating among EU ministers meeting in Dublin on Friday and Saturday for the periodic meetings of the Eurogroup and Economic and Financial Council.With the war in the Middle East continuing, Brent crude oil prices have surpassed $100 per barrel, and extreme volatility in energy prices is driving inflation higher across the bloc, which is not expected to return to the 2% target before the end of 2027.While growth indicators are still performing well this year, the European Commission expects economic growth to slow down in 2027.The EU is urging member states to pursue prudent fiscal policies and remain within the existing fiscal flexibility of 1.5% for defence spending, of which 0.3% can be used to contain energy prices.Meanwhile, the European Central Bank (ECB) is gradually raising interest rates to contain inflation.“There are several member states that put forward this initiative, it is part of our discussions," European Commissioner for Economy Valdis Dombrovskis said during a press conference on Friday, referring to the windfall tax."Member states can already implement windfall profit taxes at the national level if they decide to do so. From the Commission side, we are ready to support those member states by sharing best practices and finding a good way forward.”German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil is pressing the European Commission to present models for a windfall tax, asking to have something on the table by the next Economic and Finance Council meeting in October."You know that I have been fighting for this for a long time, together with other European finance ministers," Klingbeil said on the sidelines of Friday's meeting.The Spanish Finance Minister Carlos Cuerpo also expressed his favour for the proposal on Friday.“We are managing to lower the bill for homes, companies, industries, transport companies, and this at the expense of the taxpayer's money. We believe there may be fairer ways to distribute this cost,” Cuerpo said.French Finance Minister Roland Lescure has been more cautious about the proposal.“This [energy] shock can have a different impact on different countries. We do feel that whatever discussion we have, whatever work has been done, needs to take into account the specificities of each country," he said ahead of the meeting on Friday, specifying that France has a "bigger electricity mix".To the direct question on whether he supports the proposal or not, Lescure said that he support any work that’s being done, but that "I can’t support something before I’ve seen it"."I’ll see what the work comes out with, and then we’ll have a discussion.”Energy taxes: the bulk of pricingAlthough the energy crisis is affecting the bloc, not all member states are affected in the same way, with prices at the pump varying greatly.Finland, Denmark and the Netherlands, the three EU countries currently paying the most for diesel, impose some of the highest fuel taxes in the world, pushing retail diesel prices much higher.On the other hand, countries in Eastern Europe such as Bulgaria and Poland set excise duties far lower, keeping their pump prices down.Yet according to EU official data published on Thursday, the EU country paying the least for diesel is Malta, with €1.20 per litre charged at the pump on 14 September.The significant discrepancy in diesel prices across the EU is driven mainly by divergent national tax policies – excise duties and VAT – which make up the largest portion of the retail price of diesel.However, the difference between diesel prices before and after taxes is staggering. Per the data released on Thursday, Finland’s diesel price stood €1.48 per litre before taxes and €2.50 after taxes.Denmark also ranked high, with diesel at €1.43 before taxes and €2.50 per litre after taxes, while Dutch citizens would pay only €1.50 per litre of diesel without taxes and €2.49 with taxes.France, which has the third-highest government debt in the EU, has chosen targeted to offer assistance for the sectors most exposed to the price shock rather than cutting fuel taxes.French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu asked ministers to extend support for sectors most exposed to higher energy costs until 31 December. Meanwhile, diesel prices at the French pump stood at €2.29 per litre on 14 September, against €1.30 before taxes.Regional refining capacity also further amplifies energy pricing. All EU countries buy crude oil from the same volatile global markets, but the price motorists ultimately pay at the pump depends on whether there is sufficient refining capacity nearby, how easily fuel can be transported from other regions and how well local refineries can process the particular type of crude available.During a supply shock like the one the EU is currently suffering, EU countries with spare refining capacity, diversified import routes and strong links to neighbouring fuel markets may be able to cushion the disruption more easily.
