Headline: ‘Race-cation’ boom: Searches for 24-hour city breaks rise by 500% as runners plan marathon trips
Body: From marathons in Amsterdam to HYROX in Hamburg, autumn is shaping up to be the season of the “race-cation”. Google searches for “marathon abroad” have soared by some 1,255% in the past year, as runners increasingly combine race day with a quick city break – and new data suggests they’re already planning what to do once they cross the finish line.Findings from Bókun, a Tripadvisor-owned company, have revealed that searches for overseas marathons have hit an all-time high in 2026, and it’s perfect timing, as research shows that a quarter of marathons globally take place in October. Now, searches for 24-hour itineraries in marathon cities have surged by up to 500%, leading travel experts to predict that race-cations could drive trip bookings well beyond the summer peak. But what is a race-cation? Another trend in the world of travel, it’s popular with people interested in health and fitness who want to combine the challenge of a major race with visiting a new and exciting destination. Here’s everything you need to know about the trend - and how to do it yourself.Marathons spark growing interest in whirlwind city breaksIn addition to Bókun looking at Google search data and drawing insights from the trends observed over the past five years, it also examined social media trends. On platforms like TikTok, videos focusing on the likes of “the best locations to do a Hyrox in” and “marathon holiday itineraries” can gain thousands of views, which highlights the growing appeal of combining fitness events with travel experiences.While marathons are typically year-round events, 42% of them take place in the autumn, with October alone playing host to 23% of all events.Some of the top European sporting events this autumn include HYROX Rome and Berlin marathon in September, as well as the Amsterdam, Munich, Lisbon and Budapest marathons and HYROX Valencia in October. HYROX Hamburg runs from 28 October to 1 November. With those dates in mind, Bókun analysed Google Trends data from the past 30 days for searches relating to 24-hour trips to cities hosting major marathons and fitness events coming this autumn.It found that interest in 24-hour city break queries has increased across almost every destination ahead of these events.Hamburg saw the most traction, with a 500% surge in Google searches for “what to do in Hamburg” in the last month. Searches for “what to do in Lisbon for a day” increased by 400%, while “what to do in Munich for a day” rose by 250%.There was also a 119% increase in people googling what to do in Berlin for a day, “24 hours in Budapest” was up by 84%, and tips for a day-long trip to Amsterdam rose by 70%, all over the course of the last month.Race-cations also seem to be tapping into another travel trend: micro-adventures.While sporting events do play a part in search demand for 24-hour trips to European cities this autumn, the increase also highlights the wider trend of micro-cations, or short getaways where travellers can maximise their experience of a destination within a limited time and, often, immerse themselves in a city for just 24 hours.For marathoners and micro-cationers alike, guided tours and organised experiences are a decent way to get to know a destination and soak up the local culture. Bókun’s research also showed that search demand for day tours and experiences across different European cities has surged in the past year.Searches for “Budapest day tours” have increased by more than 400%, while search demand for “Amsterdam day tours" has increased by more than 100% and searches for “day tours in Lisbon” have increased by more than 70% in the past 12 months.It’s not just seeing the sights that matters to these travellers. Searches for “Lisbon cooking class” were up by a significant 488%, and “Rome food tour” searches increased by 94%, too.

Headline: Tajikistan celebrates its 35th independence anniversary
Body: Tajikistan marked 35 years of independence with nationwide celebrations, parades and ceremonies. However, the anniversary is also an opportunity for the country to look ahead.President Emomali Rahmon has set out his ambitions for a more industrial, technology-driven economy that is supported by green energy, modern infrastructure and a stronger workforce.Government officials emphasised sustained economic growth, energy security and accelerated industrialisation as key priorities, while investors highlighted the country’s substantial hydropower potential and significant projects, such as the Rogun Dam.The programme also examined Tajikistan’s efforts to strengthen its international relationships and attract new investment. Both officials and investors saw the anniversary as an opportunity to shape Tajikistan’s next chapter with renewed purpose.The celebrations culminated in a concert at Dushanbe’s new National Stadium.

Headline: Canada seeks to join €90bn support loan for Ukraine, Brussels confirms
Body: Canada is seeking to join the European Union's €90 billion support loan for Ukraine, the European Commission said on Friday."I can confirm that Canada has expressed an interest in joining the €90 billion Ukraine support loan," a Commission spokesperson told journalists. "We are working hard with Canada, and the respective technical talks are very much ongoing."EU leaders set up the loan to meet two-thirds of Ukraine's financial and military needs for 2026 and 2027, with the other third covered by other Western allies.So far, Brussels has disbursed nearly €15 billion, with more instalments expected soon.The €90 billion is raised through joint borrowing and generates about €3 billion in annual interest payments, which will be paid proportionally by 24 member states. (Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic secured an opt-out from the scheme.)Canada's inclusion, if successful, will allow Ukraine to procure weapons and ammunition from Canadian defence companies and bypass the "Made in Europe" requirements that govern the credit line. In turn, Ottawa will have to pay a share of the €3 billion in interest rates, depending on how much its firms benefit.The specifics of the Canadian contribution are still under negotiation."The more countries involved, the better. That can ensure that Ukraine can get the best and most suitable equipment for its defence needs," the Commission spokesperson said.The United Kingdom, a major donor to Ukraine, became the first non-EU country to join the support programme in July.The news comes as Kyiv looks to allies to plug a growing budget deficit, which is being worsened by Russia's escalation and blockade in the Black Sea.Brussels is trying to pin down the exact scope of Ukraine's additional needs and has asked other partners to step up. Norway recently announced $9 billion for 2027."It's important indeed that our like-minded partners also follow suit, including Canada and the UK," the Commission spokesperson said."That is a subject that we usually tend to take up with them regularly."Canada's move to join the scheme is seen as part of a fast-moving impetus to expand and deepen ties between Ottawa and Brussels. This week, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become the bloc's first "associate member".

Headline: Zelenskyy launches 'Carpathian Eight' alliance to boost regional investment
Body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy launched a new regional cooperation framework with seven neighbouring countries on Friday in an effort to stoke regional investment.The initiative, dubbed the "Carpathian Eight" (C8), brings together Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Austria and Hungary, with the European Union also taking part.Member states will work together on security, energy, logistics, cross-border economic ties and support for local communities."In the past, people often looked at the Carpathians mainly as a region of tourism, climate issues and support for local communities," Zelenskyy said at the summit's opening ceremony in Bukovel, western Ukraine. "Today, the Carpathians can and should become one of the key engines of economic growth, investment and energy exports."He identified transport and logistics, military mobility, critical minerals, and trade and investment as priority areas of cooperation, adding that the region could serve as a European gateway for routes from the South Caucasus and Asia via the Black Sea.According to summit organisers, some 90 joint projects requiring an estimated €9.4 billion in investment were pitched to investors during the summit's "Investment Lab".Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić and Romanian President Nicușor Dan were among those attending.While some participants U2013 including Poland and Romania – have been staunch supporters of Ukraine, others, such as Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia, have declined to provide direct military assistance.

Headline: Oasis 2027 tour: Travel searches surge for European host cities – and tickets are not on sale yet
Body: Oasis fans really are madferit, aren’t they? Even though tickets are yet to go on sale for the band’s 2027 tour, there’s already been a huge surge in online travel searches to cities set to host concerts. After a sold-out reunion tour in 2025, Oasis will be back on the road next year with gigs in Glasgow, Manchester, Munich, Barcelona, Amsterdam, Paris, Rome, Boston and Las Vegas, before shows at Ireland’s Slane Castle and a landmark return to Knebworth.Some might say that the confirmation of next year’s Oasis concert dates is great news for the bank balances of Noel, Liam and the rest of the band. However, judging by the frenzy surrounding the upcoming ticket sales, the tour could prove lucrative for the travel industry too.According to data released by global online travel agency eDreams, searches for travel to Glasgow have seen the most dramatic uplift – rising by 2,400%. The Scottish city is hosting the opening five nights of the tour, with searches increasing 25-fold compared with the same period last year.Huge increases in online searches – flight, rail, and dynamic packages – have also been recorded for Manchester (+846%), Rome (+659%), Barcelona (+655%), Dublin (+614%), Amsterdam (+592%) and Paris (+279%), eDreams said. In the US, searches for Las Vegas and Boston have risen by 692% and 487% respectively.The Oasis reunion contributed to a record year for UK music tourism in 2025 – and the early surge in travel searches suggests next year’s tour could boost the trend yet again."Fans are no longer just buying a ticket; they're building entire trips around a single show, and that's reshaping demand in cities far beyond the venue itself,” Pablo Caspers, Chief Travel Officer at eDreams, told Euronews Travel. “When Taylor Swift's Eras Tour moved through Europe, search interest in host cities like Edinburgh and Liverpool more than doubled almost overnight. We also see regular uplifts in searches for Eurovision host cities, and when festival lineups are announced for Coachella and Primavera Sound.“With these new Oasis tour dates, we're seeing the pattern play out again: Glasgow searches are up 25-fold on last year, with Manchester up 846%, Dublin up 614%, and the ripple reaching as far as Las Vegas, up 692%, and Boston, up 487%, alongside Rome, Barcelona, Amsterdam and Paris. "It shows that when an artist has enough cultural pull, they can move travel demand on a truly global scale."The 2027 Oasis tour kicks off at Celtic Park in Glasgow, Scotland, on 21 May and concludes on 19 September at Knebworth in England. Ticket sales will take place across three days next week – Friday 25 September, Saturday 26 September and Sunday 27 September – with registered fans who receive an access code allocated an on-sale window.

Headline: Women dominate Europe's health workforce but earn 19% less per hour, WHO warns
Body: Women in healthcare in Europe — a sector where they dominate— earn 19% less per hour than men on average, the World Health Organization (WHO) warns in a new report. The health and care sector is the fourth-largest employer and the single largest employer of women in the WHO European Region. Women account for 77% of the workforce in healthcare, compared with 45% in all other sectors combined. However, they make up only 55% of the sector’s top earners. “Women make up the majority of the people who keep Europe’s health systems running, yet they’re paid less than their male counterparts, a gap that compounds over a lifelong career," said Natasha Azzopardi Muscat, director of the Division for Health Systems, at WHO Europe.The gender pay gap — the difference in average wages between men and women who are engaged in paid employment — in hourly pay is widest at higher wage levels, ranging from a 2% gap among the lowest earners to over 22% at the top of the wage distribution. The sector is especially important for women’s employment, the report found. It represents almost 17% of all women’s employment, compared with 5% for men.These findings follow the same pattern documented across the wider labour market: heightened structural inequality that intensifies at higher wage and seniority levels. Globally, the health sector mirrors Europe, with women earning on average 24% less than men — a wider gap than in many other industries. What is behind this difference?The authors noted that some of the healthcare sector’s pay gap can be explained by differences in work-related factors such as age, education, sector of employment — public versus private and employment type — full-time versus part-time. Adjusting for those four factors brings the hourly pay gap down from 19% to 6% and the monthly pay gap down from 28% to 10%. However, the remaining pay gap can’t be explained by anything measured in the data.“Most of this gap isn’t down to women working fewer hours, being younger or working in different parts of the sector," Azzopardi Muscat explained. “It comes down to how the sector values women’s work. Age, education, working hours and public versus private sector employment only helps explain some of it.” According to WHO, the report points to deeper structural factors, such as the undervaluation of care work, occupational segregation and potential discrimination in pay-setting practices. The more feminised an occupational category is, the less it pays — a pattern that holds across managerial, professional and technical roles alike. Managerial jobs in health and care, for instance, employ more women than management roles in other sectors and pay less for it: €22 per hour on average, against €24.70 in comparable roles elsewhere. The broader cost of the gapThe gender pay gap remains one of the most persistent forms of labour market inequality, the WHO noted. Considering how many women work in health and care, this gap can have important economic and social consequences. The report noted this inequality may lead to lower lifetime earnings and pension entitlements, increase women’s risk of poverty, reduce returns to education and undermine sustainable economic growth. “It means lower pensions, less financial security in older age, and a higher risk of poverty for women who’ve spent their working lives caring for others,” said Azzopardi Muscat. “This isn’t a coincidence, and it isn’t about qualifications. Women are being paid less for the same work and passed over for the roles that pay more.” Closing gender pay gaps is therefore both an equity imperative and an investment in a stronger and more sustainable health workforce, the international health agency noted.To that end, they suggest targeted actions, from ensuring salary transparency and facilitating female representation in decision-making positions to addressing gender norms and stereotypes.

Headline: Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'Resident Evil' - How to resurrect a dead franchise
Body: Being a video game fan is a tough gig when it comes to film adaptations. Unless you count recent TV series like The Last Of Us and Fallout, console-to-screen transformations have historically resulted in cinematic poison.One video game franchise which has had a particularly rough time of it is Capcom's Resident Evil, which has been cursed with six live-action films, one dire 2021 reboot, and a failed Netflix series which was promptly cancelled because an actual viral infection would've been preferable to a second season.When the news dropped that horror's indie darling Zach Cregger was helming a brand-new reboot of the maligned IP, there was every reason to be skeptical or depressed. Or both. After two critically acclaimed films (Barbarian and the Oscar-winning Weapons), it seemed like Cregger was cashing in already and happy to take some Playstation / Sony bucks in exchange for silencing his original voice.We should have kept the faith, as it turns out the director knew what he was doing. It's taken 24 years, but thanks to Cregger, Resident Evil fans finally have an adaptation they can be proud to champion.  The 2026 premise discards the high-concept lore and events of the games, lets go of Milla Jovovich’s Alice, and takes things back to basics. We meet Bryan (Austin Abrams), a hapless medical courier who’s about to head home to his girlfriend, who has just informed him she's pregnant. Instead of clocking out, he accepts a double-pay gig that involves him transporting a high-priority package to Raccoon City General Hospital.He believes he's dropping off a vital organ. It's not.On the road, he hits a woman with his vehicle, who is alive but seems to be in shock. She's not. Thus begins the longest night of Bryan's life, during which he'll battle a lack of phone service, struggle with guns he doesn't know how to reload, and contend with A LOT of pesky padlocks.Oh yeah, and there's a virus that rewrites DNA, strips the infected of their humanity, and transforms them into flesh-craving zombies, cartwheeling multi-limbed monstrosities, tentacled mutants and kamikaze fleshbags. Those will all be a hindrance too.Cregger gets so much right here, to the extent it's borderline heroic considering previous adaptations. He perfectly doses the gore, the nail-biting dread, some well-timed (and never gratuitous) jump scares, and adds a surprising amount of humour. This comedic element proves to be crucial, as Cregger and his co-writer Shay Hatten understood the merit of injecting some relatability into a mix which includes Brian Yuzna-levels of body horror and creatures which look like they've escaped from John Carpenter's The Thing.This is made possible in large part thanks to Austin Abrams, who played the homeless drug addict in Weapons. His character is a squealing and bumbling everyman who possesses none of the heroic, action-savvy qualities you'd expect from a leading man. He's just an average guy on an A-to-B mission, trying to survive whatever is trying to kill him. Abrams understood the assignment and absolutely nails it.The first half of Resident Evil is undeniably its strongest, as once Bryan runs into an Umbrella Corporation scientist and a security agent (Paul Walter Hauser and Kali Reis), the white-knuckle ride gradually starts to become a bit more repetitive. It's during this second half that you're reminded you're in a Resident Evil adaptation; the unavoidable inclusion of the nefarious biotech company and a few POV shots to keep gamers happy feel slightly jarring within the everyman fight for survival. It's never not deliriously entertaining though, all the way until an afterthought ending which does let the film down. Not in how bluntly and almost hilariously abrupt it is; that part feels in keeping with the film's increasingly loopy tone. It's the way it undercuts Brian's character arc and reduces it to a Society-shaped punchline which ends things on a bit of a bum note.Still, for a large part of Resident Evil ’s runtime, Cregger pulls off not only the best Resident Evil film but the first great movie game adaptation. Granted, both very low bars to clear, but plaudits nonetheless go to a smartly handled reboot. Goes to show that when you hire the right talent behind and in front of the camera, even a doomed IP can be revived.Resident Evil is out in cinemas now.

Headline: Spain is set to become a leader in green hydrogen in Europe with a 1,000 million project led by Moeve
Body: Moeve has begun construction in Palos de la Frontera, Huelva, on the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley, a project the company presents as the largest of its kind in Europe.It aims to place Spain in a central position in the development of this new energy industry.The first phase, called 'Onuba', will initially have 300 megawatts (MW) of electrolysis capacity, with the option of adding a further 105 MW, and will involve a total investment of more than €1 billion, including the associated infrastructure and a photovoltaic plant for self-consumption.During the development, construction and commissioning phases, Moeve estimates that the project will create more than 8,000 direct jobs, as well as indirect and induced employment along the entire value chain, and will support activity at more than 400 small and medium-sized enterprises and local self-employed workers."Once again, we are turning ambition into a tangible reality", says Moeve's chief executive, Maarten Wetselaar. "Today we are turning the page on green hydrogen pilot projects and moving into the chapter of large-scale construction."Speaking to Euronews, Wetselaar argues that 'Onuba' can help reinforce Spain's role in Europe's energy transition and reduce external dependence. "We need European energy that is decarbonised and produced by us, and that is exactly what this project delivers," he explains.The company expects the facility to produce around 45,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen a year, avoiding some 250,000 tonnes of CO₂ emissions annually.The hydrogen will be used to support more sustainable production of fuels for road, air and maritime transport, as well as contributing to the decarbonisation of other industries.Sánchez hails construction of the plantThe start of construction was marked on Thursday (September 17) in Palos de la Frontera at an event bringing together representatives of the Spanish government, the European Commission, the regional government of Andalusia and the town councils of Palos de la Frontera and Huelva, along with executives from the companies involved in the project.Among those attending were the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, the president of the regional government of Andalusia, Juanma Moreno, the third deputy Prime Minister and minister for the Ecological Transition, Sara Aagesen, and the European Commission's executive vice-president for a Clean, Fair and Competitive Transition, Teresa Ribera.The Prime Minister welcomed what he described as a "huge industrial opportunity" which, in addition to creating jobs, shows that "the energy transition is already driving investment", both public and private."For decades, Spain and Europe have depended too heavily on energy coming from elsewhere. We still do. Unfortunately, every international crisis reminds us of the huge price we are paying for that dependence," he said at the event."We cannot leave our supply at the mercy of unjustified wars, of tensions elsewhere, of the legitimate geopolitical interests of other powers that are not our own, nor, of course, keep picking up the tab for those who turn energy into just another piece in their power games."Spain at the heart of productionFor Moeve, Spain's conditions, and those of Andalusia in particular, offer an advantage for the development of green hydrogen. The company highlights the availability of solar and wind power, land for large renewable facilities and conditions that make it possible to produce renewable electricity at competitive cost."Spain has abundant solar energy, very good wind power and space to build large renewable parks," Wetselaar said. In his view, given that renewable electricity accounts for a large share of the cost of producing green hydrogen, the availability of renewable resources could make the country one of Europe's leading producers.The 'Onuba' project is led by Moeve, which holds a 51 per cent stake in the initiative. Hy24 and Cofides together hold 29 per cent, while Enagás Renovable and Alter Enersun control the remaining 20 per cent.The project has been recognised by the European Union as a Project of Common Interest and has received €304 million in funding from the Spanish government through the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan, financed by the European Union via NextGenerationEU.A 2 GW project'Onuba' is the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley, which Moeve plans to develop to reach a total electrolysis capacity of 2 GW at its energy parks in Palos de la Frontera and San Roque, in the province of Cadiz.The company also intends to connect production in Huelva with other European industrial hubs through pipeline or maritime transport solutions."We want to scale up this plant and connect Huelva with other industrial centres in Europe," Wetselaar explained.The development of hydrogen is part of a broader transformation of Moeve's facilities in Andalusia. The company plans to invest a total of €2.4 billion in energy transition projects in the region, including 'Onuba' and a second-generation biofuels plant that will produce sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel.For Wetselaar, rolling out these projects could have effects that go well beyond energy production. "If Spain scales up, we are talking about thousands of jobs, a significant impact on GDP and, of course, political clout," he said. In his view, the ability to produce and export renewable energy could reshape Spain's energy relationship with the rest of Europe.

Headline: EU sanction deadlock deepens as Luxembourg complicates the picture
Body: Luxembourg has deepened the deadlock over the EU's sanction list renewal, tying a French demand to delist Russian businessman Alisher Usmanov to the case of Mikhail Fridman, who is suing the Grand Duchy over his frozen assets.Last week, Paris joined Slovakia in demanding the removal of Usmanov from the sanctions list pending renewal. Now Luxembourg says that if Usmanov comes off the list, Fridman should too."France risks setting off a race to the bottom, which is the absolute opposite of what the EU is signalling politically, given the Russian escalation in Ukraine but also against EU member states in recent weeks," an EU diplomat told Euronews on condition of anonymity.Slovakia has long pushed to delist both Usmanov and Fridman, oligarchs whom Brussels placed on the sanctions list for being close to the Kremlin. Both men deny the allegations.Under EU rules, the list of 1,600 sanctioned entities and individuals must be renewed with the unanimous support of the bloc's member states every six months. The deadline was set to expire on Tuesday, but was extended by one week to allow time for a diplomatic solution.Earlier this week, it also emerged that France's request to delist Usmanov was intended as a trade for the release of French citizens detained in Azerbaijan, a revelation that caused frustration among other member states.Luxembourg raised the stakes further on Friday, telling a meeting of EU ambassadors that if France succeeds in delisting Usmanov, Fridman should be delisted as well.Fridman is locked in an ongoing legal battle with Luxembourg over its implementation of EU sanctions, seeking compensation for his frozen assets in the country, which are estimated to run to around $16bn. He has also sued the Council of the EU before the European General Court.For other member states, Luxembourg's latest demand illustrates exactly why national interests should not be allowed to shape individual sanctions listings, since doing so risks a domino effect in which other capitals begin pushing their own agendas.EU ambassadors will reconvene on Monday. A Luxembourg official did not reply to Euronews' request for comment."Putin only speaks the language of power. If Paris really wants to push this through, France risks making the EU look weak," the diplomat added.

Headline: Russians vote in elections with no party opposing Putin or war in Ukraine
Body: Russians began voting Friday in a tightly controlled three-day election that will likely see President Vladimir Putin tighten his grip on power after 26 years at the helm, as Russia's all-out war in Ukraine continues well into its fifth year.Only parties backing Putin and his war in Ukraine are on the ballot: the ruling United Russia, the Communist Party, A Just Russia, the nationalist LDPR and New People.Yabloko, Russia's only publicly anti-war party still operating inside the country, was barred from participating. The party saw a surge in social media support, particularly among young people, after it was initially allowed to stand.An unnamed European diplomat said the elections were "pretty much a sham" but described them as "a ritual the Kremlin considers necessary," adding that it would seek to ensure a high turnout.Independent observers have previously documented the use of state resources to influence results, including bussing voters to polling stations, pressuring employees of state institutions to vote for the ruling party, and pushing online voting as it is easier to monitor and control."As in the Soviet era, elections must demonstrate the loyalty of citizens," Russian political scientist and Head of Analysis of Transformation Processes at the NEST Centre Nikolai Petrov said.The election will fill 450 State Duma seats and the governorships of 11 federal regions, with the country's only remaining anti-war party excluded from the ballot and fears of mobilisation overshadowing the vote.Running from 18 to 20 September, the election will also choose deputies to regional legislatures in 39 federal subjects.Voters will choose eight of the 11 regional heads directly, while regional parliaments will elect the remaining three. Polling stations have been opened at Russian border crossings with Poland and the three Baltic states.Half of the 450 Duma seats will be allocated through nationwide party lists and the other half through single-member constituencies.Voting in Russian elections is also taking place in parts of Ukraine occupied by Moscow's troops, a move that neither Kyiv nor the West recognises as legitimate.Kremlin pushes pro-army narrativeAlmost 200 candidates in these elections have taken part in Russia's war in Ukraine, according to electoral commissions.The Kremlin has promoted them as part of Russia's "true elite," but the initiative is primarily a recruitment tool to boost Moscow's troops on the front lines, with few standing any real chance of being elected.Ahead of the vote, Putin urged Russians to vote to show troops that "behind our fighters stand millions of people" and to deliver an "answer to those who want to weaken Russia".Meanwhile, Russians fear another wave of military mobilisation, despite Putin personally denying plans for a call-up twice in three days in September alone.Independent Russian media have counted 17 official denials of an imminent mobilisation. Russia called up 300,000 reservists in the autumn of 2022 in a move that triggered significant public alarm and a mass departure of men of fighting age from the country.Tatiana Stanovaya of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Centre, which is banned in Russia, said she considered a new draft unlikely."They have put so much effort into persuading Russians not to worry about this," she said. "I would be very, very surprised if it happened."In the streets of Moscow today, few visible signs indicate an election is even under way.Fears of mobilisation have been further compounded by Ukrainian long-range drone strikes on Russian infrastructure in a bid to defund its war machine, causing fuel shortages and economic losses running into billions of euros.Many Russians feel the attacks break what Stanovaya described as the Kremlin's tacit bargain with the population over the war.In prison, in exile, deadAll of Putin's main political opponents are in prison, in exile or dead. Alexei Navalny, his most prominent challenger, died in a Russian penal colony in 2024.Putin's political opponents have mostly been driven into exile and his main opponent Alexei Navalny died in an Arctic prison in 2024.Russia's exiled opposition has urged anti-Kremlin Russians not to boycott the elections but instead vote "against Putin's party".Navalny's widow Yulia Navalnaya also called on anti-war Russians to cast their ballots at noon on Sunday.Yabloko — which critics say outlived its usefulness after the Kremlin allowed it to exist for many years to create a pretence of political plurality as a catch-all for liberal and discontented voters — disagreed, arguing that it was better not to vote."You are suggesting that we once again go, like sheep, dancing to their tune, and vote for those who have caused the deaths of people in Russia and Ukraine?" party chairman Nikolay Rybakov said this week.'Mad printer'Parliamentary elections were previously a source of significant political tension: in 2011, mass fraud during the Duma vote and Putin's return to the presidency from the post of prime minister triggered the largest street protests in Russia since the collapse of the Soviet Union.Putin has ruled Russia since 1999 and his United Russia party has dominated politics since the early 2000s.Under Putin, the Duma's powers have been substantially curtailed, reducing it largely to approving legislation initiated by the Kremlin — a role that has earned it the popular nickname "the mad printer" to mock the speed at which it rubber-stamped highly restrictive and controversial laws.Any criticism of the war is treated under Russian law as "discrediting the army" and can carry a prison sentence.Older voters remain among Putin's strongest supporters, although many still complain about living standards.

Headline: A new wave of listings: Tashkent prepares companies for global markets
Body: Uzbekistan is preparing to bring some of its biggest state-linked companies to public markets, with national telecommunications operator Uztelecom now the most advanced candidate for an international listing.The programme extends across telecommunications, aviation, banking and energy and is designed to attract more private and international capital while bringing major companies under the transparency and governance requirements expected by public investors.For international investors, that could open access to some of Uzbekistan’s largest corporate assets. For Uzbekistan, it is a test of whether its capital-market reforms can move beyond UzNIF’s London debut to a broader pipeline of publicly traded companies.The process is being driven through the National Investment Fund of Uzbekistan (UzNIF), managed by Franklin Templeton, which holds stakes in 13 major Uzbek companies and made its own London market debut in May.The next step: listing the companiesUztelecom is furthest along in the potential IPO pipeline, according to Marius Dan, CEO for Central Asia at Templeton Global Investments.The company is already listed on the Tashkent Stock Exchange. UzNIF is considering an international listing and an increase in the number of shares available on the domestic market.An international offering could allow more investors to buy shares in the company and could also provide fresh capital for future investment.Responding to questions from Euronews, Dan said preparations included assessing Uztelecom’s financial reporting, governance and operational readiness.Five equity-adviser selection processes are also under way for Uzbekistan Airways, Uztelecom, Regional Electric Networks, the National Electric Grid of Uzbekistan and Sanoat Qurilish Bank (SQB).“Over the next 24 to 36 months, roughly 78% of the net asset value of the fund will move from unlisted to listed companies,” Dan said.That would mean most of UzNIF’s value would eventually be held in companies whose shares are publicly traded.A presidential decree provides for six UzNIF portfolio companies to be listed by the end of 2028. The fund said no final decision has yet been taken on the timing or sequence of individual transactions.Changing how companies are runUzNIF and Franklin Templeton are also changing corporate governance across the portfolio, including the composition of supervisory boards and the way companies plan, manage finances and report performance.“We've made changes across all 13 companies. We've appointed the members of our investment team and recruited 10 very reputable international directors that were appointed on the supervisory boards in certain cases of more than one company,” Dan explained.Ten independent non-executive directors have been elected across the portfolio, while 11 of the 13 companies now have supervisory boards on which independent directors and Franklin Templeton representatives form a majority.Nine transformation plans have been completed, with four more expected in the coming months.At Uzbekistan Airways, for example, the fund has identified 120 initiatives covering growth, efficiency, profitability, customer experience and expansion.Those changes are important because a stock-market listing involves more than selling shares. Companies also need reliable accounts, clearer decision-making and governance structures that can withstand outside scrutiny.Inside UzNIF’s €2.28bn portfolioUzNIF’s net asset value stood at around €2.28bn as of 31 July 2026.For the first half of 2026, the fund reported €147mn in net profit, including a €156mn fair-value gain and €24mn in dividend income.Energy-related holdings represented around 37% of the fund’s net asset value.Dan said a new regulated asset base framework was among the factors affecting valuations at several energy companies. The system determines how regulated utilities can earn returns on infrastructure investment and how tariffs are calculated.Initial tariff adjustments took effect on 1 August, with further details expected by the end of 2026 or in the first quarter of 2027.IPOs could bring fresh capitalThe potential listings could also bring money directly into the companies rather than simply allowing existing shareholders to sell stakes.Dan said the government would have priority if it chose to sell shares, while UzNIF could also sell part of its own holdings if needed to ensure sufficient market liquidity.“The companies will also have priority to raise capital as part of these IPOs because these are all incredibly exciting assets. They have significant capex programs, more investments that are needed,” he said.The distinction is important: selling existing shares changes ownership, while issuing new shares can give companies money for aircraft, telecom networks, power infrastructure or other investment.The final structure of each transaction will be decided later.2026 is the first full year in which Franklin Templeton has managed UzNIF, after taking over in May 2025.Dan said this year’s results should provide a fuller basis for assessing profitability and future dividend capacity. The first UzNIF dividend would be considered in 2028, based on the fund’s 2027 financial results.

Headline: Australian government breaks silence on EU 'associate member' pipe dream
Body: In comments to Euronews, the Australian government has responded to European Parliament President Roberta Mestola’s hint that Australia and New Zealand could also be invited to be "associate members" of the European Union.While Australia's relationship with the EU has “never been stronger or more important”, the spokesperson said Canberra is focusing on finalising the EU-Australia trade deal “which will bring us even closer together”.“This once-in-a-generation deal gives our farmers, exporters, producers and businesses access to 27 EU countries and 450 million consumers,” the spokesperson said.“Australia is a trading nation, and in a time of global uncertainty, deepening our trading partnerships makes economic sense.”A spokesperson from the New Zealand government also clarified in comments to Reuters that "there have been no discussions with the EU about New Zealand ⁠becoming an associate member."It follows the news of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen opening the door to Canada to become an EU associate member at her landmark State of the European Union address in Strasbourg on Wednesday.On top of this, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is expected to meet European Council President António Costa and von der Leyen on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly on Monday in New York.European Commission Deputy Chief Spokesperson Arianna Podestà said that the meeting would be a stocktaking exercise between Canberra and Brussels as the duo cooperate with "very closely" on matters such as trade.When pressed as to whether the discussion would focus on EU associate membership, she said: "We will not be speculating about other countries" aside from the confirmed news of Canada's invitation.Negotiations on the EU-Australia trade deal were concluded last March. However, both sides still have to go through a ratification process, which might be troubled by farmers’ concerns on both sides over the meat quotas included in the agreement.The deal sets quotas for sensitive products, including Australian beef (30,600 tonnes) and mutton/lamb (25,000 tonnes) per year.But EU farmers complain that the quotas pile up with preferential access granted in other trade agreements, such as the Mercosur deal, while the Australian beef sector was seeking some 50,000 tonnes for its meat.The deal has also faced significant pushback from the Australian opposition, with the Liberal-National Coalition calling on Australian Trade Minister Don Farrell to renegotiate.Australia ranks as the world’s second-largest beef exporter after Brazil. Talks between Brussels and Canberra had previously broken down in 2023 over disagreements about agricultural quotas.

Headline: South Korean president urges Trump dialogue with Pyongyang
Body: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Friday that his US counterpart Donald Trump "clearly" wants to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang and that he was "urging" him to do so.Lee told reporters at the presidential Blue House that South Korea was continuing "preliminary coordination efforts" to facilitate talks between the North and the US, adding that a meeting "remains difficult" but was "not impossible.""I cannot say for certain how likely it is, but it is also clear that we must make every possible effort to turn that possibility into reality," he said.Trump announced in August that he intended to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un later this year as he once again touted the pair's relationship, although he gave no further details on the plan - which would be their first meeting since Trump's first term in the White House."You know what, the fact that I get along with him, that's a good thing not a bad thing. He has 57 very powerful nuclear weapons. Should have never allowed it to happen," Trump said at the time.North Korea, which has reestablished increasingly close ties with Russia in recent years, has offered little response to Trump's comments.IranLee also told the media that South Korea would not deploy troops to the Middle East in a way that could involve the country in conflict."There will be no involvement or intervention in the war. We will not deploy troops or military assets in that manner," he said, adding that South Korea would "carry out the minimum necessary activities" to defend its merchant ships and oil shipping routes in the region.Seoul had reportedly been weighing deploying troops to the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway and crucial oil and gas transit chokepoint that has been at the centre of tensions between Washington and Tehran since the Iran war broke out in late February.It comes after Trump in August announced that he had ordered US forces to scale back "costly" joint military drills with South Korea, which he said sent an "inappropriate and hostile" signal to Pyongyang."While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, 'No thanks!'" Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social of his decision.Kim's sister slams US drillsHopes for an imminent meeting may have been doused slightly after Kim's powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong, hit out at the US over recent military drills in the Western Pacific, which she labelled a "US-led war rehearsal.""The present situation, in which new records are set in terms of practical action hostile toward the DPRK, stresses the need to break records in our responsive action, proportional or more offensive in its nature," Kim Yo Jong said in a statement shared by North Korea's KCNA state news agency on Friday.She added: "Our will to defend our sovereignty will be expressed in clearer action and there will be never ever change in the course of intensifying the nuclear war deterrence."The US, South Korea and Japan wrapped up Exercise Freedom Edge 26, which US Pacific Command said advanced "trilateral readiness across the Indo-Pacific," on 11 September.

Headline: Police fire shots in the air as thousands of migrants moved to new facility in Ceuta
Body: On Friday, Spanish authorities began moving thousands of migrants to a new facility in Ceuta, with police struggling to maintain order as people fought to secure a spot at the new site after weeks of living on the beaches and streets.The operation, which saw migrants moved from the Trampolín and Benítez beaches to the port of Ceuta, got underway shortly after 6:30 am, with several Civil Guard patrols deployed to gather people and escort them on foot to the new settlement, around two kilometres away.The transfer quickly became difficult to manage.As the first groups from Trampolín beach reached the area of Benítez beach, the number of migrants sharply increased as they joined up with those staying there, with some breaking into a run as officers worked to contain the crowd.The tented facility - which reportedly has beds and showers - in Ceuta's port has capacity for around 1,700 people, while it is estimated that there were more than 4,000 migrants coming from the two beaches. An exact figure will not be known until all transfers have been completed and all the migrants have been registered.It is the fifth temporary reception space set up by the Spanish government to deal with the crisis, which began in late July when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta from Morocco.The port campThe new camp has been surrounded by controversy and has also faced legal challenges.On Thursday, Spain's National Court rejected a request from the Unified Police Union (SUP) for an interim injunction that had sought to halt the installation of tents at the port, which is considered critical infrastructure for the city.Ana Alarcón, a spokesperson for SUP, said on Friday that "the port is not a safe place.""It is not a solution in terms of security (…). If anything happens, we are going to demand that people be held responsible," she told Antena 3.For his part, the vice-president of Ceuta, Alejandro Ramírez, accused the government of improvising and said everything had been "done in a rush.""The number of incidents in the port has gone from 80 to more than 1,000 in 50 days," he told Onda Cero.Foreign Minister seeks to 'anchor' Ceuta and Melilla to the EUIt comes after Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares presented a package of measures to the Committee of Ministers this week aimed at moving towards the full integration of Ceuta and Melilla into the European Union - a plan that he has already outlined to the presidents of both autonomous cities.The measures include establishing a permanent seat for Ceuta and another for Melilla in the European Committee of the Regions, as well as increasing Frontex's presence in both territories, according to a statement from the Foreign Ministry.The government is also working to ensure specific treatment for Ceuta and Melilla in the EU's next Multiannual Financial Framework.In addition, the Foreign Ministry has begun coordinating with the ministries of Economy, Finance, Agriculture and Territorial Policy to advance the integration of Ceuta and Melilla into the EU Customs Union and to determine the most appropriate arrangements given their particular geographical and socio-economic circumstances.

Headline: Expected years in retirement: For how long do Europeans receive their pensions?
Body: Retirement ages are rising across Europe as people live longer, but there are significant differences between countries in how many years people are expected to live after entering retirement.As of 2024, the retirement age in the EU is 64.7 years for men and 64 years for women according to the OECD.As people become eligible to receive a pension once they reach retirement age, Euronews Business used life expectancy at the retirement age in each country.They can expect to receive a pension for that number of years if they meet other requirements such as the required number of years in work. Of course, some pensioners continue working after reaching the retirement age.18.4 years for men, 21.8 years for womenMen in the EU are expected to live for an average of 18.4 years after retirement, compared with 21.8 years for women. These figures are based on life expectancy at their retirement ages, according to Eurostat and OECD data from 2024.For men, the expected number of years receiving a pension ranges from 14.7 years in Bulgaria and Hungary to 27.3 years in Turkey. Within the EU, Luxembourg has the longest period, with men expected to receive a pension for 22 years.This gap mainly stems from two factors: differences in retirement ages and life expectancy.Male pensioners in Greece (21 years), France (20.7), Slovenia (20.7), Switzerland (20.4) and Malta (20.2) are also expected to spend more than 20 years in retirement.The expected number of years in retirement is also above the EU average of 18.4 years in Cyprus (19.8), Sweden (19.4), Portugal (19.3), Belgium (19.1), Ireland (19), the UK (19), Austria (18.8) and Finland (18.7).Germany has the lowest retirement years among major economiesThis shows that, except for Germany, men in the other major European economies are expected to spend more years in retirement than the EU average. In Germany, the figure is 1.1 years below the EU average, creating a significant gap with France, Italy and Spain.By contrast, in addition to Bulgaria and Hungary, male pensioners are expected to spend the fewest years in retirement in Latvia, Romania and Lithuania, all below 16 years.For women, the expected number of years in retirement is 21.8 in the EU, while it ranges from 18.6 years in Hungary to 34.5 years in Turkey. It is also above 25 years in Luxembourg.Women in Slovenia, Greece, France, Spain, Switzerland, Malta, Italy, Portugal, Cyprus and Finland are also projected to spend more than 22 years in retirement, meaning they are expected to receive a pension for over 22 years.Among women, not only Germany (20.3) but also the UK (21) is below the EU average.Besides Hungary, women are expected to spend less than 20 years in retirement in several countries. These include Bulgaria (18.8), Romania (19.1), the Netherlands (19.2), Croatia (19.6), Denmark (19.7), Latvia (19.8) and Iceland (19.8).Retirement age and expected age at deathAs of 2024, Turkey is an outlier among the 32 European countries, with a current retirement age of 52 for men and 49 for women.Apart from Turkey, retirement ages range from 62 to 67 years for men and from 60 to 67 years for women across the other countries on the list.The retirement age in the EU is 64.7 years for men and 64 years for women. Men are expected to live to 83.1 years, compared with 85.8 years for women.Gap between men and women at retirementOn average in the EU, women are expected to spend 3.4 years longer in retirement than men. This gap ranges from 1.6 years in Iceland to 7.2 years in Turkey.The gap is also four years or more in Estonia, Lithuania, Latvia, Bulgaria, Romania and Poland. However, labour force participation rates in these countries are comparatively lower.Another aspect is the gender pension gap. Across OECD countries, women receive 23% less in pensions than men on average, while the gap reaches 37% in the UK.Labour exit age and TurkeyHowever, the average effective labour market exit age can differ from the retirement age. For example, in the EU, the retirement age for men is 64.7 years, while the average exit age is 63.8 years. For women, the exit age is 62.9 years, compared with a retirement age of 64.The most striking difference between the retirement age and labour market exit age is in Turkey. While men can retire at 52, their average exit age is 60.8. For women, the figures are 49 and 60.5 years. Expected years after the labour market exit would be 18.2 for men and 22.6 for women in Turkey. This suggests that although expected years in retirement are the highest in Turkey, the figure would be significantly lower when the labour market exit age is considered.Pensions are the main source of income for older Europeans and pension levels vary widely across Europe, both in nominal terms and in purchasing power.

Headline: Russia seizes control over assets of Nestle, French firms
Body: A little-known Russian company called L.E.V. Management has been handed temporary control of 16 businesses linked to Nestlé, Auchan and several other Western groups.President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on Thursday placing the management of stakes and shares in the 16 Russian companies under the control of the firm.The move tightens Moscow’s control over Western-owned assets amid its confrontation with Western countries over sanctions imposed following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine."Of course, one of the factors taken into account when making this decision was that these are unfriendly countries, which are currently most actively involved in military operations against our country," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said at a press conference on Friday.The businesses concerned include Nestlé Russia, Nestlé Kuban, French retailer Auchan’s Russian subsidiary, two local FM Logistic entities and Le Monlid, which operates the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain under the Lemana Pro brand.The measure does not formally confiscate the businesses or change their ownership, according to Russian lawyers cited by business newspaper Kommersant. However, temporary administration has previously preceded the sale or transfer of Western-owned assets to Russian buyers.L.E.V. Management was registered in Moscow in October 2024, and its shareholders are not publicly disclosed. According to Kommersant, the company showed no active business operations in its publicly available 2025 accounts.Andrei Krayushkin was appointed its general director on 10 September, one week before the decree was issued. Independent outlet Novaya Gazeta Europe reported that his name and date of birth match those of a Russian interior ministry major general. This has not been independently confirmed.Most Western companies quickly sold or ring-fenced their Russian businesses after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Russia has since made it increasingly difficult for foreign companies to leave, requiring presidential approval for deals and placing some assets under temporary administration.In a statement, Nestlé said it was “assessing the situation and its options”.“Nestlé is committed to taking all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders, particularly its employees,” it said.Nestlé has around 7,000 employees and six factories in Russia. It has suspended most non-essential sales, imports and exports, as well as advertising and capital investment, while continuing to supply products it considers essential.Jean-Philippe Bertschy of Swiss investment bank Vontobel said the financial impact was expected to be limited because Russia now accounts for around 1% of Nestlé’s group sales, down from approximately 2% before the war.Auchan Retail Russia told Russian business news outlet RBC that it had asked the authorities to clarify the decree and would comment further after receiving more information. It said its stores and other facilities continued to operate normally.Auchan employs around 30,000 people and operates approximately 230 stores and an online business in Russia.Lemana Pro told Kommersant that it had not yet received official information from the authorities and continued to operate normally.Leroy Merlin’s French parent company, Adeo, transferred control of its Russian business to local management in 2023. The operation was subsequently rebranded as Lemana Pro and now has 112 stores.FM Logistic had not publicly commented at the time of publication.The move echoes Moscow’s 2023 takeover of Danone’s Russian business. It was initially placed under the management of Yakub Zakriev, a nephew of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov, before Danone sold the operation at a substantial discount in 2024.

Headline: Barcelona has a bold plan to protect its vulnerable coastline – and it could be prize-winning
Body: This summer, Barcelona recorded its highest temperature in more than a century. It’s part of a worrying trend: the Mediterranean is warming around 20 per cent faster than the global average, while record-warm waters are fuelling stronger storms, sea level rise and coastal erosion.The collapse of a stretch of a storm-hit promenade on Barcelona’s northeast coast in 2023 underlined the need for climate resilient infrastructure. Around 70 per cent of the artificial sand added in 2010 has since disappeared.“Cities like ours must learn to live with climate change while protecting the places and communities that define them,” says Jaume Collboni, Mayor of Barcelona. The Spanish city’s ambitious coastal resilience project is now in the running for a prestigious environmental award.Barcelona is a finalist for The Earthshot PrizeBarcelona has been announced as a finalist for The Earthshot Prize in the Revive Our Oceans category. First launched in 2020 by Prince William, the awards recognise environmental solutions to “repair” the planet.The Spanish city is pouring €150 million into restoring one of Europe’s most intensively used urban coastlines. The project will create 22 hectares – roughly the size of 31 football pitches – of climate- and heat-adapted public space along the Sant Martí seafront, integrating restored marine habitats, natural coastal protection and waterfront access.It is hoped that it will become a blueprint for coastal cities around the world facing increasingly severe sea-level rise, stronger storms, flooding, biodiversity loss and extreme heat – something The Earthshot Prize will help with by boosting visibility and knowledge-sharing opportunities. “Every year, our Finalists give me renewed optimism,” says Prince William, President and Founder of The Earthshot Prize. “They show us that, even as the environmental challenges remain urgent, extraordinary people around the world are already proving that progress is possible.” ‘Climate-resilient infrastructure designed for everyone to enjoy’Instead of repeatedly rebuilding its vulnerable northeast shoreline, Barcelona is intentionally moving parts of the waterfront inland, including relocating a popular seafront football pitch, and moving the sea walls back. This will allow for wider beaches that act as natural buffers, absorbing wave energy and creating more space for storms, erosion and rising sea levels, as well as providing a vital refuge during increasingly severe heatwaves.Scheduled for completion in spring 2027, Passeig Marítim de la Mar Bella will encourage sustainable use of the coastline while boosting air quality and biodiversity with a 15,000-square-metre linear park.Visitors will be able to stroll along a 12-metre-wide pedestrian path or cycle down bike lanes – stretching all the way to the Fòrum – resting at energy-producing solar pergolas along the way.“The choice facing coastal cities is no longer whether to adapt, but how,” says María Buhigas, Chief City Architect of Barcelona. “This is not a defensive structure added to the edge of the city; it is a new piece of climate-resilient public infrastructure designed for everyone to enjoy.”Who else is in the running for The Earthshot Prize 2026?From nearly 7,000 nominations across 169 countries, 15 finalists have been selected for The Earthshot Prize.Each is aligned with one of the five ‘Earthshots’: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate – with winners in each category poised to receive a £1 million (€1.17m) prize.For the first time, positive tipping points were part of the selection process, rewarding innovations where progress builds on itself, costs fall with scale and recovery becomes self-propelling.Other European finalists include Ørsted (Fix Our Climate) – the Danish renewable energy company behind some of the world’s largest offshore wind projects – and PFAS-Free France (Build a Waste-Free World), the policy and civil-society campaign that helped securing, and is now implementing, France’s ‘forever chemical’ phaseout in  everyday products. Further afield, Argentina’s Satellites on Fire is being recognised for its AI-powered wildfire detection and alert platform, alongside zero-emission shipping alliance ZEMBA, and India’s electric three-wheeler pioneer Mahindra Last Mile Mobility.Reconnecting a vast mountain landscape across Canada and the US so wildlife can move freely once again, conservation collaboration Yellowstone to Yukon is among the contenders for the Protect and Restore Nature prize.“Seeing solutions work gives us all confidence to act. When they succeed, they inspire others and accelerate change,” says Prince William.The five winners of The Earthshot Prize 2026 will be announced at an awards night in Mumbai, India, on 17 November.

Headline: Spain leads quantum computing: 'Made in Spain' chips manufactured in Barcelona
Body: The Spanish National Research Council (CSIC) has inaugurated in Barcelona the new Quantum Nanofabrication Area of the Clean Room at the Barcelona Microelectronics Institute (IMB-CNM), regarded as the largest research infrastructure of its kind in Spain.The new space will make it possible to manufacture and analyse devices and circuits on the nanoscale for the development of quantum technologies and advanced microelectronics.The facility, which has involved an investment of more than six million euros, is funded by the PERTE Chip and the Complementary Plan for Quantum Communications, through Next Generation EU funds.The area includes state-of-the-art equipment, notably the most advanced electron-beam lithography system in Spain, as well as microscopes and metrology tools capable of inspecting structures with nanometric dimensions.This equipment will be available to researchers and companies, and will help advance the design, manufacture and prototyping of technologies that can be applied in fields such as quantum computing and communications, health, energy and security.With this new infrastructure, CSIC aims to strengthen Spain's capacity in semiconductors and quantum technologies and to facilitate the transition from research to industrial development.The initiative also forms part of the organisation's strategy to consolidate its position in the quantum field, which includes the creation of the QuARC-CSIC Quantum Science and Technologies Centre.A new centre to concentrate quantum talentThe Spanish National Research Council (CSIC), a public research organisation attached to the Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities, has announced the creation of the QuARC-CSIC Quantum Science and Technologies Centre (Quantum Advanced Research Center). The new centre will bring together research groups from different CSIC institutes with the aim of fostering cutting-edge research, attracting talent, opening up new lines of work and strengthening collaboration with other groups, both in Spain and abroad.CSIC president Eloísa del Pino presented the Quantum Science and Technologies Strategy, the long-term planning document that underpins the launch of the new centre. Del Pino explained that the development of quantum technologies is advancing rapidly worldwide, with strategic investment in Europe, the United States and China that is shaping an increasingly competitive ecosystem. For this reason, she argued for the need for a new organisational model that will allow CSIC to implement a long-term strategy and strengthen Spain's quantum ecosystem.According to Del Pino, QuARC-CSIC is an opportunity to consolidate a stable, nationally leading structure devoted exclusively to this field, at a time when the institution is preparing for what she has called "the third quantum revolution": the shift from laboratory experimentation to the integration of these technologies into industry and society.A headquarters in Madrid bringing together physics, computer science, mathematics, engineering and chemistryThe new centre will bring together CSIC's existing capabilities in quantum sciences, with research lines spanning physics, computer science, mathematics, engineering and chemistry. It will have a physical headquarters in Madrid, located in the former premises of the Cajal Institute, now part of the Cajal Neuroscience Centre.The choice of this location reflects the concentration of leading quantum groups that CSIC has in the Madrid region, 13 research groups belonging to ten institutes, which will make it possible to pool existing capacities and create favourable conditions for interaction among researchers.The centre will also be strengthened by the recruitment of new staff through competitive selection processes already launched, in which several posts have been reserved for this speciality, and will serve as a hub for research, training and collaboration with other centres.

Headline: Brussels seeks 'credible' outcome in EU-China talks after key negotiators’ call
Body: The European Commission stepped up pressure on China on Thursday, calling for tangible results with Beijing following a one-hour video call between Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao.The EU executive hopes to secure commitments from Beijing to rebalance the trade relationship, as the bloc's trade deficit with China has been widening by €1 billion a day.However, Beijing wants to secure access to the EU’s market of 450 million consumers, resisting calls from the Europeans to reduce its exports.“While genuine engagement remains a priority, it is equally important that first concrete outcomes are delivered at the second session of the Trade and Investment Council in Beijing in October, which the Commissioner will co-chair – a signal that we are moving from rhetoric to results,” the Commission said in a statement after the call.“That outcome needs to be credible,” the statement added.The EU-China Trade and Investment Council was launched in June as a dialogue between the two sides, with the Commission setting October as a deadline to reach tangible results.During the call on Thursday, Šefčovič and Wentao discussed market access on both sides and Chinese export controls on rare earths.China has a near-monopoly over the production and processing of these strategic materials, which are essential to the EU’s green technology, defence and automotive industries, giving Beijing significant leverage in the negotiations.The EU is seeking assurances that China will not halt its exports of rare earths again, a year after blocking them amid a trade war with the US. Securing the necessary export licences is essential for EU businesses.EU leaders expect resultsThe coming weeks will be crucial for the negotiations, with EU officials expected to make another trip to China for technical discussions before Šefčovič himself travels to Beijing on 8–9 October.In her State of the Union address to MEPs on Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also pushed for concrete results in the EU-China talks.“Words are good. But deeds are better,” she said, making clear that the EU was ready to use all its trade defence instruments to rebalance the trade relationship.China is also expected to feature prominently on the agenda when EU leaders meet in October. They have tasked the Commission with securing tangible results from its dialogue with Beijing.In an interview with Euronews, Šefčovič also made clear that, without a “deliverable” to present to EU leaders, “the political interest would be to look for the solution through other instruments.”The EU has several trade defence instruments such as anti-dumping duties or tariffs against unfair subsidies.A diversification tool is also in the pipeline, aimed at reducing EU firms’ reliance on Chinese critical minerals for strategic technologies by helping them diversify their sources of supply.Such a move would come as relations between Beijing and Brussels remain strained, following the Commission’s introduction of several legislative proposals aimed at protecting the EU market. One of them would introduce a European preference for products made in Europe, prompting China to threaten retaliatory measures.Last summer, China also urged its companies to stop cooperating with the Commission in antitrust investigations, after the EU executive opened a probe in May into e-commerce giant JD.com over concerns about subsidies.

Headline: Turkish actor and World Cup star among 16 held in Istanbul drug raids
Body: A Turkish actor and a footballer who helped the national football team finish third at the 2002 World Cup were among 16 people detained in anti-drug raids across Istanbul on Friday as part of a probe into celebrities, venue operators and social media influencers.Hasan Şaş, who earned 40 caps for the Turkish national team and played for Galatasaray during its most successful European period, and actor Aras Bulut İynemli, known abroad for Netflix Turkey productions, were detained alongside actor Melis Sezen, rapper Sefo and 12 others.Authorities had not located two further suspects by the time of publication.Bakırköy Chief Public Prosecutor's Office said the investigation concerns allegations of using narcotic and psychotropic substances, facilitating their use and mediating their supply.Authorities ordered biological examinations alongside the searches and detentions.Others detained include actors Nilperi Şahinkaya, Melisa Şenolsun and Afra Saraçoğlu, YouTuber Melis İşiten, sports journalist Yağız Sabuncuoğlu, model Yeliz Yeşilçimen, content creator Aydan Osmanlı, singer Anıl Durmuş and businesswoman Hande Demir.Friday's operation is the latest in a series of similar anti-narcotics raids targeting well-known figures in Istanbul since late 2025.In December 2025, singer Aleyna Tilki, actor İrem Sak and influencer Danla Bilic were among those taken into custody and later released after biological samples were collected.In May of this year, authorities detained 20 people from a list of 25 suspects that included actors Serenay Sarıkaya and Onur Tuna, singer Mabel Matiz, and television presenter Mirgün Cabas.In July, searches and biological sampling were carried out on a further 25 suspects including singers Sıla Gençoğlu and İlyas Yalçıntaş and producer Fatih Aksoy. Yalçıntaş was subsequently arrested.

Headline: Russia shares AI-generated Putin selfie as use of artificial content spreads among Europe's politicians
Body: The Russian embassy in South Africa has shared a picture that appears to show Russian President Vladimir Putin taking a group selfie with the 10 BRICS world leaders during September's summit.The 18th BRICS Summit took place in New Delhi, India, on 12 and 13 September.The verified X account posted the picture, which garnered more than 2 million views, alongside the caption "BRICS is a superpower".However, this selfie is not real.No credible news organisation has published the image as real, and the official website of the summit did not share it either.The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, has also run it through image detectors, which revealed it to be AI-generated. For instance, after running the image through OpenAI, the tool revealed to have found "a SynthID watermark that originated from OpenAI".Furthermore, the official logo and slogan of BRICS India 2026 do not match those portrayed in the AI-generated picture.This summit's theme was "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability", while the AI-generated picture states "Stronger together for a brighter tomorrow".At no moment does the Russian embassy in South Africa disclose that the picture was generated using AI.A rising phenomenon among politiciansWhile the image appears harmless, it is becoming increasingly common for European politicians and public institutions to publish AI-generated images without labelling them as such.Sometimes they are used for disingenuous purposes, and often they can erode trust among the public.Recently, the leader of the Portuguese far-right Chega party, André Ventura, posted an AI-generated video of a woman with six fingers, seemingly to push an anti-immigration narrative.The video depicts a hijabi woman supposedly looking up and down at a white, non-hijabi woman wearing a short dress, alongside the caption "if it were the other way around, it'd be racist and xenophobic. They come to our countries... Why do they not get used to respecting our values?"Despite many comments from users stating the video was clearly AI, Ventura didn't disclose that the video was AI-generated, and it remains active on his profile as of the time of publication.The phenomenon of politicians using AI-generated content to publicise their policies isn't confined to Europe: high-profile figures such as US President Donald Trump are infamously using more and more AI-generated images and videos in their communications and on their social media channels.What are the consequences of politicians' AI use?A 2026 study from the European non-profit AI Forensics showed that AI is being used not only to create photorealistic images "but also for stylised, cartoonish imagery to reinforce key campaign messages, including anti-immigrant narratives".The research, which focused on the French municipal elections, found that the use of AI remains most pronounced among right and far-right parties, and that the lack of disclosure could put public trust in the electoral process in danger.Most of the material looked at by researchers carried no explicit AI disclaimer, even when watermarks were present. Since August of this year, the EU's AI Act has generally required realistic AI-generated or manipulated material to be clearly disclosed as such."Providers of generative AI have to ensure that AI-generated content is identifiable," the Act states. "On top of that, certain AI-generated content should be clearly and visibly labelled, namely deepfakes and text published with the purpose to inform the public on matters of public interest."

Headline: Portuguese prime minister outlines plan to tackle rising living costs without changing VAT
Body: "Here I am, putting myself on the line," said the Portuguese prime minister, Luís Montenegro, in a televised address to the nation on Thursday night. Timed for the main evening news bulletins, the speech was used to set out the measures against the cost of living, in particular those triggered by rising fuel prices. Some elements of the plan were already known.  This is the case of the pension bonus and the cut to personal income tax (IRS) bands, announced last week in Parliament when the government survived a no-confidence motion. But they have now been formally approved by the Council of Ministers.Montenegro explained how the pension bonus will be applied: 200 euros for pensions up to 537 euros; 150 euros for pensions up to 1,704 euros and 100 euros for pensions up to 1,611 euros. The amount will be paid in December.The Council of Ministers also approved a reduction in six IRS bands, with the remaining bands also affected because of the tax’s progressive nature.  According to Montenegro, this measure is aimed above all at "middle-class households".At the same time, the government’s portal published the table of IRS withholdings, with simulations, (source in Portuguese) but this is still a draft law that must be approved by the Assembly of the Republic.On fuel price increases, the main strategy will continue to be the discount on the tax on petroleum products (ISP). Montenegro says this discount will remain in place until the end of the year, amounting to a total reduction of around 1.3 billion euros.The prime minister also said that this discount "will probably rise to 25 cents as early as next week", from the current 23 cents, in anticipation of further increases in fuel prices.The government will also once again support the sectors most exposed to rising fuel costs, with a total package of 38 million euros. This support covers taxis, freight transport, social solidarity institutions, firefighters’ associations and farmers.  The solidarity bottled gas scheme will also remain in place.The package also includes extending the green rail pass to the urban areas of Lisbon and Porto. The pass, costing 20 euros a month, allows travel on all rail lines except the Alfa Pendular high-speed service.Government steers clear of VATThe speech also served for Luís Montenegro to spell out what he will not do: tamper with the consumption tax, VAT."I will not swap cutting VAT on some foodstuffs from 6% to zero for the 800 million euros we are returning to families through IRS and the pension supplement," said the Portuguese prime minister.The measure has long been demanded by the Socialist Party (PS, centre-left) and by Chega (far right). This has also been the strategy in several European countries to tackle the rising cost of living."I have every respect for the choices of the opposition parties and for the choices of my fellow heads of government in the European Union," Montenegro said. "I will not trade our fiscal and financial policy for that of other countries, even those closest to us, such as Spain, France or Italy."The Spanish case is particularly relevant for Portugal. Fuel is cheaper in Spain, prompting consumers in Portugal to cross the border to fill up.To defend these choices, Montenegro repeatedly invoked the past during his address to the nation, referring to the international bailout programme the country was subjected to."Do not count on me, or on the government, for illusions today that come with a heavy price to pay tomorrow," he said.Luís Montenegro also made it clear that "the situation may drag on". In the morning, at a conference, he had criticised what he called the "stupid" course of the conflict in the Middle East.
