Headline: Anthropic warns AI is getting closer to building its own successor
Body: Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic said on Thursday that AI systems are increasingly capable of building future versions of themselves, adding to mounting concerns about the dangers of the powerful technology.The debate over the risks of AI has intensified in recent months, fuelled by several incidents and apocalyptic warnings from industry professionals.Anthropic said its Claude chatbot now leads more than a quarter of its research and development work and collaborates with human staff on more than 90% of tasks.The company said it was publishing the information to give the public, third parties and governments "better visibility into the pace of AI development" as the world "considers slowing" its pace.Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called this month for AI development to slow down, with rapid advances in the technology fuelling concerns over job losses and the soaring energy demand and environmental impact of data centres.Fears that designers of AI agents could lose control of their creations also mounted after several models from Anthropic and rival OpenAI reportedly broke out of their confined environments on their own, accessed the internet and intruded on websites and platforms."Models accelerating their own development could make it more challenging for humans to understand or control these systems," Anthropic said in a report."It is therefore important to share these metrics to understand how close the world is to reaching recursive self-improvement (a model fully autonomously building its successor)."As of August, Claude leads 26% of Anthropic's research and development, meaning it can complete most of a task from start to finish with human supervision.Anthropic said Claude could not yet operate "fully autonomously".The firm said it had about 30,000 AI agents doing research and engineering work, referring to bots that have the potential to carry out tasks.Anthropic is expected to beat OpenAI to the public markets with a blockbuster IPO later this year, despite concerns around industry regulation.

Headline: Nul points? UK MPs want to know why Britain keeps flopping at Eurovision
Body: Britain's Eurovision woes are officially becoming a matter for Parliament.UK MPs are set to scrutinise the country’s "dismal" record at the competition, in the hopes of figuring out why one of Eurovision’s former powerhouses now so frequently finds itself at the bottom of the leaderboard.The UK has won Eurovision five times and is one of the "Big Five" countries guaranteed a place in the final. But in recent decades, those glory days have largely given way to immense disappointment.Since 2016, the UK has finished in the top 20 just three times. It has come 24th or lower six times, including three last-place finishes - and in 2021, James Newman’s 'Embers' managed the full Eurovision humiliation ritual of "nul points."This year's UK entry, Look Mum No Computer’s 'Eins, Zwei, Drei' managed to just edge ahead of Newman’s efforts with a grand total of one point. Another last-place finish.Now, a cross-party committee of MPs wants to find out what is going wrong.The Digital, Culture, Media and Sport committee will examine how the UK’s Eurovision acts and songs are selected, with BBC News reporting that it will investigate whether the country’s poor results are down to its song choices, performers or something else entirely.Dame Caroline Dinenage, a Conservative MP and chair of the committee, told the broadcaster: “We want to get to the bottom of who chooses our entrant, on what basis and whether our dismal record of achievement in recent years is the result of bad song choice, weak performance... or something else.”The hearing will take place “over the coming months” with the committee expected to hear from the BBC, which broadcasts Eurovision in the UK, as well as music industry experts.Despite the UK's run of poor form, there has been one notable recent bright spot in the form of the magnificently maned Sam Ryder. He finished in second place with his catchy anthem 'Space Man' in 2022, scoring 466 points and finishing just behind Ukraine’s Kalush Orchestra. Ryder became the only UK act in the last 15 years to finish higher than 15th place.The investigation comes as the UK looks ahead to the 2027 contest in Bulgaria - 30 years after its last Eurovision victory, when Katrina and the Waves won with "Love Shine a Light".The competition itself is continuing to face a wider political storm following the decision of Iceland, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Spain to withdraw from last year's competition over Israel’s participation amid the war in Gaza.Ireland has already said it will boycott the 2027 contest for a second year, citing the "appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza." Dutch broadcaster AVROTROS has also withdrawn, saying the contest no longer aligns with its principles of "trustworthiness, independence and humanity".

Headline: 'Remarkable': Scientists discover new wild cat species for first time in 100 years
Body: For the first time in more than a century, scientists have discovered a new species of wild cat.The Tilcayo tiger cat is a small feline with a spotted, leopard-like coat, and was first identified in the mountainous Yang's region near La Paz, the capital of Bolivia.At first, locals who spotted the animal presumed it was a domesticated cat. But DNA studies found that it is actually in a class of its own.New wild cat species discoveredBiologist and National Geographic explorer Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, who was part of the research team, described the discovery as a "remarkable event".A new wild cat species hasn't been described in 100 years, with the last discovery dating back to 1923.The nickname "tilcayo" given to the animal by locals inspired its new scientific designation: Leopardus tilcayo. It is slightly smaller than a domestic cat, measuring around 45 centimetres (18 inches), with rounded ears.A pair of tilcayos, the only such creatures found so far, have undergone whole genome sequencing, Nogales-Ascarrunz says, referring to a type of in-depth genetic testing.A male tilcayo is living at an animal shelter in Yungas, after it was handed over by a family who had taken in the creature, while a female was rescued and released into the wild after being attacked by locals.Research on the species was published on Thursday in the journal Current Biology, capping off research that scientists began in 2021.Introducing the Tilcayo tiger cat"So far, it's only been detected in Bolivia" and not "anywhere else on the planet," Nogales-Ascarrunz adds.Little is known about the elusive creature, but Nogales-Ascarrunz says they're classified as vulnerable to extinction, and could soon be considered "at much greater risk" of dying out.Mystery remains on what these cats eat, or get eaten by, how they reproduce and many other facets of their day-to-day lives in the wild.Researchers now hope that the methods they used to identify the new cat can be used to find even more cat species around the world, and develop on ways to protect them.Tigers are often referred as environmental warriors due to the profound impact they have on the natural world. Tigers help reduce carbon dioxide by existing in protected habitats that can allow vasts stretches of forest to act as natural carbon sinks.As top predators, tigers hunt large plant-eating animals such as deer, which can prevent herbivores from overgrazing, allowing trees and plants to grow fully and absorb even more carbon.

Headline: From Madrid to Zagreb, Europe's autonomous vehicles are multiplying
Body: Europeans started to get excited about more autonomous and semi-autonomous mobility options earlier this year when multiple EU Member States began approving Tesla's Full Self-Driving Supervised (FSD) mode.Just two months later, Google's self-driving taxi venture Waymo announced plans to launch its first EU operations in Munich, Germany by 2027.And the good news keeps coming.Recently, the Region of Madrid approved Uber, WeRide and AVOMO to begin mapping and testing autonomous passenger rides in Madrid, with the first rides expected by the end of 2026.AVOMO is a subsidiary of the Spanish Moove Cars Group, focusing on rolling out autonomous vehicle services in the United States and now also Europe.WeRide also secured a permit and a partnership with Zurich Airport to shuttle passengers from the terminal to planes at remote positions using their driverless buses.Pony.ai and Verne announced the first autonomous test drives from Zagreb Airport to the business district of Croatia's capital using their technology powered by Nvidia chips. The consortium expects a larger rollout of this service in Zagreb in the near future.Verne is a spinoff of the Croatian carmaker Rimac, which also demonstrates that European companies can compete in the top league of autonomous driving technologies.On 15 September, the Swedish transport company Einride announced that, in partnership with the German retail giant Lidl, it had received approval for the Society of Automotive Engineers Level 4 Standard from the German Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA). Einride will deploy electrified lorries on German roads.From September 2026, these driverless trucks will connect Lidl warehouses with stores. While this is still a pilot project, Lidl hopes to address driver shortages by adding autonomous delivery vehicles, thereby enhancing its supply chain resilience.Germany's road rules are seen as among the toughest in the world, and such approval should make technology enthusiasts in Europe and beyond feel positive about the future of further AV rollouts.EU Tech Loop previously reported that seven out of 10 fatal accidents could be prevented by introducing driverless cars in the European Union. That could save up to 13,000 lives per year.Technology pessimism is often associated with European rulemaking. The good news is that in autonomous mobility, we can see a massive shift by European regulators towards embracing innovation on the road.The potential for road safety and consumer convenience is huge, and the good news doesn't seem to stop.This story was originally published on EU Tech Loop and has been shared on Euronews as part of a syndication agreement.

Headline: Europeans still believe in the European dream. They just don't think it's within reach, study finds
Body: In her State of the Union address, Ursula von der Leyen warned of a "battle of narratives" seeking to weaken confidence in Europe. A new study, 'Future Nostalgia: Europe's Unfinished Song', published by the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) and the European Cultural Foundation (ECF), suggests that the confidence problem is real, and its authors call it an "imagination gap": most Europeans still want a stronger, more united continent, but a majority doubt it will ever get there The findings, based on nearly 6,000 interviews across six countries, paint a picture of a public that hasn't abandoned the European project, but has largely lost confidence in its ability to deliver.A continent bracing for declineOn average, 68% of respondents describe Europe's current situation in terms of "general deterioration or loss of normality." Just 12% see it as a moment of "awakening or renewal." The gloom varies by country: it's most pronounced in France, at over 80%, and least widespread in the UK, where it still affects a majority, but by a narrower margin.Asked to name Europe's biggest challenges, war and security topped the list at 43%, rising to 47% in Poland and the UK, where the war on Europe's borders and its consequences weigh most heavily on public opinion. Economic pressure follows at 33%, but its weight differs sharply from country to country: 41% of Italians call it Europe's main challenge, compared with just 23% in Poland and the Netherlands.The verdict on Europe's response, whatever the concern, is blunt: 74% say the bloc is handling its challenges poorly, and 56% believe its future is genuinely "in danger," against just 21% who disagree.The dream isn't deadDespite the pessimism, the study finds little appetite for retreat. Some 73% of respondents still hold what researchers classify as a "positive vision" for Europe's future, against 14% with a negative outlook and 13% who express no clear vision at all. Asked to describe their hopes for Europe two decades from now, respondents most often pointed to greater unity and political integration, followed by peace and security, and prosperity and shared wellbeing.That's the paradox at the heart of the report: Europeans haven't given up on the idea of a stronger, more unified Europe.Even those who feel most anxious about where the continent is heading tend to remain attached to the European project rather than turning against it. What they've lost faith in isn't the vision itself, but whether it can actually happen.Why trust is erodingThe study identifies specific, recurring reasons behind that doubt.Nearly a third of respondents (32%) describe Europe as too slow to act, a complaint that rises above 40% in Germany and the Netherlands, where the issue has become a fixture of domestic political debate. It's a criticism von der Leyen herself seemed to anticipate in her address, telling MEPs that "in today's economy, speed is of the essence" as she pushed her simplification agenda to cut administrative burden.Almost as many (30%) see Europe as inconsistent, failing to live up to the values it claims to represent.Perhaps most tellingly, 44% of respondents, nearly half, could not name a single recent example of European action going right. Researchers say this absence of visible "wins" is central to why the public struggles to imagine a credible path from today's Europe to the one it wants.An imagination gap, not a legitimacy crisisAccording to ECFR senior fellow Pawel Zerka, the study's lead author, the findings shouldn't be mistaken for rising euroscepticism. Even among the most anxious segments of the public, attachment to the European project remains strong. The problem is one of credibility, not commitment."For many of the people we spoke to, the problem is not that they have stopped wanting a stronger Europe, but that they no longer believe it is achievable," Zerka said. "People can picture the kind of Europe they want to see, but struggle to imagine a credible path from where it is today to where they want it to be."The report argues that closing this gap will require less emphasis on grand promises and more visible proof that European cooperation can deliver results people notice in their daily lives.In her address, von der Leyen called on Europeans to "fight back" against forces seeking to divide the bloc and undermine confidence in the European project. The study suggests that the fight will be won less with rhetoric than with evidence.

Headline: European stocks edge lower as oil prices and bond yields retreat
Body: Major European stock markets opened slightly lower on Friday as investors took profits after Thursday’s rally and digested another round of monetary tightening by global central banks.The pan-European STOXX 600 fell around 0.2% in early trading. The DAX lost 0.42%, the EURO STOXX 50 declined 0.19%, the CAC 40 fell 0.34%, and the FTSE 100 slipped 0.18%.Investors were also focused on the latest economic data. UK retail sales volumes rose by 0.5% in August and by 2.4% compared with a year earlier, beating expectations. German producer prices increased by a stronger-than-expected 4.6% year on year.Bond markets stabilised after their recent sell-off. The US 10-year Treasury yield retreated to around 4.94%, while Japan’s equivalent slipped to approximately 2.97%. Eurozone yields remained elevated, with Germany’s 10-year yield at around 3.49%, France’s at 4.47% and Italy’s at 4.36%.Easing US and Japanese bond yields supported precious metals. Gold gained around 1.2% to trade close to $4,395 per troy ounce during the European morning, while silver rose approximately 2.8% to around $67 per ounce.In Asia, Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 gained 1.9% to 65,332.57 after the Bank of Japan raised its key interest rate from 1.0% to 1.25%, a 31-year high.The move had been widely priced in, coming after the Federal Reserve also raised its key rate this week. Pressures have been coming from the US for Japan to raise rates because of concerns about the weakening yen.The nations intervened together recently to prop up the yen. But the efforts haven't had a big impact.In currency trading, the euro was broadly flat against the dollar at around $1.148, while the pound gained approximately 0.1% to trade at about $1.337 in the European opening. The US dollar rose to 157.55 Japanese yen from 155.95 yen.South Korea's Kospi jumped 2.3% to 6,866.83. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 was little changed, slipping less than 0.1% to 8,731.50. Hong Kong's Hang Seng edged up nearly 0.7% to 24,769.80, while the Shanghai Composite added 1.0% to 3,916.08.Falling oil prices and easing pressure from the bond market helped Wall Street reverse many of its losses from the prior day.The S&P 500 jumped 1.1% for just its second rise in the last nine days. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 316 points, or 0.6%, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.7%.Stocks received a boost after the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil slid from the nearly $110 it reached earlier in the week on worries that the war with Iran will keep oil bottled up in the Middle East instead of going to customers worldwide.During the European morning, Brent futures fell by more than 2% to $102.50 a barrel for next-month delivery. Benchmark US crude declined by nearly 2%, trading a few cents below $100 by 10:00 CEST.Brent is still more expensive than the $72 per barrel that it cost earlier this summer.The Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised the short-term interest rate that it controls, the federal funds rate, by a quarter of a percentage point for its first hike in more than three years. Officials also hinted that they may raise the federal funds rate one more time this year as they try to get high inflation in the US under control.The signals sent Wall Street on a roller coaster. Stocks initially remained higher for the day after the Fed made its announcement Wednesday. They then slid sharply before recovering a chunk of the losses before trading ended.On the upside for markets, the shift to higher interest rates built confidence that the Fed is committed to getting inflation back to its target of 2%. On the downside for markets, higher rates undercut prices for stocks and other investments.

Headline: Could the EU Kids Act unwittingly widen the transatlantic AI divide?
Body: Brussels wants to shield children from Big Tech. It may end up handing Silicon Valley an even bigger competitive edge.The EU Kids Act, unveiled this week, promises age limits, parental controls and a crackdown on the "addictive" features baked into social media, video platforms and AI chatbots alike.But as the bloc moves to police the tech giants, a harder question looms: can Europe regulate its way to child safety without regulating itself out of the AI race it is already losing?The stakes could hardly be higher. Europe has just one significant AI company to speak of, Mistral, dwarfed by its US rivals OpenAI and Anthropic in both valuation and investment.The bloc has never really left the starting blocks when it comes to scaling digital platforms to rival America's, relying instead on the strength of its single market and its power to regulate.Now, as AI becomes the defining technology of the decade, that trade-off — rules versus growth — is seen as a "make or break" moment for the bloc.What the Kids Act actually proposesThe legislation includes a number of measures aimed at protecting children online, including age restrictions, parental controls and limits on potentially addictive features.The proposals have been welcomed by some in the tech industry, but Stanislas Marchand, a former mobile gaming lead at French unicorn Voodoo, says Europe must also consider the potential consequences for its own digital sector.He argues that Europe "must prepare for the potential consequences by investing more urgently than ever in its homegrown AI capabilities".The European Commission's proposals come amid growing pressure on governments to protect children from the risks posed by social media and other online platforms.In the last couple of years, though, Big Tech has come under increasing scrutiny for its failure to protect children online, from cyberbullying, harassment and grooming to exploitation, extortion and misinformation.Australia famously implemented the world's first social media ban for under-16s in December last year, a move that was watched keenly by governments around the world, prompting many to follow suit in implementing their own bans or exploring the possibility of doing so.France, Greece, Austria, Denmark, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Germany, Poland and the Netherlands have all been considering or advancing national legislation on social media bans, piling pressure on Brussels to present an EU-wide measure and avoid fragmentation.Meanwhile in the US this year, social media companies have faced and lost landmark liability cases, with many choosing to settle instead — such as Meta's recent $17bn (€14.9bn) deal to end a lawsuit brought by 47 US states.Beyond social mediaThe EU Kids Act calls for a total, blanket social media ban for under-13s, while those up to 15 years old would be able to make "mini accounts" — limited, highly supervised profiles linked to a parent's profile.Not only that, these accounts would also come with mandatory one-hour daily limits and a complete ban on "toxic or addictive features" like infinite scroll, endless autoplay and engagement rewards.Marchand welcomed the proposed ban for under-13s, but said the proposal "should have been extended to everyone under 16" rather than permitting mini accounts for teens.He argues the message from the Commission should have been that the platforms in question are "unsuitable for children" because they are "engineered to maximise attention".The Kids Act goes well beyond social media.It encompasses video-sharing platforms such as YouTube and Twitch, online video games like Roblox, Fortnite and Minecraft, and more recent entrants like AI chatbots and companions such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini.It would also require app stores and operating systems to integrate strict age-assurance filters to prevent underage users from downloading restricted apps and software in the first place.And implementation, for Marchand, is where the problem lies, because the EU is asking platforms to "verify children's ages, operate parent-controlled accounts, enforce daily limits, restrict contacts and features, and prove that the resulting product is safe."These requirements altogether could increase the cost and complexity of launching a product in Europe."Every one of those responsibilities creates another potential point of failure, and history gives us little reason to trust social media companies to execute them properly."That concern is particularly relevant given that Europe's digital sector is dominated by American firms, and the continent has somewhat failed to make sure Big Tech follows the rules.Meta has been fined twice for illegally transferring European user data to US servers, breaching GDPR in 2023 and the Digital Markets Act in 2025.TikTok was fined €530m last year for failing to protect children's data and illegally transferring it to Chinese servers.Elon Musk's X, which has had the most acrimonious relationship with EU lawmakers, was fined €120m last December over its deceptive "blue checkmark" verification and for denying researchers access to data.Google, too, has been fined repeatedly for breaching antitrust rules, amounting to €10.38bn so far.A patchy enforcement recordAll of these fines are pocket change for Big Tech, and with the arrival of potentially even larger firms in the shape of AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic — again based in the US — it could become even more difficult for Europe to shape and enforce its own digital rules.Marchand fears the Act could also make the EU a less attractive market to launch new products, while doing little to support European alternatives."If the Kids Act requires separate European products and costly ongoing assessments, US labs may delay launches here while smaller European developers struggle to compete," he warns.He also points out that frontier AI companies already face enormous computing costs and uncertain paths to profitability, while some advanced Anthropic models have already been restricted outside the US and withheld from the UK's AI Security Institute.For Marchand, the result could be an unintended consequence of the EU's attempt to protect children online."My feeling is this will further add to the transatlantic AI divide."

Headline: Greece: Police bust gang using AI to clone relatives' voices for cash
Body: A criminal organisation that used Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools to clone the voices of relatives in order to make telephone scams more convincing has been dismantled by the Directorate for Combating Organised Crime.The gang is alleged to have defrauded citizens using various pretexts, posing among other things as employees of the Hellenic Electricity Distribution Network Operator (HEDNO), mobile phone companies and fibre-optic service providers. They would then exploit voice-cloning technology to create the impression that a relative or other trusted person of the victim was on the line.The organisation’s activities were brought to an end following a police operation by the Financial Crime Squad’s Sub-Directorate in Nea Ionia, Attica, where two of its members, aged 23 and 25, were arrested. The two suspects are believed to have acted as the gang’s "collectors" and were caught just after removing valuables worth around 30,000 euros from a home.The case file for criminal organisation, fraud and aggravated theft also includes four more individuals, three of whom have already been identified. According to the police, the gang’s illegal gains are estimated to exceed 1 million euros.How the AI scam workedAccording to the investigation, the organisation had established clear roles, with "management" figures, "callers" and "collectors". Its operation is thought to have begun at least in early July 2026.The "callers" searched for potential victims and contacted them using different pretexts. They usually convinced them that they had to take some action related to the installation of fibre optics or another supposedly technical procedure.When a victim expressed doubts, the perpetrators urged them to get in touch with a relative or another trusted person, supposedly in order to confirm the process.They then asked for the telephone number of that person and called them, pretending to represent a telecommunications company or another service provider.During this brief conversation they recorded a sample of their voice. Using an Artificial Intelligence tool, they then created a cloned version of that voice.The next step was to call the original victim again. This time, through voice-cloning technology, they reproduced the relative’s voice, creating the impression that this person was indeed on the other end of the line and was confirming what the scammers had previously claimed.In this way, the perpetrators sought to dispel victims’ doubts and make the scam more convincing.Five more incidentsSo far, the gang’s involvement has been confirmed in five further cases using a similar modus operandi.At the same time, the police investigation led to the solving of a vehicle theft reported on 14 September 2026, which, according to the findings, the organisation’s members were using as an "operational vehicle".In total, the searches led to the seizure of a public-use vehicle and two mobile phones.The two detainees were brought before the competent prosecutor and referred to the examining magistrate, while the investigation continues to determine the full extent of the criminal activity.Police warn about scams using cloned voicesIn light of this case, the Hellenic Police are renewing their warning about telephone scams in which perpetrators pose as employees of utilities, public services, telecommunications companies, banks or other organisations.They place particular emphasis on the fact that recognising a familiar voice is no longer, in itself, a reliable way of confirming the caller’s identity, as the voice may have been technically manipulated or reproduced using AI.Citizens are urged to:hang up immediately on suspicious phone calls,avoid disclosing personal or financial information,avoid giving details about who lives in their household or when they are away from home,call their relative or trusted person themselves, on a number they already know, in order to confirm the communication,use, wherever possible, a pre-agreed safety word or phrase,not open the door to strangers simply because someone has asked them to do so over the phone, even if the voice sounds like that of a relative,not hand over money or valuables and not place them in locations indicated to them over the phone,verify any scheduled work by contacting the competent organisation themselves, using its official telephone number,and inform the police and their relatives immediately about any suspicious call.The police remind the public that no genuine technical inspection ever requires the handover of cash, jewellery or other valuables, nor disclosure of where such items are kept.Special care is advised for elderly family members, as even a completely familiar voice on the phone may now have been created or reproduced using Artificial Intelligence technology.In the event of a suspicious phone call or the presence of unknown persons at a home, citizens are urged to contact the Hellenic Police immediately on 100 or their local police station, keeping, where possible, the number from which the call was made and any other relevant information.

Headline: Trump administration moves to cut protections for endangered species
Body: The Trump administration has issued a sweeping new directive that could see the unintentional killing of protected wildlife no longer treated as unlawful.A memo from Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) director Brian Nesvik distributed to FWS field offices earlier this week called for a reinterpretation of "take," a term relating to the pursuit, killing or capture of a species under the 1973 Endangered Species Act (ESA).The definition would now be altered to "affirmative conduct intentionally directed against a particular animal or animals," effectively excluding incidental harm caused by economic activities from being considered "take.""A vessel that inadvertently strikes a whale has not taken it, because the vessel's course was not set against the whale," the memo says, quoting former Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia in a 1995 case. "Felling a tree is not a take of the bats roosting in it unless the tree is felled for the purpose of killing or capturing them".The document, which was obtained and shared by the Center for Biological Diversity, comes after a previous rule change that rescinded the definition of "harm" under the ESA.The Interior Department confirmed the memo’s authenticity to the AFP news agency."The memorandum accurately reflects the US Fish and Wildlife Service's guidance for implementing the Endangered Species Act following the final rule rescinding the regulatory definition of 'harm,'" the department said."Under the guidance, the ESA's prohibition on 'take' continues to prohibit conduct including harassing, pursuing, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capturing or collecting protected wildlife," it added.The move has drawn strong criticism from environmental groups.Brett Hartl, the government affairs director at the Center for Biological Diversity, said the move "stabs at the very heart of the Endangered Species Act by giving federal approval to the killing of some of America’s most beloved wildlife.""The Trump administration is desperate to annihilate environmental protections, but this incredibly radical measure is both cruel and profoundly unlawful. Killing endangered wildlife is illegal, whether that’s your purpose or not," Hartl added in a press release.

Headline: Eurovision 2027: Ireland follows Netherlands in boycott of song contest for second year in a row
Body: Ireland will boycott the Eurovision Song Contest for the second year in a row in protest at Israel's participation, according to Ireland's national broadcaster RTÉ. RTÉ said in a statement: "RTÉ feels that Ireland's participation cannot be justified given the ⁠appalling and ongoing loss ⁠of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there which continues to ‌put the lives of so many civilians at risk." RTÉ added that they also remain "deeply concerned by the continued denial of independent access to international journalists to the territory". They also said they would not be broadcasting the competition, which will take place in Bulgaria in 2027 after singer Dara's victory for the country in May. Ireland has won the competition seven times between 1970 and 1996, a joint record holder alongside Sweden. Eurovision director Martin Green said he "regretted" RTÉ 's stance, but "fully respect their decision". In 2026, RTÉ withdrew from the contest in Vienna, after the European Broadcasting Union confirmed that Israeli public broadcaster KAN would be allowed to take part. Ireland's decision to boycott Eurovision 2027 follows that of Dutch broadcaster AvroTros, who announced last month that they would boycott next year's show as it was no longer consistent with "trustworthiness, independence and humanity". It said the competition can no longer be considered neutral while a participating country remains involved in a large-scale military conflict. Both Ireland and the Netherlands were among the five countries who decided to opt out of the 2026 competition, along with Spain, Iceland and Slovenia. It remains to be seen whether Spain, Iceland and Slovenia will follow suit.Hamas launched an attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in the last three years of Israeli bombardment. Organisations including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the United Nations have described Israel's actions as "genocide". A report published in June by a UN independent commission found that "Israeli authorities and security forces have deliberately targeted Palestinian children, resulting in genocide and atrocity crimes in the Gaza Strip and war crimes in the West Bank." A previous report last September found that Israel had committed genocide and claimed that these acts were incited by senior Israeli officials, including prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Israel has repeatedly labelled the accusations as “defamatory” and “distorted”.Eurovision 2027 contest will take place in Burgas, Bulgaria, with the Grand Final being held at the Arena Burgas on 15 May.

Headline: Burning the bard: 'Macbeth' defies fiery curse as Lisbon's Teatro D. Maria II reopens
Body: After almost four years closed, the National Theatre D. Maria II, on Rossio in Lisbon, is finally reopening its doors after the biggest renovation in decades. It is doing so with a "cursed play" and with tickets almost sold out."Macbeth" by William Shakespeare, which was on stage at the National Theatre D. Maria II when a fire destroyed the building in 1964, is the production chosen for the reopening.It is a deliberate choice by artistic director and director Pedro Penim and serves as a provocation in the face of the many productions that have been plagued by accidents. In the show he signs, real fire is used on stage in a symbolic gesture, recalling the tragedy that reduced the theatre to ashes."It was a kind of trauma in the theatre's history, it was a very defining moment, and this play, which is believed to be a cursed play, full of superstitions, was never staged again," says Pedro Penim, director and artistic director of the National Theatre D. Maria II, in an interview with Euronews.The Shakespearean tragedy has, over the centuries, accumulated stories of disasters backstage: injured actors, props swapped for real weapons, spectacular falls and deaths on stage."Whenever this play is staged, some misfortune seems to happen. So I decided to challenge not only fate but also to draw a parallel with the theatre's own history, given that we are reopening as the National Theatre D. Maria II celebrates its 180th anniversary," the director adds.But putting together a production of this scale did not come without setbacks. The initial intention was to use the translation by Brazilian poet Manuel Bandeira, the same used by the Rey Colaço-Robles Monteiro company in the ill-fated 1964 staging. However, the holders of the poet's rights never responded to the requests and Pedro Penim found himself 'cornered' into translating Shakespeare's text himself.The translation signed by Penim will now be published as a book. "The idea was to find a Portuguese that retained the decasyllabic verse while at the same time looking for words that would not be inaccessible to a contemporary Portuguese audience and, in that way, to find something that did not lose the poetry."As for the staging, it seeks to leave the work open to interpretation by audiences. "It is a work that allows thousands of readings." However, there is an inevitable parallel that connects this tragedy to the 21st century. "There is a dimension linked to the idea of fascination with evil, the way evil shows itself off, struts around our society; it is present in our lives when we turn on the television, look at our mobile phone, in people's conversations. Suddenly, evil is no longer ashamed to show itself," Penim explains."The seductive language Macbeth uses is a kind of poetry that enchants, but which at the same time carries a very significant weight in terms of the execution and the imagining of the crime," reflects the director.This production also pays tribute to the theatre itself: Joana Sousa's set reproduces the façade of the emblematic building on Rossio, and one of the characters is Queen Maria II herself.The refurbishment work on the building has also improved the technical and artistic conditions of the main auditorium, breathing new life into "Macbeth". The stage now rotates and can be raised. There have also been upgrades to lighting, sound and stage machinery."It is a play that has been staged many times with many different visions, many different casts and very diverse directors, as well as very different set designs. In this case, we wanted to bring this proposal right to the heart of the National Theatre D. Maria II and turn the theatre itself into the set after so many years in which this play was, in fact, not staged or not presented on this stage," Pedro Penim explains.To give substance to this two-and-a-half-hour curse, Pedro Penim has opted for a cast he has worked with before, with particular emphasis on the leading pair. In the role of Macbeth is José Raposo, "one of the country's most beloved actors", as the director is keen to point out, who plays one of the greatest villains in drama."It is a production that carries a lot of weight, also because of the symbolism of this whole bridge that Pedro Penim has built with the fact that the theatre burned down in 1964. And now, after these works, it has that charge that makes us feel an even greater sense of responsibility," the actor tells Euronews.Taking on the role of Lady Macbeth is actor Bárbara Branco, who drives the plot. "Technically, it is a hugely ambitious production. Pedro [Penim] is making full use of all the features the theatre has, the platforms, fire, water, etc. We are making use of everything, and I think that technical difficulty means the responsibility goes beyond the play itself, beyond these characters. Beyond the reopening of the theatre."The cast also includes Ana Coimbra, Ana Tang, Bernardo de Lacerda, Hugo Van Der Ding, João Grosso, José Neves, June João, Sandro Feliciano, Stela and Vítor Silva Costa.The anticipation surrounding the return to the Garret auditorium at the D. Maria II is already visible at the box office: with a season longer than usual, tickets have sold out quickly, leaving only seats with restricted visibility."Macbeth" premieres on Friday 18 September and will run until 31 October.

Headline: Revolut hack: criminals steal data of 700 European clients, demand $3m ransom
Body: The public prosecutor's office in Reggio Calabria has opened an investigation into a case involving the banking services company Revolut, founded in London, which is now reportedly being blackmailed.A group of hackers requested sensitive data from the bank using a compromised institutional email account belonging to the Reggio Calabria prefecture.The digital bank has confirmed that data belonging to around 680 European customers has been affected, but that their funds have not been touched.According to the Financial Times, which contacted the cybercriminals via Telegram, the group calls itself "iamnotavillain" and posted on its website on Wednesday afternoon a ransom demand for 3 million dollars, equivalent to 2.61 million euros.If they do not receive the money within 24 hours, the hackers are threatening to sell the sensitive data to other criminal organisations.The National Anti-Mafia and Counter-Terrorism Directorate is also working on the case, as it concerns a government body. The cybercrime division of the police says it was a highly sophisticated operation, but several points still need to be clarified.An unusual ransom demandThe group posted the ransom demand on its site on the dark web. The Financial Times (source in Italian) notes that making such a demand public is unusual; typically, ransom and extortion attempts are made privately at first and only made public if the targets refuse to pay.In this case, however, the British newspaper received a message demanding that Revolut transfer "6,000 XMR / 3,000,000 $… otherwise all the data will be sold and you will have blood on your hands".XMR is the ticker symbol for the cryptocurrency Monero, often used in illegal contexts because it is difficult to trace.The criminal group also told the newspaper that this was the first time it had used its site for a ransom demand and that it had not yet contacted the bank to open negotiations.After making the ransom demand public, the hackers sent the Financial Times a 60-second screen recording showing an unidentified user scrolling through a collection of documents, possibly belonging to Revolut.The information contained in the documents taken from Revolut is said to include passport details, driving licence data, other identity documents and photographs. The hackers claim to hold a total of 147 gigabytes of data.How far the investigation has progressedProsecutors are considering the offence of intrusion into an IT system of public interest. An initial report from the cybercrime police indicates that the operation, which lasted for months, was highly sophisticated, and it is still not certain whether a computer at the Reggio Calabria prefecture or at Italy's Interior Ministry was compromised.Experts are also trying to establish whether the institutional email account from which the requests originated was infiltrated or cloned.Alongside the national Anti-Mafia and Counter-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office, the Italian data protection authority has also stepped in, immediately launching checks for possible security breaches at Italian banks and urging data-protection officers to carry out a "prompt review" and, if any vulnerabilities are found, to notify the authority immediately.The Italian privacy watchdog has also contacted its counterpart in Lithuania, where Revolut's registered office is located, starting an exchange of information to strengthen efforts to counter the threat.The investigation will determine how the offence was carried out and whether other public bodies were also affected.

Headline: The EU and Canada are getting closer than ever. And the world is watching
Body: With Canada, the European Union has opened the door to a new way for the European project to affiliate with third countries that aren't even on its own continent. The rest of the world will be watching closely.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spearheaded the idea of an alliance of middle powers in his seminal speech in Davos earlier this year. A few months later, Canada might provide the blueprint for how the EU integrates third countries.On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become "the first associate member of the European Union," proposing an unprecedented arrangement that still has to be fully defined.Whichever framework Brussels and Ottawa manage to agree on will have consequences well beyond Europe, as there is international attention on whether the EU can create an attractive blueprint to pull other democracies into its orbit."A Canada-EU alliance would create a beacon for other democracies. An alliance not defined by what we oppose, but about what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability," Carney told the European Parliament on Thursday.Unprecedented arrangementThe EU does not currently envisage an "associate membership." The idea was first floated by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as an innovative way to integrate Ukraine into the EU, but the proposal was rebuffed by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.So far, the Union has consisted solely of member states and candidate countries. Canada, meanwhile, has no intention of joining the bloc, as Carney has made clear, and its treaties would not permit it in any case, given that Canada is not a European country."The precise nomenclature is a question for Europe," the Canadian PM said, arguing that what mattered was the substance.The EU treaties do allow some flexibility, as they state that "the Union may conclude with one or more third countries or international organisations agreements establishing an association involving reciprocal rights and obligations, common action and special procedure."What exactly this associate status would entail is still not clear. Carney proposed deep cooperation across the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space and payments.But while the details remain to be hashed out, what appears clear is that whatever deal Brussels and Ottawa reach will be a highly influential precedent for how the EU engages with other partners.Trusted partnersThe idea of making Canada an associate member of the EU was first made public via a WSJ report earlier this week."We are on the same page," Australian Trade Minister Don Farrell told the Sydney Morning Herald. "We will take great interest in what Carney does."In an exclusive interview with Euronews, European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said that Australia and New Zealand might follow Canada's path, as the EU seeks to deepen ties with like-minded countries.MEP Tobias Cremer (Germany/S&D), the European Parliament's rapporteur for Canada, told reporters he was receiving an increasing number of media requests, not only from Canadian outlets but also from Australian, British and Japanese ones.Meanwhile, the UK is reportedly feeling left out of Brussels' newfound love for Canada, as some in London believe the EU is more interested in closer relations with Canada than with the UK."We need to think of partnerships that go beyond EU membership," Austria's Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger wrote on X. "Let's make that a model for the future — one that Europe also offers to other partners: Norway, Iceland, Japan, South Korea, New Zealand."In other words, the success of the special relationship with Canada might put the EU at the centre of a new international alliance, as democratic countries that have lost faith in the US as leader of the Western world realign.International orderThe newfound alignment between Brussels and Ottawa might be one step closer to the realisation of Carney's vision of an alliance of middle powers, meant to strengthen each other's sovereignty by weathering shifting geopolitical realities together."I want to be precise about what I am not proposing. I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival, only with better manners," he said."We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law," Carney continued.In Brussels, officials tend to point out that, while member states taken on their own might be middle powers, the EU as a whole is not, and might actually emerge as a leader of a democratic coalition to support the faltering rules-based international order."We are by definition a convening power of middle powers in the way we function. I think that makes us actually attractive to many other middle powers, because the EU, like no other global player, has in its DNA leveraging small and middle powers without trampling on their interests," Cremer said.At the same time, as the EU pursues global ambitions to forge deeper ties with democracies on other continents, some fear it might lose sight of its most immediate neighbourhood.Unsettled candidatesThe acceleration of the EU-Canada partnership, and the entirely new format on offer, has fallen flat especially among countries that have been standing in line to join for decades, such as in the Western Balkans.It is not the first time the EU has floated a new membership structure. Candidate countries have seen, in close succession, the growth plan, reverse enlargement, gradual integration and now a tiered form of membership.There is also a risk that the move further strains transatlantic relations with the US, with President Donald Trump already threatening possible retaliation, which might put pressure on candidate countries to pick a side between the two blocs."I don't feel comfortable with the constant new ideas over membership and the lack of discussion concerning the acceptance of new members," Obrad Kesić, the head of Bosnia and Herzegovina's mission to the EU, told Euronews."Canada is a large country, it could have negative ramifications for small candidate countries if the discussion becomes too broad. It changes the contour of the debate," Kesić said. "Conceiving memberships as going beyond Europe opens up a new set of issues."

Headline: Energy crunch and inflationary fears loom over EU finance talks
Body: Hello, this is Mared Gwyn holding the newsletter pen in Brussels. This morning: Eurozone finance ministers gather amid mounting economic pressures, and EU ambassadors make another push to break the Russia sanctions deadlock.Economic jitters: Finance ministers from eurozone countries gather in Dublin, Ireland, today, against a fraught backdrop of mounting energy costs, rising inflation and weak growth.Painful at the pump: Oil prices have surged rapidly in recent days, driven by a reduction in global supplies and exacerbated by recent attacks on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, which have been attributed to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels. European leaders are rushing to mitigate the rising prices and their impact on the broader economy. French President Emmanuel Macron has ordered a "mobilisation" to tackle fuel prices, as my colleague Marta Pacheco explains.Windfall tax on the table: Finance ministers could today respond to calls from some capitals for a windfall tax on energy companies.Speaking to our correspondent Shona Murray in Dublin ahead of the meeting, Irish Finance Minister Simon Harris — mindful of the neutrality required while chairing the EU Council presidency — spoke plainly about the soaring profits being posted by energy companies as ordinary taxpayers struggle to fill their tanks.“Energy companies are making extraordinarily large profits on the back of this energy crisis,” he said. “And they're not making those profits on the basis of being more enterprising or being innovative."“This isn't about rewarding enterprise. They're making the profits because of the chaos that we're seeing in the energy markets as a result of the strait of Hormuz being closed.” Watch.Not about Ukraine: Harris also disputed US President Donald Trump’s claims that petrol and diesel prices were skyrocketing due to Ukraine’s targeting of Russia’s refineries, which are part of the Kremlin’s war machine. “The reason there's a major energy crisis in the world right now is because the Strait of Hormuz is closed,” he said.The volatility of the global bond market and signs of rising inflation are also of concern to eurozone ministers, our economy reporter Eleonora Vasques writes, with European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde set to join the discussions after the institution raised interest rates on 10 September.All 27 EU finance ministers and central bank governors will also meet today and tomorrow for informal talks on the same issues, joined by finance ministers from Canada, the UK, Ukraine and Switzerland, as well as International Monetary Fund (IMF) director Kristalina Georgieva. Yet another try: Meanwhile in Brussels, EU ambassadors will meet this morning to try, once again, to renew the individual sanctions against Russia, which are due to expire next week if no deal is struck in time, Jorge writes.The chief obstacle remains that France wants to remove oligarch Alisher Usmanov from the blacklist in an attempt to secure the freedom of several French citizens detained in Azerbaijan. The demand has put Brussels in an unprecedented conundrum: never before have the EU sanctions been entangled with a prisoner release. While some diplomats feel sympathy for Paris, others wonder why Azerbaijan cares so much about Usmanov. The vast majority, though, remains opposed to delisting the billionaire. “We need the regime to stand,” a diplomat said. “Couldn’t this really be solved in another way, without delisting heavy Russian oligarchs?”Consultations intensify: France, as the bloc’s second-largest member state, carries considerable weight around the table and its veto is something that you can’t just shake off. Intense consultations have been going on between capitals to find a palatable solution for everyone. The Irish presidency of the EU Council and the External Action Service (EEAS) are also involved. As of now, the contours of a unanimous agreement are still blurred. Also, let’s not forget that Slovakia also wants Usmanov out, though for different reasons.Fresh support: Jorge also reports that the European Commission will disburse €3.3 billion for Ukraine to procure missiles and drones later today. Von der Leyen confirmed the move on Thursday after talks with President Zelenskyy over Ukraine’s budget deficit, which Brussels is still trying to pin down. US drawdown: Meanwhile, the Pentagon is weighing a drastic withdrawal of as many as 25,000 troops from Europe, reducing the US’s military presence on the continent by about a third, NBC News reported overnight citing seven current and former US and Western officials.While no final decision has been taken, according to the report, the recommendation is set to be laid out to Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth as part of a six-month review of US military presence in Europe later today.Analysis: Bruised by Trump, the EU and Canada find solace in each other’s armsThe blossoming EU-Canada alliance cannot be understood without the long shadow of Donald Trump, who has alienated both sides with his punitive tariffs, annexationist threats and scathing attacks.The breakup has been painful, to say the least. After all, both the EU and Canada have long defined the United States as their closest ally, their main security provider, their trade partner of choice. But Trump's return to the White House abruptly overturned these long-held assumptions, forcing them to reckon with their place in a cruel, cold world.Bruised and battered by the mercurial commander-in-chief, Brussels and Ottawa this week found solace in each other’s arms, my colleague Jorge Liboreiro writes in his post-Strasbourg analysis.More from our newsroomsBrussels seeks 'credible' outcome in EU-China talks after key negotiators’ call. The European Commission stepped up pressure on China on Thursday, calling for tangible results with Beijing following a one-hour video call between Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao. Peggy Corlin has the details.Tusk: Intelligence sees Russian plan for drone strikes on Poland, allies. The Polish Prime Minister has outlined the "most likely" scenario for the months ahead, warning of serious events and hybrid attacks on Poland and other Ukraine backers, Aleksandra Galka Reczko reports.Trump determined to end Iran war soon, US president's senior adviser tells Euronews. Massad Boulos, senior adviser to the US president on Arab and Middle Eastern affairs, has told Euronews that Donald Trump is working to end the months-long war. More from Jane Witherspoon.We're also keeping an eye onEurogroup ministers meet in Dublin, followed by an informal gathering of EU finance and economy ministers. European Commission Executive Vice-President Teresa Ribera attends a Conference on International Antitrust Law and Policy in the US.NATO Military Committee Conference starts in Copenhagen, Denmark.Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk heads to Kyiv.That’s it for today. Jorge Liboreiro, Vincenzo Genovese, Shona Murray, Eleonora Vasques and Marta Pacheco contributed to this newsletter. We'll be back on Monday.

Headline: Before the skyscrapers: Dubai’s oldest building, Al Fahidi Fort, set to reopen with new museum
Body: Think of Dubai and many people will imagine a metropolis of gleaming skyscrapers, mega shopping malls, palm-shaped islands and some of the world’s top luxury hotel and hospitality brands. But away from all the glitz and glamour, which often dominate the headlines, there’s another side to the city that doesn’t always get the attention it deserves: Old Dubai, and in particular the historic Al Fahidi area.Located on the southern side of the Creek, in this neighbourhood you’ll find traditional houses, cultural attractions, as well as Al Fahidi Fort, Dubai’s oldest standing building at more than 230 years old. Originally built as a defensive stronghold around 1787, over the centuries the fort has also been a residence for the ruler, a centre of governance and administration, and a prison before it became Dubai’s first museum in 1971, the same year that the United Arab Emirates was formed. ‘A witness to Dubai’s history’Al Fahidi Fort has been closed since 2021 as part of an extensive restoration project. Five years later, it is set to welcome back visitors “in the coming weeks or months”, according to Ayisha Khansaheb, Director of Al Fahidi Fort and Specialised Museums at the Dubai Culture & Arts Authority. Speaking to Euronews Travel at Arabian Travel Market, Khansaheb believes the contemporary museum experience is going to be a “gateway into the story of Dubai itself” and a great starting place for visitors to truly understand the history of the city. For a destination that’s known for its futuristic skylines and modern infrastructure, Dubai’s cultural heritage has sometimes been overlooked as a key attraction for international visitors. However, the reopening of the fort marks a new chapter in the city’s story. “I think cultural heritage is important as an ecosystem for cultural tourism, but also for residents, for locals, and for schools to educate the students on the cultural history and heritage of the city itself,” said Khansaheb. “I think we need to have offerings for everyone and I think this is something that you've been seeing more of in Dubai and in the wider region as well. It addresses a growing need to emphasise that there is a soul, there is a culture, and there is history here.”What can visitors see at Al Fahidi Fort? The revitalised museum combines the historic architecture of the fort with artefacts, archival material, and interactive technology to tell the story of the building and its place in Dubai’s development. Visitors begin their experience in a new underground extension, where contemporary galleries explore themes including defence, leadership and craftsmanship, before moving into the historic fort itself. Among the highlights is “The Vault”, a light and sound experience that follows the evolution of Dubai’s defence capabilities. Another gallery, “A Landmark Across the Ages”, explores the fort’s changing role over more than 230 years, while visitors can also see a major collection of Islamic arms and armour. Interactive learning experiences designed for children have also been incorporated into the museum. But one of the most important exhibits is the fort itself, where visitors can walk through its historic walls and explore its watchtowers, gates and courtyard. “You experience history through architecture,” Khansaheb said.

Headline: Trump touts 'major progress' towards setting up US military base in Poland
Body: US President Donald Trump on Thursday said there had been "major progress" towards the creation of a US military base in Poland as he hailed what he described as a "historic step" in relations with Warsaw."Thanks to the bold leadership of my friend, Karol Nawrocki, President of Poland, major progress is being made toward establishing a U.S. Army base in Poland," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social Account."If this happens, the location will be announced very soon. This will be a historic step for our Great U.S./Polish Alliance," he added.The US currently has around 10,000 rotational forces in Poland as well as 11 installation sites, with the US Army Garrison headquartered in Poznań.Earlier this year, the Trump administration threatened to pull troops out of Poland as part of a push to reduce the US' military presence in Europe following repeated criticism of European NATO allies' defence spending.However, Trump later reversed the move and announced that an additional 5,000 troops would be sent to Poland - which Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has dubbed a "model ally" - citing his conservative ally Nawrocki's election in 2025.It comes as the State Department also announced $4 billion in military aid for Poland in September.Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, Poland's defence minister, thanked Trump on Thursday for his efforts towards "establishing a permanent US base in Poland.""Good cooperation between presidents also yields positive results. This is a significant affirmation of our strategic partnership," he wrote on X.

Headline: Macron to host King Abdullah II and Lebanon's Aoun to discuss support for Lebanese Armed Forces
Body: French President Emmanuel Macron is set to host Jordan’s King Abdullah II and Lebanese President Joseph Aoun in Paris on Thursday, ahead of an international summit, aimed at mobilising support for the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF).According to an Elysée source, the talks — which are part of the Aqaba Process launched by Jordan in 2015 — will bring together senior officials and military experts from France, Britain, Jordan, Lebanon and the US to discuss plans for deploying the LAF, as well as wider efforts to stabilise the region.At present, Lebanon is seeking international support for its armed forces and working to avoid a security vacuum in the south.This follows the UN Security Council's decision to end the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL’s) on 31 December 2026, followed by a year-long drawdown and withdrawal — a move supported by the United States. It currently has around 7,500 peacekeepers from nearly 50 countries.Thursday’s meeting will focus on “direct operational matters” as France and its partners seek to assess how to assist the Lebanese Army with financial aid, equipment, intelligence and, if needed, operational guidance, according to an Elysée source.UNIFIL was established in 1978 to oversee the withdrawal of Israeli troops from southern Lebanon and assist the government in restoring its control of the area. At the time, Israel's three-month long occupation was sparked by the March 1978 "Coastal Road Massacre" — a deadly hijacking carried out by militants from the Palestinian Fatah group, which killed more than 30 Israelis.In 2006, following the war between Israel and Hezbollah, UNIFIL's mandate was expanded to help prevent Hezbollah and other armed groups from maintaining a military presence in southern Lebanon.European efforts to establish a post-UNIFILIn June, France and Italy announced they would lead efforts to establish a post-UNIFIL international coalition in support of Lebanon during the autumn of 2026, at a Franco-Italian summit.Meanwhile, EU Foreign Policy Chief Kaja Kallas said on 1 September that more than 10 EU member states were willing to provide personnel and resources for a new civilian and military mission to support Lebanese forces, stressing that the EU was not seeking to “replace” UNIFIL, but instead to invest in “Lebanon's capacity to provide security for itself."Ahead of his France trip, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun told Agence France-Presse (AFP), Aoun stressed the importance of a new force for Lebanon — whether it be European or not.“Whatever the nature of this force, that poses no problem for me: European, non-European, American, another United Nations force, Asian, or even a mix of European, Arab and Asian forces,” he stated, adding that “the best and most optimal option remains extending UNIFIL's mandate”.Aoun said that any new force in southern Lebanon, part of which is occupied by Israel, would be “temporary until the (Lebanese) army can deploy”.Although he stressed that the goal was to strike a security agreement with Israel “primarily to end the state of hostility and the deployment of the army on the border”, he cautioned “we cannot jump directly to a peace agreement”.The ongoing conflictLebanon was drawn into the wider regional Middle Eastern conflict after Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Shiite militia, launched rockets at Israel in early March in retaliation for US-Israeli strikes on Iran — prompting an Israeli military response across the country.More than six months after the conflict erupted, and despite a ceasefire agreed in June, Israeli airstrikes, military operations and demolitions have continued in southern Lebanon, leaving villages abandoned and residents displaced.Meanwhile, Hezbollah has continued to attack communities in the north of Israel, causing civilian and military casualties, as well as leading to the displacement of residents from communities along the Lebanese border. Multiple rounds of US-mediated talks between Israel and Lebanon have yet to resolve the conflict. Hezbollah has rejected calls for its disarmament, while Israel has linked its full withdrawal from southern Lebanon to the group’s disarmament and the removal of its military infrastructure.Meanwhile, hardline right-wing politicians, such as Israel's Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, have called for Israel to annex southern Lebanon up to the Litani River. Israel and Lebanon have experienced repeated periods of armed conflict and renewed hostilities since the 1948 Arab-Israeli War.Speaking to AFP ahead of his Paris trip, Aoun said that Lebanon remained determined to disarm Hezbollah, describing the issue as “neither negotiable nor open to discussion."Despite this, Lebanon’s armed forces have struggled to enforce the government’s decision to establish a state monopoly on weapons, amid Hezbollah’s refusal to disarm.Hezbollah has long maintained a substantial arsenal, which it has used to fight repeated wars with Israel, while also playing a major role in Lebanese politics. It operates both as an armed group and as a political party, with members in parliament and ministers serving in the government cabinet.France's role in the processKarim Émile Bitar, associate research fellow at the Institute for International and Strategic Affairs (IRIS) said that in his view, Hezbollah's disarmament campaign was an "impossible" task.“The army is a cross-community institution in Lebanon and it faces an impossible mission. It is being asked to disarm, within a few weeks, a militia that has been more powerful than the state for decades. This army lacks everything, from logistical resources and financial means. Politically, it is also not easy to confront Hezbollah, which continues to enjoy significant support from the Lebanese Shia community", he told Euronews.Bitar said Thursday's meeting serves as an example of France’s longstanding role in Lebanese affairs (from 1920 to 1943, Lebanon was governed under a French mandate)."Today, France views itself and has often been viewed, as the guarantor of unity, of sovereignty, of territorial integrity for Lebanon. These three things are now threatened: territorial integrity is absent as Israel occupies 6% of Lebanon's territory, sovereignty is because Hezbollah is refusing to hand over its military arsenal to the army and unity is being challenged in light of rising extremism, polarisation and fragmentation", Bitar told Euronews.The US and Israel's decision to exclude France from ceasefire negotiations between Israel and Lebanon earlier this year left Beirut in a difficult situation, stressed Bitar."For Lebanon, this posed a problem because the United States is not perceived as an 'honest broker.' The Lebanese would have liked countries such as France, Italy and Saudi Arabia to have been involved in these negotiations, so that they would not have found themselves confronted with Israeli intransigence, supported by the United States", he said.

Headline: Europe Today: Canada welcomes EU's 'associate member' offer, but what next?
Body: On today's show:Angela Skujins analyses what Canada's newly offered "associate member" status with the EU actually means in practice, after Mark Carney told the European Parliament in Strasbourg that he welcomes "much closer ties" with Europe.Shona Murray reports from Dublin, where EU finance ministers and central bank governors are gathering for two days of talks as part of Ireland's EU presidency. She interviews with Simon Harris, Irish Minister for Finance.Andrew Caruana Galizia, Head of Europe and Eurasia at the World Economic Forum, joins Europe Today to discuss a new WEF study on high energy costs as a drag on European competitiveness, two years on from the Draghi report on reviving the EU economy.Adnan Leal takes to the streets to ask people about the EU's newly unveiled Kids Act, which bans social media accounts for under-13s and stops AI chatbots from acting as "human friends" to children.Cecilia Bonefeld-Dahl, Director General at tech lobby DIGITALEUROPE, also reacts to the proposed EU Kids Act that will restrict social media access for children under 15.When and where to watch Europe Today?You can join Euronews’ anchors Méabh Mc Mahon and Stefan Grobe live on TV and Euronews' website, as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 8 am Brussels time.In just 20 minutes, we bring you the day's key events plus crucial analysis of all the stories shaping the EU and beyond. Also available as a newsletter and podcast.
