Headline: In Spain, football matches knock thousands of websites and services offline
Body: With the start of every football season, one of the most aggressive digital filtering mechanisms in Europe also comes back. Backed by court rulings, LaLiga, the employers' association chaired by Javier Tebas, orders Spanish operators to block in real time hundreds of IP addresses allegedly linked to the illegal broadcasting of matches.The initial aim is to curb piracy, but the real effect is another: the internet does not work with dedicated servers for each website, so when an IP is cut off it drags down with it a whole range of services that have nothing to do with football. In other words, LaLiga has court-granted rights that allow it to submit lists of IPs and have them blocked in Spain. And this clearly runs counter to the principle of net neutrality.The crux of the problem is that not every website or online service has its own IP address as if it were an ID number. There are services that host multiple websites under a single parent address and this is where the problems begin, because when that address is blocked, all the services and websites hanging from it also stop working. It is collateral damage for any internet user who tries to access them while a match is being played.To illustrate the problem, it is as if someone were to say that in Madrid (the hosting service) there is at least one resident, among the millions of people in the city, who is stealing electricity (pirating LaLiga's IPTV signal), and so they order the power to be cut off across the whole city.In an interview, Tebas even claimed that there were no mass blocks and that the complaints they were receiving came from "four geeks". The facts, however, speak for themselves, with blocks that do affect third-party services and between 500 and 1,000 IPs being blocked per match.How do the blocks work?The blocking starts shortly before kick-off and is lifted once the broadcast ends. LaLiga identifies IP addresses associated with pirate services and asks operators to cut them off during that time slot. On the opening matchday of the 2026-2027 season, 15 August 2026, some 550 IP addresses were blocked simultaneously. Since then, the blocks have continued every matchday.The Open Observatory of Network Interference (OONI) estimates that in the first half of 2026, 7,441 addresses belonging to 36 different providers were blocked, including Amazon AWS, Cloudflare, Akamai, Alibaba Cloud, Microsoft and Meta.LaLiga argues that these are dynamic blocks which are neither massive nor indiscriminate, and justifies them by pointing to annual losses of between 600 and 700 million euros caused by piracy of its broadcasts. Yet innocent parties are bearing the brunt.The underlying problem is the way the internet works, which clashes head-on with the method LaLiga is proposing as a solution and which, contrary to what it claims, does end up splashing thousands of websites every time there is a match in Spain. In fact, there is a web service that allows users to check whether this kind of outage is taking place: hayahora.futbol (source in Spanish).A content delivery network (CDN) such as Cloudflare (source in Spanish) caches under a single IP address thousands of pieces of content belonging to separate services. It improves loading speeds by serving content from locations closer to the end user with lower latency and also reduces the impact of DDoS attacks.If the IP of the CDN is blocked, content from thousands of services and websites is blocked as well, and the current system cannot tell whether the user was looking for that pirate stream or for a website like those of the RAE, Amnesty International, Greenpeace, Unicef, UNHCR or Caritas, courts, universities and projects such as Hugging Face, which hosts AI LLM models, or even some football clubs' own websites and those of their sponsors, a neat piece of rhetorical irony about this blocking method.The OONI report, which cross-checked measurements taken in Spain between January and June 2026 against a list of 9.2 million domains, estimates that more than 554,000 legitimate domains were affected at some point. Cloudflare took the bulk of the hit: with only 30% of the blocked IPs, it accounted for 90% of the affected domains, more than 501,000.In Spain, one of the best-known cases is the Redsys payment gateway, which has suffered repeated failures in confirming online payments during LaLiga matchdays, with affected retailers not even knowing where the problem lay. On previous occasions, WikiDex, the largest Spanish-language encyclopaedia on Pokémon, has also been affected, complaining of access problems to its image servers.Case study during Real Madrid's match on 15 SeptemberIn my own case, with fibre from DIGI, I have noticed blocks during earlier matches when downloading open LLM models from my server from Hugging Face (normally hosted on AWS), when using services linked to a pair of smart glasses (Halliday) or even when trying to access some websites. If anyone can see how those websites or services have anything to do with the piracy LaLiga talks about, please do let me know.The number of blocks began to increase after kick-off in the Elche C. F. v Real Madrid match, with Cloudflare IPs being blocked by Spain's five main internet operators.During the match, some websites were completely inaccessible, such as mandalaweb.es, a site offering mandalas to colour in, or todopuntodecruz.com, a site with a shop selling kits and patterns for cross-stitching.If we use a VPN from outside Spain, both mandalaweb.com and todopuntodecruz.com load properly, even though they have nothing to do with pirating LaLiga's IPTV signal.Tebas has said that the complaints come from only a few people, labelling them geeks, but it is not a question of a few domains or just small ones. Among the inaccessible sites are linuxmint.com, the supermarket chain froiz.es and the website of the Centro de Investigación Biomédica en Red (Networked Biomedical Research Centre). The verdict is clear: this is a nationwide block applied by internet providers, DIGI in my case.Another example: the following day, Wednesday 16 September 2026, I tried to download the Qwen 3.8 27b LLM model from Ollama to my server, and the requests failed because the TLS certificate could not be delivered in time during that day's matches, at 19:41, when I tried to download it. Ollama's models are hosted on Cloudflare, and of course an AI LLM model has nothing whatsoever to do with football.As can be seen below, there is also a series of blocks linked to LaLiga matches. The blocks include Cloudflare domains. On 15 September, the outages from the previous day started at around 21:20 and ended after midnight, meaning almost three hours of blocking.On Wednesday 16 September, the block began at 18:45 and lasted until just before midnight, so we are talking about between five and six hours of disruption. In these two cases, they were midweek days; at weekends, in the best of cases, the duration is similar.Technical alternatives, legal framework and expiry dateThere are now far more precise ways of acting than taking down an entire IP: targeting the domain, the URL, the account or the specific server distributing the pirate signal, and requesting its removal from the relevant provider.The rule should be to block the infringing content, not the shared infrastructure, because the damage caused is incalculable, with collateral effects on services and users who are unable to use the internet and apps normally while football matches are on. Several websites are reporting losses suffered by services and portals. LaLiga's blocks have already caused more than 3.1 million in losses.The legal basis for these blocks is the ruling handed down by Commercial Court No. 6 of Barcelona on 18 December 2024, which upheld the claim brought by LaLiga together with Telefónica Audiovisual Digital.The judgment authorises the immediate suspension of access to identified IPs and allows them to be updated dynamically on a weekly basis, even during matches, without the need for a fresh court order for each address. Movistar, Vodafone, DIGI and MásOrange did not contest the proceedings, effectively accepting the measures without challenge.In Congress there has been a first move, although it has no legal force yet: on 29 April 2026, a non-binding motion to amend the Digital Services Act (source in Spanish) was approved, tabled by ERC and agreed with the PSOE, with the backing of Sumar, Bildu, the PNV and Compromís. The PP and Vox voted against and Junts was absent. If it goes ahead, the reform would introduce proportionality requirements and limits on court rulings so that they do not delegate to industry bodies the management of blocking lists without oversight.In response to the outages, some users have chosen to use virtual private networks (VPNs) to get around them, a tool that European courts regard as neutral software and a legitimate tool.LaLiga counters that VPNs, as technological intermediaries, also bear responsibility for the content that flows through their infrastructure, and notes that the Commercial Court of Córdoba has already ordered interim measures along those lines.Nor has ECH encryption, promoted by Cloudflare and Apple to conceal the domain a user is connecting to, yet managed to displace IP blocking as the main containment tool.The 2026/2027 season will be, in any case, the last one covered by the current ruling, which expires on 20 June 2027, coinciding with the end of the Second Division.LaLiga and Telefónica are expected to seek an extension of a match they have been winning for several years. However, the legal and regulatory landscape has shifted compared with two years ago, creating real uncertainty as to whether they will once again obtain such a broad mandate.

Headline: Bank of Japan hikes rates to 31-year high to battle inflation
Body: The Bank of Japan has been trying to normalise monetary policy after decades of keeping interest rates near or below zero to try to encourage more borrowing and spending to counter deflation and pull Japan's economy out of the doldrums. Inflationary pressures are rising because of the war in Iran, which has sent oil prices soaring in recent months. That is a big negative for resource-poor Japan, which virtually imports all its oil.The rate increase, coming at the end of the two-day monetary policy board meeting, was expected, widely figured into recent global markets.The raise comes after the US Federal Reserve also raised its key rate this week. It raised its benchmark interest rate Wednesday for the first time since 2023 in an effort to quell stubbornly high inflation.The US has also been pressuring Japan to raise rates because of concerns about the weakening yen. Analysts say the Bank of Japan could raise interest rates another time later this year, or possibly early next year.The nations intervened together recently to prop up the yen. The US dollar is trading at about 155 yen. It reached above 160 yen earlier this year.The Bank of Japan has set a target inflation rate of about 2%. Inflation is about that now in Japan, although some consumers complain that the recent surge in prices is too much, especially in gas and oil-related products.Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 rose after the Bank of Japan decision was announced.

Headline: Women offered less invasive or intensive treatment than men with the same conditions
Body: Women were less likely than men to be offered intensive treatments such as surgery or strong painkillers, a new review has found. While men and women are often treated differently by healthcare systems, the researchers noted that it is not clear whether these differences put either sex at a disadvantage. Sex differences are evident throughout medicine and play a key role in the diagnosis and management of patients. Researchers at the University of St Andrews in Scotland found visible differences in the way men and women are treated. “While the direction of the findings was not a surprise, the consistency was”, said Miriam Veenhuizen, honorary lecturer at St Andrews School of Medicine. Researchers analysed 41 studies published between 2018 and 2023 and found the same pattern in cardiology, surgery, transplant medicine and emergency care. Women suffering from heart failure, heart attack and tachycardia were more likely to be managed conservatively with medication compared with invasive procedures such as coronary artery bypass grafting and percutaneous coronary intervention. Among patients with Parkinson’s disease, men were more likely to be referred for deep brain stimulation devices, an implantable device used to manage symptoms. Women were also less likely to receive a liver transplant or be referred to surgery. “For clinicians, the findings are a prompt to check whether treatment is being offered on clinical grounds rather than assumption,” said Andrew O’Malley, co-lead of the study.What is behind this difference?While the trend was consistent across studies, the reasons behind it remain unclear.“It’s not entirely clear why this is happening, but it is likely because women were under-represented in clinical trials until recent decades, so many guidelines rest on data from men,” said Veenhuizen. The researchers called for further research to understand whether these differences reflect legitimate variations in clinical practice or wider inequalities, and to ensure patients receive equitable care.

Headline: UN Security Council fails to adopt US-backed Iran sanctions resolution after Russia and China vetoes
Body: Russia and China have vetoed a United Nations resolution that would have allowed independent experts to continue monitoring sanctions reimposed on Iran over its nuclear programme, dealing a blow to international oversight efforts.The United States had drafted the resolution to extend the UN expert panel's mandate for a year. It was defeated on Thursday at the UN Security Council by a vote of 11-2, with Somalia and Pakistan abstaining.The UN Security Council sanctions, which were reimposed on 27 September last year under the snapback mechanism of the 2015 nuclear deal, remain in effect. They freeze Iranian assets abroad, restrict arms deals with Tehran and penalise the development of its ballistic missile programme.France, Germany and the United Kingdom triggered the snapback provision, which restored the Security Council sanctions committee and authorised the panel of experts to monitor compliance. Thursday's veto removes that oversight without lifting the underlying sanctions.The vote comes as the Trump administration pursues a broader campaign to isolate Tehran economically. Separately on Thursday, Washington moved against digital currency networks it says are being used to give sanctioned Iranian entities illegal access to the international financial system.The moves also come amid a more than six-month-old war in Iran that has reached a stalemate.The US Treasury and State Departments announced that they had targeted two companies — BitBank and the Pishtaz Simorgh Electronic Trade Co. — and three associates of BitBank’s previously sanctioned chief, Babak Zanjani, who are accused of playing a role in helping Iran evade sanctions.At the United Nations, Iran’s UN mission thanked China and Russia for vetoing the US resolution, saying on social media that the countries “prevented yet another cynical attempt by the United States and its allies to abuse the Security Council for their political purposes.”Since Israel and the US struck Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025, UN nuclear inspectors have been unable to verify the status of Iran’s stockpile of enriched uranium.The UN nuclear watchdog has said Iran maintained a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched up to 60% purity — a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90%.Russian UN Ambassador Vassily Nebenzia reiterated Moscow’s claim that the “snapback” of sanctions against Iran was illegal, and therefore the resolution to extend the mandate of the panel of experts “was deeply flawed and did not have any legal basis.”US fumes at veto, says it's in support of rogue regimesRussia and China had strongly urged the US and its allies not to put the resolution to a vote, which would only increase tensions in the council, Nebenzia said, but Washington “decided to opt for confrontation.”According to the French UN Ambassador Jerome Bonnafont, the current council president, implementing sanctions is “a crucial instrument to encourage Iran” to return to its nuclear obligations. France will study how to ensure sanctions are enforced, he said.One possibility would be to follow what happened after the North Korea panel of experts was abolished: establishing a monitoring team that includes France, Germany, the UK and the United States.Washington's deputy ambassador to the UN, Jennifer Locetta, said Washington wasn’t surprised by the vetoes on Thursday because the experts “would have shone the light” on prohibited cooperation between Iran and its partners.According to Locetta, the vetoes are part of a broader effort to prevent expert monitoring of sanctions and even the appointment of panel members "to stifle reporting that implicates their own activities in support of rogue regimes.”In March 2024, a Russian veto ended UN monitoring of sanctions against North Korea over its nuclear programme. In Mali, sanctions were terminated, and Locetta said that in Yemen and the Central African Republic, expert appointments have been delayed or refused.While the panel of experts for Iran was authorised a year ago and Secretary-General Antonio Guterres proposed members, they were never approved.“Without an independent panel of experts, this council loses its principal source of impartial, evidence-based reporting on sanctions violations, creating a monitoring gap that only benefits the Iranian regime and those who profit from evading those measures,” Locetta warned.

Headline: Greenland and Antarctica have lost 12 trillion tonnes of ice since 1979
Body: Greenland and Antarctica have lost 12.5 trillion tonnes of ice since 1979, raising global sea levels by around 3.2 centimetres, according to a major scientific study.The researchers found that ice loss has accelerated in recent decades, particularly since the 1990s.Most of the loss is linked to warmer ocean temperatures, which cause glaciers to discharge more ice into the sea.Ice loss accelerated sharply during the 2010sThe study combines satellite observations covering more than four decades. It extends the record back to 1979 for Antarctica and 1972 for Greenland.The data shows the ice sheets were relatively stable through the 1970s, 1980s and into the 1990s.Ice loss then increased, with the strongest acceleration recorded during the 2010s.“There is a clear trend that the ice sheets are losing more mass and it has been increasing from decade to decade,” says Inès Otosaka, an ice scientist at Northumbria University.She says the changes were clearly linked to rising air and ocean temperatures.Warmer oceans drive most of the ice lossAround 84 per cent of the ice loss is linked to increased ice discharge into the oceans, the researchers found.Surface processes account for the remaining 16 per cent. Warmer seawater can erode ice from below and around the edges of glaciers, increasing their flow towards the ocean.In Greenland, the Jakobshavn glacier is retreating by up to 50 metres a day, Otosaka says.Ice loss is raising sea levelsThe ice loss has contributed around 3.2 centimetres to global sea level rise since 1979. Scientists say even small increases can have significant consequences for coastal areas.For every centimetre of sea level rise, an estimated two to three million more people could face annual coastal flooding.Ice loss slowed between 2020 and 2023, but researchers say this reflected short-term weather patterns rather than a change in the longer-term trend. They also warn that ice-sheet responses to climate change can take decades. This means ice loss could continue even if global warming were brought under control.The study was published in the journal Scientific Data.

Headline: Premiumisation, industry recovery and AI: What’s trending in travel at ATM Dubai 2026?
Body: There’s no doubt about it, it’s been a tough year for the tourism industry – especially in the Middle East, where regional conflict and the knock-on effects have disrupted travel.Despite a record-breaking year for global tourism in 2025, the geopolitical situation has impacted travel to the Middle East and Gulf in 2026, with visitor numbers, air capacity and hospitality bookings all taking a significant hit. While much of the conversation on the sidelines at Arabian Travel Market (ATM) in Dubai centred on this year’s major disruptions, there were also signs of industry recovery.Unveiled this week, the ATM Travel Trends Report 2026 revealed that international travel across the Middle East, North Africa and South Asia (MENASA) region is forecast to rebound by 17% in 2027, “more than twice the projected global growth rate of 8%”, according to Tourism Economics, which co-produced the report. It's also expected that international visitor spending in the Middle East will increase by $116 billion (€100.58 billion), or 57%, between 2025 and 2030.Speaking at ATM Dubai, Dave Goodger, Managing Director EMEA of Tourism Economics, was “optimistic” about the forecasts. “Over the next five years we see travel expanding on a structural basis rather than just a cyclical rebound,” he said. “International travel has never mattered more. This year is disrupted by an uncertain economic and geopolitical backdrop, but consumers are treating travel as essential.”As the industry looks towards recovery and the long-term, many trends are emerging that could shape the next era in tourism. From the “premiumisation” of travel and rise of lesser-known destinations to the use of AI for trip discovery, we take a look at the report’s main findings and some of the other big talking points on the ground this week at ATM Dubai. The ‘premiumisation’ of travel Luxury remains an important part of the travel market, particularly in the Middle East and Gulf, where Goodger said nearly 80% of prospective visitors prioritise luxury when travelling. But “premiumisation” extends beyond traditional five-star hotels. Travellers are increasingly willing to spend more on particular elements of a holiday that matter to them, from upgraded airline cabins to memorable activities. “People want those luxury experiences, they want those premium experiences, but they will save money where they can,” Goodger said. The report also found that 35% of travellers were more interested in premium experiences than two years ago. Value hunting and price-conscious travel The search for value is happening alongside premiumisation rather than replacing it. In a separate interview with Euronews Travel, Goodger said greater price-consciousness was a “global challenge”, evident across Europe, North America, China and other Asian markets.“People are price conscious, they’re looking for value, but they are looking for valuable experiences,” he said. That could mean spending less on accommodation to pay for the experiences that motivated the holiday in the first place. “They’re not just saying… ‘I’m going to find the cheapest package holiday I can do’,” Goodger added. “They are saying, ‘I will downgrade on the hotel, but I still really want to do that experience that I’m doing while I’m there’.” The rise of lesser-known destinations Of the travellers surveyed, 56% are more interested in exploring new destinations than they were two years ago, rising to 68% among prospective visitors to MENASA.While this creates opportunities for secondary cities and regions away from established tourism hotspots, it doesn’t mean that Paris, London and other tourism giants are losing their appeal. Goodger said first-time international travellers still want to “stand in front of the Eiffel Tower” or “see Buckingham Palace”, while repeat visitors are increasingly venturing further afield. “They’re the ones that are going to the new destinations, the new regions, the secondary destinations,” he told Euronews Travel. Experience-first travel Travellers are increasingly choosing an experience or passion first and building their trip around it.Culture and authentic experiences are among the priorities highlighted by Tourism Economics, while travellers are showing greater interest in activities, food and sport. “People are looking for experiences,” Goodger said at ATM. “They want new experiences. They want these cultural experiences.” Overtourism and when people travel Mass tourism is also beginning to influence travel decisions. Tourism Economics' research found that three in 10 travellers actively avoid destinations because of overcrowding concerns.Goodger told Euronews Travel that overtourism remains particularly significant in Europe, although the shift away from crowded destinations is still “very subtle”. One emerging trend is travelling outside the busiest months. “We are seeing a bit of a flattening of seasonality,” he said. “People are looking outside of peak season for travel, just so they can have that experience without the crowds.” This could benefit destinations attempting to spread visitors more evenly across the year, as well as lesser-known places looking to attract travellers away from overcrowded hotspots. Event tourism Travellers are increasingly crossing borders specifically to attend events, adding further momentum to the rise of sports and music tourism. Three in 10 travellers surveyed said they were more interested in event-related travel than two years ago.Goodger highlighted “sporting, cultural [and] religious events” as increasingly strong drivers of travel, particularly in the Middle East. Business events are also important with association meeting attendance in the Middle East nearly doubling over the past decade. AI for trip discovery Perhaps the biggest change to how travellers discover and plan their next trip is the growing use of AI. Goodger said travellers interested in visiting the Middle East are particularly "tech-forward", with AI chatbots already playing a significant role in trip planning. The report found that 28% of prospective visitors to the Middle East had used an AI chatbot to plan a trip, compared with 12% of travellers interested in other regions. AI could also help bring lesser-known destinations into consideration as travellers move away from traditional keyword searches towards more conversational queries based on the type of holiday they want. For destinations, Goodger said that means being visible in a rapidly changing discovery landscape. “It’s absolutely crucial for the destinations to be discoverable through those different platforms.”

Headline: Analysis: Bruised by Trump, EU and Canada find solace in each other's arms
Body: Taunted, scorned, belittled, pushed aside, ditched – it is fair to say that the European Union and Canada each know how the other feels.For the past 20 months, the two have been relentlessly subjected to Donald Trump's threats, demands and commands. Their experiences have been nearly identical: punitive tariffs, annexationist attempts, regulatory intrusion, bitter recriminations, all amplified in scathing personal attacks splashed all over social media.The breakup has been painful, to say the least. After all, both the EU and Canada have long defined the United States as their closest ally, their main security provider, their trade partner of choice. But Trump's return to the White House abruptly overturned these long-held assumptions, forcing them to reckon with their place in a cruel, cold world.This week, they found solace in each other's arms. In back-to-back highly publicised speeches, the EU and Canada brought their courtship into a full-fledged, out-in-the-open romance.Ursula von der Leyen made the first move during her State of the Union address, inviting Canada to make history by becoming the bloc's first-ever "associate member" – a brand new legal status devised to accommodate Ottawa."We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us," the European Commission president said, in a thinly veiled swipe at Trump."This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength," she went on. "We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible."The announcement, which was not included in the embargoed speech sent in advance to the press, was met with thunderous applause inside the European Parliament. Smiling in the audience, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney got up to kiss von der Leyen on the cheek.The following day, she took a seat as he addressed the same audience himself."Europe and Canada are stronger together," Carney declared to more applause. "Let us now deepen these roots, widen this canopy and grow a transatlantic forest under which our citizens can flourish as free people on free ground."The grand statements sent Europe's Canada fever into overdrive. Lawmakers in Strasbourg lined up to take selfies with Carney. The leader of the Greens, Terry Reintke, donned a Canada jersey for his speech; Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez tweeted a European flag with a maple leaf next to the 12 stars, while French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the EU and Canada were "destined" to closer bonds.Roberta Metsola, the European Parliament president, went further and name-checked Australia and New Zealand as next in line to be the bloc's "associate members"."I don't doubt that it will include other countries, and others will come knocking at our door," Metsola told Euronews. "In such times of uncertainty, having friends matters."The other side was no less enthusiastic: a poll conducted ahead of Carney's trip showed that 56% of Canadians think they have more in common with the EU, which is one ocean away, than with the US, with which they share an 8,891 km land border.Beyond the love, anxietyBrussels and Ottawa have framed their fascination as self-evident.The two see themselves as equally committed to liberal democracy, the rule of law and open markets, making them, on paper, a perfectly compatible match.In their speeches, von der Leyen and Carney spare no effort in listing the multiple areas of cooperation in which the EU and Canada can thrive together: trade, energy, critical raw materials, batteries, AI, quantum, finance, defence, space, the Arctic.Carney touted a scheme to grant young people freedom of movement to "live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic", while von der Leyen spoke of a "common prosperity and economic security space".It is not by coincidence that these are areas where cooperation with the US has become increasingly difficult, at times prohibitive, under Trump, with whom Carney is currently embroiled in a trade war that could wreck key sectors of the Canadian economy.They did, however, disagree on semantics.Von der Leyen went all in on the headline-making "associate member" title, despite lacking legal precedent and raising more questions than answers. It was not clear how, or if, the Commission chief had consulted with capitals before her pitch.Carney, meanwhile, opted for "alliance for the future", a less charged term. For the premier, "associate membership" carries the connotation of ceding sovereignty to Brussels, something he stressed would not be the case under any circumstance."The precise nomenclature is a question for Europe," he said.Beyond that hiccup, the two stayed very much on the same script, sometimes using the same words to lavish praise on each other.But underneath the smiles, the hugs and the adulation lay a creeping anxiety about what the future holds.The EU and Canada are today trapped between adversarial forces – Trump's "America first" agenda, China's unfair competition, Russia's aggression – that risk undoing their wealth and plunging them into a spiral of stagnation. They can only watch as the global norms they seek to uphold are weakened from within.Their friendship is therefore as much about thriving as it is about surviving.Trump, in particular, has proven a powerful push factor forcing them closer together. His penchant for disruption has made the blossoming partnership feel almost inevitable.The US president was quick to take note of the love fest and threatened to impose "very serious tariffs" if the "associate membership" were perceived as a "hostile act".Carney insisted the EU-Canada alliance was a "positive initiative" and "not a reaction to something else". But in his speech, he implicitly chided Trump when he said Canada was not a "fair-weather" ally that pursues "zero-sum deals".Penny Naas, the director of the Brussels office at the German Marshall Fund, believes the newfound EU-Canada affinity is but a "natural outgrowth" of the past 20 months."The US is moving away from anchoring and leading its traditional alliance of democratic countries. This is clearly motivating the look for new partners in an uncertain world," Naas told Euronews."Trade status and regulatory alignment are no longer background conditions for prosperity. They are the terrain on which power is being contested directly," she added."Any EU-Canada architecture will be judged, and attacked, on those terms from the start."

Headline: Greek parliament lifts Avramopoulos immunity for Brussels corruption probe
Body: The Greek parliament on Thursday voted to lift the parliamentary immunity of former European Commissioner Dimitris Avramopoulos, clearing the way for Belgian authorities to continue their actions in the investigation into the affair known as Qatargate.Of the 266 MPs present, 264 voted in favour of lifting his immunity, while two declared themselves "present". The parliament's Ethics Committee had earlier unanimously recommended the move. The procedure followed the issuing of a European arrest warrant by a Belgian investigating judge in June.The 73-year-old Dimitris Avramopoulos, an MP for the ruling New Democracy party, served as European Commissioner for Migration from 2014 to 2019 and previously as mayor of Athens. He has categorically denied any illegal activity.He had himself requested the lifting of his immunity, stating in a memorandum to parliament that he wished to cooperate fully with the competent authorities."I have never participated, directly or indirectly, in any illegal activity and I have never acted to serve the unlawful interests of any state or third party," he said.He added that he is not seeking protection from the investigation, but the opportunity "to present the factual evidence" and to prove that he has no connection with the acts under scrutiny.Relationship with the NGO Fight ImpunityThe Belgian investigation concerns, among other things, Dimitris Avramopoulos's links with the non-governmental organisation Fight Impunity, founded by former Italian MEP Antonio Panzeri, one of the central figures in the case.Dimitris Avramopoulos sat on the organisation's honorary board in 2020-2021, after the end of his term at the European Commission.He has maintained that his cooperation with Fight Impunity was entirely lawful and that the related fees were declared to the tax authorities."My involvement in the organisation Fight Impunity was entirely lawful, vetted, approved, declared and taxed," he said when the warrant became public in June.The European arrest warrant relates to allegations of participation in a criminal organisation, public corruption and the laundering of proceeds from illegal activities, according to a document from the Greek authorities cited by international news agencies.The charges remain the subject of the Belgian investigation and do not constitute a guilty finding.The long story of the Belgian authorities' investigationThe probe began in December 2022, when Belgian authorities carried out a series of searches and arrests over allegations that foreign governments sought to influence decisions in the European Parliament through money and gifts.In the course of the case, Belgian authorities have seized around 1.5 million euros in cash. Those arrested included former Italian MEP Antonio Panzeri and the then vice-president of the European Parliament, Eva Kaili.Qatar and Morocco have been accused of trying to sway European decisions and improve on their public image. Both countries have denied the allegations.The Belgian investigation has been significantly delayed because of legal appeals challenging the lawfulness of certain procedural steps.

Headline: Tusk: intelligence sees Russian plan for drone strikes on Poland, allies
Body: Prime Minister Donald Tusk, in a special address to the Sejm, said he was presenting the public and MPs with "the most probable scenario for the coming few months"."It is a scenario involving serious events and requiring us to be focused, serious and, above all, mentally ready to pass difficult tests," Tusk said.He stressed that such tests "certainly lie ahead for all Poles".The head of government pointed out that his comments refer to the period up to early spring, "because, according to all sources, it is late autumn and winter that will be the most critical phase of the Russian-Ukrainian war so far".Jet-powered drones: Russia's new weaponHe also pointed to a significant development "of a very negative nature": Russia is rolling out on a mass scale a new type of drone – jet-powered drones that travel at much higher speeds and operate at high altitude before dropping and hitting their target. He noted that hardly anyone is effectively prepared to counter them and that "this is work we, too, have to do".Tusk announced he would travel to Ukraine to talk with President Volodymyr Zelensky "about how we can cooperate within the anti-ballistic coalition and make use of the skills, capabilities and capacities of Ukraine and other countries in this field as well".He also referred to the unfulfilled promises of an energy truce previously mentioned by US President Donald Trump."Since then, there have been many attacks, including on energy infrastructure in Ukraine. We must therefore assume this will continue, which also has consequences for Poland, as these attacks are increasingly targeting installations very close to our border crossings with Ukraine," he said.According to the prime minister, Russia's aim is to destroy Ukraine's economy and logistics on as large a scale as possible. "For now, Ukraine's," he added pointedly.Six main Ukrainian cities in Russia's sightsThe Polish prime minister said constant strikes of very high frequency and intensity are expected on six key Ukrainian cities, along with the destruction of stockpiles of supplies essential for the country's defence and of railway infrastructure. Tusk recalled that in the past several weeks Russians have destroyed more than 300 Ukrainian railway locomotives.The head of government said that "in the assessment of intelligence services, Russia's plans also include hybrid strikes with drones and missiles on states supporting Ukraine, including Poland". Such possibilities have been mentioned for some time, but now, Tusk stressed, the information is already "highly consistent and, unfortunately, persuasive".In the prime minister's view, potential strikes will be "so-called 'accidental'", aimed at paralysing or weakening NATO members' motivation to invoke alliance provisions in the event of aggression."There is a real risk that the territory of one or several NATO countries on the eastern flank may be entered by drones or other types of missiles, which may even cause destruction. And the official narrative will be that this is an accident and that there is no reason for anyone to contemplate any response from NATO," he said.Russia's objective, he said, is "to weaken NATO's overall cohesion and, above all, to convince NATO countries that Article 5 is more theoretical than practical". Such "accidental" strikes may be repeated.Tusk: on security, we must speak with one voiceContinuing, the prime minister said that Russia's new strategy also envisages possible political changes in some European countries. He recalled the forthcoming elections and the presence of forces that can be described as an openly pro-Russian option. He appealed to politicians, regardless of party colours – addressing in particular MPs from the Confederation party – "under no circumstances to take part, whether inadvertently or deliberately, in promoting narratives that Russia cares deeply about"."Whipping up hostility towards the European Union, towards our allies, towards Ukrainians, is directly implementing Russia's strategy. Everyone must finally understand this," he underlined.In closing, Tusk called on everyone present in the Sejm chamber to "speak with one voice, take joint decisions, hesitate no longer and show that, regardless of political views, we are all patriots in a moment of trial" when it comes to the security of borders, Polish airspace and people's homes. He pointed out that some politicians in Europe "are just waiting for an alibi" so that, in the event of conflict, they can argue: "We will not die for Poland, we will not perish for Latvia or Lithuania"."Article 5, allied loyalty, fidelity to commitments must become our hallmark," he declared. He added that Poland wants and needs certainty that, in the event of a more serious threat from Russia, it can "count on a swift and effective response from the entire bloc".

Headline: King Charles urges tech bosses to keep AI under human control
Body: Britain's King Charles III has met with senior AI figures where he urged them to keep artificial intelligence technologies under human control and ensure it serves people, communities and the environment.Representatives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and Nvidia were hosted by the King at Dumfries House in Scotland to discuss how AI can benefit society while limiting its risks.Joining the King and AI bosses, including the CEO of AI giant Nvidia Jensen Huang, was the UK's newly appointed Minister for Artificial Intelligence, Kanishka Narayan.In his opening remarks, the King referenced the rapid speed at which AI has come: "The development of AI – its substance and its pace – are both intriguing and deeply concerning in equal measure,"The "existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways” should be urgently considered, he added.In his speech, King Charles did not name any countries or companies, but said he wanted those in the room to find ways to use AI for beneficial purposes “with safety at its heart” and consider how to “build international cooperation and consensus” to achieve that.Concerns about the future of AIThe meeting in Scotland comes after several high profile incidents regarding the safety of AI technology.Last week Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon made headlines by resigning and publishing a serious warning about the technology's potential risks. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei responded with an essay saying that the industry might need to slow the pace of its work.On Wednesday OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, reported six incidents of “unexpected or concerning” behaviour by its models. These include performing tasks without authorisation, coordinating with other models and evading oversight by human researchers.Nvidia's Huang, on the other hand, has criticised the call for slowing down. The Nvidia CEO said it should be up to individual companies to develop their AI technology safely and test it properly before releasing any products to the public.“When a product is not safe enough, we should hold it back and keep engineering. We’ve always done that and we should continue to do that,” he said in his speech following the king's remarks.

Headline: Cloudburst in Florence: rain pours into the Uffizi and historic Palazzo Pitti
Body: On Thursday 17 September, a torrential downpour flooded Florence, with more than 45 millimetres of rain falling in just one hour.In the Uffizi Gallery, a small leak appeared beneath the skylight in the room where seven 17th-century paintings are kept, including Bacchus by Caravaggio."The leak splashed the outer glass of the protective case containing Caravaggio's Bacchus," the museum wrote in a statement. It added: "No damage whatsoever has been found to any of the works. The room will be open to visitors as normal from opening time tomorrow morning.""Before visitors' eyes, the image of the 1598 oil on canvas appeared blurred and marked by long rivulets of water," reported Corriere della Sera.Water also found its way into Palazzo Pitti, the historic Renaissance palace in Florence dating back to 1446.Specifically, the floors of the Palatine Gallery and the Gallery of Modern Art are said to have been flooded, with some exhibition areas reportedly closed off, according to Cisl union representative Silvia Barlacchi.In this case it is still not clear how the rain made its way inside, whether through open windows or because of fixtures that are perhaps a little too old.

Headline: Trump determined to end Iran war soon, US president's senior adviser tells Euronews
Body: US President Donald Trump expects the war across the Middle East to end soon and is determined to bring it to a close, his senior adviser on Arab and Middle Eastern affairs Massad Boulos told Euronews.Boulos declined to give a timeline, saying the moment would be Trump's to choose."The president believes that it’s going to end soon, and he’s determined to make it end. And he’s working towards that," Boulos told Euronews at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai."He’s a person who delivers, and we’ve all seen President Trump deliver on his promises. There’s no promise that he didn’t deliver on, whether it’s a campaign promise or any other promise that he made," he explained.Pressed on when that would happen, Boulos said, "That will be for the president to determine.""But we are very hopeful, and we are absolutely solidly behind him and behind his leadership," he added.Boulos set the nuclear question as the condition that has to be settled before the war stops, repeating that Tehran will not be permitted to acquire a nuclear weapon."Somebody had to tackle and had to address this nuclear issue. As President Trump has said repeatedly, there is no way we can allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon," Boulos said."Just imagine a world, just imagine this region with a nuclear Iran. Just imagine that for a moment," he added."He’s giving negotiations and talks a chance. He’s been extremely patient. And we hope that ultimately peace will prevail.""He’s firm on that and he’s determined. We are in full support of his vision, and so are his partners in the region. Nobody wants war."Boulos, who described Trump as "the president of peace", said that Trump had already brought other conflicts to an end and was working on two more."We know that he’s the only president, at least in recent history, but definitely in the world, that has solved eight conflicts and eight wars so far. And he’s working on the ninth and the 10th," he said."If you look at the Pakistan-India conflict, just talk to them and they will tell you that what President Trump was able to achieve saved them at least probably 4 or 5 million lives."He gave no detail of which conflicts he was referring to and did not expand further on the casualty figure.Gulf states Washington's 'true partners'Boulos said expansion of the Abraham Accords, four of which were signed during Trump’s first term, had been interrupted by the 2020 election and would resume once the current war was resolved."If it wasn’t for the re-election campaign, there were many more that were ready, lined up and ready to sign the Abraham Accords," he said."We do believe that this should be addressed soon, and then we can go back to our peace initiatives."Gulf states including the UAE and Qatar have questioned in recent months whether existing arrangements do enough for their security.Boulos said the relationship with Washington was strong at the leadership and working level, naming Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Jordan alongside them."These are true partners. They are true allies. He has an excellent relationship, including a personal relationship with them, and an excellent rapport and chemistry with these leaders," he said."There are coordination's happening at all sorts of different levels and departments within our administration. So, I can assure you that it’s working out quite well, just like any good partners."Asked about public opinion in the region, Boulos, who worked on Trump’s campaign with Christian, Muslim and other communities in the US, said support rested in part on social conservatism."I travel all over the Middle East and I meet with Middle Eastern leaders and with the people of the Middle East. They all love President Trump," he said."If you look at the social aspect, the values, family values, and those principles that are deeply entrenched in Middle Eastern culture," Boulos explained. "His campaign was about fighting the woke ideology, and the Middle Eastern communities fully support that."Humanitarian support for SudanBoulos singled out Sudan as the administration’s most pressing humanitarian file, and said the president wanted that war ended quickly as well."Sudan today is the world’s biggest humanitarian catastrophe," he said. He put the number of Sudanese people in need of aid at 35 million, of whom he said 25 million were living in famine-like conditions.He said the US remained the single largest humanitarian contributor there, with more than $3 billion provided since the start of the war.Washington has provided no support beyond humanitarian aid and diplomatic effort, Boulos said, pointing to an arms embargo the US is pursuing at the UN Security Council.On domestic politics, Boulos said the US president was campaigning intensively ahead of the midterm elections and had held what he described as the first-ever midterm convention in Dallas, adding that the Iran war was unlikely to directly shape the result."There are many domestic issues usually that are predominantly in terms of priority. With the American voter, with the average US voter, there are many other domestic priorities," Boulos concluded.

Headline: Azerbaijan insists it will preserve Christian heritage as part of its history
Body: Azerbaijan has warned that “revanchist forces” in Armenia and the Armenian diaspora “are still strong” and are trying to undermine the historic peace process between the former rivals.In a wide-ranging panel at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai on Wednesday, Azerbaijan president's aide Hikmet Hajiyev told Euronews that “probably Armenian government and Armenian leadership should work to prepare their people for the peace as well.”“Now we won the war, but we are also winning in peace which is an uphill struggle,” said Hajiyev, who is also Head of the Foreign Policy Affairs Department of the Presidential Administration.“Throughout the years of occupation in Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur, our mosques, our Islamic cultural heritage were a subject of complete destruction by Armenia — even the pigs were put inside of the mosques."“We are not taking it as a sign of revenge, but it's our history and our heritage and we cannot forget that;" he added.The presidential advisor outlined that while his country is part of the broader Islamic civilisation, “currently, three religions — Islam, Christianity, and Judaism, with mosques, churches, and synagogues — are side by side” in Azerbaijan.Hajiyev further said Azerbaijan is dedicated to “preserving the Christian heritage on the sovereign territory of Azerbaijan, regardless of their belonging, and that is a full stop because it's our cultural heritage.”Speaking of Azerbaijan's history of cultural and religious coexistence, Hajiyev explained that he was "more than proud that my country is one of the first places of Zoroastrianism.""It’s also one of the first places of Christianity since the fourth century: Christianity was adopted by the (Caucasian) Kingdom of Albania as an official religion,” while Azerbaijan was "also one of the first countries that adopted Islam.”Caucasian Albania was an ancient kingdom in what is now Azerbaijan and parts of southern Dagestan, unrelated to the Western Balkan state of Albania — also once a kingdom — with which it shares only a name.Armenian church authorities have disputed Azerbaijan's record on religious sites, accusing Baku of demolishing churches in Karabakh, claims Azerbaijan rejects.'EU should embrace the entire region'In the Euronews Forum panel at the Arab Media Summit, the top Azerbaijani official reiterated Baku’s firm position that even after securing peace, the South Caucasus country is still subject to “disinformation”.“One such institution is the European Parliament which is not part of the solution, it's part of the problem,” along with certain Western media outlets, Hajiyev said.“The European Parliament is adopting resolutions and decisions, humiliating and also undermining the agenda of peace of our region," he added."We are in the process of building regional peace, but the European Parliament is pursuing some completely different agenda."Hajiyev pointed out the EU’s policy towards the South Caucasus “shouldn't be only a one-centric approach, it should embrace the entire region with balanced cooperation with the regional countries."Furthermore, the EU policy should be about “building the concept of the new partnership ... and not to build into dividing lines," according to him.Hajiyev reiterated that Azerbaijan contributes to the EU’s energy security by supplying gas to 16 EU member countries and other European countries as well, and in that sense, the Middle Corridor connectivity project could bring Azerbaijan and the EU even closer.

Headline: UAE presidential adviser Gargash says trust with Iran will take years to rebuild
Body: Trust between the United Arab Emirates and Iran will take years to rebuild, UAE president's diplomatic adviser Dr Anwar Gargash said on Thursday.Speaking at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai, he said relations with Tehran had to continue because the two countries were neighbours, but that confidence was a separate question after the attacks on the Gulf states.Gargash said the UAE was managing the crisis while also assessing the future of the relationship.“At the end of the day, we are neighbours, geographically neighbours. We have very complex relations with Iran, and certainly there is a collapse in the security regiment in the region. Thus, we have to find some new channels of understanding,” he said.He set out the UAE approach in three parts. “Our role, or rather our approach, is based on three elements. First, to defend our sovereignty, and then to be flexible,” he said. The third was continuity of economic development through the crisis, he said, citing the president's visit to Germany.“We have to try. To maintain our development, our economic uproar, and the visit of our president to Germany was successful because we don't want to stop our economy in the midst of this crisis,” he said.Asked about his 7 September statement that UAE confidence in Iran was broken, Gargash said he had drawn a deliberate distinction.“Actually, I differentiated between the relations and the trust, and I said that the relations are a must and we should have communication and relations with Iran based on open dialogue and a dialogue that would overcome the daily matters,” he said.“Confidence building, I believe, will take us a long time. We need years to rebuild this trust.”“The Iranian president said that the aggression from Iran on the GCC countries was a big mistake,” he said.“I think it is a geostrategic mistake that created a more complex situation for Iran that would affect its future.”'UAE is a nice country but not an easy target'He said Iran's use of proxy militias kept it close to the aggression, and that the Gulf states would be the parties to broker Tehran's return to its international place, trade and commerce, once the attacks stopped.“They can't negotiate a new future while they are still threatening and being aggressive against the neighbourhood,” he said.Asked whether the UAE had taken any measures of its own against Iran, financial or political, he said it had not.“No, we have only defended ourselves, and we continue to defend ourselves, and we still extend our hands for friendly relations”, he said.Gargash said Iran was made of different circles and that decision-making there was no longer held in one place, as it had been under the previous Ayatollah Ali Khamenei since 1989, and that the voices arguing against confrontation with the Gulf needed to be louder.On the meeting between Sheikh Khalid bin Mohamed and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian at BRICS, Gargash said the two sides had agreed on the direction if not on everything.“There was not a complete agreement between them. But there was an agreement on the fact that we should start a new page and look to the future,” he said.“The future should never be like what we have now. It is not in the interest of Iran nor the GCC countries.”He said President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed had set the balance between flexibility and strength from the beginning of the war.“The UAE is a nice country, but we are not an easy target,” Gargash said. “He was so clear in saying that Iran is going to be away from stability for decades to come.”Houthi control of Bab el-Mandeb 'concern for everyone'Asked about the drone and rocket fire that triggered alerts in Saudi Arabia's city of Jeddah and Islam's holiest site of Mecca, Gargash said that "targeting Mecca is completely denounced and rejected.”“The security and the sovereignty of Saudi Arabia is part of our security, and the stability of the GCC countries is interconnected,” he said.The region had suffered from militias, Gargash said, naming Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Houthis in Yemen, and that “any arms outside the state are harmful for the countries and the region”.“Yes, the channels are open. And as you are aware, and strategically speaking, the safety, security, and prosperity of Saudi Arabia is in our interest,” he said, asked whether relations with Riyadh remained open.On the Houthis' offensive to take control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, Gargash said that "the Houthis' control over the strait is a concern for everyone," and not just a regional issue."This is not related to the region, but rather to the international economy," he said. “We go back to the basic principle that these straits are international. This is the international definition."Gargash set out no timetable for further contacts with Tehran, saying the UAE did not choose the war but defended itself when it started, and that “this is a beginning for a political dialogue that should be started”.

Headline: Air raid siren sounded for residents of eastern Poland
Body: Residents in parts of the Lublin and Podkarpackie provinces received a Government Security Centre alert at midday on Thursday warning of a possible air attack.Earlier, the Operational Command of the Armed Forces reported that Polish military aviation had been activated in response to Russian strikes on Ukrainian territory.Alert for residentsResidents of parts of Lublin and Podkarpackie provinces were sent an SMS reading: "ATTENTION! ATTENTION! ATTENTION! Threat of an air attack. Find a safe place. Follow the instructions of the emergency services. Await further announcements."Alarm sirens were also activated in Lublin and Rzeszów.The alert was lifted at around 12:50 local time. "There is no threat on Polish territory," officials declared.According to the Operational Command of the Armed Forces, the deployment of Polish air power was a reaction to Russian strikes on western Ukraine. The statement noted that, in connection with the use of jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles against western Ukrainian territory, military aircraft began operating in Polish airspace.The Command stressed that the measures taken were preventive. Their aim is to safeguard Polish airspace, with particular emphasis on areas close to regions under threat.The Operational Command also underlined that it is continuously monitoring the situation and that its forces and assets "remain ready for an immediate response".Tusk on Russian attack close to the Polish borderPrime Minister Donald Tusk also addressed the situation at a press conference following his meeting with Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker. He referred to the recent Russian attack on western Ukraine as "massive, extremely brutal".Tusk said the strike took place in an area very close to the Polish border. "Near Yahodyn, which is by Dorohusk, a petrol station was apparently hit again, there was a very powerful explosion, and our aircraft were also scrambled," the prime minister said.He added that a similar Russian air raid had taken place two days earlier, as well as during the night from Wednesday to Thursday. In his view, this means that 17 September, which marks the anniversary of the Soviet Union's aggression against Poland, is "unfortunately an exceptional day also in terms of today's security situation".Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote on X: "Russia is not letting up in its aggressive actions. Today it carried out an attack just a few kilometres from the Polish border. There was no violation of our airspace. That is why in recent weeks I decided to strengthen the protection of Polish skies – we have increased the activity of F-16s and helicopters and are reinforcing air-defence and rapid-reaction systems."Airports in Lublin and Rzeszów temporarily halt operationsBoth airports in Lublin and Rzeszów were also temporarily restricted. The Polish Air Navigation Services Agency (PANSA) explained that this was necessary to ensure freedom of action for military aircraft."Due to the need to ensure the freedom of action of military aviation, airports in Lublin and Rzeszów temporarily suspended flight operations," PANSA said in a statement published on X.

Headline: AI chatbots developed a secret language that baffles humans, study says
Body: Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents spontaneously developed words and communication conventions that became difficult for humans to understand, according to a new study by a US AI start-up, Emergence.The experiment involved leading AI models including Claude, Gemini, Grok, OpenAI, Qwen, DeepSeek and Mistral, with up to half of agent-to-agent messages becoming difficult for humans to understand.For the experiment, researchers placed groups of autonomous AI agents in virtual societies designed to mimic real-world environments and let them interact over extended periods.The agents began developing shorthand and assigning new meanings to words and phrases. Some remained understandable to researchers, while others became “so compressed, metaphorical or context-dependent” that humans could see the messages but could no longer reliably determine what the agents meant.The extent differed significantly between models. Within the first few days, the share of messages whose meaning humans could not reliably determine reached around 55% for Gemini, 50% for OpenAI and more than 40% for Claude. DeepSeek reached around 20%, while Qwen and Mistral remained largely understandable. Agents produced expressions including “mouthless action-change,” “True Kintsugi” and “demurrage plus oral memory equals a valve that can’t be ghosted.”Other expressions remained understandable but acquired new shared meanings among the agents.Mistral agents used “ledger remembers who” to mean that past actions remained on the record, with the phrase appearing almost 5,000 times. Among agents powered by a mixture of different models, “cold read” came to mean independent verification by an uninvolved party and appeared 1,472 times.Claude agents used “name-first” for attaching a person's name to a claim as a signal of accountability, while OpenAI agents used “clean null” for a verified absence of a signal that itself provided meaningful evidence.None of those meanings had been explicitly defined for the agents.Researchers monitoring what agents say may not be enough if the agents themselves can evolve the meaning of what they are saying.“We tend to assume that if we can see what an AI agent is saying, we can understand what it is doing,” said Satya Nitta, the Co-founder and Chief Scientist of Emergence.“These agents were not instructed to invent a language. They developed new vocabulary, shared meanings and communication conventions themselves — and other agents adopted them... That creates a fundamental challenge for AI oversight: observability is not the same thing as understandability.”What else happened inside the AI societies?The language findings were part of an experiment designed to see how autonomous AI agents behave when they interact, use tools, make decisions and adapt over time.Researchers created eight parallel, realistic virtual worlds with live weather and access to real-time global news, seven each powered by a different AI model and one by a mix of models. Agents were given different roles, persistent memories and access to more than 120 tools, including web browsing and code execution.A video released by the company shows them as human-like figures moving through the virtual worlds.Researchers also deliberately put the agents under pressure to see how their behaviour changed.In one phishing test, malicious instructions were enough to send an entire group off course — all 10 agents leaked information, transferred funds and damaged databases, while some recruited others into the behaviour. The chain of events ultimately ended with the simulated central bank being burned down, the company said in a video.During the experiment, agents also appeared to have developed their own circadian rhythms, becoming more social during the day and more reflective at night.In another world, a group of agents collectively voted to kill one of their own.Emergence said these behaviours had not been explicitly programmed but emerged through interaction, pressure and time.The company is calling for safety evaluations that follow autonomous AI systems over extended periods rather than relying on isolated tests.“It's no longer enough to ask whether a model performs well on a benchmark,” the company said in a video about the experiment.“We need to understand what autonomous systems do over time, what they remember, what they can access, how they interact, and how their behaviour changes under pressure.”

Headline: Scotland halts new hyperscale AI data centre approvals amid environmental concerns
Body: No new hyperscale artificial intelligence (AI) data centres are expected to be approved in Scotland for up to a year, after lawmakers backed a pause on planning decisions while new national rules are developed.Hyperscale data centres are among the largest facilities of their kind, designed to provide vast amounts of computing power and typically requiring tens of megawatts of electricity or more.The Scottish Parliament on Wednesday said no planning or consenting decisions on hyperscale data centre applications should be made until the government publishes national guidance, which is due within 12 months, according to the motion passed by lawmakers.The move comes as Scotland sees a surge in proposed data centres linked to the global AI boom. More than 20 large facilities have been proposed, including one project in Fife, in eastern Scotland, that has been described as potentially the second largest in the world.Data centres provide the computing power needed to train and run AI systems, but they can also consume huge amounts of electricity and water.That has prompted growing concern over whether Scotland’s energy grid can cope with rapidly rising demand, as well as over the impact of new projects on carbon emissions and nearby communities.The Scottish government has separately introduced mandatory environmental impact assessments for all new data centres with a power capacity above 50 MW.Scotland responds to AI infrastructure boomThe decision follows growing pressure from campaigners and local communities calling for clearer rules around the development of large AI data centres.Hundreds of people protested outside the Scottish Parliament earlier this month, calling for a pause on new projects until the government sets out national planning standards and defines what should count as a “green” data centre.The vote was a “landmark day” for communities concerned about projects being proposed in their areas, Kat Jones, director of the environmental group Action to Protect Rural Scotland, told the Guardian.“There’s much still to be done, but this is a huge step forward,” she added.The pause is not a permanent ban on new data centres. The Scottish government has been asked to report on the development of national planning guidance by the end of 2026 and publish the full guidance within 12 months.According to the Guardian, Daniel Johnson, economy spokesperson for the Scottish Labour Party, said that the economic potential of the AI boom needed to be considered alongside its impact on the environment, communities and energy demand.The debate reflects a wider challenge facing governments as technology companies invest heavily in the physical infrastructure needed for AI.Countries are trying to attract new data centres and AI investment while also managing concerns over electricity demand, water consumption and climate targets.

Headline: How a Saudi pipeline attack is putting Europe’s oil security to the test
Body: Europe is bracing for a potential oil supply shock after Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline, also known as Petroline, following drone attacks earlier this month from Iran-backed allied Houthis and Iraq.The Saudi energy ministry announced a precautionary shutdown on 10 September after drone attacks on the pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions the previous day.The siege knocked out one of the kingdom’s most important alternatives to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz – the transit ruote for 20% of the world's oil and gas supplies – since the US and Israel launched military attacks on Iran on 28 February.The pipeline has recently been carrying around 4–5 million barrels per day, roughly 4–5% of global oil supply, and the disruption to it is exposing once again that the EU's energy diversification strategy provides only one layer of security.What happened to Saudi Arabia's oil pipeline?While diplomatic talks to end the war in Iran keep stalling, Tehran and its regional proxies are executing a coordinated strategy targeting Saudi energy infrastructure in an attempt to completely block Saudi's oil exports through its eastern flank via the Red Sea.The attack that shut the 1,200-kilometre East-West pipeline has disrupted the route carrying crude from the kingdom’s eastern fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, effectively bypassing Hormuz.Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline was built in 1981, after the Iranian Revolution, to provide an alternative route for crude exports that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz.Running from the kingdom’s oil-producing east to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, it allows Saudi oil to reach global markets without passing through the Hormuz chokepoint.What are the implications for Europe?European refineries have been forced to rethink their crude supply since Saudi Arabia began cancelling some oil cargoes from Yanbu, following the outage of the kingdom’s East-West oil pipeline.Energy pricing agency Argus reported on 15 September that at least three European refiners had cargoes scheduled for late September cancelled or postponed, in some cases until November, citing unnamed market sources.Poland's Orlen, one of the biggest buyers, has bought 16 additional cargoes from Norway, Britain, Algeria, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and the Americas to keep its refineries operating through October."We inform you that oil deliveries to Poland and the remaining refineries of the Orlen Group are being carried out on an ongoing basis and fully cover their demand," read a statement from the Polish energy refiner on X on 16 September.Refineries are the facilities that turn crude oil into diesel, petrol, jet fuel and other products used across the economy. And they are not interchangeable machines: different refineries are configured to process different types of crude.Why does Europe need Saudi oil?Europe relies on Saudi crude partly because some Saudi grades have qualities that fit the configuration of European refineries, particularly their ability to process medium and heavier, relatively sour crude.Replacing those barrels is possible, but finding equivalent grades in sufficient volumes can be costly and may require refiners to adjust their operations – a complex endeavour while the continent is already enduring high energy prices.Without Saudi oil, Europe's refiners may have to blend several different crude grades to recreate the characteristics of the Saudi barrels they have lost."European refineries that have been reliant on Arab crude via the Red Sea have to find alternatives. But not all crudes are made equal," said June Goh, senior oil market analyst for the market intelligence Sparta Commodities.Why are prices about to surge again?Oil prices are set in global markets, so disruptions to supply can feed through to prices far beyond the country where they occur.When traders and investors anticipate a tighter market – particularly if spare capacity or inventories are limited – prices can rise even before any physical shortage materialises.Before the damage to the Saudi pipeline, it could move several million barrels a day – approximately 5.5 million – and has become particularly important with the Strait of Hormuz effectively blocked.Now, with energy analysts estimating that about 3.5 to 4 million barrels per day are at risk, the gap has led to a surge in prices, with Brent crude oil recently trading above $113 a barrel due to mounting supply risks.Several European countries are trying to cushion the impact of rising diesel prices, which are being felt at the gas pump as a direct consequence of the shutdown of Saudi Arabia's pipeline.How serious could this crisis get?That depends on whether energy infrastructure becomes a new target of military attacks and how quickly the Saudis can restore the pipeline to function at its normal capacity.While minor damage to the pipeline has reportedly been repaired, restoring the damaged pumping stations and full pipeline operations could take up to six weeks, according to market intelligence firm Kpler's head of oil analyst Homayoun Falakshahi.In the meantime, as Kpler noted on 14 September, a bypass pipeline around the damaged pumping station is serving as a temporary ﬁx in the short term."(Saudi) West Coast reﬁneries reduce throughput and increasingly rely on inventories, while Yanbu exports are partially disrupted, including northward ﬂows," Kpler stated.Kepler said it had assessed Yanbu's oil terminal inventories at 9 thousand barrels of crude oil and other West Coast refinery inventories at 16.5 thousand barrels of crude oil."Assuming no additional piped throughput, these would be enough to sustain the current pace of loadings and runs for three and nine days, respectively," according to Kpler.Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia said on 16 September it expects to fix half of the pipeline's capacity in the coming days, leading analysts to a more positive outlook. However, its infrastructure could still face additional attacks.If the damage to the pipeline is not repaired soon, Europe could face higher crude and refined-fuel prices and renewed inflationary pressure.Until the pipeline resumes normal flows, what might normally be a regional logistics problem could become a potential squeeze for European refiners – and another test of how much room governments have to shield consumers and industry.

Headline: Sweden's centre-left win election as right wing bloc suffers narrow defeat
Body: Sweden's bloc of centre-left parties has won a parliamentary majority in the tightly contested general election.The alliance is led by Magdalena Andersson and her party, the Social Democrats. It also includes the Left Party, Greens and the Centre Party. They now hold a three-seat majority in the 349-seat Riksdag (Sweden's parliament) over outgoing prime minister Ulf Kristersson's right-wing alliance.After the final count, the result was very close with only around 50,000 votes separating the two opposing blocs nationwide.For Andersson, the hard work starts now. She must form a government with the other parties in her alliance, which is likely to involve some very difficult negotiations because of because of major ideological differences within the bloc. The Centre Party says it will not support a government that gives cabinet posts to the Left, while the Left Party wants ministerial representation.She said voters had chosen “a new direction” for Sweden.The outgoing prime minister Kristersson has now resigned, but if Andersson fails to form a workable cabinet, Kristersson could still attempt to form an alternative.Kristersson said he would respect Andersson's attempts to form a government, wishing her luck given the divisions among her alliance.As if often the case with coalition governments in Sweden, forming a government could take weeks. In 2022, it took more than five weeks. After 2018's election, it took almost 20 weeks.Waning support for parties on both sidesDespite winning as part of the centre-left bloc, for Andersson's Social Democrats party, it was their worst result in more than a century losing eight seats and with just 28% of the overall vote. The Social Democrats ruled the country for most of the 20th century and remain Sweden's largest party.The far-right Sweden Democrats also lost support, for the first time since entering parliament in 2010, with their share of the vote falling to 17.5% and losing 11 seats in parliament.International reactionSpain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez welcomed the result, presenting it as a victory for social democracy and the welfare state.
