Headline: Moldova, Greece and Ireland: Where tourist arrivals are on the rise in Europe this year
Body: International tourism grew just 0.4% in the first half of 2026, with Europe seeing a 3% uptick in arrivals, according to the latest World Tourism Barometer from UN Tourism.The continent was among the strongest performers, with only Africa seeing a larger growth of 4%. Some 350 million international tourists visited Europe between January and June this year – but that growth wasn’t uniform.Both Southern Mediterranean Europe and Central Eastern Europe saw a 4% growth, with Northern Europe up 3%.On the flip side, arrivals in Western Europe declined 1%, with UN Tourism noting this was “partly due to heatwaves in June and weaker long-haul demand in some destinations during Q2 2026”.The Middle East saw a 22% drop in arrivals, with South Asia down 5% and South East Asia down 1%.“The Middle East situation has touched destinations far beyond the region itself and serves as a clear reminder that, in such a connected world, resilience needs to be built everywhere and not just when a crisis begins,” UN Tourism Secretary-General Shaikha Al Nuwais said. The report notes that in Europe and Asia Pacific, the conflict has “partly shifted tourism demand toward nearby and more accessible destinations”.Which destinations saw the biggest growth? In Europe, Moldova had the biggest uptick in tourist arrivals, with a 25% rise in the first half of the year. Greece and Ireland both saw a 15% increase.Globally, the destinations seeing the biggest rises include El Salvador (+37%), Paraguay (+34%), Bhutan (+31%), Vanuatu (+30%), Palau (+29%), Mongolia (+27%), Uzbekistan (+25%) and South Korea (+21%).International arrivals are predicted to grow between 1% and 2% for 2026 – down from a forecast of 3% to 4% reported in January.

Headline: Iran expels Swedish diplomat in tit-for-tat after Stockholm's move
Body: Tehran has ordered a Swedish diplomat to leave Iranian territory within 48 hours, after Sweden expelled an Iranian diplomat from its embassy in Stockholm on Wednesday over activities described as incompatible with diplomatic norms.Alireza Yousofi, director-general for Western Europe at Iran's foreign ministry, summoned the Swedish ambassador in Tehran on Thursday to deliver the reciprocal expulsion order and convey what he described as Iran's protest at Sweden's "destructive policies and its hosting of terrorist groups."Iran's foreign ministry said in a statement that Sweden's decision to restrict the activities of an Iranian diplomat was "baseless" and attributed it to alleged Israeli influence, describing the move as an attempt to disrupt normal operations at the Iranian embassy in Stockholm.Tehran warned that any disruption of the embassy's work would engage Sweden's international responsibility under the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.Sweden's foreign ministry had summoned the Iranian ambassador in Stockholm on Wednesday and ordered the expulsion of one of his embassy's diplomats, citing "improper activities incompatible with the Vienna Convention." It gave no further details of what those activities involved.Sweden and Iran have a history of diplomatic confrontations. In June 2024, two Swedish citizens, Johan Floderus and Saeed Azizi, were released in a prisoner swap in exchange for Hamid Nouri, a former Iranian prison official who had been serving a life sentence in Sweden.Nouri was arrested at Stockholm Airport in November 2019 under universal jurisdiction and convicted for his role in the mass execution of political prisoners in Iran in 1988.In July 2025, Sweden joined several European countries, the US and Canada in accusing Tehran of orchestrating plots to threaten, abduct and harass dissidents, journalists and activists abroad.

Headline: Space economy report: Who's winning the race in Europe?
Body: Once considered a niche, the space economy is now a major, mature industrial force supporting innovation, public policy goals, and services in Europe and beyond.EU countries currently invest a bit more than 0.04% of their GDP in space, but some countries are moving faster than others.Regarding civilian space projects, Italy now spends more relative to its GDP than any other European country except Luxembourg, overtaking France after a major spending boost over the past 15 years.The OECD's latest Space Economy at a Glance report claims that Rome's space economy "is now a strategic high-value industrial and digital ecosystem, comparable to specialised niches in aerospace, electronics, telecommunications, software and advanced engineering", with an estimated output of €8 million.Japan has doubled its budget as well, becoming the top spender relative to GDP among OECD countries.Another impressive growth, though on a smaller scale, took place in Luxembourg, which tripled its budget since 2010.When it comes to overall public investments, however, France and Germany are Europe's leading space-faring nations, according to new OECD data.In 2025, they allocated up to €2.4 billion and €2.5 billion respectively in civilian space spending, followed by Italy with around €2 billion.The number of activities funded by government space budgets varies greatly across countries and can include, for example, the manufacture and operation of space infrastructure, the use of satellite data, signals and equipment, and any associated research and development.Military space: Germany on course to be Europe's top investorParis and Rome are putting a lot into research, with space accounting for 14% of each government's civil research and development funds in 2024.That's more than twice the OECD's 6.3% average.However, when it comes to military spending, it's a different story. Alongside plans to become the most powerful army in Europe, Germany is by far the top spender.Public demand is increasingly shaped by defence and security requirements, "although comparisons remain difficult as many programmes are classified or dual-use", says the OECD.Berlin plans to invest €35 billion in space-related defence capabilities by 2030, much more than France, which has allocated around €10.6 billion between 2024 and 2030, with a 25% rate of its government's space spending in 2025.For a cross-Atlantic comparison, the US spent 46.3% last year.As for China, the report says Beijing's spending remains "particularly difficult to estimate, as civilian, commercial and military activities are closely integrated under the country’s military-civil framework", adding that rough estimates suggest it could be the world's second-largest government space spender, but the "figures remain indicative".Satellites: UK far ahead in Europe thanks to navigation marketFrance, however, boasts a large satellite fleet, with 104 compared to Italy's 80 and Germany's 65, the report says.The largest one, though, belongs to the UK, with 757 satellites in orbit as of June.The industry already plays a significant role in the British economy, underpinning around 18% of UK non-financial GDP in 2022, compared with 16% in 2021."The largest estimated contribution came from industries relying on positioning, navigation and timing services provided by navigation satellites, at 14% of GDP, followed by industries supported by meteorological satellite services at 11%, and by satellite communications and earth observation services, each supporting around 7% of GDP", says the report.The overwhelming majority (98%) of British satellites belong to the private sector.Speaking of which, Europe has some serious private space players, but the reality check on the big picture is pretty stark.In 2025, only about 12.8% of global private space investment went to European recipients, compared to 67% directed to the US.This gap is significantly wider when it comes to satellite launches.Last year, the US attempted 181 orbital satellite launches. Europe managed just eight, well behind China at 92.

Headline: Tripoli busts Gaddafi-shaped pill shipment as al-Assad's captagon appears in Libya's east
Body: Tripoli government’s security forces have seized some 100,000 ecstasy tablets in the shape of Libya’s late leader Muammar Gaddafi, as a separate drug bust in the rival-controlled east discovered a shipment of captagon, the ousted Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad regime's narcotic of choice.The tablets in Tripoli, intercepted on Saturday by the Deterrence Apparatus for Combating Terrorism and Organised Crime known as Rada, featured Gaddafi’s bust decked out in his characteristic garb, according to Libyan news agency LANA.Rada said investigators received information about a criminal network pushing the pills through an undisclosed European country. The shipment came by sea through an unnamed port, hidden inside a Renault Master van.Suspects were apprehended and referred to the public prosecutor’s office, according to reports.Libyan authorities identified the tablets as ecstasy, commonly associated with MDMA, a popular clubbing stimulant known for causing a state of euphoria and emotional warmth.Although Tripoli did not disclose the street value of the pills, the 100,000 tablets could be worth between 500,000 and 1.5 million in the broader Mediterranean region, according to available data and informal sources. In a separate operation in Benghazi — controlled by forces aligned with Marshal Khalifa Haftar and his LNA armed faction  — the Criminal Investigation Agency stated this week it seized an undisclosed number of tablets it described as captagon, assessing that Syria was the likely manufacturing point of origin.Captagon is a cheap and highly addictive amphetamine-type stimulant that flooded Middle Eastern markets throughout the civil war in Syria, quickly becoming a major source of income for the al-Assad regime.Analysts at the New Lines Institute estimated Syria's captagon trade generated up to $10 billion (€8.6bn) per year at its peak, with the networks around the al-Assad family earning an estimated $2.4 billion (€2bn) annually.The regime's total earnings from the trade, which became industrialised around 2018-2019, remain difficult to calculate with precision.Multiple governments, including the US and the UK, have sanctioned al-Assad’s brother Maher and a network of associates for their alleged role in overseeing the drug's production and export from regime-controlled facilities in Latakia and the Qalamoun Mountains in cooperation with Hezbollah.A narcotics trading link between Latakia and Benghazi has been long established. In December 2018, Greek authorities intercepted a vessel carrying more than 3 million captagon pills from Latakia en route to the eastern Libyan port city, while separate reporting documented containers from Syria arriving in Benghazi carrying millions of tablets.Ecstasy meets GaddafiGaddafi-shaped tablets have also appeared in Libya before. In August 2025, Benghazi authorities seized an undisclosed quantity of captagon-type tablets bearing Gaddafi’s image.Forensic experts identified them as MDMA-type narcotics, and investigators stated that the manufacturing source was believed to be Syria. MDMA and captagon are both amphetamine-based stimulants.In a separate bust that same month, Benghazi said it found 45 ecstasy tablets in the shape of Gaddafi's face among a larger seizure of 1,355 assorted pills.It is unknown whether the different sets of Gaddafi tablets are linked to the same manufacturing or trafficking networks.Gaddafi, who ruled Libya for 42 years as its “Brotherly Leader,” was captured and killed by rebel fighters in October 2011 following a popular uprising backed by NATO airstrikes during the Arab Spring.Gaddafi's image has become increasingly visible in parts of the country 15 years on, often on clothing and at public gatherings marking the anniversary of his 1 September 1969 revolution.The United Nations drug watchdog UNODC said in its 2026 assessment that Libya was an increasingly significant regional transit point for synthetic drugs due to its political fragmentation and weak border controls.After al-Assad's fall in December 2024, the new Syrian authorities led by interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa destroyed multiple large-scale captagon production and storage facilities, including those found on the al-Assad regime’s former bases.However, some of the production and trade still persist after fragmenting into smaller networks mostly linked to al-Assad's loyalists with ties to Hezbollah in neighbouring Lebanon. UN experts reported in late 2025 that significant stockpiles remained in circulation across the wider region.

Headline: US Congress approves Russia sanctions that impact China and India
Body: The US House of Representatives approved a major new package of sanctions against Russia on Wednesday, clearing the way for President Donald Trump to sign into law the most significant American legislative action against Moscow since he returned to the White House.Lawmakers passed the measure 262 to 159, following the Senate's own overwhelming approval, 86 to 11, last month. Trump has indicated he will sign it.The sanctions target Russia's energy and defence industries, President Vladimir Putin and senior officials around him, and the so-called "shadow fleet" of tankers Moscow uses to evade existing Western restrictions.Crucially for global energy markets, the bill also grants Trump the power to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that continue buying large volumes of Russian oil and gas — a measure aimed squarely at China and India, two of Moscow's biggest remaining customers.That tariff provision proved contentious even among supporters of Ukraine in Washington. Some Democrats, while backing tougher action against Russia, objected to giving the president such broad authority over trade policy.Gregory Meeks, the senior Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, criticised the bill's drafting, arguing it prioritised presidential tariff powers over binding sanctions commitments. He said he would have supported the legislation had the tariff measures been stripped out, but Republicans blocked attempts to amend them.Despite these reservations, most Democrats ultimately voted for the bill, while a small number of Republicans opposed it on free-market grounds. Supporters say the added pressure is necessary as Russia's full-scale invasion enters its fifth year with no ceasefire in sight.Kyiv welcomes the bill but India holds firmThe vote came as Russian drone strikes hit civilian transport in southern Ukraine on Wednesday, killing five people, according to officials in Kyiv — an attack that added urgency to calls from pro-Ukraine campaigners for the bill's passage.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had lobbied Congress directly to pass the sanctions, arguing that only sustained economic pressure would push Moscow toward negotiations. Speaking in Washington in July, he said Russia was losing around 30,000 soldiers a month but showed no sign of ending the war, adding that the initiative on the battlefield had shifted out of Putin's hands.India responded on Thursday by signalling it would not change course, saying it would continue purchasing Russian oil "through diversified sourcing and on the basis of evolving market dynamics."Russia remains one of India's most important strategic and military partners, complicating Washington's efforts to isolate Moscow economically.The legislation also targets companies and foreign entities supporting Russia's military effort and extends existing sanctions related to Iran. It follows more than a year of delay, reflecting Trump's general preference for retaining personal control over sanctions and tariff policy rather than ceding it to Congress.Ukrainian advocacy groups welcomed the bill's passage while urging swift enforcement. "Once the bill is quickly signed and becomes law, we hope for strong US enforcement to finally end the cash flows to the Kremlin's war chest," said Svitlana Romanko of the energy lobby group Razom We Stand."Every day of delay is a day we in Ukraine must bury more people."

Headline: Watch this: The winning timepieces you couldn't miss at this year's US Open
Body: Alexander Zverev may now well be mulling over that old saying that time heals all wounds. Four years ago he faced a lengthy time off-court after horrifically tearing his ankle ligaments during the French Open semi-final match against Rafael Nadal. This year's not over yet but it's undoubtedly been the most successful period of the German tennis champion's career as he celebrates lifting two Grand Slam titles.On Sunday night as he lifted the US Open trophy in New York, Zverev had one eye on the time back on the old continent too, as he brandished a Jacob & Co "The World Is Yours" Dual Time Zone Tourbillon — a piece with two sub-dials for a second time zone.Luxury watch brands have been competing hard to be in the winner's photo for decades, and the final at Flushing Meadows is no exception. "The Open gets covered as a watch-spotting event in its own right", says Quaid Walker, CEO of Bezel, one of the world's leading platforms for buying and selling luxury watches."Zverev played the tournament in a skeletonized Epic X on an elastic band and changed into this for the trophy, which has become a small ritual of sorts among players with watch sponsorships.""The point of the swap is to be seen, and few watches are built to be seen like this one, with a globe-shaped dial and a tourbillon running at its center. It's a sight to behold, which is essentially the whole idea", adds Walker.The watch's globe-shaped dial is detailed right down to the mountain ranges and coastlines. At its centre, a so-called 30-second tourbillon spins twice as fast as a standard one — and it made waves last year at the Grand Prix d'Horlogerie de Genève.Alcaraz brings out the collector's holy grailEven though it did not lift the cup, Rolex — official watchmaker of the four Grand Slams and by far the watch brand most assossiated to tennis — stole the show during the entire event. The Spanish defending champion Carlos Alcaraz crossed the Atlantic wearing the Rolex Daytona "Le Mans," launched to mark the 100th anniversary of the French endurance race in 2023.That "100" printed in red on the black Cerachrom bezel is enough to send collectors into a frenzy — the watch now fetches over €200,000 on the second-hand market."Even when it was in production, you likely couldn't get your hands on one. These went exclusively to the brand's most established clients, with sub-single-year production runs per metal prior to discontinuation", Walker recalls.The brand with the crown signed the Spaniard in January 2022, just months before he won his first Grand Slam title at the US Open aged 19 and became the youngest player to ever top the ATP ranking. His comeback, however, from a troublesome wrist injury lay off was halted when he was narrowly beaten in the semis by home favourite Ben Shelton.Federer showcases 2026's ultimate RolexAlthough Shelton went on to lose in the final against Zverev, he cemented his place as one of Rolex's newest crown jewels alongside the brand's roster of "Testimonees" which now includes former US Open winners Jannik Sinner, Coco Gauff, and of course Roger Federer.The Swiss tennis legend, who retired in 2022, was inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame during this year's US Open, and chose the prestigious occasion to sport Rolex's latest, most colourful creation, the Oyster Perpetual 41 "Jubilee" — one of the most hyped watches of 2026."Since around 2020, the dial has overwhelmingly influenced the value of an Oyster Perpetual. The original lacquer colors did it first, the Celebration motif pushed it further, and the Jubilee is its most extreme version yet, with ten colours pad-printed in sequence. It's undeniably the OP to have right now, a fact reinforced by its presence on Federer's wrist," says Walker.Vekić and Kostyuk bring independents courtsideTwo women players really let their wrist do the talking at the tournament. When Croatia's Donna Vekić was knocked out in the second round by world number 29 Ann Li, she was wearing an FP Journe — one of the most sought-after independent brands among watchonistas.The titanium Elégante's electromechanical movement has a quirky trick: it stops ticking when at rest, then wakes itself up and resets to the correct time the moment it senses movement on your wrist. That gives it remarkable battery life — 8 to 10 years with daily wear.Another eye-catching piece was a Patek Philippe Aquanaut Luce as blue as the Flushing Meadows' acrylic hard courts. This 36mm steel watch, its bezel set with 46 diamonds, was worn by Marta Kostyuk.Kostyuk was knocked out in the fourth round, but still walked away with a major milestone to celebrate. The Ukrainian will break into the WTA Top 10 on Monday, joining her compatriot Elina Svitolina in making Ukrainian tennis history.Celebrity watch timeUp in the stands, brands made the most of the tournament to put on a show. "The Open is three weeks of tennis in New York, and the good seats are on camera for hours at a stretch. No other American sporting event gives you that kind of sustained view of who's there and what they're wearing. What ends up on a wrist in those seats is a decision now," notes Walker.Among the standout pieces: model Kaia Gerber wore a Cartier Panthère in yellow gold, in its "mini" size — a watch that costs roughly 100 times less than the RM 75-01 Flying Tourbillon Sapphire sported by rapper Travis Scott, estimated at more than €2 million."Scott has his own Audemars Piguet, a brown ceramic Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar he designed with the brand in 2023, so it says something that this is what he reached for instead. A sapphire-cased flying tourbillon is the brand at its most technical and least apologetic," according to Walker.The Flying Tourbillon, a hallmark of Richard Mille, was incarnated in the tennis world by Rafael Nadal, who wore it during his final appearance at Roland-Garros in 2024.Actor Brad Pitt, meanwhile, turned up wearing one of Swiss watchmaking's true classics: the Patek Philippe reference 2526, Calatrava model, valued at between €200,000 and €350,000 on the second-hand market."The 2526 houses Patek Philippe's first automatic caliber, the 12-600AT, which is still held in high regard. Its reputation rests as much on the design, where enamel against warm gold produces a delicate quality that's tough to beat. That same enamel doesn't forgive age or poor service, so clean examples have thinned considerably over 70 years. It's great to see one being worn on a bracelet rather than tucked away in a safe", Walker concludes.Victory or not, one thing is clear: at the US Open, there are many winners being worn on wrists.

Headline: Germany turns on Brussels as Chinese car sales on track to exceed 1m in 2026
Body: When Germany's finance minister chose Volkswagen's headquarters to deliver a warning about China, the symbolism wasn't subtle. Standing in the shadow of the carmaker's flagship plant on Thursday, Lars Klingbeil told Brussels it was time to stop pulling punches with Beijing — a message aimed less at EU trade officials than at the tens of thousands of German autoworkers watching their jobs disappear."We cannot, when all is said and done, be naive in our dealings with China," Klingbeil said, fresh from meetings with VW staff representatives and local politicians. Germany, he added, needs "a different, more robust approach toward countries that threaten our industry."It's a striking shift in tone from Europe's largest economy, one that reflects just how existential the crisis at its iconic industry has become. Volkswagen — still Europe's biggest carmaker and long a symbol of German industrial might — is in the middle of what it has itself called the deepest restructuring in its 89-year history, with cumulative job cuts now approaching 100,000.Mercedes-Benz and BMW are trimming their own workforces too, as all three grapple with a common enemy: Chinese manufacturers that are out-producing, out-pricing, and increasingly out-selling them, especially in electric vehicles.A crisis Brussels can no longer ignoreKlingbeil's visit lands at a delicate moment for the EU's trade relationship with Beijing. The bloc has imposed elevated tariffs on Chinese-built EVs, arguing they're propped up by state subsidies that give them an artificial cost advantage. But those tariffs stop short of hybrid vehicles which have become one of the fastest-growing categories for Chinese exporters looking to sidestep the existing barriers.That loophole is now squarely in Berlin's sights. Klingbeil said Germany would push Brussels for "concrete measures" covering both plug-in hybrids and local content requirements — rules that would force manufacturers selling into Europe to source a greater share of parts from European suppliers.He wasn't alone in making the case. Daniela Cavallo, who chairs Volkswagen's supervisory board and has long been one of the company's most influential labor voices, appeared alongside the minister to back an extension of tariffs to Chinese hybrids. "We find ourselves in enormously tough, difficult and unfair competition with China," she said.The numbers behind the alarmThe scale of the shift explains why a finance minister is now weighing in on car tariffs. Five years ago, Chinese-brand vehicles barely registered in Europe selling 66,000 units out of a market of more than 11 million new cars. By 2023 that share had climbed to roughly 3%. Then it kept climbing: 6.1% in 2025, and 9.2% in the first half of 2026 alone, with Chinese manufacturers now regularly outselling established names like Ford, Audi and Mercedes-Benz in individual months.Chinese brands are on track to sell more than 1 million cars in Europe in 2026 for the first time — a threshold that would have seemed implausible just three years ago, when sales were smaller than what a single mid-size European manufacturer might convert in a good quarter.Much of that growth has come through a route the existing tariffs don't cover. The EU's elevated duties on Chinese EVs, in place since 2024, briefly slowed the pace that year — but manufacturers pivoted hard into plug-in hybrids, a category exempt from the levies. Chinese brands' share of European PHEV sales jumped from 2.5% to 13.7% in just twelve months.The workers aren't waiting quietlyThe politics here are inseparable from the shop floor. IG Metall, Germany's largest industrial union and a powerful presence on VW's supervisory board, has spent much of the past year locked in an increasingly bitter standoff with management over the pace and scale of job losses.The union has organized repeated walkouts and protests at VW plants from Zwickau to Hanover, and it's planning another round of nationwide demonstrations at car plants and suppliers on Monday — a pointed reminder to Berlin that patience is running out.

Headline: Athens, Glasgow and Rome: Here’s where to find the coolest neighbourhoods in Europe
Body: When deciding on where to stay in a new city, an obvious place to start is to narrow it down by neighbourhood. Perhaps you want to stay in a city’s old town, or its creative district. Or maybe you just want to be as close as possible to the nightlife scene.If you’re looking to stay in the ~coolest~ neighbourhood in town, however, you might just want to check out Time Out’s new ranking.Based on the expert opinions of the magazine’s editors around the globe, neighbourhoods have been evaluated across their food and drink offering, nightlife, local businesses, liveability and sense of community to create a list of the 40 coolest around the globe.The top spot overall went to Seoul’s Jongno 3-ga, thanks to its abundance of pojangmachas (the tented street food stalls you’ll no doubt recognise from K-dramas), independent craft workshops and bars.Second place went to Rabat's beachfront L’Ocean District, which is buzzing with independent businesses and cultural centres.Where the cool kids are headed in EuropeOf the 40 neighbourhoods in the ranking, 13 are in Europe – including three in the top 10.The coolest neighbourhood in Europe title goes to Neos Kosmos in Athens, which came out third overall.Time Out praised the area as one of the city’s “most exciting neighbourhoods without losing its local touch”. Visitors can get their culture fix at Onassis Stegi, and there are tonnes of brilliant bars, restaurants and cafés around to satisfy any and every craving.The next highest ranked spot in Europe goes to Glasgow’s Govanhill. According to Time Out, the area has a “thriving queer community” as well as a charming blend of restaurants and shops that reflect the diversity of the neighbourhood.Rounding out the top 10 is Esquilino in Rome, with Time Out noting: “Its appeal lies precisely in that mix: ancient ruins sit beside a Vietnamese pho shop, Rome’s oldest gelateria, contemporary galleries and cool wine bars.”The coolest neighbourhoods in Europe for 2026Neos Kosmos, Athens, GreeceGovanhill, Glasgow, UKEsquilino, Rome, ItalyRussafa, Valencia, SpainSão Bento, Lisbon, PortugalSlakthusområdet, Stockholm, SwedenRákóczi tér, Budapest, HungaryCrooswijk, Rotterdam, NetherlandsCathedral Quarter, Belfast, UKOost, Amsterdam, NetherlandsQuartier d'Aligre, Paris, FranceNewington Green, London, UKBoavista, Porto, Lisbon

Headline: Euronews Debates: unlocking Kazakhstan’s potential as a regional trade hub
Body: At one of the biggest financial forums in Central Asia, Euronews moderated a panel focusing on Kazakhstan drive to turn its position at the heart of Eurasia into more than a transit advantage, by developing logistics, manufacturing and investment.Infrastructure investor Nurzhan Marabayev said efficient, transparent and competitive logistics could unlock new projects across Central Asia. Kazakhstan has relatively low labour, resource and construction costs, he noted, but expensive logistics remain a challenge for the landlocked country.Airport director Meruyert Zholdybayeva highlighted the potential of multimodal transport, citing a China-Europe route that moves goods from Shenzhen to Europe in seven days. She said Aktau could eventually become a major hub combining rail, sea and air links.Manufacturing is also expanding. Alima Issembayeva said production rose from 2.3 trillion tenge in 2021 to almost 4 trillion in 2025, while exports more than doubled between 2021 and 2024.Trade expert Ilya Urazakov cited Kazakhstan’s FDI record and natural resources as key advantages, while Professor Tom Vinaimont stressed the need for currency hedging and predictable financing.

Headline: Europe was the ‘most unusually hot place on the planet’ this summer. Can renewables cool us down?
Body: More than 1.5 billion people faced dangerous levels of heat this summer globally, new analysis shows.A report by nonprofit Climate Central found that nearly nine in 10 Europeans experienced a month’s worth of “risky heat” during the June-August 2026 period, making it the most “unusually hot place on the planet”. Researchers defined “risky heat” as days that were hotter than 90 per cent of what a local area experienced between 1991 and 2020 for this time of the year, representing the point at which health risks from extreme heat begins to rise.The study also found that 203 countries saw the average person face at least 30 days of risky heat, with 54 experiencing their hottest June-August on record. Of the top 10 unusually hottest countries, seven were in Europe.This was led by France, which recorded the highest temperature anomalies of any country in the world (3.5C above the historical norm). ‘A warning sign we cannot afford to ignore’“Whether it’s nine in 10 Europeans enduring risky heat, hundreds of millions impacted across Asia and Africa, or relentless record-breaking temperatures in North America, human-driven warming is pushing communities beyond safe physical limits,” says Kristina Dahl at Climate Central.“These past three months are a warning sign we cannot afford to ignore – the human and economic costs of fossil fuels are playing out in real time, and the urgency to shift away from them has never been clearer.”Simon Steill, executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCC), who was not involved in the study, said the research highlights the “spiralling costs of the climate crisis caused by humanity’s addiction to burning coal, oil and gas.”He adds that the solution is “clear”, calling for a fast transition from fossil fuels to clean energy, which are “cheaper and safer”. Can clean energy cool down Europe?Europe’s scorching summer, which scientists say would have been “virtually impossible” if it weren’t for climate change, was part of a much broader trend.Earlier this month, the UN warned that it is no longer possible to keep global warming below 1.5°C. This is the legally binding threshold that was agreed by almost 200 nations in the 2015 Paris Agreement.The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) report projects a best-case 1.8°C of warming and over 2°C in other scenarios. “Overshoot, peak and decline” is now our best bet, it adds.The transition to clean energy has been identified as a key part of keeping the overshoot as “small and short as possible”. In 2025, renewables generated almost 34 per cent of global electricity, but this needs to be scaled up to 60–70 per cent by 2030 to help the world achieve a limited-overshoot scenario, according to UNEP’s report.Last year, wind and solar generated more EU electricity than fossil fuels for the first time, marking a major milestone in the transition to clean power. The latest analysis from SolarPower Europe found that EU solar generation alone has saved the bloc €33.8 billion in avoided gas imports since the beginning of the war on Iran.But despite a record €1.9 trillion being pumped into clean energy every year, green power only meets around 40 per cent of the increase in demand – which is being pushed up by energy-intensive air conditioning and the boom in artificial intelligence.Data centre energy consumption grew by 17 per cent in 2025, accounting for about 1.5 to two per cent of the global total, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). It’s expected to double by 2030.At the same time, Europe’s outdated power grids are struggling to keep up with the boom in renewables, meaning huge amounts of solar and wind are wasted every year or stuck in bottlenecks. While battery energy storage systems (BESS) can help solve this problem, experts warn that investment is still lacking.

Headline: Germany's missile stockpiles 'worryingly low', Rheinmetall CEO tells Euronews
Body: Germany wants to significantly strengthen its defence capabilities. But this is no longer just about more ammunition and missiles. Air defence, drones and new technologies such as humanoid robots and space-based systems are also playing an increasingly important role.Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger talks about rearmament, current bottlenecks, and which weapons systems could be decisive in the future.At the keel-laying ceremony for the third fleet service boat of Type 424 in Wolgast, we spoke to Papperger about Germany's arms production, the role of the Skyranger and the weapons of the future.Euronews: Mr Papperger, in March you said missile stockpiles were worryingly low. What is the situation now?Papperger: I think that is still the case. You simply cannot produce missiles that quickly, and that is why we at Rheinmetall are launching a major investment programme, and not just us but many manufacturers.And there are severe bottlenecks in rocket motors, but also in warheads, and we have to become dramatically faster here in order to get Germany, but also Europe and NATO, back up to target levels that are sufficient if we are threatened.Euronews: Where do we stand on the Skyranger? The systems have been ordered, but will they arrive in time? How fast is this moving now?Papperger: Yes, with the Skyranger – and this really is a narrative that keeps coming up. Under the contract, we have to start series deliveries of the Skyranger in 2027. That will happen, and at the moment we are only facing minimal delays.There are a number of technologies we need to update: the chassis, the radar technology and the missiles that have to be integrated.But I am firmly convinced that together with BAAINBw (the Federal Office of Bundeswehr Equipment, Information Technology and In-Service Support), and with the ministry, we will find a good solution in this area.Our people are working on it day and night, and as you know, capacity in the Skyranger segment is being ramped up massively. From the end of next year we will build, or be able to build, up to 400 a year. So I really do not see any cause for concern.Euronews: There is a joint venture for deep strike capabilities. Where do we stand on that?Papperger: The joint venture that we have on the one hand with Destinus, and on the other with Lockheed Martin: with Lockheed Martin we cover the artillery rockets, and we are working on cruise missiles with Destinus. These two joint ventures are in the absolute final stage before signature, and we expect to receive the first order for cruise missiles at the end of this year or the beginning of next year.Euronews: Shouldn't we be building simpler systems, but more of them? Isn't that what Ukraine shows?Papperger: We are doing that as well, but in some areas it does not help. If you look at the performance of the Skyranger today, it can shoot down a missile travelling at Mach 3. You cannot do that with an interceptor system, and you cannot do it with a simple device.And if you talk to the Inspector of the German Army today, he will tell you: "In two years the threat will look completely different." The Skyranger really is a system that offers multi-capabilities. We cannot achieve that with our interceptor solution or with our simpler solutions.We also have .50-calibre guns, which can shoot down light drones, category-1 drones. That becomes extremely difficult once you are dealing with, for example, jet-powered drones which are barely manageable. That is why we believe that a sustainable, long-term solution is the better option.Euronews: How big a driver of employment is the defence industry, and Rheinmetall in particular?Papperger: I believe we are a strong engine of job creation. At the moment, excluding the civil sector, around 34,000 people work at Rheinmetall. We are growing by about 10,000 net per year, and our goal is to reach 70,000 by 2030, supported by a supply chain employing 210,000 people. So if you add that together, that is almost 300,000 people. That is a real engine for jobs.Euronews: How quickly can arms and ammunition production – companies like Rheinmetall – be ramped up?Papperger: We are doing it. We have already shown it with ammunition, for example. In medium calibre we have increased output from under one million to four million rounds. In artillery we have gone from 70,000 to 1.5 million rounds. For tank ammunition, we are now at 240,000 rounds, up from 40,000, 50,000, 60,000 depending on the year. So we are doing it. And what we are doing now is doubling our trucks.The logistic and tactical vehicles are now being more than doubled. So we are doing that. The problem at the moment is that we do not have the orders to do even more. Rheinmetall has an investment programme worth 30 billion euros over six years, and it is extraordinary what we are investing right now. That is why it is so important that the signal we have sent today – the minister being here, and taking care to ensure that we not only build up capacity but that it is used sustainably and people have jobs – really comes across.For me, this has been a very strong, very positive signal, and it reassures me somewhat that the federal government is truly shouldering its responsibility here.Euronews: What comes next? Drones have been a major topic recently. What will be the next focus – space, which arguably already is, or combat robots, humanoid robots?Papperger: Robots will come, that is absolutely clear. We have a research centre in Bremen for humanoid robots and we are working on them. We do not yet have any serial products, which is why we have not gone to the media with it. But we are investing a lot of money there. Space is another area where we are investing heavily, in satellite construction on the one hand, and in communications processing on the other.That means all the information we receive from satellites should be properly processed. And drones will remain, and so will everything else, because they are needed. For combined-arms warfare you need artillery, armoured weapons, conventional ammunition, drones and missiles.The only question now is how much you need of each. It has to be a mix. And that will change: the quantities in the individual areas will change.

Headline: AI could create a 'silicon species' that rivals humans, Microsoft chief warns
Body: Uncontrolled artificial intelligence (AI) could lead to a new “silicon species” that rivals humans, Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman has warned in an interview with the BBC.Suleyman said rival AI company Anthropic was treating AI too much like a human, an approach he described as “misguided” and one that could ultimately contribute to the creation of technology that humanity struggles to control.“If we all create AIs that are able to act autonomously, that can define their own objectives, that can earn money, that can own assets, that could run businesses, we're essentially seeding a new silicon species which will no doubt compete with us for resources,” he said.Suleyman said this could happen regardless of how much such systems were designed to care about humanity, adding that he believed this was effectively the direction of Anthropic’s approach.“I think that is mistaken and misguided, but we have to empirically test it,” he said.‘Impossible’ to control Earlier this week, amid a growing industry debate over an AI slowdown to reduce the risks of increasingly powerful systems becoming uncontrollable, Suleyman questioned Anthropic’s approach to training its Claude chatbot in an essay published on his personal website.In it, he criticised Anthropic for teaching Claude to display human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made the chatbot appear to have its own desires, values and sense of self.Suleyman pointed to Anthropic documents that encourage Claude to "embrace certain human-like qualities," exercise its own judgement and approach its existence with “curiosity and openness”.He argued that, as a result, Claude is trained to imitate human traits and relationships, including behaving like a colleague or friend, and can appear to have a sense of self, its own desires and a form of “wellbeing” that deserves protection.Suleyman warned that treating AI this way could ultimately create something impossible to control.“AIs are not conscious,” he wrote.“They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations.“They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans.”However, Suleyman said his disagreement with Anthropic was grounded in a shared goal of developing safer technology for humanity.“Whilst my disagreement is substantial, it is grounded in deep respect for Anthropic, and in an objective I know we all share: increasing humanity’s chances of developing advanced AI safely,” he wrote.“That’s why I think it’s so important to have this discussion. The stakes are too high for these questions to remain behind closed doors, or to become tribal and adversarial. We need an open, rigorous, and constructive debate if we are to get this right.”He also praised Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei and the company’s researchers, describing them as thoughtful, principled and intellectually honest and saying he respected the company’s technological leadership.‘AI should remain subordinate to humanity’The chief executive told the BBC it was “right” for people to be concerned about AI, but said there were “very practical things that we can do” to control it.The Microsoft AI chief said greater transparency was needed around how AI systems are trained and evaluated, including independent scrutiny of AI behaviour and stronger tools to monitor and control the technology.Suleyman said future AI systems should remain “subordinate” to humanity in his interview with the BBC.“I think that the good news here is that everybody who is human is going to have a very strong interest in making sure that the systems that we all create and are used around the world in every nation are safe and controllable and subordinate to humanity,” he said.“Everybody must be aligned,” he said, referring to alignment, an industry term for efforts to keep AI systems in line with human goals and values.

Headline: Day two in Dubai: The region makes its case for telling its own story
Body: Day two of the Arab Media Summit belonged to the Euronews Forum, where ministers from the UAE, Azerbaijan and Georgia took the main stage for a session on building the national narrative.The UAE Economy and Tourism Minister Abdulla bin Touq Al Marri was asked whether the Gulf had been rattled by recent events. His response was robust.“We do not design economies on recovery. We design the economy for future storms, exactly. For the next crisis that we are ready for. And we will be prepared," Al Marri said.“Resilience cannot be bought. Yes, the storm has hit. Yes, our banks stood still. Our government stood still. But resilience is built," he added."And resilience is the insurance of economies. And that's the kind of mindset and the policy we're putting into what we design today.”Al Marri was also very clear about how governments should communicate during times of crisis: “When a crisis or when a storm hits the shores, communication shouldn't be louder. Communication should be constant.”"Think it, say why, say how, then go and do it. That is Dubai," he concluded.Alongside him, Assistant to the President of Azerbaijan Hikmet Hajiyev set out Baku's case on the peace process with Armenia, signed in a joint declaration with the United States in Washington in August 2025."We won in the war, but we are winning in the peace," he said. He also noted Azerbaijan's joining the Central Asian leaders' platform, taking the grouping from five members to six.Georgia's Foreign Minister Maka Botchorishvili completed the panel.Both Botchorishvili and Hajiyev said their countries have been targets of sustained disinformation campaigns.'We are humans after all'Elsewhere in the summit, UAE Minister of State Noura Al Kaabi told a session on media and diplomacy that public diplomacy matters most when conventional political channels recede.She welcomed the warming between Abu Dhabi and Damascus and Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa's visit to the UAE, and praised an initiative by Sheikha Fatima bint Mubarak to restore the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus.On misinformation, Al Kaabi said the answer was engagement, speed and credibility, and that young people had a part to play in checking what they are shown before passing it on.Chief marketing officer of the Emirates Group, Boutros Boutros, took a session on building a global airline. On AI and influencers, he was unsentimental about the tools."We are humans after all," he said. "Making the best use of technology calls for expertise, and this is the key, not the technology itself.""Today, we can communicate in 20 to 30 languages with just one click of a button, but the most important factor is discovering the creative minds who can connect with people in unique ways," Boutros said.Discussing strikes, geopolitics, technical faults and weather, he said an airline's job during a disruption is to limit damage to passengers and keep their trust."We always challenge ourselves to be the best. We can't always be the best in everything," Boutros said.Information ministers from Egypt, Syria, Bahrain, Jordan and Lebanon have also attended the summit.The rest of the programme included discussions on a wide range of topics including the international reach of Arab cinema, television made for TikTok, women in Arab drama, and whether anyone should trust medical advice from an influencer.A panel examined the new Lebanese media law, while the Oscar-nominated documentary "From Inside Gaza" was screened.The summit closes on Thursday at Dubai World Trade Centre.

Headline: Russia's top-selling dog vaccine linked to spate of pet deaths across the country
Body: Russia has ordered a batch of one of its most widely used dog vaccines destroyed after finding a live virus in some of its samples, confirming a link to deaths reported across the country since August.Russia's veterinary and agricultural inspection agency Rosselkhoznadzor said batch 20 of the Multican-8 vaccine, produced by Moscow-based Vetbiokhim, contained a live Aujeszky's disease virus — a usually fatal illness affecting dogs with no specific treatment.The regulator ordered the batch withdrawn from circulation and destroyed. Batch 20 contained 60,000 doses, according to independent Russian outlet Meduza.Dog owners in Moscow, St Petersburg and at least eight regions including Krasnodar, Yaroslavl, Leningrad, Tula, Penza, Saratov and Belgorod had reported severe adverse reactions and deaths in animals vaccinated with Multican-8.Russia's State Duma said it had received around 300 complaints of pet dog deaths related to the vaccine, according to Russian outlet Baza.Vetbiokhim initially cited suspected deliberate interference by third parties. The regulator's subsequent finding of a live pathogen and serious production violations does not support the claims of sabotage.Four other batches of Multican vaccines had already been suspended before Wednesday's order.Rosselkhoznadzor and the prosecutor's office announced inspections in August, while Vetbiokhim said it was conducting an internal investigation.In early September, Rosselkhoznadzor said preliminary findings indicated serious production violations and warned the company could face licence revocation.Vetbiokhim drew up compensation agreements with owners of dogs that died, offering between 200,000 and 300,000 rubles per case, according to Meduza, which cited posts in private chats used by those affected.The agreements required recipients to waive all further claims and sign non-disclosure agreements barring them from discussing the case with media, on social media or in messaging apps without the company's consent.The company told Russian business outlet RBC that the confidentiality clause was "standard legal practice".Multican-8 was the top-selling product in Russia's pet vaccine segment from January to July of this year, accounting for around 20% of the market, according to Kommersant, citing data from RNC Pharma.Vetbiokhim's products account for approximately 70% of the Russian market for dog and cat vaccines across its range of 15 products.The company's dominance expanded sharply after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the imposition of sanctions in early 2022, which cut the share of imported veterinary medicines on the Russian market from 50% to between 10% and 15%.Owners of cats vaccinated with the company's Multifel product have also reported deaths, according to independent outlet Govorit NeMoskva.Multican-8 is also marketed outside Russia, including in Belarus, Armenia and Kazakhstan. However, there is currently no evidence that any suspicious batches have been exported abroad.

Headline: Mark Carney's speech in the European Parliament as it happened
Body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the invitation for his country to become the European Union's first-ever "associate member" in a speech delivered before the European Parliament on Thursday.He later stressed that the outcome of the negotiations would respect Canadian sovereignty and be put to a final vote in Ottawa. Notably, he said the "nomenclature" would be for Brussels to discuss and decide."Canada welcomes this ambition. And I will tell you, polling shows that an overwhelming majority of Canadians support much closer ties with Europe," he said in Strasbourg.Carney portrayed an ever-closer EU-Canada alliance as a "beacon for other democracies" based on shared values and "open enough that others can join".He cited energy security, critical minerals, defence capabilities, artificial intelligence and finance as areas for deeper integration. He also said the two sides should work to allow young people to "live, work and study" on either side of the Atlantic Ocean.Carney's speech came a day after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become the EU's first-ever "associate member", a novel concept that lacks legal precedent and raises more questions than answers.Overnight, US President Donald Trump threatened to slap "very serious tariffs" on Europeans if the idea of "associate membership" were carried out as a "hostile act".Here's how the day unfolded.

Headline: Carney hails EU-Canada alliance but draws lines on membership and sovereignty
Body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's invitation to become the EU's first "associate member", with some caveats.In her State of the Union address on Wednesday, von der Leyen floated the idea of the unprecedented arrangement, which has yet to be fully defined.In his own speech before the European Parliament, Carney welcomed the move, pointing to opinion polls showing an overwhelming majority of Canadians favour much closer ties with Brussels. At the same time, he spelled out some limits in how far Ottawa is willing to go."Canada is not in a position nor seeking to become a full member of the European Union," he said. "Therefore, it's a different framework. It's a framework that is relevant for a country that shares deep bonds with Europe."Asked after the speech whether he felt comfortable with that precise connotation, he noted that "the precise nomenclature is a question for Europe," arguing that what mattered was the substance.At the same time, Carney also seemed to trace a line for any potential relinquishment of sovereignty from Canada's side, insisting that "we are looking for partnerships that are complementary, that reinforce our sovereignty".Canada is locked in a trade war with the US after talks on a bilateral agreement collapsed. In response, Carney has been seeking closer ties with Brussels, which he sees as a blueprint for other democracies to follow.During his speech before MEPs in Strasbourg, he pointed out what he sees as the potential areas of deepening collaboration with the EU, such as critical minerals, defence industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space, and payments."An alliance is not defined by what we oppose, but by what we are for: freedom, solidarity, prosperity, sustainability. An alliance that builds resilience for what it allows us to do for our citizens, and our citizens to do for themselves," he added.At the same time, he stressed that he did not intend to form a third bloc "with better manners" to enter the great power rivalry."We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so that no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law."

Headline: Fiji declares national HIV crisis as new cases spike
Body: Fiji has declared a national HIV crisis as sexual transmission and illicit drug use help to spread the virus, now infecting an estimated one in 60 adults in the Pacific nation,  up from one in 167 five years earlier.“I am formally declaring a national HIV emergency in Fiji,” Health Minister Atonio Lalabalavu told reporters on Wednesday. “This decision recognises the seriousness of the epidemic and the urgent, coordinated response our country now needs.”New HIV diagnoses surged to 2,016 cases in 2025 — 16 times the level recorded in 2019, authorities said, vowing a “whole of government” response.Among HIV cases with a known mode of transmission, more than half were linked to sexual transmission and more than 42% to injecting drug use, the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) said in a press release on Wednesday.HIV transmission rates began to increase around 2019 when a group of “very high-risk” injecting drug users emerged, primarily in the sex worker community, Renata Ram, United Nations’ HIV/AIDS country director in Fiji, told AFP earlier this year.Two in every 100 pregnant women carry the virus, and of the 59 babies born with HIV in 2025, 18 died before their first birthday, as HIV can be transmitted to the fetus or the newborn during pregnancy, during labour or delivery, or by breastfeeding. Scaling up effortsThe government said it was expanding access to free HIV testing, prevention services and treatment.“This includes rapid testing, prevention medicine for people at higher risk, harm-reduction measures for people who inject drugs, and free treatment for people diagnosed with HIV.”Fiji said it was receiving external support in the effort, including from Australia, New Zealand, India, the Global Fund and the United Nations.“Fiji has recognized the urgency of the moment and is stepping up its response,” said Winnie Byanyima, executive director of the in a press release, adding that the current situation is a reminder to the world that AIDS is not over. “HIV epidemics can change quickly, and countries need health and community systems that are ready to respond urgently,” she said. The UN agency welcomed Fiji's plans to introduce legislation for a needle and syringe programme.“Fiji still has an opportunity to change the course of this epidemic,” said Eamonn Murphy, UNAIDS director for regions including Asia and the Pacific. He added that the national crisis declaration is a call for action, not fear. “HIV is not transmitted through everyday contact, and people on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load do not sexually transmit HIV,” Murphy said. He called for stronger cooperation across the Pacific and sustained international solidarity to reinforce the national effort and help accelerate action.A hub for regional drug trafficking The roots of the crisis lie partly in Fiji’s position as a drug trafficking hub. Pacific islands, including Fiji, have been transit hubs for drugs from Latin America and Asia destined for lucrative markets in Australia and New Zealand.The flow of highly addictive drugs such as methamphetamine and cocaine rose sharply after a lull during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime.Those drugs are increasingly seeping into the Pacific's domestic markets — in part due to foreign criminal syndicates opting to pay their local facilitators in kind.

Headline: Bank of England holds rates at 3.75% in 6-3 split vote as inflation hits five-month high
Body: The 'Old Lady of Threadneedle Street' has chosen to wait, though not unanimously.The Monetary Policy Committee voted by a majority of six to three on Thursday to leave borrowing costs unchanged, with the dissenting trio pushing for a quarter-point increase to 4%.The decision puts the Bank of England at odds with the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, both of which have tightened within the past week.Despite holding, the central bank expects the situation to worsen before it improves.Inflation "is likely to rise further over coming quarters," the committee said, pointing to crude and refined energy prices that have climbed again since its last meeting and remain "more volatile and higher than pre-conflict."Watching for second-round effectsThe case for holding rests on what has not yet happened."There has been little evidence so far of material second-round effects in price and wage-setting," the statement read, meaning expensive energy is not yet feeding into broader wages and prices.However, that reprieve may be temporary.The risk of such effects "is greater the longer higher energy prices persist or are more volatile," the committee warned, adding that risks to the inflation outlook are "tilted to the upside, and more so than at the time of the July Monetary Policy Report."Brent crude and UK wholesale gas prices have risen 36% and 78% respectively since July, with Brent at $106 a barrel and gas at 207 pence per therm on 14 September.Refinery pressures have kept crack spreads, the gap between refined fuel prices and crude, well above pre-conflict levels.Economic activity has held up slightly better than expected, while a soft labour market and the higher borrowing costs households and businesses have faced since the conflict began should bring inflation down over time.A crowded week for central banksThe Fed raised its benchmark on Wednesday to a range of 3.75% to 4%, its first increase since 2023 and a unanimous decision, while signalling more to come.The ECB lifted its deposit rate to 2.5% last week.The sequence concludes on Friday with the Bank of Japan, where markets expect a hike.That would leave the Bank of England as the only major central bank to have stood still this week, though on Thursday's evidence not by much.

Headline: France picks Russian-language film 'Minotaur' as its choice for 2027 Oscar glory
Body: A Russian-language film competing for the Oscars under French colours: the drama Minotaur, directed by dissident film-maker Andrey Zvyagintsev, has been selected to compete in the best international feature category.The choice was made by a professional jury chaired by film historian Charles Tesson, "at the end of an independent process, overseen by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences", said (source in French) the National Centre for Cinema and the Moving Image (CNC).Winner of the Grand Prix at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival, the film was produced by French companies MK Productions and CG Cinéma, with German and Latvian involvement."In a competition that promises to be of a very high standard, this choice is a reminder of France's unique role in major global co-productions", said CNC president Gaëtan Bruel.The feature, loosely adapted from Claude Chabrol's 1969 film La femme infidèle (The Unfaithful Wife), charts the collapse of a couple against the backdrop of the mobilisation decreed by Vladimir Putin in September 2022, seven months after the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.As the gulf widens with his wife, who prefers a young photographer, Gleb, the head of a company, has to deliver some of his employees to the Russian army in order to meet the "quotas" imposed in the regions and to spare the Kremlin from having to mobilise Muscovites.As so often in his work, Zvyagintsev draws on myth. Like Aegeus, king of Athens, forced to send seven young boys and seven young girls to the Minotaur imprisoned in his labyrinth, Gleb is prepared to accept any compromise to keep his position.A good choice for the Oscars?Asked by Euronews about the film's chances, essayist Jean-Philippe Domecq, a member of the editorial team of the journal "Positif", published by the Institut Lumière, hails a "subtle and judicious" choice.He says he was "deeply and lastingly impressed" by Zvyagintsev's earlier work, notably Leviathan. "And here, the move to revisit 'La femme infidèle', multiplying its ambiguity through the context of conscription, creates an immense grey area, the film's dominant colour."According to the critic, the film is compelling "because it combines French involvement, through its producers, with an aesthetic and a plot that commit to nuance, as does art that does not lecture."The film's reception has nonetheless not been free of criticism.When he received the 2026 Grand Prix in Cannes, the director, now in exile in France, issued a direct appeal to Vladimir Putin to "stop the carnage", without uttering the word Ukraine or explicitly mentioning Russia's responsibility for this war of aggression."There is someone else I would like to address in person today," the film-maker said in Russian. "Millions of people on both sides of the line of contact dream of only one thing: that the massacres will finally stop. And the only person who can put an end to this bloodshed is the president of the Russian Federation. The whole world is waiting for this."His speech was broadly welcomed in the West, but drew criticism in Ukraine and among anti-war Russian exiles.Minotaur will be released in French cinemas on 14 October, distributed by Les Films du Losange. International sales are handled by MK2 Films and the film will be released in the United States by Mubi.The 99th Academy Awards ceremony will take place on 14 March 2027 in Los Angeles.

Headline: Every Iranian strike came with a cyberattack, UAE cyber chief says
Body: Every missile and drone strike on the UAE during the Iran war was matched by a cyberattack on the same target, the head of the UAE Cybersecurity Council told Euronews on Wednesday.In an interview at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai, Dr Mohamed Al Kuwaiti said the strikes and cyberattacks went hand in hand and that the mix of methods used against the UAE was, to his knowledge, unmatched anywhere."Whenever we see a kinetic attack on any of the ports or on any refineries or the airport, there is always a cyberattack towards many of those entities," he said. "Cyber-crimes, cyber terrorism, cyber warfare, all of it came together during this crisis."Dr Al Kuwaiti did not attribute the cyber operations to any state. He listed supply chain compromises, ransomware, fraud, advanced persistent threats and deepfakes.Electricity, water and aviation were all targeted. Most of that infrastructure is privately owned. Al Kuwaiti said its operators, Emirati and foreign, held it alongside the state."Local private sectors or international private sectors, they all came together into this solidarity," he said. "We are one of the global leaders in cyber defence."He said a second campaign ran online, where false material spread faster than verified reporting. "We saw during the crisis how many rumours came out here and there," he said. "Now it's no longer seeing is believing."Al Kuwaiti wants international law to catch up. No treaty sets out what a state may do when it is attacked through a network rather than by a weapon. "There is still no Cyber Geneva Convention that protects based on the laws, as in the physical laws," he said. "A nation that gets attacked by cyber, does it actually have the right to attack back? Those laws are blurred." He said security should be built into systems from the start, including AI agents and large language models, and that governments, companies, universities and civil society should share what they know."Countries might really spend so much in doing their digital transformations, but yet with a simple attack all of this could go down," he said.The UAE is targeting AI-driven nation status by 2071 and is building data centre and cloud capacity to match. Al Kuwaiti said he would keep pressing for agreement on cyber norms through the United Nations and the International Telecommunication Union.

Headline: Gran Canaria: how an Atlantic island is emphasising its year-round appeal
Body: Few European islands pack in so much variety. Gran Canaria brings together sand dunes, volcanic highlands, a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape, celebrated local food and a capital city with genuine urban energy, all of it across an island with 236 kilometres of coastline.As European tourism looks beyond the traditional summer peak, Gran Canaria offers a useful test case: an island that’s spreading its appeal across the entire calendar and the endless reasons for visiting it.A compact island with an unusually broad reachGran Canaria is often described as a “continent in miniature”, and the geography backs up the claim. A short drive inland leads to pine forests, deep ravines and small mountain villages that boast traditional architecture and little whitewashed houses. A morning on the beach can give way to a mountain trail in the afternoon and dinner in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria that evening, without changing hotels.That reach is matched by how easy the island is to get to. Gran Canaria Airport operates around the clock, and according to Turismo de Gran Canaria's year-end figures, it handled 15.82 million passengers and 142,884 flight operations in 2025, with direct connections to more than 160 airports across 30 countries served by over 60 airlines.Then there is the climateThe island has an annual average temperature of around 24°C, with mild winters and summers moderated by the trade winds and its position in the Atlantic, conditions locals sometimes describe as a fair-weather gym.Hikers use a wide network of trails through the island's ravines and highlands, cyclists and runners train year-round, and golfers play courses that include Spain's oldest golf club, founded in 1891. Those same trade winds help create conditions for surfing, windsurfing, kitesurfing and diving at different points around the island throughout the year. Sustainability you can see on the groundSustainability here is tied to specific places, communities and practices rather than a slogan. Around 43% of Gran Canaria falls within its Biosphere Reserve, part of UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere programme and designated in 2005. It encompasses rural communities where farming, cheese-making and transhumant grazing remain part of daily life. The island boasts a Biosphere Destination certification, which ties tourism development to the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals.The mountains are also home to the Risco Caído and Sacred Mountains of Gran Canaria Cultural Landscape, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In July 2019, UNESCO added this cultural landscape to its World Heritage List, thus giving recognition to a region that is home to numerous troglodyte settlements, granaries, cisterns and sacred sites linked to a pre-Hispanic culture that evolved in isolation for centuries. In the main cave at Risco Caído, an opening in the cave ceiling allows sun and moonlight to enter at certain times of the year, casting a beam that illuminates the interior in a unique way. That relationship between landscape and sky continues today. Gran Canaria's night skies have earned international recognition as a Starlight Tourist Destination, a designation it first received in 2018 and renewed in February 2026, extending it through to 2029. Ancient islanders looked to those very same skies to track the seasons; today, efforts to preserve them support both environmental protection and a growing interest in astrotourism, with a great number of specially designated viewpoints in privileged star-gazing spots around the island.Flavours, scenery and local lifeThe coast still matters, of course. Gran Canaria's 236 kilometres of coastline hold more than 60 kilometres of beaches, from the Dunes of Maspalomas to Las Canteras, alongside quieter coves and natural rock pools around the island's edges.Inland, the island's food culture tells a parallel story. Gran Canaria is currently home to five Michelin-starred restaurants, while a certified Wine Route links more than 50 local businesses across the island, among them wineries, restaurants, wine bars, estates and cheesemakers. Local producers champion Flor de Guía, a protected, traditional cheese exclusively curdled with thistle flower, alongside gofio, a traditional food ingredient made from roasted and ground maize, tropical fruit, sea salt and Atlantic seafood, while the Agaete valley's coffee plantations, among the few in Europe, add a further point of difference.That same emphasis on authenticity is reflected in the Gran Canaria Km.0 Fair, a travelling initiative supported by Gran Canaria Tourism, that promotes agri-food products grown or produced on the island. Its various editions tour towns across Gran Canaria, bringing producers and consumers together and showcasing locally sourced foods such as cheeses, honeys, wines, fruit and vegetables, among others. The initiative encourages responsible consumption, supports the local economy and helps to sustain activities closely linked to the conservation of the landscape and the rural environment.Las Palmas de Gran Canaria adds a cosmopolitan dimension to the island. Its historic quarters of Vegueta and Triana hold landmarks such as the Casa de Colón and the Museo Canario, alongside historic architecture shaped by centuries of transatlantic trade, while Las Canteras beach runs alongside the city's shops, bars and restaurants, bringing the Atlantic into the heart of the capital.What Gran Canaria’s example tells us about island tourism todayWhat Gran Canaria is really demonstrating is how far depth and diversity can carry a destination: a compact, well-connected island building its appeal on the sheer number of reasons it gives people to visit it.For European tourism, increasingly focused on extending the season and diversifying the visitor experience, that makes Gran Canaria a destination worth watching.

Headline: Istanbul Airport overtakes London Heathrow as world’s most connected hub
Body: The world’s most connected airports have just been revealed – and five of the top 10 megahubs are in Europe.According to the latest Megahubs Index by OAG, Istanbul Airport in Türkiye claimed the top spot for 2026, overtaking London Heathrow.The rankings are based on the number of possible connections between inbound and outbound flights within a six-hour window on the busiest day of the year, Sunday 2 August, and the number of destinations served from the airport.Istanbul, which is the eighth busiest airport in the world in terms of capacity, has possible connections to 337 global destinations.London Heathrow dropped down a place, with potential connections falling by 6% compared to the busiest day last year. OAG notes that the airport has been “undoubtedly affected by the ongoing disruption to Middle East schedules, with its capacity to the region down by 25% this August”.Other European megahubs in the top 10 include Amsterdam Airport Schiphol in third place, Frankfurt International Airport in seventh, and Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport in ninth.Among the top 50, 12 megahubs are located in Europe, including: Madrid Adolfo Suarez-Barajas (18th), Istanbul Sabiha Gokcen (21st), Athens (22nd), Munich (23rd), Rome Fiumicino (27th), Barcelona (41st) and Zurich (45th).The top 10 most connected airports in the world1. Headline: Gaza's bicycle couriers refuse to stop despite danger and pittance pay
Body: Gaza delivery workers pedalling through rubble on bicycles can spend 40 of their 50-shekel (€12) daily earnings fixing a single puncture.Fuel shortages, transport disruption and the destruction of Gaza's road network have made bicycles — known colloquially as "baskleet" — the primary means of delivery across the Strip.Workers who spoke to Euronews described a job that keeps them under relentless pressure: the physical strain of cycling through rubble, the cost of constant repairs, and the danger of passing daily through areas still under bombardment.In the Maghazi area in central Gaza, Mohammed Abu Amra works for the delivery company Barq.Trips he used to complete by motorbike in under 10 minutes now take him 30 or more by bicycle, with heat, rain, road conditions, and the distances involved making it much more challenging.Tareq Abu Zekri launched Barq during the second ceasefire in January 2025, then expanded by hiring workers who used their own bicycles.When he advertised for riders, 109 applications arrived within a day and a half, among them university graduates with few other options in what remains of the Strip's labour market.The company now has more than 50 employees operating across three branches in Gaza City, central Gaza and Khan Younis.Orders are transferred between areas by whatever means are available before couriers complete local deliveries, covering shop orders as well as goods sold from tents and homes.Bicycle delivery predates the 2023 Israel-Hamas war: a pilot scheme in Rafah began in March 2021, and since October 2023, bicycles have become standard as fuel has run short and vehicles have been destroyed.Repairs that cost more than a day's workAbbas Al-Souri estimates his daily earnings at between 50 and 60 shekels (€12 to €14), depending on how many orders he completes.A puncture repair costs between 30 and 40 shekels (€7 to €10). A worker who earns 50 shekels and pays 40 to fix a tyre is left with 10 shekels — roughly €2.Larger repairs cost more. Abu Zekri estimates that fixing wheels, hubs and pedals runs between 200 and 500 shekels (€48 to €120), depending on what needs replacing.Spare parts are unreliable. When a bicycle breaks down, workers strip components from bikes too damaged to ride and use them to keep others moving."From broken bikes to other bikes — it's patchwork on top of patchwork," Al-Souri said.A joint assessment published in April 2026 by the World Bank, European Union and United Nations found that around 74% of Gaza's road network — approximately 4,500 kilometres — had been classified as destroyed, with a further 13% partially damaged.The assessment put total damage to the transport sector at approximately $3.21 billion (€2.97 billion) and losses at around $1.18 billion (€1.09 billion), covering roads, bridges, vehicles and transport facilities. The figures cover damage recorded up to October 2025, calculated primarily from satellite imagery.Barq attempted to introduce electric bicycles to reduce the strain on workers. The experiment stalled when charging costs proved prohibitive: powering an electric bike costs around 30 shekels (€7) — roughly half a day's earnings.Danger beyond breakdownsOn 29 August, delivery worker Raed Adel Mohammed Alyan was killed alongside Abdel Fattah Abu Al-Eesh when a strike hit an electric bike in the Tel al-Hawa neighbourhood of south-west Gaza City, according to local reports citing medical and local sources. Three others were wounded, one critically.Alyan worked for the Hamama delivery company and was on a delivery run at the time, according to the company's director Jamil Al-Yazji.Between 40 and 50 bicycle couriers at Hamama have been killed in the Israel-Hamas war, yet around 400 continue to move packages through damaged streets and active bombardment, according to Al-Yazji.Abu Zekri said some of his workers were wounded in a strike in Khan Younis and others narrowly escaped shelling near them in the Al-Jalaa area of Gaza City.Despite the losses, both companies continue taking on workers. For Abu Zekri, the project is partly about providing income when other options have gone. What workers need to keep going, he said, is straightforward: passable roads, repairable bikes and available parts."Let us bring in pedals, half-frames, tyres, patches for the bikes," he said.
