Headline: US denies Palestine leader Abbas a visa to UN summit for second year running
Body: The Palestinian Authority on Thursday sharply criticised a decision by the United States to deny visas to its officials ahead of next week's UN General Assembly in New York, a measure that also affects its president Mahmoud Abbas.In a statement, the Palestinian foreign ministry called it "an unjustified measure that runs counter to efforts to rebuild trust, develop Palestinian–US relations, and create the necessary political climate for implementing the two-state solution and achieving peace and stability".The decision marks the second consecutive year in which Abbas has been prevented from traveling to New York for the General Assembly, after a similar visa denial last year forced him to address the meeting by video instead.The State Department said Palestinian officials, including Abbas, had failed to live up to their commitments under previous agreements to seek peace with Israel. In its statement, the department said that "as a consequence of their failure to reform, contrary to their commitments to the United States, and their ongoing activities that undermine the prospects for peace, the United States will extend sanctions that deny visas to PLO members and PA officials."The restrictions extend beyond Abbas himself. Similar rejections were issued to dozens of other Palestinian Authority officials who had hoped to travel with him. According to the Times of Israel, one notice seen by a Palestinian official cited Section 212(a)(3)(B) of US immigration law, which prohibits issuing a visa to anyone who has engaged in terrorist activities or been associated with a terrorist organisation.Despite the ban, Palestinian representation at the summit will not disappear entirely. The Palestinians will still be represented at next week's high-level meeting by diplomats already accredited to the United Nations, and Abbas is expected to again appear by video.The US State Department's statement also noted that it would maintain a waiver allowing members of the Palestinian Mission to the UN to continue operating from New York.The UN General Assembly is expected to vote on a measure that would once again allow Abbas to participate remotely, a mechanism it first used last year.The renewed visa denial comes at a politically sensitive moment as a number of key members are expected to recognise a Palestinian state at this year's General Assembly.In 2025 France officially recognised the State of Palestine, joined by the United Kingdom, Australia, Luxembourg, Belgium, Portugal, Malta and Canada. Four of the five permament UN Security Council members now recognise Palestine.When Washington first imposed the restriction last year, the move drew criticism from European governments including Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez who described the visa decision as "unjust", writing on X that "Palestine has the right to make its voice heard at the United Nations and in all international forums".

Headline: 'Napoli on the Road': London pizzeria crowned world’s best at global awards
Body: London has officially got the world's best pizza. Napoli on the Road, the Chiswick pizzeria founded by chef Michele Pascarella, has taken the top spot at the 50 Top Pizza World Awards 2026, beating out hundreds of contenders from around the globe.The win was announced in Naples – the original birthplace of pizza – where Pascarella celebrated a remarkable journey. He launched Napoli on the Road in 2016 from a three-wheeled Piaggio Ape fitted with a wood-fired oven, serving pizzas at London’s streets and farmers’ markets.A decade later, the business has grown into restaurants in Chiswick, Richmond and Soho, with the latter branch offering a pizza tasting menu inspired by Pascarella’s childhood in Caserta in the south of Italy."I’m in shock. Headline: Macklemore donates $1 million to Palestinian aid: 'I invite Robert Kraft to match my donation'
Body: American rapper Macklemore has said he will donate his $1million (€871,000) net earnings from Ed Sheeran's tour to organisations supporting the Palestinian people. The rapper, who has been dropped from the tour for making pro-Palestinian remarks on stage, has challenged Jewish billionaire Robert Kraft to match his donation. "I will be donating the entire $1 million of my net earnings from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour to six organizations working directly to support the Palestinian people," wrote Macklemore. "And I invite Robert Kraft to match my donation. Whatever we disagree about, perhaps we can agree on this: Palestinian lives are worth protecting. A Palestinian life is no less valuable than any other life on this earth." Macklemore has shared that his net earnings will go to organizations including Palestine Children’s Relief Fund, Heal Palestine, Gaza Soup Kitchen, Medical Aid for Palestinians, UNRWA USA National Committee and Anera. Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium, intervened towards Sheeran and made the decision to ban Macklemore from the Gillette Stadium because his venue would not "provide a platform for hate speech". The tycoon and Israel donor predictably accused the Grammy-winning rapper of having "a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric" - something which Macklemore denies. In fact, Kraft's accusation can be dismissed when looking at the footage of Macklemore on stage."To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace; love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality," said Macklemore. "So I say Free Palestine, I say Free Lebanon, I say Free Cuba, I say Free Congo, Free Sudan, I say Free all people in America living in fear of this terrorist organization, ICE. None of us will be free until we are all free."Kraft has now responded by saying that he and Sheeran have pledged $2m (€1.7m) each "to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis" - although, rather crucially, he did not specify which organisations or charities would receive the money."Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis," Kraft said in a statement. "Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges." "I have dedicated much of my life to building bridges between all people. I believe deeply that all lives are worth protecting," Kraft added.Earlier this week, Sheeran said he was "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," and described the "suffering and pain caused on both sides" as a human tragedy in a lengthy Instagram statement. "I am not complicit," he added. "I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care." Sheeran also said that "Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine", adding that the rapper's contract for the tour "was with the promoter, not me". Despite Sheeran's attempts at damage control, the final leg of his tour remains in crisis as all the other artists scheduled to perform as part of his tour pulled out in protest.Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe, Irish folk band Beoga, Danish band Lukas Graham, and Finneas, the brother of pop star Billie Eilish, all announced they were dropping out.  Rowe said that Sheeran had been a friend to him, “but as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation”. “I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children. I would lose all respect for myself to carry on as normal.” Beoga stated on Instagram that they would no longer be a part of Sheeran’s band “following the silencing of Macklemore by zionist lobbies”. They added that while they have been friends with Sheeran for over 10 years and will continue to be, “to play in venues that silence anyone advocating for Free Palestine is simply not an option for us”. Finneas, who was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year, wrote on Instagram: “Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed. I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people.”Elsewhere, many are calling Sheeran out for not standing up for Macklemore and his fellow artists. Some are calling Sheeran's stance "morally bankrupt" and labelling the singer as a "lowlife coward whose music sounds exactly like he is."Sheeran has also faced backlash from other musicians and celebrities, who have expressed support for Macklemore and argue that the rapper's removal represented a chilling effect on free speech.Massive Attack are the most recent band to share their stance on the situation. Taking to Instagram, the band shared: “Entertainment can never be bigger than resisting the apartheid & genocide of fellow human beings. ‘Neutrality’ in the face of the slaughter of more than 20,000 children can never be neutrality.” They also said that “no artist should tolerate the censorship of another artist, however many millions of dollars are in play” and that the “arc of state, corporate and media silence that allowed a genocide to take place seeks to coerce high profile artists and actors into that silence.” Concluding, they added that they “stand in solidarity with all artists risking their careers in defence of the rights of the Palestinian people, & against the illegal occupation, apartheid, war crimes & ongoing genocide perpetrated by the State of Israel.” Sheeran has yet to respond to his support acts pulling out, or to the comments from Massive Attack.

Headline: Is curtailing AI an illusion for the EU, despite von der Leyen's pledge?
Body: Ursula von der Leyen wants the world to believe Brussels will set the pace of the rapid AI development that is threatening to reshape economies and labour markets, as well as security infrastructures, faster than governments can respond.The trouble is, the EU is barely part of the race.In her State of the European Union address this week, the European Commission president vowed that Europe would help write the rules for artificial intelligence, positioning the bloc as a rule-setter on a par with Washington and Beijing.But the EU has no dominant model, no equivalent to OpenAI, Claude or DeepSeek, and precious little leverage over the companies actually building the technology.Michael McNamara, an independent Irish MEP from the Renew group says Von der Leyen's pledge is little more than "lip-service" at the moment."Many of the most significant AI developers are outside of Europe, and will have little regard whatsoever to her comments," the MEP, who is co-chair of the European Parliament's working group on the implementation and enforcement of the AI Act, said.McNamara pointed to what he calls a wildly inconsistent record from von der Leyen's Commission on AI safety.It championed the AI Act, the bloc's risk-based rulebook for AI systems, and an AI Liability Directive, which would have made it easier to sue over AI-caused harm, in the last mandate, then withdrew the liability proposal in this one.Later, it pushed to strip safeguards and pressured the Council and Parliament to carve entire sectors out of the AI Act during the recent Omnibus trilogues, only to reverse course again in the State of the European Union speech."Given the contradictory positions she has advanced in quick step, it’s hard to expect AI developers to pay much regard to her latest position," McNamara continued.He did however agree with Von der Leyen's pledge to work with "like-minded partners like Canada, the United Kingdom and others, particularly on model evaluation, verification and security."Meanwhile, Italian MEP Brando Benifei, who also co-chairs Parliament's AI working group and was co-rapporteur of the AI Act, praised von der Leyen, saying she is right to claim "the AI Act positions Europe to lead on AI safety"."It binds every frontier model offered here, American or Chinese. Allied cooperation with Canada and the UK on safety is a welcome step that must be backed by sovereign capacity: European cloud, chips, unified capital, and a public CERN for AI to turn regulatory leadership into technological power."Is the EU even part of the race?In yesterday’s State of the European Union speech, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen set out EU plans for the AI industry and called for a slowdown in the development of AI models to “pace the frontier".Her wording on the issue matches pleas issued by Anthropic’s Dario Amodei in an essay published earlier this week.“If the people developing the technology are clear, then we should be too,” she told the European Parliament.Europe currently lags behind the US and China in the AI race and in a number of ways.The continent captures less than 5% of the estimated $1 trillion (€871.6tn) global AI investment, compared to 75-80% going to the US and another 10-14% to China.Its only significant AI company, Mistral AI, is valued at just $24 billion (€20.9bn), a figure dwarfed by US firms OpenAI and Anthropic, each valued at $852 billion (€741.2bn) and $965 billion (€839.6bn) respectively.Even China’s AI scene, which is more pluralistic than America’s, has market leaders such as DeepSeek, valued at $52 billion (€45.2bn), Moonshot AI, at $31.5 billion (€27.4bn) and Zhipu AI at $141 billion (€122.7bn).The only area it can reasonably be argued that the EU is leading is regulation, with the introduction of the EU AI Act in 2024 and transparency and governance rules coming into effect in August this year.The Commission president, however, believes the EU AI Act is “a crucial piece to putting guardrails in place” that “puts Europe in the position to shape global efforts on how to tackle this”.She also announced that the EU would seek to work with its allies, including Canada, the United Kingdom and others. “We want to team up on model evaluation, verification, early warning, AI security and much more.”Plans for talks in November with industry leaders, entrepreneurs and government officials to see how AI can be implemented in key sectors including health, transport, agri-food, advanced manufacturing and defence and space were also mentioned.Von der Leyen also promised to table a "Quality Jobs Act" by the end of 2026, to "help develop skills, improve the quality of jobs and give workers a fair chance".

Headline: Frankfurt issues malaria warning after two new cases
Body: Frankfurt am Main's public health authority has issued a warning after the city recorded two further cases of malaria, bringing the total number of people who have fallen ill since July to six. Malaria is a tropical disease transmitted by mosquitoes. Two of the cases in Frankfurt have proved fatal.The new cases involve people from the Schwanheim district, close to the airport, and the public health authority is investigating whether there is a link. Airport employees have been particularly affected by recent infections. It is thought that mosquitoes from malaria-affected regions occasionally travel on flight routes, survive in Frankfurt and then transmit the disease when they bite.What is malaria?Malaria, a tropical disease, can be treated effectively if is diagnosed early. At first, however, the symptoms resemble flu or a common cold. "It is therefore crucial to consider a possible malaria infection at an early stage when such symptoms occur," the city of Frankfurt am Main said.Typical symptoms of malaria infection include fever, shivering, headaches, and pain in the limbs, as well as gastrointestinal complaints. "Such signs are therefore often mistaken as a flu-like infection or a stomach and intestinal infection," the Robert Koch Institute also explains.Not all types of malaria are fatal, such as malaria tertiana, quartana or Plasmodium knowlesi malaria. The most dangerous form is malaria tropica, which can be deadly without prompt diagnosis and treatment and Germany's Federal Foreign Office describes it as a life-threatening disease.The illness is not contagious from person to person; transmission requires the bite of an infected mosquito. When malaria is not contracted in an endemic area but instead reaches other countries via mosquitoes carried on flights, it is often referred to as airport malaria.Recommendation: consult a doctor if you develop unexplained feverPeople who work at Frankfurt Airport or in its surroundings, spend time there or live close to the airport should see a doctor if they develop unexplained fever.During the consultation, it is important to mention their place of residence or any stay in the vicinity of the airport.Residents of Frankfurt am Main can also obtain information via the public health authority's hotline, which can be reached by phone from 9 am to 6 pm on 069/212-30030.Preventive measures are also possible by protecting yourself from mosquito bites, for example, through the use of insect repellents. Products containing diethyltoluamide (DEET) and icaridin have so far proved effective worldwide, according to a guide from the Federal Foreign Office. Wearing long clothing and using insect nets can also help over the longer term.Airport malaria in EuropeAccording to the Robert Koch Institute, cases of airport malaria are very rare in Germany. A recent study also shows that more than 99% of malaria cases recorded in Europe were imported from endemic regions.From 1969 to early 2024, databases recorded 145 malaria cases in which the patients were infected within Europe. More than two-thirds of these were classified as airport malaria. The countries most affected were France (52 cases), Belgium (19 cases) and Germany with nine cases, eight of them in Frankfurt and one in Munich.Here, too, many of those affected had links to an international airport. According to the city, the two newly infected people from Frankfurt's Schwanheim district are currently being treated in hospital.

Headline: Fact check: Will Marine Le Pen hold a Frexit referendum if she becomes president of France?
Body: A number of social media posts claim that Marine Le Pen, the far-right candidate in France's 2027 presidential election, is promising a referendum on the country's EU membership if she wins the keys to the Élysée Palace next year.The posts, primarily in Spanish, provide no further detail, and that's our first clue that the claims are false: Le Pen is not calling for a Frexit referendum if she becomes president.It is true that the National Rally politician is a harsh critic of the EU and once championed the idea of France leaving the bloc.She celebrated the Brexit result when the UK voted to leave the EU in 2016. She made leaving the bloc and giving up the euro two of her flagship proposals in her 2012 and 2017 presidential campaigns.But she has since abandoned these proposals. During the 2022 election, she instead advocated radically reforming the EU from within, stripping Brussels of most of its power and transforming the bloc into a looser alliance of nations.Le Pen's change in position reflects a wider trend among far-right parties across Europe. Before the Brexit vote, far-right politicians in the Netherlands and Italy, among others, regularly pushed for their own referenda, but now those calls have generally quietened.Nevertheless, Geert Wilders, leader of the far-right Party for Freedom, revived his call to reconsider the Netherlands' EU membership on Wednesday, telling Dutch MPs that "Nexit" was necessary to stop migrants and asylum seekers from entering the country.Even if Le Pen did become president and held a Frexit referendum, she'd be unlikely to win: a study by Pew Research earlier this year showed that support for the EU in France has risen from 38% in 2016 to 52% in 2026. Similar increases were recorded elsewhere in Europe, including in the UK.A YouGov poll from late 2025, meanwhile, found that 49% of French respondents would vote to remain in the EU, compared with 27% who would vote to leave.While a Frexit referendum is currently not on the cards, Le Pen, who's currently leading in first-round polling with roughly 33 to 36%, has suggested putting other issues to a public vote if she wins the presidency next year. This may have fuelled some of the online rumours about an alleged EU referendum.Her proposals include a referendum on combating so-called "Islamist ideologies", including banning the wearing of the veil in public, and a vote on amending France's constitution to restrict immigration.The National Rally did not respond to a request for comment.

Headline: Australia and New Zealand could follow Canada into associated EU membership, Metsola tells Euronews
Body: European Parliament President Roberta Metsola has told Euronews that countries including Australia and New Zealand could follow Canada in becoming “associate members” of the European Union as like-minded nations seek closer ties.Speaking exclusively to Europe Today ahead of a speech by Canadian Prime MInister Mark Carny on Thursday, Metsola described the proposed status as a third way between full EU membership and candidate status.“There are countries with which we want to deepen our relationship,” Metsola said."I don't doubt that it will include other countries, and others will come knocking at our door...In such times of uncertainty, having friends matters."The EU already has trade agreements with both countries, providing a potential starting point for closer cooperation. A similar relationship has been proposed with Canada, which signed a comprehensive trade agreement with the EU in 2016.Asked about the technicalities of what associate membership would look like, Metsola acknowledged that talks are still at an early stage, while pointing to deeper trade relations, access to critical raw materials and common regulations on issues that “like-minded” countries care deeply about, such as social media and the protection of minors.On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed “associate membership” for Canada in her annual State of the Union address.Canadian Prime Minister Carney is exploring closer ties with the bloc amid a trade war with the US, Canada’s biggest trading partner, with prohibitive tariffs in place. Under pressure from President Donald Trump, Ottawa is rethinking its place in the world, while Carney has been vocal in calling for an alliance of “middle powers”.No reason for retaliationAfter the announcement, Trump told reporters he would consider imposing fresh tariffs on the European Union if the bid for associate membership turns "hostile".Washington and Brussels have a trade deal in place, under which the EU faces a 15% tariff on goods.Metsola played down the threats, saying the EU views its relationships with the two countries separately. She said that the EU does not work against anyone but acts as an advocate for rules-based cooperation.She also pointed to the trade deal agreed last summer and ratified this year.Separately, a spokesperson for the European Commission said: “The proposed strengthening of our partnership is not against anyone, but for our common strength.”Carney is due to address the European Parliament on Thursday at 11.30am.Peggy Corlin contributed to reporting.

Headline: Anger over Thaçi war crimes sentence spills into protests at Kosovo EU mission
Body: The internationally backed Kosovo court's verdict sentencing former President Hashim Thaçi to 25 years in prison for war crimes sparked shock and anger among most Kosovars on Wednesday.Judges of the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague found Thaçi and three other former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leaders guilty of illegal arrests, torture, murder and cruel treatment during the 1998-1999 war for independence from Serbia.But among many Kosovo Albanians, Thaçi and his co-defendants are still widely lauded as heroes of the independence movement — and their simmering anger threatened to escalate into wholesale riots.In Prishtina, a crowd of young men marched towards the headquarters of the European Union's Rule of Law Mission in Kosovo (EULEX), waving KLA flags and chanting the guerrilla group's name.Some scuffled with riot police and threw stones at the building. A small group remained in front of EULEX until Wednesday night, blocking traffic and defying police orders to clear the road and disperse.The group eventually left for Prishtina airport to welcome Thaçi and Veseli's sons, Endrit Thaçi and Klestor Veseli, upon their return from the sentencing.In The Hague, angry demonstrators who had gathered near the court briefly clashed with police, with some climbing onto a police van as officers held them back from the court building.Police dispersed the crowd with water cannon.Earlier on Wednesday, thousands gathered in the capital Prishtina to watch the verdict on a large screen.As the sentence was delivered, silence settled over the attendees, leaving many visibly stunned after weeks of preparations by Thaçi's supporters for a possible acquittal."This process was not about justice, but politics," said pensioner Tahir Bytyqi, one among the crowd that quickly dispersed after the proceedings finished.'Unacceptable injustice'The trial has remained deeply controversial in the Western Balkan nation of some 1.6 million, with Premier Albin Kurti calling the verdict "a great and harmful punishment" and urging it to be "corrected" on appeal."These are unjust findings, but they are not final and will be subject to review on appeal," Kurti said in a Facebook post."The reason the KLA was born was not, and cannot, be punished or tarnished."Thaçi was sentenced alongside former senior KLA figures Jakup Krasniqi, Rexhep Selimi and Kadri Veseli. Krasniqi was sentenced to 25 years, Selimi to 13 and Veseli to 18.The court said they had "contributed significantly" to a common criminal purpose targeting perceived opponents of the KLA's political and military goals.All four were acquitted of charges of crimes against humanity and can appeal the sentence.During the appeals process, Thaçi and his co-accused will remain detained in The Hague. Thaçi also faces a second trial over alleged obstruction of justice related to this case, for which prosecutors have requested a sentence of six years.The 58-year-old resigned as president and surrendered to the court after his 2020 indictment. He has been detained in The Hague since, with time served counting towards his sentence.After the war, Thaçi remained a central political figure and played a key role in Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence.During the trial, images of the 58-year-old — who also served as prime minister and foreign minister — regularly appeared on huge billboards across the country, and his supporters organised rallies demanding his acquittal.Murders and severe beatingsAlthough based in the Netherlands and staffed by international judges, the KSC was established under Kosovo law specifically to prosecute alleged crimes committed by KLA members during the war.Deeply unpopular from its foundation, the court's use of evidence supplied by Belgrade has further inflamed accusations of political bias.But its mandate is heavily backed by international allies, and the court has previously convicted several people for crimes committed during the war.Reading out the verdict, Judge Charles Smith said the "scale and nature" of the men's crimes were "very serious", including 96 murders of ethnic Albanians, Serbs and Roma, some of whom were their political opponents."Murder victims in this case were shot to death, and others died because of the severe beatings," Smith added.The court said many of the victims' bodies were found in a condition that amounted to a further outrage upon their dignity, he said.The crimes were committed between April 1998 and June 1999, during and just after the Kosovo war, which claimed some 13,000 lives and ended in a NATO intervention that pushed out Serbian forces.Belgrade was not happy with Wednesday's verdict either, but for different reasons."We in this moment have no reason to neither rejoice nor grieve," Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić said on Thursday, criticising the court for allegedly not taking into account crimes against ethnic Serb civilians and claiming anti-Serb bias."As I said, in the six counts that concern the hardest and the most important criminal acts of crimes against humanity (the defendants) were not found guilty," Vučić told the press.“There can be binding judgements, or non-binding ones, it’s all the same, Serbs will always be (war) criminals and all the others will be liberators and heroes, and everyone else will be allowed this, but the Serbs.”Thaçi has maintained his innocence throughout the process, telling a Kosovo outlet in August that he expected a full acquittal.

Headline: A chunk of the Sun blasted off and could trigger storms on Earth
Body: A large cloud of material released by the Sun is due to reach Earth on Thursday and could trigger a minor geomagnetic storm, according to a report from astronomy outlet EarthSky, co-written by a NASA solar scientist.The Sun's outer atmosphere contains extremely hot, electrically charged gas. Sometimes huge amounts of this material are blasted out into space in what scientists call a coronal mass ejection (CME), according to NASA.The current event began with an eruption on Monday from active region AR4528. The following day, the astronomy outlet reported that further analysis showed part of the material was travelling towards Earth and could arrive around Thursday, based on modelling from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).Forecasters say the effects could build gradually over the day rather than all at once, since fast solar wind from a coronal hole is adding to the CME's push.What happens when a solar eruption reaches Earth?When this material reaches Earth, it can disturb the planet’s magnetic field, causing what is known as a geomagnetic storm.Depending on its strength, such a storm can affect satellites, navigation and communications, while more severe events can also disrupt power grids.They can also produce the northern lights. Charged particles from the Sun interact with gases high in Earth’s atmosphere, creating auroras.During stronger geomagnetic storms, the lights can spread much farther away from the polar regions and become visible in places where they are normally rare.For now, however, the expected storm is weak.NOAA is forecasting G1 conditions, the lowest level on its five-point geomagnetic storm scale.At G1, the agency says weak fluctuations in power grids are possible and satellites may experience minor effects. Auroras can also occur, but they are generally expected at high latitudes.That means most people are unlikely to notice any technological disruption from this event, while the current forecast does not point to an unusually widespread display of northern lights across Europe.The impact will depend on how the incoming solar material’s magnetic field interacts with Earth’s own magnetic field, EarthSky said.

Headline: EU defence chief says a ‘painful response’ to Russian hybrid threats is needed
Body: European Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius said Europe can respond to Russia in a “painful way” through the development of an anti-hybrid warfare playbook.“We can find ways for how Russia will pay quite a painful price for their provocations,” he said in exclusive comments to Euronews’ flagship current affairs news programme, Europe Today.“This is what the Commission president spoke about.”He was responding to comments made by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at her agenda-setting State of the European Union speech on Wednesday, in which she proposed that Europe must develop a mechanism to be able to respond to hybrid warfare incidents.Recent drone incursions have rattled Europe’s Eastern flank, as have many other incidents inhabiting the grey zone of warfare, such as cable-cuts and weaponised migration.The steady drumbeat of incidents last month prompted five Baltic European Commissioners to demand a stronger response from the EU executive to support the region.Von der Leyen used her State of the European Union address on Wednesday to outline a new European response to threats “which fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security”.Among the proposals the Commission president unveiled was a mechanism to complement NATO's Article 4, which would be referred to as the Emergency Security Protocol.“When triggered by one member state, all member states would convene to coordinate a European response," von der Leyen explained, "to deter further escalation and to mitigate the impact.”Coming togetherKubilius told Euronews that the European Commission is working on plans for how it can assist countries particularly impacted by hybrid threats.“The European Union is a solidarity union,” he said.But the security effort does not stop there, with von der Leyen also touting a potential new leader’s format, titled the European Security Council.According to her, the group would include not just EU member states but also like-minded countries such as Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Norway and Canada, banded together to address the biggest geopolitical issues facing Europe — among them an increasingly brazen Russia and the retreat of the United States from Europe's security architecture."For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent," von der Leyen said. "This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play."In practice, leaders like Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are already frequently invited to European Council meetings. The new format would institutionalise this relationship, giving it a dedicated framework to discuss security matters.The big question is how the group would not duplicate the efforts of the 77-year-old NATO, of which 23 EU countries are members.European Commissioner for the Economy Valdis Dombrovskis said the European Security Council would “complement NATO” and not “compete with NATO”.“We see the war in Ukraine has been turned into a drone war and Russia is producing millions of drones a year,” he said on Europe Today. “We need to strengthen our drone defence capabilities.”Asked whether duplication could occur through the proposed Emergency Security Protocol or the European Security Council, a NATO official told Euronews they welcome European Allies and partners stepping up to do more in support of shared security.“As again underlined at the Ankara Summit, NATO is the bedrock of our collective defence and we will continue to work closely with the EU in pursuit of our shared agenda — including to ramp up defence industrial production and to ensure continued support to Ukraine,” the official said.

Headline: Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappé breaks silence on Ceuta shirt controversy
Body: Kylian Mbappé has explained for the first time why he, along with teammates Vinícius Júnior and Ibrahima Konaté, only partially wore a shirt in support of Ceuta before Real Madrid's match against Elche. The French forward insists the gesture was not meant as a rejection of the people of Ceuta, and has expressed solidarity both with the city's population and with the migrants who have died."I want to explain it properly so that people understand," Mbappé told the newspaper AS. He explained that the initiative to wear the shirt had come from the clubs, and that the players were expected to put it on. "The first thing I want to say is that I stand in full solidarity with Ceuta and with all the victims. Because before being a player, I am a human being," he said.Mbappé said he had also wanted to use the gesture to remember the migrants who have died and those still in difficult situations. "I also wanted to have a gesture and a thought for all the migrants who have lost their lives and who are also living in harsh conditions," he said.The striker acknowledged that it was a "difficult" position, and denied that his decision meant he was against the people of Ceuta. "I have nothing against them, and I support them 100 percent — my thoughts are with them. But I also wanted to spare a thought for all the people who are suffering," he explained.The controversy began before Tuesday's match, when the three players only partially put on the shirt, covering the message "We are all mackerel" — a reference to the nickname for Ceuta's inhabitants. The slogan was completed by the phrase "Our city, our homeland."The initiative had been proposed by Elche, as the home side, and accepted by Real Madrid. LaLiga president Javier Tebas later criticised the three players for not wearing the shirt properly.Mbappé insisted his intention had been to convey a broader message of solidarity. "I'm a guy who wants the best for the world we live in. I am trying to send a message of positivity and peace, and I hope this is resolved quickly," he concluded.

Headline: European markets open higher after Fed hike as US dollar hits seven-week high
Body: Investors in Europe took the Federal Reserve rate hike in their stride.Both the Euro Stoxx 50 and the broader pan-European Stoxx 600 traded over 0.6% higher at the start of Thursday's session.France's CAC 40, Germany's DAX 30, Italy’s FTSE MIB, Spain's IBEX 35, the Netherlands' AEX and Switzerland's CH20, all traded between 0.2% and 0.7% higher than their Wednesday close.The UK's FTSE 100 led the pack and rose more than 1%.Carmakers and industrials led the Paris index, with Renault gaining more than 2%, Stellantis 1.6% and Schneider Electric 1.3%. Technology went the other way, with Dassault Systèmes falling 2.4%.The calm followed a rougher session in New York, where the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed 1.2% lower on Wednesday and the S&P 500 fell 0.4%, while the Nasdaq was broadly flat.Asian markets were mixed overnight with Tokyo's Nikkei 225 rising 0.2%, Seoul's Kospi gaining 0.9%, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng lost 0.7% and the Shanghai Composite 0.4%.Reactions were "pretty much expected since the rate hike was also in line with market expectations", said Lorraine Tan, director of equity research for Asia at Morningstar, adding that the Iran war is likely to keep pressure on inflation.A stronger US dollar and higher yieldsThe more consequential moves were in currencies and bonds.The US dollar climbed to its highest in seven weeks against a basket of major currencies, lifted by the jump in short-dated Treasury yields that followed the decision.The euro was trading around $1.146, down 0.5% from Wednesday's open.A stronger US dollar makes European exports more competitive in American markets, but it also raises the cost of anything priced in dollars, which includes oil and gas, which compounds Europe's energy bill at a difficult moment.In bond markets, the two-year Treasury yield, the maturity most sensitive to rate expectations, jumped to around 4.72% from 4.67% before the decision, holding near that level on Thursday.The 10-year sat close to 5%, reflecting both the war-driven energy shock and mounting investor concern about American government debt.Traders now fully expect another rate hike by December and put the odds of a move as soon as October at around 50%. Goldman Sachs became one of the first major Wall Street banks to forecast consecutive hikes, reversing its previous view that this month's move would be the only one.Attention turns next to the Bank of England, which announces its decision later on Thursday and is expected to hold rates steady, and to the Bank of Japan on Friday, where a hike is anticipated.

Headline: The 'Canada effect': Which European companies could benefit from closer ties?
Body: The US-Canada trade war is pushing Ottawa closer to the European Union. For European companies, that shift is already creating opportunities in defence, aerospace and industrial technology.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney got a standing ovation in Strasbourg on Wednesday, not something that happens often to a foreign prime minister in the European Parliament.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen later gave that welcome a political meaning.“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” she said during the annual State of the Union address.Von der Leyen described the broader relationship as an “Alliance for the Future”, covering defence, energy, technology, critical minerals and the Arctic.What does an "associate member" mean?There is no established “associate member” category in the EU treaties and no template Canada can simply join.Creating one would require agreement among member states and complex legal negotiations.Ten, including France and Italy, have yet to ratify Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) fully, almost a decade after the trade agreement between Canada and the European Union was signed.Carney has also said Canada is not seeking full EU membership. Ottawa instead wants a “unique alliance” that extends beyond a conventional free-trade deal.For now, the proposal is more political signal than legal blueprint.However, recent contracts show that the commercial relationship is already moving ahead.EU–Canada trade already has a head startTrade in goods and services between the two sides has grown by more than 81% since 2016, the year before the CETA took provisional effect, reaching just over €130 billion in 2025, according to the Council of the EU.EU goods exports to Canada amounted to €48.9 billion. Services exports added another €29.4 billion.Germany shipped roughly €12 billion of goods to Canada last year. Italy followed at €6.3 billion, ahead of France at €4.4 billion.Machinery, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and transport equipment dominate European sales to Canada.European machinery sales to Canada hit a record €9.5 billion last year. Electrical equipment climbed from €2 billion in 2022 to €3.3 billion, and cars rose from €2.9 billion to €4.4 billion over the same period.Aerospace moved hardest of all. Sales of powered aircraft went from €449 million in 2022 to €1.2 billion last year.European defence companies stand to gainDefence provides the clearest evidence that Canada is looking beyond its traditional American suppliers.In July, Ottawa selected Germany's TKMS AG & Co. KGaA, the naval shipbuilder spun off from Thyssenkrupp AG last October, as preferred supplier for up to 12 new submarines.While the final contract has not been signed yet, the decision places a European company at the centre of one of Canada's largest military procurement programmes.Sweden’s Saab has also gained ground. Ottawa selected the company as its preferred supplier for six GlobalEye surveillance aircraft, ahead of alternatives from Boeing and L3Harris.The GlobalEye is built on business jets made by Canada's Bombardier Inc. and Saab has offered to carry out much of the work in Canada, combining European sensors and mission systems with Canadian airframes.The aircraft use jets produced by Canada’s Bombardier. Saab has offered to complete much of the work in Canada, combining European technology with Canadian manufacturing.Canada also became the first non-European country admitted to procurement under the EU's SAFE defence programme in June.That gives Canadian manufacturers access to joint European purchasing, and it makes it easier for European defence groups to build supply chains that include Canadian firms.Airbus and Siemens already have a strong footholdThe opportunity extends beyond military equipment. Air Canada has placed a firm order with Airbus for eight A350-1000 aircraft.The government has also contracted Airbus for four new A330 tankers plus five conversions, part of a C$3.6 billion (€2.2bn) programme whose first new-build aircraft flew in July.Ottawa has committed a further C$1.5 billion (€930mn) to keeping the fleet in the air.Germany’s Siemens is investing C$150 million (€97 million) over five years in a Canadian research centre for AI-powered battery manufacturing.French groups Keolis, Systra and SNCF Voyageurs are also part of the Cadence consortium selected in 2025 to develop Alto, the planned high-speed railway between Toronto and Quebec City. Canada has allocated about €2.4 billion to the project’s development phase.Critical minerals could become the next opportunityCanada’s reserves of nickel, lithium, copper and other critical minerals offer another potential area of cooperation.Europe wants to reduce its dependence on concentrated and politically risky suppliers.Canada wants more investment, processing capacity and customers outside the United States.In March, the European Investment Bank and the Canadian government signed a letter of intent to explore financing for Canadian critical-minerals projects.The agreement does not yet contain financial commitments.However, it could eventually support European companies involved in mining technology, processing, recycling and battery production.The price of deeper European accessCETA had eliminated 99% of tariff lines by 2024. A new alliance would therefore need to offer more than another reduction in customs duties.The next gains would probably come from government procurement, investment, digital trade, professional mobility and the mutual recognition of standards.Greater access could also require Canada to align some of its rules with the EU in the sectors covered by any future agreement.However, it is too early to assume that Canada would adopt European rules on everything from agriculture to data protection. That will depend on what “associate membership” eventually means.Angelo Katsoras, a geopolitical analyst at National Bank of Canada, said in an August note that Brussels is “increasingly using procurement rules, subsidies, tariffs and local content requirements to encourage more manufacturing within Europe”.That could create difficulties for Canadian companies trying to enter the European market.“Diversifying trade beyond the United States to regions such as the EU will likely be more challenging than many people anticipate,” Katsoras said.The same logic applies in the opposite direction. European companies are more likely to succeed in Canada when they invest locally rather than rely entirely on exports.Can Europe replace the United States?The short answer is no.The US absorbed 71.7% of Canadian merchandise exports in 2025. The EU, by comparison, represented 8.7% of Canada’s total trade in goods.Canada cannot quickly replace the pipelines, railways, factories and cross-border supply chains built around its southern neighbour.The more realistic outcome is a gradual redistribution of investment and government contracts.Defence and rail can move first because governments choose the suppliers. Critical minerals, battery technology and energy infrastructure could follow as financing and supply chains develop.Canada’s European pivot is therefore less an economic divorce from the United States than a decision to stop relying on a single partner.For European companies, the biggest winners will not necessarily be those exporting the most.They will be the groups prepared to turn European technology into Canadian production, investment and jobs.

Headline: These are the best food and drink tours to travel for in 2026, according to Tripadvisor
Body: With the ubiquitous nature of social media, plenty of us have travelled with our eyes, seeking out the most photo-friendly spots while away. Others still have planned their trips with their ears, as gig-tripping begins to rival sports tourism.Someone who prefers to travel with your stomach? Then you might just want to check out this new ranking of the ultimate food and drinks tours across the globe.Part of TripAdvisor’s 2026 Travellers’ Choice Awards, the newly unveiled rankings are based on reviews and ratings collected over the past 12 months.“Food is at the heart of how we experience a destination, and these awards recognise the restaurant and culinary experiences travellers consider among the very best,” Laurel Greatrix, chief communications officer at Tripadvisor Group, said. “From cooking classes with locals to incredible food tours and restaurants, these are the kinds of experiences that can become a highlight of a trip – or even a reason to take one.”The best food, wine and beer tours in EuropeTopping the food tours list in Europe, and overall, is the Reykjavik food walk, which offers tastings of dishes like Icelandic hot dogs, cheeses and ice cream.Taking place over three hours, guests visit half a dozen local spots, ranging from food trucks to fine dining restaurants, exploring the lesser-known cuisine.On the wine and beers front, a Tuscany wine tasting tour in Florence came out second overall. The half-day tour takes you to different wine estates, with tastings of wine, olive oil, cheese and cured meats, and also including a traditional Tuscan lunch or dinner.European experiences dominated both lists, with top options including a food and wine tour in Lisbon, a Greek food walking tour in Athens, and a historic pub tour in Prague.Top 10 food tours around the worldReykjavik Food Walk - Headline: Heat and drought: Why beer at Oktoberfest could soon be in short supply
Body: Heat, parched soils and significantly smaller hop cones: for many hop farmers in Austria this year's harvest is proving sobering. The Mühlviertel, one of the country's most important hop-growing regions, is particularly hard hit."The heat and the drought have taken a heavy toll on us. Some of my plants are completely ruined," says Stefan Hofer, chair of the Mühlviertel hop growers' co-operative, speaking to ORF.Even the plants that survived the dry spell have not developed as well, he says."The others simply haven't been able to form cones in the same way. Everything is about half the size of a normal year."But the problem does not stop at the Austrian border. In Germany too, one of the world's most important hop producers, increasing aridity is posing major challenges for farmers.This is particularly evident in Bavaria. The Franconian town of Spalt, together with three other German growing regions, is one of the areas that supply around 40% of the world's hop production.Extreme weather events are placing farms under growing pressure. Longer dry periods not only hamper plant growth but also encourage pests such as spider mites. When infestations are severe, crop losses can be considerable.Is Germany therefore facing a beer shortage?Drought is becoming a problem for hop growing.At least for this year's Oktoberfest, beer lovers do not yet need to worry: so far there have been no warnings of a shortage of beer at the festival.However, the problems in the hop fields could ultimately also be felt by breweries. Hops are one of beer's key raw materials and are responsible for its bitterness and a large part of its aroma.How far this year's harvest will affect prices and production cannot yet be said with any certainty on the basis of current forecasts. Alongside the volume harvested, factors such as existing stocks, long-term supply contracts and the development of cultivated areas also play a role.One thing is clear, though: the sector increasingly has to grapple with the question of how to grow its raw materials under drier conditions. Producers are relying on different approaches.Irrigation to prepare hop growing for droughtOne of the most obvious responses to increasing dryness is additional irrigation. For many hop farms, water supply is becoming a central question for the future.Growers in Austria's Mühlviertel region are already reacting. Irrigation systems have now been installed on around 20% of the hop acreage. In view of more frequent dry spells, demand is likely to rise further.Larger irrigation projects are also being planned in Bavaria. In the Spalter Hügelland, a system is to be built that will pump water in winter from a bank filtration well on the River Fränkische Rezat into a new storage basin. From there, around 400 hectares of hop fields are to be irrigated during dry months. Using bank filtrate is also intended to protect groundwater.The costs are estimated at up to €20 million. The Free State of Bavaria is expected to cover around half, with the participating farmers having to finance the remainder.In the Hallertau (source in German), Germany's largest hop-growing region, work is also under way to secure long-term supplies of water. The local irrigation association brings together 461 farms covering a total of around 12,000 hectares. Bavaria is supporting plans for new irrigation infrastructure with €9.5 million.But additional irrigation alone is unlikely to be enough. "Simply turning on the tap is not sufficient," said Manuel Starlinger, managing director of the Mühlviertel hop growers' cooperative, speaking to ORF.And in fact the brewing industry is not only focusing on hops. Another key raw material is also suffering from the drier conditions.Winter barley instead of spring barleyFarmers and breweries are therefore also looking for alternatives when it comes to barley. On average, about 60 to 75 grams of spring barley are needed for half a litre of beer. Yet this particular variety of grain is finding it increasingly hard to cope with rising levels of drought.Spring barley "has a big problem; it only ripens under stress and does not grow properly," brewmaster Jörg Kirchhoff told broadcaster rbb.A brewery in Potsdam is therefore experimenting with winter barley in the Uckermark. Initial trials are being run on two hectares to see whether it is suitable for cultivation and, subsequently, for the brewing process.The crucial difference lies in the sowing date. "Winter barley is drilled in October and thus benefits from all the moisture of autumn and early winter," Kirchhoff explains. "By January it is generally already green and has a huge head start in terms of growth."While spring barley carries out a large part of its development in the increasingly dry spring and summer months, winter barley is better placed to benefit from the moisture of the cooler seasons.The experiment is being accompanied by the Terrathesis project at the Film University Babelsberg, funded by the Volkswagen Foundation, which looks at the concrete consequences of climate change in Brandenburg."Everyone talks about the weather changing and things getting drier. But what does that actually mean? Among other things, it means that your local brewery is running into problems," says project leader André Nebe.The project, which aims to bring together science, agriculture and the brewing industry, is scheduled to run until the end of 2029.

Headline: Europe Today: Metsola exclusively on Euronews as Carney addresses EU Parliament amid Trump's tariff threat
Body: On today's show:Maria Tadeo reports from Strasbourg as Canadian PM Mark Carney addresses the European Parliament this morning, a day after EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed making Canada the EU's first "associate member". US President Donald Trump has called this plan "laughable" and threatened with "very serious tariffs."We speak exclusively to European Parliament President Roberta Metsola, who reacts to this plan and the State of the Union speech yesterday.We also hear reactions to the State of the Union from European Commissioners Valdis Dombrovskis, Maroš Šefčovič, Wopke Hoekstra, and Andrius Kubilius, and from MEP David McAllister (EPP, Germany).Jorge Liboreiro breaks down whether the speech will move the needle, why von der Leyen announced nothing new on Ukraine support or Russia sanctions despite expectations, and what comes next for her after her biggest speech of the year.When and where to watch Europe Today?You can join Euronews’ anchors Méabh Mc Mahon and Stefan Grobe live on TV and Euronews' website, as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 8 am Brussels time.In just 20 minutes, we bring you the day's key events plus crucial analysis of all the stories shaping the EU and beyond. Also available as a newsletter and podcast.

Headline: One wallet, 27 systems: can the EU build an untraceable Digital ID?
Body: By the end of 2026, every EU country must legally offer citizens a European Digital Identity Wallet. This smartphone app holds a person’s government ID, driving licence, diploma, and other verified documents in one place and is designed to work across all 27 EU countries.Digital rights groups warn the technology and the safeguards meant to protect it are not ready and that the wallet could become exactly the kind of surveillance tool it was designed to prevent.“We are at maybe 50-60% of the technical standards that are needed to build this wallet,” says Thomas Lohninger, executive director of Austrian digital rights group epicenter.works and a board member of European Digital Rights (EDRi). “The other 40% are not there yet. They do not exist.”The “honeypot” problemCentralising a person’s identity, health data, driving licence, and financial credentials on one device raises the cost of a single security failure. A stolen phone, malicious app, or cloud breach could expose everything at once. Unlike a leaked password, a compromised credential carries a cryptographic signature of authenticity, making misuse far more damaging.“If you put all your eggs in one basket, then that basket hopefully never fails,” Lohninger says. “Imagine if this little wallet gets hacked or has downtime of just a few hours or a week. People would be locked out of their social media. They couldn’t use public transport. Their driver licence would no longer be with them.” He calls the wallet “critical infrastructure” connecting the public and private sector “like we’ve never done in Europe” and a target not just for cybercriminals but state-level actors.The regulation mandates technical defences: tamper-resistant cryptographic hardware to store keys, credentials bound to a specific device so they can’t be copied, authentication for any organisation requesting data, and a rule requiring users to be notified within 24 hours of a revoked credential. The European Data Protection Supervisor points to secure hardware elements as a key safeguard against theft. But losing a phone still means a race to freeze and recover a wallet before a criminal exploits it. EU auditors note that recovery remains only partly tested.Tracking by designThe wallet’s core privacy pledge is selective disclosure: someone proving they are over 18 should be able to share only that fact, not their name, address or ID number. The EDPS calls this “authorisation without identification”, a defence against tracking and profiling that a physical ID card can’t offer.Lohninger frames the risk as “over-identification.” Verifying someone’s identity online is currently slow and costly; banks and mobile carriers pay to do it under anti-money-laundering rules. The wallet could make identification very fast, cheap, and widely available, he warns. This creates an incentive to strip away anonymity that currently exists on social networks or in email sign-ups.He also raises what EDRi calls the “panopticon” risk. The same wallet could be used for taxes, healthcare, public transport, banking and logging into Facebook; previously separate areas of life could become linkable through one system. “These areas of life could become connected,” he says. “There’s this big risk of a panopticon where you can really see everything from everyone.” EDRi has pushed for a legal principle called unobservability, intended to stop wallet providers, governments, or potentially Google, from seeing what users do inside the system. Draft implementing rules, EDRi argues, currently weaken exactly this safeguard, while pushing mandatory biometric facial checks not foreseen in the original law.Unfinished cryptographyMuch of the technology meant to make the wallet both secure and private doesn’t exist yet, Lohninger says. Zero-knowledge proofs, cryptographic techniques that let someone prove a fact, such as being over 18, without revealing the underlying data, are “the frontier of cryptographic science.” “There is a triangle between privacy, security, and usability,” he says. “It’s very hard to get all three to 100%. The wallet certainly will cut some corners here.”That leaves an open question over which corner gets cut first. A credential system can be cryptographically secure, with strong keys, valid signatures, no obvious hack, and still leak information about a person’s behaviour if the same identifier or attribute is reused across services, letting verifiers link separate transactions to the same individual even without a name attached.The cross-border weak linkBecause the wallet relies on mutual recognition, a bank or government office in one country must trust identity checks carried out under another country’s enrolment, certification, and security standards. Lohninger doesn’t expect most national systems to be equally robust by the deadline. “Even countries that spend a lot of money on this, like France and Germany, are not ready,” he says. “They will not make it completely to the finish line.”That unevenness is itself a security risk: a system built for 27 mutually trusting implementations is only as strong as its weakest national deployment, slowest incident response, and least rigorous enrolment process. Lohninger’s advice is caution for now. “Let’s wait and not be early adopters here. I want an audit, an independent academic and civil-society investigation into what the governments bring us before we jump on these systems.”Why the stakes are risingThe security debate is intensifying as governments across Europe, including France, Denmark, Greece and Austria, push new age-verification laws for social media, with an EU-wide announcement expected soon from Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The wallet is being positioned as the enforcement tool, pairing a high-value identity system with, as Lohninger puts it, “the most dubious companies that we interact with on a daily basis.”To monitor how the system is used once live, epicenter.works is building an open-data platform called “Who Identifies Me,” designed to let journalists and civil-society groups track which companies and border agencies requests people’s data, a watchdog function Lohninger sees as essential once real security incidents begin.“The public’s trust is really the scarcest resource in all of this,” he says. “We have seen in regions around the world, when these big government digital identity systems are rolled out and they have problems, people run away.”

Headline: EU plan to make Canada an 'associate member' draws Trump’s ire
Body: Expectations are high after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday offered to create a tailor-made status of “associate EU membership” for Canada, and pitched closer collaboration on tech, energy and defence (if you missed von der Leyen’s landmark annual speech, here are our five takeaways).Trump strikes back: The announcement has already created ripples across the Atlantic, with US President Donald Trump overnight describing the invite as “hostile” and “laughable”, threatening “very serious tariffs” or to even “stop trading with Europe”.It’s a nightmare scenario for Brussels. The bloc has been treading carefully in its rapprochement with Ottawa, refraining from taking sides or intervening as a negotiator in the escalating trade spat between the North American neighbours.Carney’s dash to the UK: Carney returned to Strasbourg late last night after a quick dash to the north of England where he met UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Manchester. Both leaders held bilateral talks at the home of Everton football club, which they both support.Burnham and Carney discussed defence cooperation, with Canada formally applying to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force, a UK-led northern European military coalition.Questions linger over special status: Meanwhile here in Strasbourg, questions are mounting over what “associate membership” – a status that does not yet exist – would mean in practice. Von der Leyen’s announcement is widely understood to be an aspirational political signal, but as the Irish deputy prime minister said in Strasbourg yesterday, “the devil is always in the detail”.Several third countries are “associated” with the EU through association agreements, from the Western Balkans to Eastern Europe and the Middle East. But no country so far is an “associated member”, a definition that seems to align with Carney’s pitch for a “unique alliance” with the bloc.Canada’s status could entail a preferential trade relationship, building on the EU-Canada trade deal known as CETA, institutional cooperation and a close defence partnership. Talks on joining EU programmes such as Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe are also ongoing, as my colleague Luca Bertuzzi reports.The picture could come clearer after an EU-Canada summit in Montreal at the end of October, when Brussels and Ottawa are expected to put some meat on the bones. EU leaders are also expected to gather for a summit in Brussels in mid-October.More clues could also come from Carney’s speech in the hemicycle today and from the following press conference in Strasbourg. Meanwhile, the Canadian Prime Minister met separately on Wednesday with von der Leyen and Parliament President Roberta Metsola, who gave him a steel combat helmet used by Canadian forces in France during the Second World War.“We have so much in common,” Metsola told our EU Editor Maria Tadeo in an interview, adding that this will “absolutely” open the door for more countries to seek associate status.“I think in the big picture (...) friends matter, and if we can do more things with our friends, then let’s do them,” Metsola said. Watch. Lasting love: The rapprochement between Brussels and Ottawa is not just a “short-term honeymoon”, as Socialist MEP Tobias Cremer, author of a parliament report on EU-Canada cooperation, put it during a dinner with reporters in Strasbourg.There’s no love lost, however, among parliament’s political groups over the crisis in Ceuta.Ceuta crisis divides chamber: After a heated debate on Tuesday, the chamber is set to vote today on a resolution “on the recent hybrid attacks and instrumentalisation of migrants”, following the massive influx of 80,000 irregular migrants into the Spanish exclave last July.Each political family put forward a different version of the text, with right-wing parties attacking the Spanish government and left-wing forces denouncing the exploitation of the crisis by the far right. The deadlock could produce the unusual situation of no resolution being adopted at all.After all, in the European Parliament, every word matters — and political battles are not confined to the chamber.Even an exhibition in the corridors has become a political flashpoint. “Just EUman”, a display currently on show and promoted by a conservative MEP with a pro-life association, features pictures of a fetus developing during pregnancy.The Socialists and Democrats, the Left and the Greens/EFA have called on President Metsola to withdraw it, as they consider it to be “part of a broader anti-choice campaign”, with a “clear attempt to question access to abortion, even if this is not explicitly stated”.Inside von der Leyen's pitch for a new EU security architectureA new European Security Council, an emergency protocol and a new strategic enabler initiative: three key pillars of a new European security strategy pitched by Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday, and which my colleagues Angela Skujins and Luca Bertuzzi break down for you in this must-read piece.Among the most significant proposals is a new security-focused political format dubbed the European Security Council, a special configuration of the EU leaders' summit that will include partners such as Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Norway and Canada.Von der Leyen also called for the EU’s own version of NATO’s Article 4 – which allows members to formally request emergency consultations when they believe their security is under threat – as hybrid threats across Europe grow increasingly kinetic.Oana Lungescu, NATO's former spokesperson, told Angela and Luca that while it's welcome that the Commission President wants closer EU-NATO cooperation, it's hard to see how this would actually deter Russia. "Protocols and playbooks already exist in both organisations," she said.Finally, von der Leyen announced a new instrument to scale up Europe’s so-called “strategic enablers” – which include satellites, airlift, refuelling and intelligence capabilities that allow military forces to operate effectively – amid a retreat in US military assets in Europe.How exactly the new instrument will close this gap remains unclear, as Brussels tries to work out how to incentivise national investment in the area.Read the full article.More from our newsroomsHow did Greece end up borrowing more cheaply than France? Greece now pays less than France to borrow despite carrying more debt. Petro Cingai explains how Athens rebuilt market trust while Paris lost fiscal credibility.Kosovo's former President Thaçi convicted of war crimes at Hague court. Hashim Thaçi, who served as both president and prime minister, was found guilty of murder, torture, cruel treatment and arbitrary detention by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, as tens of thousands who had gathered in Prishtina expecting his acquittal watched proceedings on a livestream. Aleksandar Brezar has the details.Mbappé, Vinícius and Konaté criticised for hiding Ceuta support message. The La Liga president Javier Tebas has criticised three Real Madrid players, including Kylian Mbappé, for not wearing a T-shirt properly in support of the people of Ceuta, a Spanish autonomous city in North Africa that has been hit by a migration crisis. Cristian Caraballo has more.We're also keeping an eye onEuropean Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and vice-president for Technological Sovereignty Henna Virkkunen present the EU Kids Act at 10.00 CET in Strasbourg. Here's the leak. The European Parliament’s plenary session closes. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to address the chamber at 11.30 CET.That’s it for today. Vincenzo Genovese, Luca Bertuzzi and Angela Skujins contributed to this newsletter.

Headline: Cuts to income tax: experts back the measures but warn situation in Portugal may worsen
Body: This Thursday, the Portuguese government will formally decide, in the Council of Ministers, to grant the bonus for pensioners and a cut in IRS income tax brackets for workers.Pensioners with pensions of up to 1,611 euros will receive an extraordinary top-up in December, between 100 and 200 euros, totalling 400 million euros.IRS will be reduced up to the sixth bracket, in an amount of up to 400 million euros. But because of the progressive scale, the higher brackets will also be affected. The measure will be applied from November.In parliament, Prime Minister Luís Montenegro said the IRS cut is intended to "support the middle class"."Families can't take any more"The Portuguese government (the centre-right AD coalition) made these announcements last week, during a debate on a motion of no confidence, which was rejected. Before that, the prime minister defended the cabinet's social and economic policy, including measures in response to rising fuel prices.The previous day, diesel in Portugal had reached its highest price ever and petrol its highest level since the invasion of Ukraine. This time, the rise was met with protests. In a go-slow march towards Galp's refinery in Sines, placards read "families can't take any more".Economist João Rodrigues dos Santos regards these measures as legitimate, as a "give-back to those who need it most", but disagrees with the method. "I consider these to be budgetary policy measures and that they should be more structural in nature, reflected in the State Budget," says the professor who coordinates the academic area of Economics and Management at the European University."The government surely has good intentions, but I think this may not be the best way to conduct budgetary policy. Public policy cannot depend every year on whether there is money in the coffers or not, can it?" he asks.Rebate mechanismAnd, in fact, there is money. Tax lawyer Tiago Caiado Guerreiro points out that, with prices rising, the state has collected more tax."The VAT take on fuel goes up as fuel prices rise. Why? The taxable base on which it is levied increases in size," says the tax expert, referring to the consumption tax."This is just one more reimbursement mechanism, in this case via IRS, with which I could not agree more," argues Tiago Caiado Guerreiro."And then the bonus for pensioners is a somewhat political measure, but it is not something that shocks me, given the low pensions that exist in Portugal," the tax lawyer concludes.João Rodrigues dos Santos also agrees that the state has taken in more VAT revenue from the rise in fuel prices, an amount that, "according to the government, could come to around 700 million euros". But he also recalls the reduction in the Tax on Petroleum Products (ISP)."It is true that this revenue should be neutralised through cutting ISP, precisely to prevent the state from benefiting fiscally from higher fuel prices," he explains.Even so, the increase in VAT receipts covers other products beyond fuel."Ultimately, if the state collects more revenue because prices have gone up and families are paying more for the same goods and services, it seems legitimate to me that part of that extraordinary fiscal windfall can be returned to taxpayers."High taxes and many bracketsBoth experts agree that taxes are too high in Portugal."Anything that serves to lower taxes or put money into people's pockets, I usually agree with," says Tiago Caiado Guerreiro.The tax lawyer argues that IRS "is extremely high in Portugal. In other words, people who work are heavily penalised by taxation".João Rodrigues dos Santos, for his part, advocates a simplification of the IRS system."There could be fewer brackets, with less steep progressivity, because the current setup is absolutely stifling," he argues.And cutting VAT?The opposition has been advocating another path: VAT cuts. The Socialist Party (PS, centre-left) is calling for zero VAT on essential goods, and Chega (far right) also says it intends to put forward a proposal along these lines.But Tiago Caiado Guerreiro warns that such a measure could be difficult to implement."Technically, cutting VAT is very difficult, because it would be reduced to a lower band, which would mean a loss of revenue that the government would not be able to manage. You cannot bring the rate down from 23% to 22% or 21%, as I saw suggested in some reports; that is not possible," says the tax lawyer, adding that in future this budgetary room for manoeuvre may not exist."I think that, given the international circumstances and the rise in the price of oil, economies in Europe and elsewhere in the world will probably start to slow. And the tax take will probably not stay on a permanently upward trajectory."European Union countries set their VAT rates, but these have to be framed within the EU directive on the tax (source in Portuguese)."A cut in VAT, for example from the maximum rate to the intermediate rate or even the minimum rate, would depend on authorisation from the European Union," explains João Rodrigues dos Santos, adding that one of the disadvantages of VAT is that it is a non-differentiated tax."VAT is a tax that affects everyone in the same way. Those who need more support and those who do not need support."Nevertheless, this economics professor believes that such a measure could end up being "an inevitability", an exception in a scenario of rising fuel prices that "will necessarily spread to the rest of the economy"."I would say that a generalised VAT reduction, above all on basic necessities, is not a measure I consider unreasonable. On the contrary, it may well be the most effective measure, because it is across the board and the vast majority of Portuguese people have very low wages," he explains."I think this will take years"Right now, the international climate is not the most promising. Last Thursday, in Frankfurt, the European Central Bank (ECB) once again raised interest rates. At the time, ECB president Christine Lagarde warned of inflationary pressures due to the conflict in the Middle East.The two experts, interviewed by Euronews, are equally pessimistic about the future."I do not know whether fuel prices will ever fall back to the levels they were at before the war, given all the instability that exists in the Middle East and other parts of the world," says Tiago Caiado Guerreiro, referring to the war in Ukraine and to blockages in the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb."We are in a period of great instability; I do not think this will be resolved quickly. And I never believed this war would end quickly, I think this will take years," he adds.In fact, the crisis is dragging on. And not only is it dragging on, it is deepening," argues João Rodrigues dos Santos.The European University professor thinks the government also has this scenario in mind."With a budget surplus of more than 2 billion euros, the fact is that this government has remained uncompromising in relation to its strategy. And, from my point of view, it has remained uncompromising because it has always understood that this crisis, which we have now been living through for more than six months, was here to stay."The economy is growing, but wages are lowIn parliament, the Portuguese prime minister said these measures "are only possible thanks to the economic performance of Portugal and the government's sound financial and budgetary management".Luís Montenegro also described the growth of the Portuguese economy as having "the best economic performance in Europe and the biggest employment growth in Europe". This despite the fact that, according to Eurostat, it was not the country with the strongest growth in gross domestic product (GDP) in the second quarter, but rather the seventh, together with Cyprus (up 0.8%)."I think we are in a good phase; we are among the six or seven best in the European Union and that usually does not happen, as you know, we are normally closer to the bottom," says Tiago Caiado Guerreiro, highlighting the contribution of some areas, such as tourism.But the tax lawyer also says this is no reason for excessive optimism."We are indeed in a very reasonable period of growth, compared with the European economy, which is rather sluggish. It is one of the slowest-growing economies in the world. So there is no reason to get euphoric about it."João Rodrigues dos Santos points to the low wages paid in Portugal, which means that tinkering with IRS will not solve families' income problems."We must not forget. In Portugal, 75% of those registered with social security have wages of up to 1,000 euros," the professor says.
