Headline: Bitcoin drops after US Senate blocks landmark crypto bill
Body: Crypto markets dropped late on Tuesday and early Wednesday, as investors digested a defeat that few in the industry had expected.The procedural motion on the CLARITY Act drew 49 votes in favour and 50 against, 11 short of the 60 required to advance, dealing a major setback to efforts to pass market structure legislation this year.The CLARITY Act, formally the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, was meant to divide supervision of digital assets between the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Securities and Exchange Commission, replacing a fragmented system in which classification has largely been settled through enforcement actions and litigation.Bitcoin fell almost 34 over the past 24 hours to below $76,000, while HYPE, the token behind the decentralised exchange Hyperliquid, which stood to benefit from the legislation, also dropped about 4% to below $78.Most major tokens fell alongside them.A deal that still was not enoughThe bill’s defeat is striking because so much had been conceded.US President Donald Trump agreed over the weekend to ethics restrictions he had long resisted, including a requirement that federal officials and their spouses divest significant financial interests in crypto issuers or place them in a blind trust, and a role for state attorneys general in enforcing those rules.Republican negotiators said that over 120 Democratic requests were written into the final text of the more than 600-page bill, representing a major bipartisan effort.Still, it was not enough.Four Republicans, Jerry Moran, Susan Collins, Josh Hawley and Thom Tillis, joined the 46 Democrats who voted against it. The Democratic Senator Chris Coons did not vote.Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren, the bill's most prominent opponent, said it "fails to adequately protect investors, our financial system and our national security," and attacked Trump's crypto ventures on the US Senate floor hours before the vote.Republican Senator Thom Tillis's vote was a procedural exception. After having publicly backed the ethics package that morning, Tillis voted no to preserve a motion to reconsider, leaving open the possibility of another cloture vote.Senator Cynthia Lummis, the Wyoming Republican who has led crypto legislation in the US Senate since co-authoring the Responsible Financial Innovation Act in 2022, was blunt afterwards."I think we're done. It's over," she told reporters before going considerably further online."The once-proud Democratic Party is anti-consumer and pro-illicit finance, anti-ethics, anti-free enterprise, anti-worker, anti-livable wage jobs and pro-socialism," she wrote in a social media post.The failed vote likely means the crypto industry will have to wait until next year for clearer rules to be discussed.The US midterm elections are in just seven weeks which complicates bringing the bill back up for consideration in the short term.Senators are scheduled to leave Washington in early October and not return until after the election and the House recesses even earlier, heading out of town already at the end of this week.Members, especially those in tight races, are eager to  return to their home states and hit the campaign trail.Regulators inherit the problemThe legislation’s failure does not mean nothing happens. It means the rules are more likely to be written by agencies instead.The US Securities and Exchange Commission under Paul Atkins and the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission under Michael Selig have already been building a framework without Congress.The two signed a cooperation agreement in March and issued a joint interpretation sorting tokens into five categories, with Atkins stating that most crypto assets are not, in themselves, securities.The SEC's own agenda includes registration exemptions for token launches, a safe harbour for projects decentralising away from central control, and rules on custody and trading venues.Analysts expect that work to accelerate now.However, the catch is durability, because agency rules can be rewritten by a future US administration, which is precisely the instability the CLARITY Act was meant to end.

Headline: 'Silk Road spirit' meets supply chains at Korea-Central Asia summit
Body: South Korea and the five Central Asian republics held their first heads-of-state summit in Seoul on Wednesday, adopting a 30-year cooperation framework targeting critical minerals, energy, supply chains and emerging technologies against the backdrop of a shared Silk Road history.The declaration established a leaders’ summit that brings together South Korea, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan every two years, and a new mechanism that brings together the six countries’ industry ministers.“The ‘Silk Road spirit’ of Central Asia that connected people, technologies and cultures of the East and West as one is needed more than ever,” South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said.The six countries share common goals: Seoul needs more diverse sources of critical materials and more resilient supply chains, while Central Asian governments want technology, investment and a larger role in manufacturing the products made from their resources.On critical minerals, South Korea is looking to diversify supplies for industries including semiconductors, batteries and electric vehicles, while Central Asian countries want more processing and manufacturing to take place inside the region.The Seoul Declaration, which builds on a dialogue launched at the vice-ministerial level in 2007 and later elevated to the ministerial level, calls for “mutually beneficial value chains” that combine Central Asian resources and local production with Korean technology and manufacturing expertise.“Today, Central Asia is no longer merely a supplier of raw materials,” Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev said. “Our countries are actively integrating into global value chains while expanding opportunities for innovation and technological cooperation.”President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said Kazakhstan has all 10 minerals classified by South Korea as strategic, and called for cooperation extending into semiconductors, batteries, electric-vehicle components and robotics.Mirziyoyev proposed a Regional Investment Alliance for Critical Minerals covering the full production cycle, and set a $20 billion (€17.3 billion) target for trade between South Korea and Central Asia by 2030.Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov pushed the regional approach further, proposing a joint investment fund to finance priority projects and make it easier for Korean companies to enter Central Asian markets.Transport chain reaching EuropeTransport was another key segment to the summit, with Tokayev proposing an “end-to-end transport and logistics chain extending from Korea, through Central Asia, to Europe”.Central to that idea is the Middle Corridor, formally known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route. It moves freight through Central Asia, across the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan and Georgia, and onwards towards European markets through Turkey or the Black Sea.The corridor has attracted growing attention as companies and governments seek alternatives to routes through Russia. Tokayev said its freight volumes had increased fivefold over the past six years.Mirziyoyev also described Central Asia as an emerging “hub of global connectivity”, while Japarov highlighted the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway and invited Korean companies to participate in industrial and logistics facilities along the route.Turkmenistan put transport, logistics, energy and industrial cooperation among its priorities for deeper ties with South Korea.Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, meanwhile, focused on water security, climate change and sustainable development.From political strategy to businessThe regional agenda moved from the leaders’ table to the business community later in the day, when more than 500 government and company representatives gathered for the first Korea–Central Asia Business Summit.Lee Jae-myung described the priorities in practical terms: broader trade and investment, cooperation across the critical-minerals value chain and new infrastructure connecting the region with international markets.Tokayev pointed to Central Asia’s combined GDP of nearly $550 billion and growth of more than 6%.“Combining these advantages with Korea’s industrial, technological and financial capabilities opens up broad prospects for mutually beneficial cooperation,” he said.Mirziyoyev similarly urged Korean companies to view Central Asia as a single market of more than 80 million people, with opportunities in AI, semiconductors and advanced manufacturing.Tokayev, meanwhile, pointed to transport infrastructure and technology as areas where Korean investment could strengthen connections across the Eurasian continent.Nineteen memorandums of understanding were signed during the regional business summit in sectors including critical minerals, industry, infrastructure and digital technologies. They set out areas for future cooperation but are not, in themselves, final investment contracts.The regional meetings in Seoul ran alongside separate bilateral talks and business programmes between South Korea and individual Central Asian states.Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan were among the countries announcing national agreements and investment projects during their leaders’ visits.The new C5+Korea format will meet again at the leaders’ level in Kazakhstan in 2028.

Headline: Hackers impersonating government agency hit Revolut customers in the UK
Body: Hundreds of European customers of digital bank Revolut had their personal information handed over to hackers after they impersonated a government agency, the company said on Wednesday.Revolut said it had identified a “sophisticated external impersonation scam” in which an unauthorised third party used an email address from a legitimate government agency domain to submit fraudulent requests for customer information.According to the Financial Times, the attack was carried out by Italian hackers who used a compromised Italian government email account to pose as officials seeking customer information.The hackers obtained data including customers’ addresses, verification photos, identity documents and information about bitcoin activity.A source familiar with the matter said around 680 Revolut customers across several European countries were affected.Revolut is a British company, but its European banking operations are legally based and licensed in Lithuania, with more than 50 million customers across Europe.Revolut said its systems and customer funds were “unaffected” and that it had contacted those affected to inform them and provide support.“Upon detection, we immediately blocked the address and alerted the relevant government agency as well as enforcement agencies, data protection and financial regulators,” Revolut said.Britain’s data protection regulator, the Information Commissioner’s Office, confirmed that it had received a report about the incident and was assessing the information provided.Europe's fintech unicornThe incident comes as Revolut expands further into the global banking sector, more than a decade after it was founded in 2015 as a fintech start-up.The company was valued at $115 billion (€98.7bn) in a secondary share sale in July.It secured a long-awaited banking licence in its home market of the UK in March, lifting restrictions on its ability to compete with established retail banks, and bagged a full French banking licence in August.This month, Revolut also secured conditional approval for a US banking licence, while on Tuesday it filed an application for a banking licence in Switzerland.Revolut initially built its business around smartphone-based currency exchange and money transfers before expanding into a wider range of financial services.It now has more than 80 million customers globally and is targeting 100 million customers across 100 countries.

Headline: Gaza: Building collapse kills 21, including 11 children as perilous conditions persist for Palestinians
Body: A building housing dozens of people collapsed in Gaza City early Wednesday morning, leaving rescuers clawing with bare hands through rubble until determining that 21 people, including 11 children, had been killed in their sleep.The six-storey building, which had four apartments per floor, crumbled overnight onto nearby homes and tents in the Tal al-Hawa area of Gaza City, according to the civil defence agency, which works as a rescue service under Hamas authority.The sudden collapse of the building, which was known to be unstable because of damage from Israeli strikes earlier in the war, underscored how perilous and desperate living conditions have grown for the majority of the enclave’s population as a ceasefire deal between Israel and Hamas stalls.Excavators bearing Egyptian flags worked to remove the debris next to rows of tents for displaced people, while rescuers and volunteers carried out the dead wrapped in white plastic body bags."My friend and neighbours live in this building. I came to help my friend retrieve some clothes and mattresses. He currently has no shelter or home," said Mohannad Al-Mashharawi.'No other choice'"The lack of options and alternatives left them with no other choice," said Aboud Majdalawi, a rescuer with Gaza's civil defence.All of Gaza’s roughly 2 million people now live in a stretch of land that makes up less than half the territory. They remain dependent on aid and are surrounded by Israeli troops who carry out strikes or attacks on a near-daily basis.In the aftermath of the collapse, people were searching desperately for loved ones or their remains.A group of men was seen carrying the headless body of a child. Others sat atop a pile of rubble, pulling desperately at flashes of color they believed could be clothing worn by a survivor. All they found were dust-caked blankets wedged in the debris.The collapse comes as rescuers in the Gaza Strip are trying to unearth hundreds of bodies from buildings collapsed by Israeli strikes earlier in the war. They have just a few working excavators, and their fuel supply is dwindling.On Wednesday, the UN human rights chief said that he worried that the bodies recovered so far are just the "tip of the iceberg."Despite an October ceasefire that has reduced fighting in Gaza, Israel has continued to carry out strikes, killing at least 1,375 people since the agreement went into effect, according to local health officials.The nearly three-year Israel-Hamas war has killed more than 73,789 Palestinians, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records viewed as generally reliable by UN agencies and international organisations. It doesn’t distinguish between civilians and militants, but says women and children make up around half the toll.

Headline: Danish pharma giant Novo to use Anthropic’s Claude to advance AI drug discovery
Body: Novo, previously Novo Nordisk, the Danish pharmaceutical company behind Ozempic, has partnered with Anthropic to accelerate the development of new medicines using artificial intelligence. “Joining forces with Anthropic will supercharge our R&D organisation and help us on our mission to bring new, transformative health solutions to people living with chronic diseases,“ said Mike Doustdar, president and CEO of Novo, in a press release Wednesday. The pharmaceutical giant will use Anthropic’s models and Claude Science to advance scientific reasoning for Research and Development (R&D), the company announced. Beyond increasing productivity in R&D, Novo’s CEO said AI tools can offer “completely new scientific opportunities” and help reasoning and understanding of human biology and drug mechanics."AI’s increasing capability brings with it the potential to compress a century’s worth of biological and medical breakthroughs into a decade," said Dario Amodei, co-founder and CEO of Anthropic.He added that by giving leading researchers access to safe, capable, and trusted frontier models, it is possible to shorten research timelines, improve outcomes, and discover medicines and treatments that significantly improve human life. This partnership comes amid Novo’s bet on AI to fast-track drug research. The pharma giant is already using OpenAI’s science GPT-Rosalind, after sealing the deal in April to use advanced AI to analyse complex datasets, identify potential drugs, and cut the time between research and patient access. In 2024, the Novo Nordisk Foundation partnered with Nvidia and the Export and Investment Fund of Denmark (EIFO) to establish the Danish Centre for AI Innovation, which operates Gefion – Denmark's first AI-ready supercomputer. Anthropic is also expanding its work in the life sciences sector. In May 2026, the tech company announced a collaboration with Bristol Myers Squibb to deploy Claude across the company's research, clinical development, manufacturing, commercial, and corporate functions.

Headline: Russia used Claude AI for espionage, disinformation and drone swarms
Body: Russia used Anthropic's Claude AI model to accelerate cyber-espionage operations against Ukrainian and European government targets, run disinformation campaigns in Africa and Moldova, and develop targeting software for autonomous kamikaze drone swarms, the US company said in a report published this month.Anthropic said it had blocked all malicious activity identified in the report, used the findings to strengthen its security systems, and shared the information with government bodies and industry partners.In one major case, a hacking group designated GTG-20006 used Claude to automate operations against more than 20 organisations, including government ministries, defence and intelligence agencies, embassies, think tanks and defence-industrial companies, Anthropic said.Ukraine was the primary target, with suppliers of military drone technology and their supply chains also among those attacked. The group also targeted Middle Eastern and Asian government departments with links to maritime activity.Anthropic said GTG-20006 is linked to Midnight Blizzard, a hacking group Western intelligence assessments attribute to Russia's foreign intelligence service SVR.The group used Claude across a range of operational modes: as an engineering assistant for writing malware, phishing kits and surveillance tools, as an executor of commands on victims' networks, including collecting credentials and extracting data under human direction, and in fully autonomous operations with minimal human oversight.Disinformation in the CAR and MoldovaWorking alongside investigators from the All Eyes On Wagner project, Anthropic identified and removed an account operated by a Russian-speaking individual in Bangui who was running a disinformation operation for Radio Lengo Songo, a station set up and financed in 2017 by the Kremlin-run mercenary Wagner group.The operator prepared daily pro-Russian content for the station in coordination with Russian state outlets RT, Sputnik Afrique and TASS, and with the local "Russian House" cultural centre — part of a network Russia uses as a political and influence hub abroad.Content consistently promoted the CAR government and Wagner, and attacked France and domestic opposition figures, according to the All Eyes On Wagner investigation.The operation was designed to appear locally run, with one person coordinating output while contracts, scripts and publications were presented as the work of a Bangui-based radio station.Anthropic investigators identified the individual through invoices for a Claude subscription issued in central Madrid.The operator was linked to Africa Politology, aka "The Company," the information and political technology arm of the African Corps — the successor to Wagner in Africa — which is reportedly controlled by the SVR.In Moldova, a former regional head of the Russian state-run Sputnik media network used Claude as a content-production tool, adapting news, polling data, and opposition material to fit pro-Kremlin narratives, Anthropic said.Autonomous swarm drone warfareAnthropic identified and shut down a group of Russia-linked developers who used its Claude Code tool to write software for kamikaze drones, including an autonomous targeting system tested on real hardware.The developers trained AI models on footage from combat operations in Ukraine and used a fixed location in the Donetsk region as a demonstration strike target.The project's stated goal was a fully autonomous swarm of FPV kamikaze drones.Anthropic linked nine accounts involved in the project to a regional Russian university and a federal research centre connected to the Russian Academy of Sciences, without naming either institution.Claude is officially unavailable in Russia, with access to Anthropic's website and API blocked and Russian bank cards not accepted for payment. The developers bypassed these restrictions by routing traffic through commercial virtual private servers (VPNs).

Headline: Canada invited to become first 'associate member' of the EU
Body: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced on Wednesday that Canada has been invited to become the first “associate member” of the EU.She announced the move during her 2026 State of the Union address in Strasbourg, to an audience including not only MEPs but also Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who attended her speech in the midst of a trade war with the US.Since late August, the Canadians have been pushing hard for the Europeans to build a closer relationship with them, though full EU membership is not an option as Canada is not a European state.During her speech before the MEPs on Wednesday, von der Leyen invited the country to become “the first associate member of the European Union".“We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world. And we will now build our shared future as well,” she added.A new statusExpectations had been high over the last week after Carney spoke about building a “unique alliance” with the EU.Canada is not a European state geographically, but it shares the same values as the EU – human rights, democracy, rule of law – which are necessary criteria for becoming a member state.Several options already exist for countries that don’t have full membership. Norway, for instance, is part of the single market, the EU’s borderless area of free movement of goods, persons, services and capital. Oslo and Brussels also collaborate on joint defence initiatives.Switzerland also has access to the single market through several agreements – and in the years since Brexit, the United Kingdom and the EU have secured the largest and broadest trade and cooperation deal in the bloc's history, coverering a wide range of sectors. The UK is now taking part in several EU programmes such as Horizon Europe, the EU’s research and innovation programme.Euronews has learned that Ottawa is already in talks with Brussels to join the Erasmus+ exchange program, Horizon Europe research grants, and mutual recognition of workers’ qualifications.However, “associate member” is a completely new status, and key questions have not yet been answered – chief among them, whether Canada will have voting rights in EU institutions. Despite their regulatory harmonisation with the bloc, Norway and Switzerland have no say on EU legislation.A new alliance with OttawaGerman Chancellor Friedrich Merz floated the idea last May of an “associate membership” for Ukraine, which is urgently seeking to enter the EU. In a letter sent to EU leaders, he argued that this status would grant Ukraine access to the decision-making bodies – the European Council, the European Commission and the European Parliament – without voting rights or a dedicated portfolio.It would also allow the country to tap into certain EU-funded programmes on a "step-by-step" basis.It’s hard to see Canada in the same category as Ukraine, a country which is at war, but von der Leyen's announcement on Wednesday nonetheless sent a strong political signal in a volatile world where historical alliances are shifting.“Europe and Canada believe in democracy. That power does not belong to the strongest, the richest, or the loudest – but to all of us,” she said. “Democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work.”She also called for a new alliance with Ottawa, which could include tech, defence, Arctic joint projects, but also energy, critical minerals and artificial intelligence.“We will move from CETA to an Alliance for the Future to create a common prosperity and economic security space,” she said, referring to the 2016 EU-Canada trade agreement that removed tariff barriers between both sides and has been provisionally applied.The economic and security cooperation between both partners is set to be pushed further during a summit in Montreal in October.

Headline: Exein becomes unicorn: Italian Physical AI security start-up valued at $1.7bn
Body: Italian startup Exein, which specialises in cybersecurity for industrial devices and machinery, has joined the ranks of digital unicorns after closing a 270-million-dollar funding round.The deal, led by global fund Headline and backed by institutional investors including the European Investment Bank (EIB), which Exein announced on Tuesday, gives the company an overall valuation of 1.7 billion dollars.In just two years the company's value has increased thirtyfold, making it Europe's highest-valued hardware cybersecurity firm."Devices are no longer just connected; they are becoming intelligent. They run models, make decisions and act in the physical world," reads Exein's website."The core idea is that every device should be able to defend itself autonomously, regardless of the security of the network it is connected to," added CEO Gianni Cuozzo in an interview with TechCrunch. (source in Italian)What cybersecurity for Physical AI means: how to protect robots, automotive systems and dronesFounded in 2018 in Rome by Cuozzo (and now with offices in Germany, the United States and Taiwan and around forty employees in total) to fix vulnerabilities in industrial firmware, Exein was set up with the mission of securing modern hardware by working closely with manufacturers.In particular, the focus is on security for Physical AI, meaning those autonomous systems driven by artificial intelligence that interact with the real world. Among them are industrial robots, self-driving vehicles, drones, medical devices, energy infrastructure and aerospace systems.In these fields, a cyberattack on the firmware entails direct physical risks, making it advantageous to have internal, ultra-low-latency protection capable of neutralising threats directly on the device.It is known as embedded security and has become a priority because of the challenges posed by today's advances and applications in artificial intelligence. If a hacker were to compromise the firmware of a self-driving car or a robotic arm, for example, the consequences would not only be data loss but also physical damage to infrastructure and people.Moreover, since AI-generated attacks unfold in just a few milliseconds, having a defence system inside the machine keeps latency to a minimum.Artificial intelligence has in fact boosted everyone's capabilities, including those of hackers. According to Cuozzo, this is made possible by open-source models that can run without protection mechanisms, making it much easier and cheaper to target physical devices in new ways.Industrial defence against threats in the age of AIIn the global cybersecurity landscape, various companies, such as Palo Alto Networks, Microsoft Defender for IoT, Claroty and Armis, analyse threats "from the outside". Others operate, like Exein, at operating-system level (for example Sternum IoT, Drivesec, Nothreat and MicroSec), but not directly in the kernel, the central core of the system that controls all hardware and software, before malicious code is executed, as the Italian start-up proposes.The global tech debate has recently raised catastrophic scenarios, following cases where AI agents have gone out of control. Before such scenarios materialise, Exein aims to provide a kind of digital immune system for connected devices.So far the company has focused on two products: Pulsar and Photon. Pulsar is a Linux defence tool that monitors and protects the device in real time using eBPF technology, which allows the core of the operating system to be controlled with very low resource consumption, and Rust, a programming language designed to be fast and free of vulnerabilities.Built on this infrastructure is Photon, the preventive platform for Physical AI, which operates in kernel space to block malicious execution paths in a timely manner before infection takes hold.Global expansion and compliance with EU directivesAccording to the company, this technology protects more than 1.5 billion devices worldwide every day, ensuring security at every level: from the software that processes data remotely (cloud workloads) to edge systems, meaning all those machines and robots that analyse information directly on site and in real time to cut response times to a minimum.Thanks to the new capital, the company is planning an expansion in the US and Asia-Pacific markets (which already generate 50% of its revenues) and the strengthening of its sites in Italy and abroad.Exein's growth is also being driven by global regulatory alignment and EU directives such as the Cyber Resilience Act, which sets strict security-by-design standards for hardware and IoT products sold within the European single market.

Headline: Celebrated playwright and novelist Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
Body: American and British playwright-novelist Bonnie Greer has died aged 77.  Her husband David Hutchins announced the news, saying: "It is with profound sadness that I announce that my beloved wife, Bonnie Greer, has died aged 77 after a brief illness.""Bonnie was an acclaimed playwright, author, critic, cultural and political commentator whose intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life." Hutchins added: "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her. Those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together." Born in Chicago in 1948, Greer moved to Britain in 1986. She became a familiar face on British television, including as a panelist on shows like Newsnight and Question Time. Greer was awarded the Verity Bargate Award for Best Play for "Munda Negra" and she was also the author of the novels "Hanging By Her Teeth" (1994) and "Entropy" (2009). Other works include the biography "Langston Hughes: The Value Of Contradiction" (2011) and the play "Marilyn And Ella" (2008) about actress Marilyn Monroe and singer Ella Fitzgerald.Greer was appointed to the British Museum's board of trustees in 2005 and later served as deputy chairwoman. She also served on the boards of the London Film School and Royal Opera House, and was appointed a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature in 2022. She also served as Chancellor of Kingston University in Kingston upon Thames, London. In 2010, Greer was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) for her services to the arts.RIP Bonnie Greer 1948 - 2026

Headline: Why this fast-growing German AI start-up is moving its parent company from the US
Body: Berlin-based Langdock has reversed the usual path taken by European start-ups by moving its parent company from the US to Germany.The decision comes amid growing debate over how Europe can build its own AI infrastructure, retain promising technology companies and reduce its dependence on US cloud and AI providers.Many European start-ups establish US holding companies in an effort to make it easier to secure funding. Langdock has now defied this trend and dismantled its US holding structure and brought its parent company under European law.“Langdock has reorganised its corporate structure into a Societas Europaea (SE), registered in Germany, replacing the previous US holding-company structure,” a company representative told Euronews Business. The company said the process began in early 2026 and cost several million euros. It is now complete.Founded in Berlin in 2023, Langdock is an enterprise AI platform serving about 13,000 organisations. It gives employees access to several AI models and allows companies to connect them to workplace data and applications, create AI agents and automate tasks.Langdock said creating a US-registered parent company was initially a “vital step” that helped it attract investors and benefit from the support and network of US start-up accelerator Y Combinator. However, its operations and customer data remained in Germany.Langdock has now replaced its US parent company with a European SE. The previous structure meant customers’ lawyers had to check whether the US parent created any legal or data-protection risks, even though Langdock said the US company had no employees, infrastructure or access to its production systems.US laws, including the Cloud Act, have created concerns across the market that American authorities could seek access to customer data.Removing the US parent makes Langdock’s European structure clearer to customers, the company said, particularly “in geopolitically uncertain times”. It added that it was now large enough to meet the stricter governance requirements of an SE.“We believe Europe is a strong place to build a global technology company, and we want to contribute to its sovereignty and competitiveness,” the company told Euronews Business.About 80% of Langdock is owned by founders and employees who live in the EU. The company said the new structure would not change its plans to serve customers worldwide or raise money from international investors.Langdock says its annual subscription revenue reached a rate of $50 million (€42 million) in August, up from $1 million (€870,000) in October 2024. The figure estimates how much subscription income the company would receive over a full year if its current sales continued.Langdock said its long-term ambition was to build “a sovereign, full-stack AI platform that can compete with US hyperscalers over time”. It plans to launch three new services by the end of the year and use its own data centre in Germany to run open-source AI models and provide computing power. The company said it would start small and expand as customer demand grew.Despite its rapid growth, Langdock has a long way to go before it can compete with US tech giants. Its $50 million annual revenue run rate compares with the $128.7 billion (€108 billion) in revenue generated by Amazon Web Services in 2025.Langdock’s decision to relocate its parent company offers a test of whether European regulation and concerns about digital sovereignty can become a competitive advantage, rather than simply a burden, for the region’s AI companies.

Headline: Earning more is not enough: house prices in Spain rise faster than wages
Body: In Spain, earning a good salary does not necessarily make it easy to buy a home. An analysis by iAhorro reveals wide disparities between regions: while salaries vary by around €10,000 a year across Spain, the price of a 90-square-metre home can differ by almost €383,000.The biggest hurdle is the money that has to be saved before applying for a mortgage. To buy a 90-square-metre home, the buyer has to put down around 30% of the price to cover the deposit and other costs. In the Balearic Islands, that comes to about €144,000, compared with €29,000 in Extremadura and €30,000 in Castile-La Mancha.Prices account for much of this gap. A 90-square-metre property costs around €480,000 in the Balearic Islands and €431,000 in Madrid. By contrast, it costs about €97,000 in Extremadura and around €100,000 in Castile-La Mancha. So a higher salary does not always offset the cost of housing.Savings also make the difference. If a family sets aside 35% of its income to save for the deposit, it could gather the money needed in less than five years in nine regions: Galicia, Navarra, Aragón, La Rioja, Murcia, Asturias, Castile and León, Extremadura and Castile-La Mancha.At the other end of the scale are the Balearic Islands, Madrid and the Canary Islands. In these territories, five years of saving would not be enough to raise the money needed for a 90-square-metre home. For someone buying alone, the effort is even greater: they would need to save for 14.2 years in the Balearic Islands, 10.7 years in Madrid and 10.1 years in the Canary Islands.According to iAhorro’s head of communications, Laura Martínez, quoted in a statement, the main problem is not so much paying the mortgage as pulling together the money to get started: “The hardest part is managing to save.”According to the analysis, young people and buyers living alone find it hardest to overcome this first barrier.

Headline: Sniffing out trouble: Customs dogs remain vital in the age of AI
Body: As artificial intelligence and advanced scanning systems transform border controls, customs services still rely on one of their oldest detection tools: trained dogs.AI can analyse images and data, identify patterns and help customs officers decide which shipments or containers warrant closer inspection.But customs officials, dog handlers, and other specialists from more than 50 countries gathered at the World Customs Organisation's 7th Global Canine Forum in Tashkent argued that this does not remove the need for dogs trained to detect scents.Antonio Lo Parco, head of the WCO's Regional Office for Capacity Building for Europe, told Euronews that dogs possess detection abilities “that AI cannot substitute”.Information from canine detection can also feed into AI systems, he added, helping customs authorities identify patterns and emerging trends.Oliver Stolper, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime's regional representative for Central Asia, also sees the two tools as complementary.AI can help customs services identify containers that require additional scrutiny and analyse images for signs of illicit cargo.“But a dog cannot be replaced,” Stolper told Euronews. “Customs organisations continue to rely on them and for good reasons, as we can see in everyday work.”Experts explained that technology can help narrow the search, while a trained dog provides an additional form of detection.The role of detection dogs is also evolving as illicit drug markets change.Jonibek Yusupov, an officer at Uzbekistan's Agency for the Control of Narcotic Drugs and Firearms, said authorities had recorded a significant rise in synthetic drugs since the pandemic.Canine units are now training dogs specifically to recognise the scents associated with synthetic narcotic substances.“If we rely solely on artificial intelligence or technology, we can only analyse images,” Yusupov told Euronews. “But narcotic substances have a smell.”How a service dog is trainedUzbekistan's National Canine Centre has been training dogs and handlers for three decades.Established in 1996, it trains canine teams for customs and other law-enforcement agencies. It was granted WCO Regional Canine Centre status in 2008.Its dogs are trained for tasks including the detection of narcotics, psychotropic substances, weapons, ammunition and explosives, as well as search-and-rescue and tracking operations.But not every puppy is suitable.At around four months old, dogs bred at the centre begin working with instructors and are assessed for characteristics including their response to noise, unfamiliar environments and heights.“Not every dog can become a service dog,” chief instructor Captain Ahmadjon Goyibov told Euronews.The centre primarily works with German and Belgian Shepherds, Russian Spaniels and Labradors.Dogs that pass the selection process are gradually introduced to environments they may encounter during operations, including vehicles and railway carriages.Specialised training begins around eight months of the dog's age and normally lasts six to seven months. Training is adapted to each dog's temperament.Dogs are also taught how to signal a detection to their handler, for example by sitting, lying down or remaining still.Goyibov rejected a common misconception that drug-detection dogs are made dependent on narcotics or otherwise forced to perform their work.“We never use force against the dogs,” he said. “We train them solely through positive reinforcement. We give them their favourite toy or their favourite food as a reward, but we never use force.”Toys, including ones with food or treats inside, are used as rewards during exercises, teaching the animal to associate a successful detection with something positive.For Goyibov, however, technique alone is not enough.“To become a good canine specialist, first and foremost, you need to love service dogs and animals and be able to show them care and affection,” he said.A regional training centreUzbekistan's centre also trains foreign canine teams.In recent years, 220 handlers from countries including South Korea, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, Armenia and Mongolia have received training or professional development there.More than 200 service dogs have also undergone specialised training, with some later deployed by customs authorities outside Uzbekistan.Elpida Kasapi of the Greek Customs Service said the forum gave participants the opportunity to study WCO criteria for canine training centres and consider how to apply them at home.“What we are doing here will be extremely useful for us,” Kasapi told Euronews, “as it will allow us to gain knowledge and information that we can then apply to the Greek context and to our practices in Greece.”According to Uzbekistan's Customs Committee, between 2023 and the first half of 2026, service dogs trained at the centre helped intercept more than 12 tonnes of narcotic substances.

Headline: Syria's al-Sharaa opens the biggest Arab Media Summit yet
Body: Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa opened the Arab Media Summit in Dubai on Tuesday with a keynote dialogue titled "Syria of the Future", the first appearance by a Syrian head of state at the event.Organisers say the three-day summit at Dubai World Trade Centre is the largest in its history, running more than 175 sessions with over 400 speakers from 23 countries across 8 forums.Al-Sharaa told Euronews that escalation in the region looked to be "on the way" but that states should keep calm and work together.Away from the main stage, the UAE gave its fullest account yet of the cyber-attacks it faced this year.Dr Mohamed Al Kuwaiti, head of the UAE Cybersecurity Council, told Euronews that every missile and drone strike on a port, refinery or airport was matched by a cyber-attack on the same target."Cyber-crimes, cyber terrorism, cyber warfare, all of it came together during this crisis," he said, calling for an international convention to govern state conduct in cyberspace.Dubai also set out new figures for its media sector. Nehal Badri, secretary general of the Dubai Media Council, said media now accounts for 1.4% of the emirate's gross domestic product, up from 0.5% when the council set its strategy in 2023. The target is 3% by 2033. Registered media companies have reached 25,000."It's not just attracting the companies to have Dubai as their home, but to retain them," Badri told Euronews.Badri has worked in the sector for more than 20 years and opened the council's programme with an address titled From Dubai: The World Films, Plays and Streams."The narrative was always other countries telling our stories,” she said. "Now you have institutions that can tell their own stories from Dubai."The definition of media has widened too. The event began as the Arab Media Forum, small and regional. It now runs eight forums covering film, gaming, podcasting and influencers alongside journalism."We had journalism, multimedia and graphic design only," Badri said. "Now you have gaming, you have films."Film, television and diplomacyThe Games Forum heard from Saifi Ismail of Yalla Group, the first UAE technology company to list on the New York Stock Exchange, and from a panel with the UNDP on the social uses of games.A television panel brought together the Gulf drama actors Samira Ahmed, Dawood Hussain and Mohammed Al Mansoor. An exhibition of early Gulf broadcast equipment, much of it still working, drew steady traffic from younger delegates. Dr Ali Rashid Al Nuaimi, chairman of the defence affairs, interior and foreign affairs committee at the UAE Federal National Council, said coverage of international relations concentrated too heavily on governments."What we need is to invest in people-to-people diplomacy, and the media should take a lead in playing that role," he told Euronews.He cited the UAE relief operation in Nepal, where flooding and landslides have affected thousands and where the UAE has flown in successive aid consignments since early September. "We have here in the UAE a community of more than 500,000 Nepalese," he said. On regulation, Al Nuaimi said the UAE, home to some 200 nationalities, asks for one thing. "We don't ask people to change. The only thing we ask them to respect is the rule of law," he said.Mona Ghanem Al Marri, vice chairperson and managing director of the Dubai Media Council and president of Dubai Press Club, said foreign direct investment in the sector reached $1.62 billion in 2024, writing for Euronews on opening day.The summit runs until Thursday.

Headline: Tributes paid to Catherine Ringer, singer of Les Rita Mitsouko
Body: Some voices you recognise in a split second. Catherine Ringer’s was one of them. A voice that could laugh, rasp, scream, sing of love, desire or madness. A voice that never wanted to be put in a box.The announcement of her death has triggered a wave of emotional reactions. Among them, French President Emmanuel Macron, who paid tribute to a personality he called "unclassifiable, irreverent, profoundly French".On X, the president accompanied his message with a clip from 2024 in which the artist sang 'La Marseillaise' during a ceremony marking the enshrining of the right to abortion in the Constitution.The Élysée also paid solemn tribute on Wednesday in an official statement. The text traces the journey of this "all-round artist", born in 1957 in Suresnes and immersed from childhood in an artistic family environment. After her first steps on stage at the Café de la Gare and then at the Palace, as well as "darker, more painful experiences" from which she managed to break free, 1979 marked a major turning point when she met Fred Chichin.Together, they created Les Rita Mitsouko, a duo with an art "free and impossible to categorise", which broke through to the general public in 1984 with the resounding success of the song 'Marcia Baïla'.Following the death of her partner in 2007, Catherine Ringer carried on her career "with deeply moving dignity", alternating solo projects with returns to the stage to revive the band’s cult tracks. Described variously as "a diva, a popular singer and an avant-gardist", she leaves, according to the presidency, "a singular, flamboyant artistic legacy" that has left a lasting mark on musical life in France.Across the political spectrum, voices have spoken up to stress that she was also a tireless activist, but without a party label – feminist through her actions long before the word became a slogan – standing up to sexists on TV shows as much as to right-thinking orthodoxies. Among them, Dominique de Villepin on X (source in French) and France Insoumise MEP Manon Aubry (source in French).Her peers pay tribute and thank herRock musicians, pop artists, rappers or icons of French chanson: all are mourning the loss of a "big sister" of the stage.On social media, the music world seemed to freeze in order to salute the woman who injected a punk streak of madness into mainstream French pop.Singer-songwriter Benjamin Biolay posted a powerful tribute on Instagram (source in French), recalling the formative shock of the album 'The No Comprendo', and honouring the memory of an extraordinary voice and the poetry of the mythical duo she formed with Fred Chichin.Singer Étienne Daho (source in French), meanwhile, posted a photo with Catherine Ringer and simply her first name.And then there are the words from legendary band Sparks, with whom Les Rita Mitsouko worked. The American band spoke of an artist that was "one of a kind", a "true force of nature", and a friend whose path they know they were lucky to cross.Tributes are also coming from far beyond the world of music. Actors and performers like Josiane Balasko, Nikos Aliagas, Michèle Laroque, Julie Gayet, Flavie Flament and Alain Chabat, among others, have shared their memories and their emotions on social media.One particularly beautiful tribute from a user spotted on X shows that the artist touched many generations, including the youngest, and will continue to do so.Finally, there is no better way to end this article than with music. The music of Catherine and Fred, the soundtrack that accompanied and lulled a large part of this writer’s life. This song in particular is forever tied to a vivid memory: a concert in October 2000, in a venue in Lyon. Seeing them play that night and hearing this track live is etched forever.'C'est comme ça' – Les Rita Mitsouko – album 'The No Comprendo' – video directed by Jean-Baptiste Mondino in 1986.

Headline: Canada in talks to join EU's Erasmus+ exchanges programme
Body: Ottawa and Brussels are in talks for Canada to join the Erasmus+ exchange programme, which would let students from both sides study at each other's universities.EU-Canada relations have rarely been closer, as Prime Minister Mark Carney has sought to build a tighter relationship with the European bloc following the aggressive trade agenda and erratic foreign policy of the second Trump administration.On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become the first "associate member" of the EU, an unprecedented arrangement short of full membership, which remains off the table for Canada since it is not a European country.While the details of that new status remain unclear, talks are already under way for Canada to join several existing EU programmes, including the flagship Erasmus+ exchange scheme, long hailed as one of the most tangible benefits of European integration.Canada would be the first non-European country to join the exchange programme, which funds people and organisations to study and train abroad."Canadians want to participate in Erasmus+. It will be expensive for them, but they are ready to do that," MEP Javier Moreno Sánchez (Spain/S&D), chair of the European Parliament's delegation to Canada, told reporters at a briefing on Tuesday.Negotiations are still at an early stage, but there is momentum on both sides of the Atlantic to bring Canada into one of Europe's most successful projects, Euronews understands.Canada is currently a recognised Erasmus+ partner country, but not an associated one. That means Canadian universities and other entities may join certain Erasmus+ actions, subject to specific eligibility criteria and conditions.Besides EU member states, six non-EU countries currently take part: North Macedonia, Serbia, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Türkiye. Canada is expected to follow a similar arrangement if an agreement is found.Moreno hailed the move as a way of strengthening the relationship with tangible benefits for ordinary people. He also said the convention that mutually recognises architects' professional qualifications should be extended to doctors, engineers and professors.Canada might also join another flagship EU programme, Horizon Europe, which funds research projects. Cooperation there is currently limited to the strands dedicated to global challenges and industrial competitiveness."Canadians are the most European people outside of Europe," Moreno said. "If we don't strengthen our relationship with Canada, then with which other country should we do it?"

Headline: 'Starship Troopers' director confirms Donald Trump's space uniforms are Nazi-inspired
Body: If the Jackboot fits...  On 6 September, Donald Trump bulk-posted a series of AI-generated images, in which he renamed New Mexico as “New America”, declared the Moon as US territory, and portayed himself as the Green Lantern.During this AI slop rampage, Trump proposed new uniforms for the United States Space Force – which was established in 2019 during Trump’s first term in office.The image Trump posted was a design mockup for a new “service dress uniform” that was “inspired by the discipline and functionality of the Starship Trooper Uniform.”Many were quick to point out that this was a curious choice of inspiration, as Starship Troopers is a 1997 sci-fi war movie which is a cautionary tale about the dangers of fascism.The cult film by Dutch director Paul Verhoeven is about a group of friends who enlist in the military and get swept up in an intergalactic war. Beyond fight against space bugs, Starship Troopers explores themes of misplaced patriotism, colonialism, xenophobia and violence decrying from fascistic rule.The movie was based on the novel by Robert A. Heinlein, which Verhoeven interpreted as fascistic, nationalistic and in favour of military rule. The director used his film to deconstruct these elements and undermine the themes, using Nazi iconography to further his point. For instance, officer uniforms in Starship Troopers are similar to those worn by the Gestapo...Verhoeven has gone on the record many times to state that he directed the film in order to turn a “right-wing book” into a film that was a dark satire about the dangers of fascism.Now, Verhoeven has said that Donald Trump's administration should be aware that the film’s heroes are all "fascists without knowing that they’re fascists”. “When [the Trump administration] talks about Starship Troopers, they should be aware that it’s based on the style of Leni Riefenstahl," Verhoeven told The Hollywood Reporter - referring to the German filmmaker who was closely associated with the Nazi regime and glorified it through films including 1935's Triumph of the Will.  “I don’t know if this president is aware that the movie says these [characters] are fascists without knowing that they’re fascists. That’s the point,” continued Verhoeven.Once again, a potent reminder that the Trump administration should really think twice before co-opting cinematic references. Trump has previously appropriated several pop culture touchstones, including Superman, Hannibal Lecter, Jedis and Spider-Man, and the references have backfired every time – not only by sparking the ire of the original creators and fans, but also for how these hijacked cultural winks display a lack of appreciation or understanding when it comes to the references themselves.That being said, Verhoeven said that he is used to Starship Troopers’ satirical intent being misread and that the film has been challenging for audiences “because its heroes are, without knowing, Nazis.""I thought people would understand and laugh about it. But that was not the case,” he added. “I’m a Dutch citizen, and I cannot vote. I’ve been here in this country [US] for 40 years and it’s still difficult for me to understand the political culture here in America.”

Headline: EU heads to COP31 with a blunt message: climate pledges are no longer enough
Body: The European Union is increasingly worried about whether nations will actually implement existing climate targets as it prepares for the United Nations' climate summit, COP31, according to a Council document seen by Euronews."(The Council highlights with concern) that current ambition and implementation remain insufficient to limit warming to 1.5°C," read the draft Council conclusions dated 14 September, referring to the Paris Agreement.Similar concerns were recently shared by the United Nations Environment Program (UNEP), which warned the world is set to cross the 1.5°C global warming threshold, but can still limit, adapt to and return from higher temperatures.Early in the summer, Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said that the latest COPs have fallen short of the urgent progress needed to tackle the climate crisis, calling their outcomes "underwhelming" compared to scientific demands.In Antalya, where COP31 will take place in November, Brussels wants to defend the Paris Agreement and keep 1.5°C at the centre of international diplomacy, but it is also shifting the emphasis towards delivery, investment and implementation, according to the draft.Rather than agreeing on new targets, the EU wants COP31 to deliver concrete outcomes: faster clean-energy deployment, a transition away from fossil fuels, greater electrification, tripling renewable energy, doubling energy-efficiency improvements and cutting methane and other non-CO2 emissions by 2030. EU ambassadors want COP31 to produce “tangible progress” in closing the global ambition and implementation gaps and to set the direction for the next Paris Agreement cycle as the bloc of 27 nations concedes that pledges alone are no longer enough without active action.The draft also calls on major polluters to raise their ambitions and minimise both the scale and duration of the overshoot, which UNEP and many other climate scientists have warned must be tackled with urgency."(The Council) urges all parties, particularly major emitters, to act with the highest possible ambition and make all efforts to return to a 1.5°C compatible trajectory and to minimise the magnitude and duration of the overshoot," reads the draft document.Ironically, COP31 host Turkey keeps prioritising fossil fuels, despite its vast potential to replace them with clean power and recent success in increasing renewable energy capacity, according to a study of the country's power sector released on Wednesday by the Climate Action Tracker. Energy transition and climate adaptationHaving becoming hostage to global price volatility due to disruption in the Middle East, the EU now frames the transition away from fossil fuels not as a purely environmental climate policy but as a matter of energy security and affordability.It argues that renewables, low-carbon energy, energy efficiency and electrification can simultaneously strengthen energy security, reduce strategic dependencies and improve resilience.On international climate, the Council is following the same energy policy touted by the European Commission, even if some divergences persist at home with consequential legislative files, such as the future of the bloc's carbon market or the ban on new cars and vans powered by diesel or petrol.The EU also suggests that climate resilience is a paramount prerequisite for safe and prosperous economies and stresses that mitigation and adaptation must go together – a reality that Europeans are increasingly facing at home after a summer marked by intense heatwaves, wildfires and drought.To address the issue, the EU wants all the nations at COP31 to incorporate their National Adaptation Plans into national investment plans and development strategies, reflecting a broader recognition that climate policy is no longer simply about preventing future warming but dealing with damage already occurring. However, climate finance is likely to be one of the harder political negotiations. Elephant in the roomIn an echo of COP30 in Brazil, the EU will call for increased finance for developing countries covering mitigation, adaptation and loss and damage. It will also reaffirm its efforts to triple adaptation finance. However, it simultaneously stresses that public money alone cannot meet the scale of investment required.The draft also highlights carbon pricing as an efficient way of cutting emissions and redirecting financial flows towards climate action. After the absence of the biggest polluters at last year's COP30, the EU will reaffirm its commitment to multilateralism and call for reforms to make the system more effective and inclusive – a key point expected to become very contentious.Given the current geopolitical scene, the EU's pursuit of multilateralism suggests COP31 will be about defending the international climate architecture as well as negotiating individual emissions measures.Reacting to the draft document, Sven Harmeling, head of climate at the NGO Climate Action Network Europe, welcomed the EU's position in backing the 1.5°C, tripling renewables, just transition and climate adaptation, but criticised the persistent lack of ambition on climate financing."The draft still avoids the central question: what will the EU actually put on the table?" Harmeling said."Reaffirming the goal of tripling adaptation finance is welcome, but without clarity on Europe’s own contribution, the mandate risks asking more of others than it commits to itself."

Headline: The Soprano: A magical evening of opera with acclaimed Greek singer Christina Poulitsi
Body: Christina Poulitsi, the internationally acclaimed Greek soprano, who has appeared at iconic opera houses around the world, was a special guest performer at this year's The Chios Festival, organised by the North Aegean Region.Together with distinguished pianist Dimitris Giakas she gave a concert at the impressive Castelli mansion in Kampos at Chios. The opera evening revolved around famous arias once sung by Maria Callas as well as the documentary by the Greek National Opera "Mary, Marianna, Maria: The unknown Greek years of Callas". (source in Greek)Maria Callas and meA native of Chios herself, Christina Poulitsi has a deep affection for her island and its people. This year marked her third appearance at the event. She studied in Germany, where she also took her first professional steps.When Euronews met Poulitsi she was keen to talk about paying tribute to the legendary American-born Greek opera singer Maria Callas and her own journey in opera:"First of all, as Greeks we are extremely proud that Maria Callas, a giant of classical music and opera, is Greek. I believe she inspires all of us through her performances, not only musically but also through the energy she brings to her arias.""Unfortunately I never had the chance to see her live, but even through her recordings you can grasp how unique she was. Whenever I sing arias, and especially Italian bel canto, I always go back to her and draw inspiration from her interpretations. I see her as a pillar, a light that opens up a distinct and different path for each of us."Poulitsi has performed on all the major opera stages, winning the love and adulation of audiences around the world and, along the way, has won several prestigious awards."My international career started in Germany, because I studied there and took my first steps there. I have sung in almost all of Germany's major opera houses, and then went on to perform across Europe, America, Asia and Oceania. It is a great joy to discover different worlds, to work with conductors and theatres with whom you are compatible and with whom you can make music at the highest level.""I was fortunate to have Zubin Mehta as my mentor, a legend in the world of opera. He was the one who wrote a letter of recommendation for me and essentially launched my career. He wanted to keep track of my progress while I was still a student and, when he felt I had reached the right level, he offered me our first collaboration, as Gilda in Florence with him. One thing led to another after that. We gave a great many concerts together. I was invited several times to Israel, to Tel Aviv, and it was there that I met Gianandrea Noseda.""I have a great love for Germany, because it is the country where I first made a name for myself and began my career. But of course I also have a profound love for Greece. It is my country. I really enjoy singing here. I have a very special relationship with the Greek audience and I love coming back again and again. Today, thanks to this concert, I feel deeply moved to be singing in my home place, because I come from Chios."What is it that attracts her to venues that are not conventionally associated with opera? How does she feel about singing on smaller stages?"This is the third year I have sung at The Chios Festival, organised by the North Aegean Region. They are doing a really excellent job. It is a week packed with lectures, documentaries, performances and events that cover a huge range of fields such as medicine, history, art, you name it. I really enjoy singing in spaces that are not strictly linked to the usual concert and recital halls. I love performing in nature. Of course the conditions are very demanding, no question, but the energy is always different.""These places win you over and give you a completely new sensation. Here we are in a Genoese medieval tower in Kampos, Chios, where all the traditional features are preserved: the orchards, the architecture, the unique building style, the waterwheel well. Here in this magnificent garden, with Chios' fragrant mandarins and lemons, the feeling is unique. It gives you inspiration to carry on into the future."A mother of two young children, the Greek soprano is trying to strike a balance between family life and the demands of the international career she has built over the years. At the moment she is trying to spend more time in Greece with her children and to avoid large-scale opera productions. Her schedule for the new season is packed:"Right after Chios we start rehearsals for a new Greek opera to be staged in Athens, called 'Theodora, Empress of Byzantium'. It is the new work by Theodoros Stathis, directed by Panos Angelopoulos. The emblematic figure from Byzantine history will come to life on the stage of the Municipal Music Theatre Olympia 'Maria Callas' on 30 September and 1 October."After that I have a recital in Athens again, at Parnassos Hall. Then we go with Plácido Domingo to Malaysia. In December I will appear at the Athens Concert Hall and give two solo recitals at the Athens Conservatoire. Then there is another recital with Plácido Domingo. This is followed by a recital with the American tenor John Osborn in Thessaloniki. I am really looking forward to it, because we have worked together before and we have great chemistry. And I finish the season with a recital in Switzerland."This year marked the fifth edition of The Chios Festival, which ran for ten days. The festival's rich programme once again left a strong mark on the island. It included performances, concerts, screenings, talks, exhibitions, side events and tribute evenings. Leading figures from science, culture, the arts, history and shipping attended the event, which is held under the auspices of the UNESCO Hellenic National Commission and the American-Hellenic Chamber of Commerce.The festival's artistic director, Dimitra Moutzouri, tells Euronews: "We have managed to create a multi-faceted festival. I think the word 'festival' does not quite do it justice. It is a blend of conference, artistic events and exhibitions. What we are trying to do is to showcase the cultural identity of Chios, to promote artists from the island and, at the same time and above all, to bring leading figures to Chios.""We want to make the island a cultural focal point for Greece every September. And we believe that, to some extent, we have achieved this. It is a festival that evolves step by step, year after year. We do not set specific targets; we simply try to improve every year. We will continue in the same way in the years to come, always aiming for what is best for Chios and its people."

Headline: How Kazakhstan is reshaping its trade beyond commodities
Body: The Central Asian nation accounts for around 2% of global oil supply and is also a major supplier of natural uranium and chromium. It is now seeking to diversify its exports beyond raw commodities.The government sees part of the solution in attracting investors to tap into rising domestic consumption, with projects aimed at substituting imports and expanding the country’s export potential.According to QazTrade, Kazakhstan recorded a trade surplus of over €7.5 billion, with trade turnover reaching nearly €62 billion.China remained Kazakhstan's largest trading partner in the first half of the year, followed by Russia and Italy. Turkey, France, Uzbekistan, the Netherlands, Germany, the United States and South Korea completed the top ten.Imports accounted for nearly 44% of total trade turnover in the first half of the year, rising 5.4% year on year.Imports reached €27 billion, driven by demand for natural gas, power-generation equipment, railway locomotives, gold, enriched uranium, petroleum products and machinery.According to the country’s trade agency, the industries best positioned for import substitution include machinery, pharmaceuticals, advanced processing of agricultural products and construction.“Localising production and implementing investment projects in Kazakhstan can help meet domestic demand while also serving growing demand in neighbouring Central Asia and Eurasian Economic Union,” said QazTrade Deputy General Director Nurlan Kulbatyrov.He noted that Kazakhstan’s economy grew 4.1% in the first half of the year, with manufacturing among the main drivers of growth.The biggest shifts driving tradeOne of the biggest shifts is taking place in the commodity export base. Oil exports fell by 3.3%, gas plunged by 60.4%, and petroleum products dropped by 51.7%. Together, the decline points to weaker momentum in parts of the commodity sector that has traditionally generated much of Kazakhstan’s trade surplus.Another shift is geographical. Exports to Turkey rose by 94%, to France by more than 45%, and to Uzbekistan by nearly 40%, while exports to Italy, Kazakhstan’s largest buyer after China, fell by roughly 15%.Italy accounts for more than 17% of Kazakhstan’s total exports, but barely features among the main destinations for processed goods, suggesting that its demand remains heavily concentrated on oil.While trade with some major partners remains heavily reliant on commodities, diversification is taking place in newer, less prominent destinations such as Turkey, the UK, where exports grew 2.5 times, and Singapore, where they rose 2.9 times.Move towards processed exportsCrude oil remained Kazakhstan’s largest export, accounting for 46.5% of the total, followed by copper and copper products, uranium, ferroalloys and wheat.Although energy and metals continue to dominate Kazakhstan’s export basket, non-resource exports are gradually gaining ground.Exports of processed goods grew nearly 18% year on year in the first half of 2026. However, Kazakhstan continues to rely heavily on imports of finished products, creating opportunities to expand domestic production.Animal feed shipments surged nearly 80% to €378 million, while sunflower oil exports rose almost 57% to €460 million.The rise of Kazakhstan’s oilseed sectorKazakhstan has the largest agricultural land area in Central Asia and natural and climatic conditions well suited to growing oilseed crops.It is already a major global supplier of sunflower oil and among the EU’s top three suppliers of sunflower meal.The country now aims to increase exports of fats and oils to €1.3 billion by 2028, around 60% above current levels.The National Oilseed Processors Association attributes the sector’s rapid growth to government support, a strong raw-material base, Kazakhstan’s geographical position and the development of export logistics.“We’re also seeing accelerated diversification towards oilseed crops. For example, sunflower has seen the largest increase in planted area, growing 2.3 times over the past five years”, said Chairman Yadykar Ibragimov.The potential goes further, with sunflower cultivation capable of expanding to more than four million hectares across the country.Attracting investment for import-substitutionOver the past four years, Kazakhstan has signed 62 investment agreements worth around €32 billion. These can provide up to 25 years of legislative stability for projects worth around €52 million.In 2025, Kazakhstan signed a further 173 investment contracts worth around €2.6 billion. Qualifying projects may benefit from tax incentives, exemptions from import customs duties on equipment and components, and in-kind state grants.  Foreign investment also increased. In 2025, gross foreign direct investment inflows amounted to nearly €18 billion, up 14.4% year on year.With trade ties to some major partners still heavily reliant on commodities, Kazakhstan is looking to attract foreign investment into import substitution and domestic production, reducing its reliance on imported goods while broadening its export base.

Headline: No comment from Riyadh on oil delivery cancellations as scale of disruption remains unclear
Body: Saudi Arabia has remained silent on reports that it has cancelled or delayed crude oil shipments to European refiners following last week's drone strikes on its East-West pipeline, as the scale of the disruption to European deliveries remains unclear.Energy pricing agency Argus reported on Tuesday that at least three European refiners had cargoes scheduled for late September cancelled or postponed, in some cases until November, citing unnamed market sources.Saudi Arabia’s state-controlled oil company Aramco told Euronews it "declined to comment" on this and other similar reports in a brief email on Wednesday afternoon.Saudi Arabia's energy ministry announced a precautionary shutdown last Friday after drone attacks on the pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions the previous day.Saudi and Iraqi authorities said the drones came from Iraq. The ministry said technical teams were checking the pipeline, but did not say when pumping would restart.The pipeline carries crude from Saudi Arabia’s eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.From Yanbu, tankers heading to Europe sail north towards the Suez Canal. Egypt’s SUMED pipeline provides another route for crude to reach the Mediterranean from the Red Sea.Oil stored at export terminals can keep cargoes moving during a shutdown. How long those stocks last depends on the amount available and how quickly pipeline deliveries resume.US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Tuesday that the pipeline interruption would be “measured in days”.Bab el-Mandeb in Houthi crosshairsThe Saudi-led coalition said on Wednesday that it had intercepted a Houthi drone south of Mecca the previous evening. The Houthis denied targeting the city.Last week, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis took control of the Bab el-Mandeb strait in the Red Sea after seizing the port of Mokha and nearby islands from Yemen's Saudi-supported internationally recognised government.Bab el-Mandeb lies south of Yanbu, on the direct route to Asia. Europe-bound tankers sailing north from Yanbu do not pass through it, but the strait is a key passage for trade between Europe and Asia.Qatar warned on Tuesday that losing access to Bab el-Mandeb would worsen the disruption already affecting shipping through Hormuz.Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, director of media and communication at Qatar’s foreign ministry, told a briefing in Doha that this would be “catastrophic for the entire world," calling for international efforts to keep the waterway open.Meanwhile, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi discussed the security of regional shipping routes in Cairo on Tuesday.El-Sisi said Saudi and Gulf security formed part of Egypt's national security, expressing support for Saudi measures to protect the kingdom and calling for a political settlement in Yemen.
