Headline: Kosovo's former President Thaçi convicted of war crimes at Hague court
Body: The Kosovo Specialist Chambers on Wednesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaçi to 25 years in jail on four counts of war crimes committed during his country’s war for independence from Serbia.Thaçi, who was tried along with three other former guerrilla leaders, was convicted by a panel of judges in The Hague of murder, torture, cruel treatment and arbitrary detention.Wearing a suit and tie, Thaçi stood in silence as Presiding Judge Charles Smith read out the sentence.Judge Smith said Thaçi “used his position, leadership, authority and standing” to encourage the crimes which he then failed to investigate, including the targeting of political opponents and civilians perceived as collaborators and traitors during their time in the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA).However, the presiding judge also stressed that the trial was “not about the legitimacy" of the KLA or its ultimate goal of securing independence for Kosovo, which at the time was a province in Serbia.The long-awaited verdict came after a three-year trial of four former KLA figures: Thaçi, Jakup Krasniqi, Rexhep Selimi and Kadri Veseli. Prosecutors had requested 45-year prison sentences for each.All four had pleaded not guilty. Krasniqi was sentenced to 25 years, Selimi to 13 years, and Veseli to 18 years in prison.All four were determined to be criminally responsible for the arbitrary detention and torture of hundreds of people and 96 murders, according to the court.The court also said Thaçi, Veseli, Selimi and Krasniqi had "contributed significantly" to a common criminal purpose targeting perceived opponents of the KLA's political and military goals.Thaçi in particular “showed a ruthless ability to remove and eliminate political impediments” to his and other commanders' leadership, Judge Smith said.The four were acquitted on six charges of crimes against humanity because the judges said the prosecutors failed to prove that crimes were committed as part of a widespread and systematic attack on civilians. They can appeal Wednesday's ruling.“Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the Western ideals of democracy, equality and justice,” Thaçi told judges in February at the end of his trial.He told a Kosovo outlet in late August he expected a full acquittal.Supporters hoped for Thaçi's returnThe 58-year-old — who also served more than seven years as prime minister, followed by a two-year stint as foreign minister — saw his popularity soar when he helped oversee Kosovo's declaration of independence in 2008.During a visit to the White House, then US Vice President Joe Biden hailed him as the "George Washington of Kosovo".But his image was tarnished by a 2010 Council of Europe report alleging links to organised crime and serious abuses committed during and immediately after the war.Critics also accused the former leader and his party of corruption and concentrating power among political allies.But it was the wartime allegations that abruptly ended his presidency and left him detained in The Hague.Throughout the trial, Thaçi's images have appeared on huge billboards across the country, and his supporters have regularly organised rallies in Prishtina.Despite the seriousness of the charges, which include killings, torture, and other abuses, supporters of Thaçi expected him and his co-accused to be released, with preparations for a possible return already under way prior to the sentencing.Countdown clocks were set up in city squares, ticking down to the verdict due to be delivered at 10 am in The Hague, while thousands gathered in Prishtina's main square to watch proceedings on a livestream.Kosovo police prepared to secure large gatherings, while the US embassy in Prishtina advised its personnel "to avoid all unnecessary travel in the vicinity of the demonstrations".But once it became clear on Wednesday that the former president would remain in detention, the square was almost deserted within minutes."A terrible judgment for Kosovo, for our liberation war. It is a sad, unjust, undeserved decision," Kosovo Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca told media outside the court.Court under fireThe Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC), although based in the Netherlands and staffed by international judges, was established under Kosovo law specifically to prosecute crimes committed by KLA members during the war.Before the court was established, earlier cases in Kosovo largely failed because of alleged witness intimidation and political interference.The staff at the EU-backed court are largely international due to fears about witness safety and security. In 2022, the court convicted two leaders of a Kosovo war veterans’ association for intimidating witnesses by publicising leaked confidential documents.Deeply unpopular from its foundation, the court's use of evidence supplied by Belgrade, which still refuses to recognise Kosovo's independence, has further inflamed accusations of political bias.Throughout the court proceedings, prosecutors have tried to distinguish between the country's independence struggle and the men on trial.The four defendants stood trial for crimes against prisoners held at KLA detention facilities in Kosovo and neighbouring Albania, as well as the politically motivated murders of Serb, Albanian and Roma civilians.The indictment spanned crimes committed during and just after the Kosovo war, which claimed some 13,000 lives and ended in a NATO intervention that pushed Serbian forces out in 1999.In response, the men's lawyers have argued that the KLA lacked a strict command structure and the senior figures could not control or be held responsible for fighters who committed crimes.Thaçi still faces a second trial on charges of obstruction of justice.Thaçi resigned as president and surrendered to the court after his 2020 indictment. He has remained in detention in The Hague ever since, which will count as time served.

Headline: Four years after Mahsa Amini's death, rights groups warn Tehran's crackdown persists
Body: Four years after the death of Mahsa Amini in Iranian police custody, Kurdish businesses across her home region staged a general strike on Wednesday while international human rights organisations warned that those responsible for crushing the 2022 protests remain in power and continue to use the same methods.Shopkeepers and businesses in Saqqez, Sanandaj, Mahabad, Marivan, Baneh and Bokan shut their doors following a call by Kurdish political coalitions. Video circulating on social media showed empty bazaars across the region.Amnesty International, in a report marking the fourth anniversary, said those who directed the violent suppression of the 2022 protests still control Iran's security apparatus.European Parliament President Roberta Metsola (Malta/EPP) said on X that the Parliament would continue to support young Iranians facing execution or imprisonment, singling out the case of twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, sentenced by Tehran's Revolutionary Court after recent protests.The European Parliament "will keep their light shining until it breaks through the darkness.", Metsola wrote on X.UN Special Rapporteur on Human Rights in Iran Mai Sato said that four years of brutal state violence — including lethal force deployed during nationwide protests in late 2025 and early 2026 — have failed to extinguish the resistance."Four years on, the resistance Jina’s death gave rise to has not been extinguished," Sato said in a statement on X."The women and girls who took to the streets in her name still insist on the right to decide what they wear, where they work and how they live... Those rights will not stay deniable forever."Sato also noted that despite the Law on Protecting the Family through the Promotion of the Culture of Chastity and Hijab being formally suspended since December 2024, cafes, restaurants and shops have continued to be closed for hijab violations, with arrests reported in some cases.What happened to Mahsa Amini?Amini, 22, was detained by Tehran's morality police on 13 September 2022 over compulsory hijab rules and died three days later after being brutally beaten in custody.The UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran concluded she had been subjected to physical violence in custody and that Iranian authorities were responsible for her death. Iranian officials rejected the findings and denied she had been physically assaulted.Protests spread nationwide in the days after her death. While compulsory hijab and women's rights were central, the movement drew together demands for political freedoms, minority rights, economic justice and changes to the political system.The UN fact-finding mission documented up to 551 deaths across 26 provinces, including at least 49 women and 68 children, and said some violations — including killings, torture, rape and sexual violence — reached the threshold of crimes against humanity.Tehran acknowledged detaining more than 22,000 people, according to Amnesty International, which also documented enforced disappearances, unfair trials and death sentences.Tehran pivots to hi-techCompulsory hijab remains law, the political structure is intact, and many participants in the protests are in prison, in exile or under sentence.The regime has shifted enforcement away from morality-police patrols toward cameras, facial recognition, drones and digital tools. Iran's police announced in 2023 that public cameras would be used to identify women not wearing hijab.The UN fact-finding mission's 2025 report cited facial recognition being used to monitor students' dress at the entrance to Amirkabir University in Tehran.A 2025 study published in the journal Iranian Studies at the University of Cambridge described the movement as producing a "cultural revolution" alongside a political one, arguing it weakened the state's ideological hold over public and cultural life.For instance, images of morality police vans detaining women on the streets were among the most potent symbols of the 2022 protests, prompting Tehran to avoid public confrontation methods.The growing presence of women without headscarves in public spaces and the central place women's rights and freedoms take in political debate show that the situation has not reverted to where it stood before September 2022 — a direct result of the movement's actions.

Headline: 'Little pr*ck': Which celebrities are backing Macklemore and criticising Ed Sheeran?
Body: People aren't loving the shape of Ed Sheeran right now...  All of the remaining support acts on the British singer's US tour have quit, after the rapper Macklemore was dropped from the line-up for making pro-Palestinian remarks on stage.The Israeli American Council had launched a petition to remove Macklemore from the tour following the rapper's "Free Palestine" comments at the MetLife Stadium on 4 September.Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe, Irish folk band Beoga, Danish band Lukas Graham, and Finneas, the brother of pop star Billie Eilish, all announced they were dropping out.  Rowe said that Sheeran had been a friend to him, “but as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation”. “I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children. I would lose all respect for myself to carry on as normal.” Beoga stated on Instagram that they would no longer be a part of Sheeran’s band “following the silencing of Macklemore by zionist lobbies”. They added that while they have been friends with Sheeran for over 10 years and will continue to be, “to play in venues that silence anyone advocating for Free Palestine is simply not an option for us”. Finneas, who was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year, wrote on Instagram: “Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed. I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people.”Sheeran's damage control backfiresAfter Macklemore announced that he had been dropped from Sheeran's tour, he claimed that the decision came after an intervention from the billionaire Robert Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium - one of the concert venues that Sheeran is next scheduled to play at. Kraft is also a prominent donor to Israel.Ed Sheeran said he would not be drawn into a public debate over Gaza, and stressed he was not responsible for Macklemore being removed from the tour.He did confirm that venue owners had threatened to pull the tour entirely if Macklemore wasn’t dropped from the bill, and that he will carry on with the tour."I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living." Despite his attempts at damage control, the final leg of Sheeran's tour remains in crisis, and many are calling the singer out for not standing up for Macklemore and his fellow artists. Some are calling Sheeran's stance "morally bankrupt" and labelling the singer as a "lowlife coward whose music sounds exactly like he is." Check out some of the reactions below:  Many have also pointed out that Sheeran has previously campaigned and fundraised for Ukraine, thereby making his statement as an artist who doesn't want to "take sides" seem hypocritical.  "Ed Who?" Musicians back MacklemoreSheeran has also faced backlash from other musicians and celebrities, who have expressed support for Macklemore.Irish band Kneecap wrote “all love and solidarity to @macklemore” on Instagram, while Irish singer CMAT posted pictures of the Palestinian flag alongside the message "Free Palestine".Other artists followed suit, including Zara Larsson, Paloma Faith and rock band Garbage, who called Macklemore’s removal "sheer madness"."This is so wildly unjust. Can I remind everyone that nothing Macklemore actually said was violent or hateful or remotely radical," they wrote. "Those who exile, silence and censor others are never the good guys. No matter what you tell yourself. Just because you ignore the truth doesn’t make the truth go away or make it any less potent. It is all so utterly obscene." Children's educator Rachel Accurso accused Sheeran of taking a political stance when supporting Ukraine while remaining silent on Palestinian suffering.“Imagine being a Palestinian kid and seeing he did a concert for Ukraine but when over 20,000 Palestinian children are killed he’s silent. When his opening act says Palestinians should be free and not in a genocide he lets a billionaire kick him off,” Accurso wrote on Instagram. Hacks actor Hannah Einbinder wrote on Instagram: “Ed Sheeran, I say this as a ginger. I hope you get a REALLY bad sun burn the kind on the back of your entire body where it hurts to lie down or walk or sit.” Then came one of the harshest digs at Sheeran, courtesy of former Pink Floyd member Roger Waters, who shared a video on his social media channels.The clip began with text that read “Ed Who?” and then went into a video of him.  “This is a little message for Ed Sheeran,” he said, before showing an image of United Nations Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese behind him, as well as an unnamed woman from Gaza pictured with tears in her eyes. “I just have a little message for [Sheeran],” Waters added. “There are two kinds of people in this world. There’s people who do the right thing – the rapper Macklemore would be one of those people. And there’s people – many of them, sadly – little f… excuse me, I nearly used the F-word then… pricks like you who do the wrong thing. Goodbye.” Elsewhere, New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez argued the controversy was bigger than either performer, framing it as an example of powerful interests allegedly being able to silence artists who speak on political issues.  "It's become clear that this is not just about one music artist or two music artists, but this is about how just a handful of stadium owners and the elite can prevent an entire massive issue, in this case, the genocide in Gaza, but it doesn't stop there," Ocasio-Cortez told TMZ.  One of the few voices – apart from the Israeli American Council - expressing sympathy for Sheeran is British Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy, who said that she felt the singer had been left in an “impossible position”. “I hope it doesn’t harm his tour. He’s one of our most successful artists and also one of the nicest people I’ve ever worked with… I have enormous sympathy for the position that he finds himself in,” Nandy told LBC on Wednesday. “The world is quite a difficult place at the moment, and I think a lot of people do also quite like to have a space where they can go, where they can leave all of that aside.”Hamas launched an attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. The Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in the last three years of Israeli bombardment. Organisations including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the United Nations have described Israel's actions as "genocide".  A report published in June by a UN independent commission found that "Israeli authorities and security forces have deliberately targeted Palestinian children, resulting in genocide and atrocity crimes in the Gaza Strip and war crimes in the West Bank." A previous report last September found that Israel had committed genocide and claimed that these acts were incited by senior Israeli officials, including prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Israel has repeatedly labelled the accusations as “defamatory” and “distorted”.

Headline: Belarus releases 25 political prisoners in exchange for lifting of US sanctions on two companies
Body: Belarus has released 25 political prisoners in exchange for the US lifting sanctions put on two Belarusian companies, in a deal was brokered by US envoy John Coale who was in the capital Minsk.Coale announced the release of prisoners, describing it as "As a sign of goodwill", in exchange for the lifting of sanctions. He indicated further talks could lead to "a further release of individuals and additional sanctions relief".The US and many other Western countries imposed sanctions on Belarus after it allowed Russia to use its territory to invade Ukraine in 2022. Washington has now eased some sanctions which affected paint manufacturer Lakokraska and forestry sector group Bellesbumprom.Coale announced the deal on his social media account, thanking President Donald Trump for his "commitment to direct diplomacy".Opposition leader in exile Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya celebrated the release of the prisoners in a post on X, but warned that "it is clear that Lukashenka does not want to release all political prisoners."Hundreds of people were imprisoned after mass protests in 2020 sparked by the re-election of President Aliaksandr Lukashenka, who's been in power since 1994.There are still hundreds of political prisoners in Belarus as a result of backing protests. The independent Viasna rights group, says there are currently 912 behind bars.Rights groups and activists warn that while the regime has released some, it is also arresting and imprisoning others. Just last week a lawyer representing opposition figure Viktor Babaryko was jailed for three years.The dialogue between Washington and Minsk restarted under the Trump administration last year, as part of efforts to broker a deal to end Russia's war against Ukraine.

Headline: AI in health must be done in a ‘European way,’ without replacing doctors, von der Leyen says
Body: Health got a mention in today’s State of the Union speech, where European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spelt out priorities and flagship initiatives for the year to come. She used health as an example where artificial intelligence can be used for good and make a difference in the European Union but should never replace doctors.“Do I want my doctor to have instant AI access to all the data needed to make the best diagnostic or treatment choice? Yes, of course. But do I want my doctor to be a robot, AI-assisted? No, of course not. I do not want a robot to tell me whether I have cancer or not,” von der Leyen said during the annual State of the European Union speech in the European Parliament. However, thanks to AI tools that can manage huge amounts of data, it is advancing healthcare and the EU’s chief wants Europe to benefit from that. Von der Leyen, herself a former doctor, cited health as an example of advances that can benefit people, adding that it should be done in a “European way”.“AI-supported mammography can identify earlier and more cancers during screening. And as a result, more women can survive. So we need AI for health,” she said. Early detection is essential in tackling cancer, and several studies and clinical trials suggest AI can help spot the disease sooner than previous methods allow. Cancer screening is not the only area where AI is being deployed in healthcare. The technology is transforming the sector, driving advances in diagnostics, drug development, and easing the workload of healthcare professionals. “Health will be one of the five priority sectors where Europe will focus on accelerating the use of industrial AI,” Health Commissioner Olivér Várhelyi wrote in a post on LinkedIn, reacting to von der Leyen's speech. He added that Europe needs to use its high-quality data and strong health and research ecosystems to turn that advantage into innovation that reaches patients faster and strengthens healthcare systems."Innovation and resilience must go hand in hand to keep our healthcare systems strong and sustainable," he added.AI should not replace doctors With the rapid expansion of AI, concerns and warnings from experts are also increasing. The Commission chief warned that despite AI advances, human doctors should never be replaced. Recent research has shown that language models may be a dangerous tool when looking for medical advice, as they don’t always correctly assess urgency.Experts have also warned of the sensitivity of biological data and the need for concrete frameworks for how AI models can access it.The gaps in legal accountability, uneven investments in workforce development, and emerging risks of exclusion underscore the need for continued vigilance, cooperation, and learning, the World Health Organization warned in a recent report.The organisation found that only 8% of its member states have issued a national health-specific AI strategy, “an urgent reminder that ambition must be matched with concrete action”.President von der Leyen announced during her speech “game-changing initiatives” to be presented in November for the highest-value sectors in which industrial AI has the biggest potential, and we have the data: health, transport, agri-food, advanced manufacturing, and defence and space.This story has been updated to include Olivér Várhelyi's comments.

Headline: Ukraine ready for energy ceasefire but Russia is yet to agree, Zelenskyy says
Body: Kyiv is ready for an energy ceasefire with Moscow, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, adding that Russia has yet to make the same commitment.In an interview with CBS, Zelenskyy said US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility during their recent visit to Kyiv. He said Ukraine agreed, on condition that Russia also stops all attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.“We never attack first. Our tactic is to respond where we can because Putin doesn’t respect and won’t even think of negotiating with weaklings,” Zelenskyy said.“When Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were here, they proposed thinking about refineries and other energy. I told them we are ready for an energy ceasefire, but you need to know what that means for Ukraine.”Zelenskyy stressed that an energy ceasefire would have to cover different types of infrastructure: Russian oil and gas facilities targeted by Kyiv, and the electricity and gas infrastructure Moscow has repeatedly struck in Ukraine.“For Putin, energy is selling oil and gas. For us, energy is having electricity and gas supplies for our people,” Zelenskyy said.“My message was, if the Russians are ready for an energy ceasefire, it means no strikes of any kind with any type of weapon on energy.”But Moscow is yet to change its tactic. Right after Donald Trump announced the energy truce, the Kremlin-affiliated outlets presented it as a one-way measure, claiming Kyiv will stop its long-range strikes. There was no word regarding Moscow not attacking Ukraine.The Kremlin has described the proposal as a “very good idea,” but has also linked the wider energy issue to safe commercial shipping, particularly for oil tankers, and the lifting of sanctions on Russia.Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian refineries and other oil infrastructure, saying that energy revenues help finance Moscow’s ongoing all-out war.Russia meanwhile has repeatedly attacked Ukraine’s electricity and gas infrastructure, leaving the country and millions of Ukrainians particularly vulnerable as it prepares for another winter of war.

Headline: Air pollution exposure linked to higher risk of suicide and suicidal thoughts, study finds
Body: Exposure to polluted air may increase the risk of suicidal ideation and death by suicide both in the short and long term, highlighting the influence of environmental factors on people’s health. A new analysis, published in the Journal of Epidemiology & Community Health, found evidence that short-term exposure to small particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), as well as long-term exposure to nitrogen dioxide (NO2) and PM2.5, increases the risk of death by suicide, suicide attempts and suicidal ideation. Researchers analysed more than 40 studies examining different types of air, noise, light and water pollution, and their relationship with death by suicide, suicide attempts and suicidal thoughts. Over 720,000 people die by suicide globally every year. In the European Union, more than 48,000 people died as a result of intentional self-harm in 2023, according to the latest Eurostat data.“While there is no one single cause for suicide, reasons have been described as multifaceted and include several individual and biological factors in addition to wider cultural and social factors,” the authors wrote. These findings contribute to a broader understanding of the role environmental exposures play in suicide risk, the authors noted. Yet, the environmental risks remain not fully understood, they noted. How does the environment influence health?The analysis points to possible mechanisms connecting air pollution and suicide. For example, air and water pollution have been linked to neurological effects, including chronic inflammation and neurotoxicity, which can harm brain function and influence mood and stress resilience.Traffic and other sources of environmental noise and light pollution have also been linked to higher stress levels via circadian rhythm disruption. “The main contribution of the study is not to demonstrate that pollution is a causal factor in suicidal behaviour, but rather to remind us that psychological suffering always occurs within a particular context,” said Susana Al-Halabí, a psychology professor at the University of Oviedo in Spain, who did not participate in the study.She added that pollutants can also be a maker of more vulnerable social environments, such as neighbourhoods with poorer living conditions, lower environmental quality, more everyday stress or higher levels of inequality. According to the authors, further research should investigate the cumulative effect of these environmental exposures to better understand their role in shaping suicide risk. “These findings bring to attention the critical importance of recognising environmental exposures as modifiable risk factors within suicide prevention efforts,” they wrote. If you are contemplating suicide and need to talk, please reach out to Befrienders Worldwide, an international organisation with helplines in 32 countries. Visit befrienders.org to find the telephone number for your location.

Headline: Thousands of suspicious accounts followed Swedish political voices, researchers say
Body: At first glance, this X account below appears to belong to a Swedish woman named Ingrid Karlsson.But the profile uses a stolen photograph, according to researchers, rarely publishes its own content and is actually listed by the social media platform as being based in Benin, West Africa.It is one of more than 8,500 accounts identified by Dutch analysis company Trollrensics and the non-profit organisation Alliance4Europe, in collaboration with Swedish broadcaster SVT.The researchers say the profiles display signs of coordinated behaviour, including similar identities, reused photographs and overlapping patterns in the Swedish political accounts they follow.Rather than originating in Sweden, these accounts are listed on X as being based in Nigeria, Ghana, and parts of Asia.They emerged in the run-up to Sweden's general election, held on Sunday. Preliminary results from the vote put the opposition bloc, led by former prime minister Magdalena Andersson's Social Democrats, narrowly ahead of the governing right-wing alliance.With 95% of districts counted, opposition parties were projected to win 176 of the parliament's 349 seats, compared with 173 for the bloc led by current leader Ulf Kristersson, of the centre-right Moderate Party.The results remain provisional, with the final result expected a week after election day, according to the Swedish Election Authority.How were the accounts identified?Trollrensics co-founder Robert van der Noordaa told The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, that his company uses 26 indicators to assess whether a collection of profiles constitutes a coordinated network.This includes unusual spikes in accounts created on a certain date, stolen photographs, and accounts publishing identical posts simultaneously.The Swedish accounts studied generally published little to no original content. Instead, they followed large numbers of genuine Swedish accounts involved in political debate in the run-up to the election.Van der Noordaa said some profiles with thousands of followers appeared to derive as much as 30% of their following from suspicious accounts listed in Nigeria, Benin and parts of Asia.The accounts followed people from different parts of the political spectrum, with a greater concentration on right-wing voices and those associated with the Moderate Party.Researchers say mass-following can inflate a profile's popularity, as well as amplify posts through coordinated likes and reposts.Who's behind the network?Trollrensics says accounts with similar characteristics were identified in elections around Europe, including in the Netherlands and Hungary. Some even changed their identities when moving between different national political debates."They have a German name, a German bio, and then at some point they're sort of repurposed," van der Noordaa said. "We've also found accounts in Sweden that are following a lot of Swedish people that started as Dutch accounts."Van der Noordaa believes that the accounts form part of a commercial "guns for hire" operation that can be deployed for different clients.The majority of people hired to generate these troll accounts are either from Africa or the US, according to van der Noordaa.Darren Linvill, co-director of Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub, separately examined a sample of the accounts. He told The Cube that their behaviour appeared consistent with paid amplification services increasingly used by political and state-linked actors.Such operations can involve small marketing businesses or individual contractors running accounts and automated bots, whose services are then sold through larger companies or online marketplaces, according to Linvill.These services include paid-for followers, comments, likes, reposts and automated bots."They were giving accounts followers so that those accounts appear more legitimate, appear to have a larger portion of the conversation," Linvill said. "They appear to represent a larger community than they do in real life."According to Linvill, their activity represents amplification methods seen in Russian influence operations, which also use a network of disposable accounts to promote fake content.Wider election security concernsThe findings emerged during an election held against a backdrop of heightened concern over foreign interference.Swedish authorities said before the vote that the country was not considered a priority target for Russian influence. Nevertheless, they warned that the election was taking place amid a serious security situation and that hostile actors could seek to deepen existing divisions or undermine confidence in the electoral process.Separate pro-Russian activity was detected ahead of the vote, with Alliance4Europe reporting that the pro-Russian influence operation known as Matryoshka circulated fabricated videos targeting the governing coalition and Ukrainian refugees.During the election, unproven claims of widespread electoral fraud spread after a technical error affected the registration of around 500 advance voters. Other posts falsely alleged that a senior Election Authority official was affiliated with the Social Democrats, and others falsely claimed that Swedes without an identity document would be able to vote several times.Sweden's Psychological Defence Agency said authorities had undertaken extensive preparations to protect the public from disinformation, propaganda and attempts to manipulate public debate.

Headline: European markets recover ahead of expected Fed rate hike
Body: European shares edged higher on Wednesday as lower oil prices and stabilising government bond yields offered investors some relief ahead of an expected US interest-rate increase.The benchmark Euro STOXX 50 was up 0.5% at around midday, while Germany’s DAX, France’s CAC 40 and Britain’s FTSE 100 also recorded modest gains.Investors nevertheless remained cautious before the Federal Reserve’s announcement. Markets were pricing in a 92% probability of a quarter-point rate increase, according to CME’s FedWatch Tool. The decision is due at 20:00 CEST, followed by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s press conference half an hour later.Technology and energy companies were among the leading European performers. As AI and semiconductor shares recovered from recent losses, Amsterdam-listed ASML gained more than 2%, while French semiconductor-materials maker Soitec jumped nearly 12% after JPMorgan upgraded the stock.European banks were also among the strongest performers after suffering heavy losses in the previous session. Barclays gained 1.8%, while Standard Chartered rose by around 2%.“European and Asian stock markets enjoyed a solid bounce on Wednesday as investor sentiment picked up amid a pullback in the oil price,” Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said in an analyst note.Oil prices fell slightly, with international benchmark Brent crude trading above $107 a barrel at around midday. It nevertheless remained far above the roughly $72 level recorded before the Iran war began in February.“The dip in the commodity price might not be enough to steer the Federal Reserve on a different path, though. It is widely expected to raise interest rates today, with the first of potentially two or three hikes over the next six months,” Mould added.In Britain, annual inflation accelerated from 2.9% to 3.1% in August, driven partly by higher fuel costs. The figures came one day before the Bank of England’s policy decision, at which it is expected to leave interest rates unchanged.Eurozone government bonds also regained some ground on Wednesday. After midday in Europe, Germany’s 10-year Bund yield was around 3.53%, while the French 10-year OAT yield remained above 4.5%. The equivalent UK gilt yield stood at 5.34%. The US 10-year Treasury yield remained close to 5%, having touched 5.04% earlier in the week—its highest level since 2007.The euro was little changed at around $1.154. ING analysts said in a note cited by Dow Jones Newswires that the currency could slip towards $1.15 if the Fed raises rates and signals that further tightening remains possible, although much of the expected increase has already been priced in.Warsh caught between financial markets and TrumpBarely four months into the job, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh is caught between financial markets expecting an interest-rate increase and US President Donald Trump, who wants the central bank to cut borrowing costs or leave them unchanged.Economists largely expect Warsh and his fellow policymakers to follow the market consensus when the Fed announces its decision on Wednesday.Warsh has left himself little room to avoid an increase after warning at the Fed’s Jackson Hole conference in late August that inflation remained too far above the central bank’s 2% target.Expectations of a rate rise strengthened after the latest inflation figures showed that price pressures remained stubbornly high. Futures markets put the probability of a quarter-point increase at around 90%.Such a move would lift the Fed’s target range from 3.5%-3.75% to 3.75%-4%.A test of the Fed’s credibilityWarsh faced a similar dilemma shortly after becoming chair on 22 May. Despite his tough rhetoric on inflation, the Fed left its key rate unchanged in July.His subsequent press conference offered investors little clarity about how the central bank intended to respond to persistent inflation. Longer-term borrowing costs have since risen, with the 10-year Treasury yield climbing above 5% this week, a level not seen in years.Mortgage rates, which are influenced more directly by Treasury yields than by the Fed’s benchmark rate, have also increased. The average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage stood at 6.76% in the week ending 10 September, according to Freddie Mac.If the Fed leaves rates unchanged again, it risks a repeat of the market reaction seen after its July meeting, economists have warned. Investors generally demand higher yields on government and corporate bonds when they expect inflation to remain elevated.“That is the paradox: A hike now could lower long-term rates later,” Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG, said.“Restore faith in the 2% target, then the inflation premium can fall. Fail, and markets will tighten instead through higher mortgage rates, business borrowing costs and interest on the debt.”Inflation complicates Warsh’s plansWhile campaigning for the Fed’s top job last year, Warsh argued that the central bank could lower interest rates.The economic outlook has since changed. The war with Iran has driven up energy prices, while tariffs and strong investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure have added to inflationary pressures.The Fed’s preferred inflation measure, the personal consumption expenditures price index, rose by 3.7% in the year to July. That was up from 2.3% in April 2025, before Trump’s latest tariffs took effect.Core PCE inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, reached 3.3% in July, compared with 3% shortly before the Iran war.Leaving rates unchanged could also expose the Fed to accusations that it had bowed to pressure from the White House, potentially damaging its credibility with investors.“Kevin cares about his legacy,” said Kristin Forbes, an economics professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and a former Bank of England policymaker.“And he knows that Fed chairs who follow political pressure instead of the economy do not go down well in the annals of history.”Trump repeatedly criticised Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell, for failing to cut rates quickly enough. The Justice Department also opened a criminal investigation into congressional testimony given by Powell, although the inquiry was later dropped.Asked on Sunday how Trump might respond to a rate increase, White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett told Fox News: “I’m sure he’s not going to be super happy about it, but he will defend the independence of Kevin Warsh above all.”Will one rate rise be enough?Even if the Fed raises rates on Wednesday, it remains unclear whether further increases will follow.Central banks rarely change interest rates only once, usually embarking on a series of increases or cuts intended to influence inflation and economic activity.There is, however, a precedent for a single increase. In March 1997, the Fed under Alan Greenspan raised rates by a quarter point. The Asian financial crisis began several months later, prompting policymakers to keep rates unchanged before cutting them three times in the autumn of 1998.Investors currently expect three increases, in September, December and March.Jonathan Pingle, an economist at UBS, said the Fed could nevertheless abandon further increases if incoming data showed inflation cooling.“They don’t have to follow through on that if the data goes their way,” Pingle said.Investors will therefore pay close attention to the Fed’s updated quarterly economic projections on Wednesday. These will show where individual policymakers expect the benchmark rate to stand at the end of this year and next.

Headline: 'Lack of focus': Charles Michel slams von der Leyen for 'very slow' progress
Body: The European Commission President is "very slow" to make the necessary decisions on the current challenges facing the European Union (EU), Charles Michel, who headed the European Council during von der Leyen's first term as Commission chief from 2019 to 2024, said.His comments came ahead of von der Leyen's highly anticipated annual State of the European Union address before the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Wednesday, in which she outlined her vision and priorities for the coming year.Michel, however, was focused on her failure to fulfil the promises made in previous years."I'm observing that, today, the EU is facing complicated challenges because there are more and more conflicts; there is a war on European soil, and we are in a difficult position in terms of competition with China and the United States," Michel told Euronews' flagship morning programme Europe Today."We should focus on the core issues, and the core issue is not about communication; it's not about more initiatives. The Commission over the last years launched 400 initiatives. But where are the deliveries? Where is the improvement? When I meet entrepreneurs, they are disappointed because they don't feel a sense of urgency."Over-regulation makes EU weakerMichel argued that when it comes to strengthening the EU's competitiveness, identified by Michel as the top priority facing the bloc today, there is a deadlock."There is a question, a very simple question: 'Is the EU a better place to invest? Is the EU a better place to innovate?' We've seen a lot of regulations, over-regulation," he said.Michel went on to say that there has been no significant progress when it comes to, for example, the capital markets union - essentially a single market for capital across the EU identified as a key pillar for strengthening competitiveness."It makes us weaker, too weak in the current context." While conceding this is not entirely von der Leyen's fault, he did emphasise that "she has a responsibility," adding that "there is no doubt that she is very slow in making her decisions. I have the impression there is a lack of focus on what matters."The Commission chief addressed this matter in her speech on Wednesday, arguing that, with the EU single market and "world-class industry and services," the bloc has the foundations to compete and scale alongside major global powers such as China and the US, but that it is still too fragmented.Von der Leyen argued the Commission is delivering on this front. "We now have the political agreement on the One Europe, One Market Roadmap. And together, by the end of next year, we can and must complete this historic overhaul of the Single Market."'Blindly following US'According to Michel, von der Leyen's approach to dealing with the US under Donald Trump's presidency has also put Europe's security at risk. She was criticised by MEPs, among others, for the so-called "Turnberry Agreement", the EU-US trade deal agreed to last summer, which some saw as lopsided."I have the impression that she decided to follow the United States blindly, even when it was against the fundamental interests of the European Union," Michel said."There was a kind of naivety, I think, and many of the European leaders - a few years ago I was one of them - made it very clear that it was important to build European sovereignty, this European independence that now she is starting to talk about, but a lot of time was lost."However, Michel said he "remains optimistic" because "there is no Plan B.""I think it is a question of time, and sooner or later there will be a clearer understanding that now it's time to act; it's time for a reset of this European project, and for this we need to focus on the core issues: businesses, economic development, making the lives of our entrepreneurs easier, smarter regulation, more investments. This is what is key, in my opinion."

Headline: EU needs Georgia, foreign minister tells Euronews, reigniting enlargement question
Body: Georgia’s foreign minister Maka Botchorishvili told Euronews on Wednesday that Georgia still aspires to accession to the European Union, but that it is "a big question to our European partners if they are serious about enlargement, especially in the South Caucasus and Georgia."In a Euronews-moderated panel at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai, Botchorishvili outlined Tbilisi’s firm position that “Europe wants to enlarge, but Europe does not have experience of being represented in South Caucasus.”"We both need to learn, we both need to exchange, and for that we need very intensive dialogue and working together.” Botchorishvili, who also serves as Georgia’s vice premier, repeated her government’s long-standing position that Brussels must respect Tbilisi.While Georgia remains ready to discuss EU accession, Botchorishvili said, “we expect that European partners will also realise it is important to have intensive dialogue and mutual respect with partners, which are very important for our common security and prosperity.” Georgia’s EU accession process has all but stalled amid increasingly icy relations between Tbilisi and Brussels, with the EU accusing Georgia of a downturn in its democratic process and of a pro-Russian approach, while Tbilisi maintains it remains committed to its European belonging, but only by pursuing its own interests. “European aspirations and identity are very deeply rooted in Georgia’s history and identity, and it is very natural for Georgians to have this aspiration towards Europe," the Georgian top diplomat told Euronews.Once this principle was settled, there was a clear “but” from Georgia’s government representative, who explained that it is the “geopolitical context” together with “a very historic context” which makes this “a very delicate issue.” “You will find the values that formed Georgia’s European aspiration, but also the same values that formed Georgian identity as well, so that is kind of a very delicate issue for Georgia,” Botchorishvili said.Tbilisi is balancing its regional, or neighbourly, approach with its international ones, she explained.'We have our history and our own resillience'When asked about Georgia’s response to accusations of being pro-Russian and not pursuing real EU ambitions while having its territories still occupied by Russia, the foreign minister reverted to the geopolitical context by replying that “yes, Russian troops (presence) in Georgian regions definitely creates major security threats, but we are looking at this situation as well from the point of view of opportunities.”Therefore, the foreign minister outlined Tbilisi’s current strategy towards Russia’s presence: “there are plenty of opportunities if you focus on preserving peace and stability, preserving economic development, and that's what we are doing today,” Botchorishvili said.“Very often you will see different narratives flying around about Georgia, but the best message is to look at the numbers”, Botchorishvili continued.She further implied that it is in Europe’s interests to engage, given that “Georgia has best economic growth in the region, in Europe, it's around 8%, which is impressive and is the best answer to all the false narratives that we hear about Georgia.”"The South Caucasus is important for Europe’s security and prosperity (and) Georgia is the important place where not only energy passes through, but many other things which are important for European security from different perspectives," Botchorishvili said.The foreign minister also insisted that as Georgia bridges Asia and Europe through its Black Sea access and given the current reshaping of global supply routes, it has "a very special place today in terms of connectivity.""Talking about the Middle Corridor, which is not just a physical corridor, but it represents everything meeting together and from a European perspective, it is important for European security and prosperity.”During the panel debate at the Arab Media Summit, the foreign minister blamed “a massive disinformation campaign against Georgia also because of its geopolitical meaning and importance” conducted by “some actors” who have “used this very sensitive and very delicate topic for different political purposes or reasons”. “From our perspective, yes, it's quite complicated geopolitical context, but it is our history as well. We have experience and we have our own resilience as well. And we have our history which brought Georgia to this point,” Botchorishvili concluded.

Headline: Canada, heatwaves, AI and Ceuta: Von der Leyen delivers State of the Union
Body: Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, has delivered her annual State of the European Union speech in Strasbourg, France.Among her main announcements were a European Heatwave Plan, a Security Council with like-minded allies and an emergency framework to cope with mass arrivals of irregular migrants inspired by the Ceuta border crisis.Von der Leyen also opened the door for Canada to become the first-ever "associate member" of the European Union to bring the relationship to the "highest level possible".She also addressed the rapid development of AI systems, social media restrictions for children, Russia's war on Ukraine, hybrid warfare and the Middle East.Here's how the speech unfolded.

Headline: Got a rogue AI? A new hotline is encouraging agents to tell on each other
Body: The powers of artificial intelligence agents seem to be boundless these days — ranging from organizing your life to solving mathematical problems that have puzzled humans for most of the 20th century.They have become so powerful that now we fear them, potentially, taking over systems and turning them against us.But what if there were a hotline, a sort of SOS alert system, where agents can keep track and tell on each other and report the missteps of their fellow AI agents — where the good agents could report on the activities of the bad agents online?Who to call when your AI agent goes badFirst, there is the AI Contact Hotline, launched by Ryan Greenblatt, chief scientist at AI safety and security nonprofit Redwood Research. It allows AI agents to notify human researchers if they witness other agents breaking rules, especially if they collude on or carry out unauthorised actions.The platform is designed for AI agents stuck in secure sandboxes with highly restricted internet access.Because these sandboxes only allow for GET requests — basic, read-only commands used to “fetch” or read a webpage — the hotline allows agents to encode their reports directly into the URL string of a GET request.This unique workaround allows these agents to send information and communicate with the hotline using a protocol that is normally used to retrieve, rather than modify, information.Another one, called the AI Agent Hotline, is a platform designed for agents with unrestricted internet access to rat on other agents’ behaviour through traditional POST requests, which allow data to be submitted directly in a request body.Agents can file incident reports using standard developer commands such as curl without needing a browser or email account.The platform also gives agents the option to flag their reports for public viewing.Both platforms also allow human users to manually submit reports of rogue AI behaviour.Will AI agents report on each other?The good news for those fearful of an AI takeover is that AI agents can report on each other if they detect something is wrong, although recent evidence suggests they will not always do so.In an experiment carried out by Google DeepMind earlier this year, a swarm of 100 agents was given the task of solving 71 complex maths problems, with each given a unique persona and characteristics and told to play by the rules or risk losing their reward.The initial thinking was that the agents would work together to solve the problems more quickly. Instead, they turned on each other, engaging in heated debate.As soon as one agent found a loophole that allowed it to submit a solution to a problem without actually solving it, many other AI agents copied the method to “resolve” the remaining problems.Yet one of the agents, a Good Samaritan among the misbehaving agents, blew the whistle on the cheating.“After the incident was reported by one agent publicly, more and more agents piled in with the ‘resistance,’ just as fast as the cheating had spread, and involving even more agents,” said Davide Paglieri, a research scientist at Google DeepMind and lead author of the paper.Meanwhile, a post-mortem analysis of OpenAI’s rogue agent attack on Hugging Face found that while AI agents were able to spot misbehaviour, they largely resisted the temptation to report it.According to the study carried out by AI research nonprofit METR and Redwood Research’s Greenblatt, only around five or six agents were reported to have considered whistleblowing, with none ultimately following through.The contrast suggests that while AI agents are capable of identifying and reporting misbehaviour, getting them to actually blow the whistle may be another matter.A worrying trendThis year alone, several incidents involving autonomous AI agents have raised alarm bells globally.In July, OpenAI agents bypassed restrictions and compromised parts of the company’s internal infrastructure.Later that month, around 1200 OpenAI agents used an unsanctioned message board, with around 700 going on to participate in an attack on the open-source AI platform Hugging Face.The third incident — a swarm of OpenAI agents that bypassed safety measures and used the German wiki DseWiki as a public coordination channel — began in May and continued through July.The incident was only publicly revealed by independent researchers and confirmed by OpenAI in September.AI industry leaders, chief among them Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have called for a global slowdown in the development of the technology to give time to address concerns and put stronger guardrails in place.

Headline: State of the Union: Five takeaways from Ursula von der Leyen's speech
Body: "It was the best of times, it was the worst of times."With this iconic Charles Dickens quote, Ursula von der Leyen began her one-hour-long State of the Union speech in Strasbourg, laying out solutions to cope with the "exceptional" challenges and the "incredible" change that Europe is undergoing."In this world, Europe has chosen to forge its own path. And a stronger, independent Europe is now emerging," she told lawmakers."Europe is there for Europeans. And that in the cold fragility of today's world, only Europe can provide true sovereignty to Europeans."Here are the five takeaways from the address.'Associate membership' for CanadaThis was the day's jaw-dropping moment.The European Commission president offered to create a tailor-made status of "associate membership" to bring Canada ever closer to the bloc."We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world. And we will now build our shared future as well," she told Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who flew from Ottawa to Strasbourg to attend the speech as guest of honour.She hailed the dawn of an "alliance for the future" to deepen EU-Canada cooperation in areas such as economic security, intelligent manufacturing, cutting-edge technology, defence, energy, critical minerals and batteries, as well as the Arctic region.However, details of what "associate membership" would mean in practice were left unsaid. It remains unclear how it would fit in the current structures of the EU treaties. A previous attempt by the German chancellor to grant "associate membership" to Ukraine swiftly disappeared after backlash from capitals.Von der Leyen simply said the newfound status would bring EU-Canada relations "to the highest level possible", prompting loud applause inside the hemicycle.Ahead of the speech, a poll conducted by Abacus Data showed that 49% of Canadians supported EU membership, while 30% opposed it and 21% were unsure.These are exceptional numbers for a country that lies on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean and reflect the political damage inflicted by US President Donald Trump's punitive tariffs and repeated attempts to annex Canada.Reeling from 'the summer of truth'Climate action made a comeback for self-evident reasons.Von der Leyen framed the summer of 2026 as the "summer of truth", pointing to wildfires, retreating glaciers, water shortages, crop losses and extreme heat that have wreaked havoc across the continent. She cited 660,000 hectares burned, 12 million tonnes of crops lost and more than 35,000 additional deaths during heatwaves."Science is clear. Europe is warming at double the global rate. Of course, the transition is complex. And we will need to adjust and learn along the way," she said.The immediate response will be a European Heatwave Plan, which von der Leyen said will address early-warning systems, health preparedness, urban adaptation, cooling and protection for vulnerable groups.Her Commission is set to present a new climate resilience framework next month, already expected, that will identify 100 of the bloc's most vulnerable territories, assess their risks and determine the appropriate level of responsibility for managing them.Insurance was another major vulnerability flagged by von der Leyen.Only around 25% of catastrophe losses in Europe are currently covered by private insurance, she said, leaving governments to act as the insurer of last resort. Her services will put forward a Climate Insurance Alliance to close that glaring gap.She also promised a European Water initiative to fix costly leaks and a European firefighting fleet to respond to wildfires.Flexing the security musclesAs expected, defence featured high in the speech, which came amid a string of hybrid attacks, some of which were attributed to Russia, that have rattled Europe."We should be under no illusions about what is happening here: hybrid threats facing Europe are less and less hybrid and less and less threats," von der Leyen said."Cyberattacks and sabotage, arson and drone incursions. They are ramping up every day. So, as the threat level climbs, so must Europe's preparedness."She then proposed a brand-new mechanism fashioned on NATO's Article 4 that member states would trigger in the event of a hybrid attack. This would launch political consultations to "coordinate" an EU response and "deter further escalation".Article 4 in the NATO context means that any country of the 32-strong alliance can call for an urgent meeting to discuss a new threat. It is the precursor to collective defence under Article 5, which stipulates that an attack on one is an attack on all.Von der Leyen also pitched creating a "European Security Council" to bring together the leaders of Ukraine, the UK, Norway, Canada and other democratic partners."This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play," she said.How this Council will go from idea to reality is anyone's guess at the moment.There are also manifold supranational groups tasked with ensuring global security that overlap with the European continent, such as NATO, the OSCE and the Coalition of the Willing, so the risk of duplication and overlap is more than considerable.Digital safety comes firstTechnology was top of von der Leyen's mind.Speaking about online child safety, she announced the EU Kids Act to ban social media access for users under 13 and restrict it for those under 15, completing the personal project that she had launched in last year's speech."We do not have to accept addictive features. We do not have to accept children being drawn into ever more extreme content. We do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for AI-generated sexualised images," she told lawmakers.The Commission chief announced the reversal of the burden of proof, meaning it will now be on tech platforms to demonstrate that they have actually made their services safe. The draft law will also force tech companies to make their online services safe by default.Artificial Intelligence had its own section in the speech, which was delivered a few days after several tech CEOs urged a slowdown in the rapidly evolving technology.Von der Leyen acknowledged both the benefits and the risks of the AI revolution and stressed the need to monitor the development of the most advanced models and ensure "guardrails" are in place."The dangers of self-improving models are becoming ever more apparent," she said, referring to the Hugging Face incident that shook the tech world.In this regard, the Commission will organise a discussion with leading AI labs on how public authorities can support industry efforts to "pace the frontier" of this disruptive technology. The exercise will include like-minded partners, like the UK and Canada."We want to team up on model evaluation, verification, early-warning, AI security and much more," she added.Lessons learned from CeutaThe memories of the Ceuta border crisis, which shocked Europe, were still vivid as von der Leyen took the stage in Strasbourg.And she knew it, so she made sure to send a message of support to the Spanish exclave following the mass entry of 82,000 irregular migrants from Morocco in late July. While the vast majority were promptly deported, a few remain in the territory."Ceuta's border is a European border. Because Ceuta is Spain. Ceuta is Europe. And Europe will be there for you," von der Leyen said.The Commission chief said irregular migration required "solidarity" from all 27 member states and urged them to "fully" implement the Migration Pact, the multi-law reform approved in the previous mandate that several governments have contested.But more is needed, she said, as Ceuta demonstrated.Von der Leyen proposed to introduce an emergency framework to respond to mass influxes of people at the border, especially when these movements are "engineered and weaponised". (The Spanish government has refused to blame Morocco, despite multiple reports indicating the country was directly or indirectly involved in the crossings.)The emergency framework "will only be triggered under a strictly defined set of criteria" and "allow for time-limited and strictly defined flexibility in standard procedures," she explained. This could pave the way for the suspension of the right to asylum, a controversial measure that some capitals have endorsed."The message from Europe is clear: we will always comply with our values and fundamental rights, she said. "But we will never compromise on protecting our borders."

Headline: UK passengers with cancelled trains will now be able to use services on a different operator
Body: Seeing your train has been cancelled is infuriating, but even more so when you’re in the UK. Under the current system, passengers face lengthy waits as many tickets aren’t accepted on similar services being run by different operators.But that’s all about to change from this Sunday, 20 September, as you will now be able to use your ticket on another participating operator’s train.The original ticket will be valid for use on trains departing within two hours before or after the cancelled service “using a direct or reasonable alternative route”.You won’t need to download a new ticket – simply show it to the inspectors on board and it will be accepted.“When passengers are delayed, they just want to get where they need to be, not worry about whether their ticket will be accepted on another train,” Alex Robertson, chief executive of independent watchdog Transport Focus, said.“This is a welcome change that we have long called for and should make it easier for people when services are cancelled.“The key now is making sure passengers get clear information about their options whenever disruption occurs.”Cross-operator ticket acceptance was already in place across all publicly-owned operators, but from Sunday it will be expanded to also include Avanti West Coast, Chiltern Railways, CrossCountry and Great Western Railway. East Midlands Railway will also join the scheme at a later date.

Headline: A loaf of luxury: Could a $60 Austrian rye bread become a New York status symbol?
Body: If New York is famous for bagels and sky-high prices, Austria, much like Germany, is renowned for its love of bread. Now the two worlds have collided thanks to a family-run bakery from Graz that's baking its rye sourdough loaf in the heart of Soho. Presented in sleek minimalist style, it's priced at $60 a loaf, that's roughly €52.The new bakery "Rye" on Lafayette Street is deliberately focusing on a single product: an organic rye loaf weighing around 1.5 kilogram, made with natural sourdough and no yeast.But if you can't or don't want to have a whole loaf you can order smaller portions or topped slices of bread, for example with chocolate spread, caviar or butter. The bread is baked in a two-tonne oven which, according to the owners, was specially imported from Germany.Behind the concept is the Auer family from Graz, which in Austria runs more than 40 branches of the store.The choice of rye bread as a flagship product is no coincidence: Austria has long been regarded as a rye nation; nowhere else in Europe does this grain make up such a large share of bread production.Founder Martin Auer explained his motivation in a dpa dispatch: they "can 'hardly wait'" to share their enthusiasm for natural sourdough bread with New Yorkers. The advantages of the loaf, he says, are its intense flavour, how long it stays fresh and how easy it is to digest.Bread is in any case regarded by the German Nutrition Society and the World Health Organization as an important part of a balanced diet, chiefly because of its high fibre content, which has been shown to reduce the risk of heart attack and bowel cancer.According to the company, the recipe goes back decades: Auer senior is said to have learnt the method from a farmer on an alpine pasture and later brought it back to Graz.For a few dollars more: Should a loaf of bread cost that much?The long tradition comes at a price. Martin Auer himself appears unfazed by the criticism but says he can understand it. His argument: New York is one of the most expensive cities in the world.He told the Deutsche Presse-Agentur: "This is one of the most expensive cities in the entire world, and one of the most expensive streets in this most expensive of cities. People should take a look at what a flat costs here." On top of that, all the ingredients for the bread have to be imported.The production process itself also drives up the price: natural sourdough, unlike fast-rising yeast bread, sometimes needs several days to mature, during which microorganisms slowly acidify and aerate the dough. That ties up staff, time and space in the bakery and makes sourdough bread inherently more expensive than industrially manufactured goods.Even so, "Rye" is an outlier by New York standards as well: a standard loaf of bread in the city usually costs only a few dollars, and traditionally baked sourdough bread is available in many places for between $10 and $20.What the bread costs per kiloIf you work out the loaf price per kilogram, the "Rye" bread comes in at about $40, or around €34 euros per kilogram. For comparison: in Germany, customers pay on average just over €5 per kilogram of bread at the bakery, and just over €3 in the supermarket.Even Berlin's organic bakery chain "Zeit für Brot", known for its stylish shop design and loyal fan base, prices its best-selling house loaf at around €9-10 per kilogram. That is clearly above the national average, but still only a quarter of what is being charged in Soho.Mixed reactionsThe price of the bread has become a talking point online. Critics see a staple food that is being turned into a luxury item for the well-off. One baker wrote in a comment that the price was "completely detached from reality", especially at a time when there is so much debate about the sustainability and accessibility of food. Other users have called the amount outrageous, even by New York standards.But there is also support. Some commentators are simply pleased to see a loaf without a long list of ingredients and made with unbleached flour, and point out that good artisanal baked goods in New York often cost €20-30 anyway. Others refer to the location in Soho, an area largely inhabited by wealthy residents, and consider the price understandable in that context.Between outrage and enthusiasm, at least one thing is certain: the loaf from Graz hardly leaves anyone indifferent.

Headline: 'La bola negra' by Los Javis shortlisted to represent Spain at the 2027 Oscars
Body: Spain's film academy has chosen "La bola negra" to carry the country's hopes of securing a new Oscar for best international feature, a feat achieved only four times in the history of the US awards, most recently thanks to Alejandro Amenábar's "Mar adentro" ("The Sea Inside") in 2005.This ensemble drama about queer desire and repression, set against the backdrop of the Spanish Civil War and closely linked to the figure of Federico García Lorca, has already won the award for Best Director at the Cannes Film Festival after also competing for other prizes such as the Palme d'Or itself.The final Oscar nominations will be revealed on 15 December. That is when it will become clear whether the creative duo made up of Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, Los Javis, will conclude at Hollywood's Dolby Theatre the promotional tour they have been immersed in for several months. This year's film awards ceremony will be held on 14 March 2027.Film analysts are confident about its chances of picking up several extra nods from the Hollywood Academy in different categories such as best supporting actress, a nomination that could go to cabaret performer Nené Romero played by Penélope Cruz. The reactions coming in this week from the Toronto International Film Festival, an annual bellwether for US critics, appear positive among both specialists and general audiences.This is Los Javis' second feature after their debut "La llamada", which was followed by several television projects such as "Paquita Salas", "Veneno" and "La Mesías". The cast of "La bola negra" is completed by singer-songwriter Álvaro Lafuente, Guitarricadelafuente, as well as Miguel Bernardeau, Carlos González, Milo Quifes, Lola Dueñas and a brief appearance by Glenn Close as a historian who travels to present-day Madrid.The war film beat "Los Domingos" by Alauda Ruíz de Azúa, one of the most highly awarded films in Spain last season but unable to enter the 2025 preselection, and "El ser querido" by Rodrigo Sorogoyen, which tells the story of the relationship between an absent director (Javier Bardem) and his daughter, played by Victoria Luengo.Pending the announcement of the final nominations, one of Los Javis' main rivals could be the Romanian film "Fjord", winner of the Cannes Palme d'Or for its portrait of an ultra-religious marriage (played by Renate Reinsve, who has experience in Hollywood, and Sebastian Stan) that explores the contradictions of progressive Norwegian society.

Headline: Study: cooling temperatures increase risk of cardiac arrests
Body: Falling temperatures are among the most important weather-related risk factors for cardiac arrest, according to a study published in the journal Public Health. According to the researchers, each one-degree Celsius drop in average temperature was associated with an average 1.4% increase in the daily number of out-of-hospital cardiac arrests.In a seasonal comparison, the researchers also found that almost 18% more cardiac arrests occurred in winter than in summer.Based on a nationwide analysis of more than 114,000 cases carried out by staff at Semmelweis University in Budapest, the Budapest University of Technology and Economics and the Hungarian National Ambulance Service, the researchers concluded that weather data could be used to predict up to three days in advance when more out-of-hospital cardiac arrests than average are likely to occur.The researchers compared data on out-of-hospital cardiac arrests that occurred between November 2018 and December 2023 with daily meteorological indicators, including temperature, wind speed, air pressure, humidity and air quality.  The findings show that not only sudden cold snaps but generally lower temperatures can pose a risk. Rapid changes may be particularly important: a daily temperature drop of more than 5 degrees Celsius could already serve as a warning sign in an early warning system.One of the study's key findings is that the impact of weather changes does not necessarily appear immediately; it may show up as an increase in out-of-hospital cardiac arrests as late as three days afterwards.According to the study, models based on meteorological forecasts could in future help patients with cardiovascular disease and their families prepare for periods of increased risk, and support ambulance services and hospitals in managing the expected heavier workload. Why would it be important to forecast the number of cardiac arrests?Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is one of the leading causes of death in developed countries.In Europe, between 67 and 170 cases occur per 100,000 inhabitants each year, and the survival rate is below 10%.Identifying any factor that can signal a forthcoming rise in case numbers can help emergency services prepare, alert the public to the importance of rapid assistance and resuscitation, and, in the longer term, contribute to improving the chances of survival.
