Headline: World Athletics chief Seb Coe: 'We stand firm against Russian athletes taking part'
Body: In an exclusive interview with Euronews, the President of World Athletics Sebastian Coe defended the organisation's decision to keep Russian athletes barred from its events.The International Olympic Committee announced in the summer that it was easing the relevant restrictions, but left it to each international sports federation to take its own decisions. Euronews asked whether, in the light of those developments and of decisions taken by other federations, World Athletics plans to change its stance.Athletics is, after all, the sport often described as "the king of the Olympic Games". Coe's answer, however, leaves no room for misinterpretation: "We will maintain our position and we will defend our position."The second question concerned the pushback (on a legal basis) in recent months from the Russian side against the hard line taken by World Athletics. Over the summer, the Russian Athletics Federation lodged two appeals against World Athletics at the Court of Arbitration for Sport in Lausanne (CAS), arguing that the decision to maintain the exclusion "affects the fundamental interests of athletics in Russia and restricts the right of Russian athletes to compete."Just last week, groups of Russian athletes appealed to the human rights commissions of the IOC and the UN, claiming that their exclusion violates their rights and is destroying their careers. Coe's response to this barrage of Russian legal action was, once again: "We will maintain our position and we will defend our position."'It is not a personal issue but one of philosophy'This stance, banning Russian (and Belarusian) athletes from all World Athletics competitions, was recently described as "Coe's personal obsession" by the executive director of the Russian Athletics Federation, Boris Yarisevsky."It is clear that there is something personal here. I believe this is simply his personal position. It is not the position of World Athletics. The sanctions against the Russian Athletics Federation are unprecedented. No other sports federation is facing such strict restrictions.They not only prevent smooth day to day operations, they also hold back the development of athletics in Russia, especially among young athletes who cannot represent their country on the international stage.We are seeking the lifting of the sanctions through the courts and are preparing our next steps to restore justice", Yarisevsky. told Russian media.Euronews asked Coe, a British Olympic champion who won four medals in Moscow 1980 and Los Angeles in 1984 to respond, and once again he was unequivocal, although this time more verbose: "Fighting for the integrity of competition and the integrity of competitors and the primacy of an international federation to decide how it determines eligibility is not a personal issue, it is one of philosophy."It should be noted that World Athletics imposed the current sanctions and full exclusion on Russian athletes in March 2022, as an immediate response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.It was the first major sports federation to take such a decision and has kept it in place almost four and a half years later, even though the International Olympic Committee and other federations such as the international wrestling, judo and fencing federations and World Aquatics have already relaxed theirs.Lesson from the 'Ultimate Championship'Sebastian Coe spoke to Euronews on the sidelines of the Ultimate Championship, the new World Athletics event staged last weekend in Budapest. He sees the competition as one of the key legacies he will leave to his successors when his term as World Athletics president ends in a year's time."I hope it's a very, very strong legacy because we're looking at the sport in a very different way. We want this to feel different, to look different, particularly for the athletes. The prize money is significantly larger than we've ever had before, $10 million. And the format is significantly different because it's not a full world championships with 2,000 athletes. It's 381 from 65 different countries. But it really does determine the best of the best.", Coe said at the outset.The World Athletics president went on: "I think there are things we're going to learn from this that we're gonna be able to take into our world championships, maybe the Olympic program, around event presentation, around just being more exciting and more innovative in the stadium and what it looks like on television".The legacy of Coe's 12-year presidencyCoe was a candidate for the presidency of IOC a year and a half ago, in a process held in Ancient Olympia. Kirsty Coventry ultimately came out on top.Sebastian Coe will therefore complete his third and final four-year term as president of World Athletics in 2027. The federation's statutes were amended at his initiative in order to avoid presidents staying in office for life, as was sometimes the case in the past.He took over the leadership of what was then the IAAF (International Association of Athletics Federations) in 2015, after elections held on the sidelines of the World Athletics Championships in Beijing, where, a year from now, his successor at the head of World Athletics will be chosen. The IAAF was renamed World Athletics in 2019.We asked him for a brief assessment of his most significant achievements. He chose to highlight the following:"We are now the best governed sport in the Olympic movement, by some distance. All the work that's been done by the ASOIF Governance Review (Association of Summer Olympic International Federations) shows that, and that's not where we started.We've worked really hard to put governances, safeguards, checks, and balances in place. We have an athletic integrity unit that now has made independent all our drug testing, but also our integrity programs, the way we manage ourselves during elections all that is is very very differentI'm very pleased that we are the only olympic sport that has a gender balance council we have twenty six members thirteen men thirteen women and each and every one of them is there on meritAnd that is important and in the last four years we've increased our revenues significantly and people want to invest in our sport. Across a whole series of metrics, we're in much better shape than when I took over".'No comment' on Infantino and the OlympicsSebastian Coe has achieved all this at a time when global sports governance appears to be in crisis, as shown by the growing pressure on FIFA president Gianni Infantino to step down from the head of world football's governing body, and by the resignation of Edgar Grospiron, president of the organising committee for the 2030 Winter Olympic Games in the French Alps.Given that Coe is himself the president of what he calls "the best governed" sport federation, and also served as president of the London 2012 Olympic Games Organising Committee.When asked for his view, he provided a diplomatic answer: "I'm not really interested in other sports and I'm not really interesting in other organising committees. My responsibility is to chair the boards at World Athletics and I am satisfied that not only have we come a long way in improving our governance, we are the best governed sport in the world and I have a council that is accountable and responsible and those are the foundation stones for a very promising future.", Coe replied."So, could everyone learn from you?" we asked, picking up on his remark. Coe, smiling, was quick to reply: " I'm not even saying that, I'm just saying that we've done what we have done in the best interests of our sport and that is the only way to manage an organisation."

Headline: Where in Europe are homes most at risk of a break in?
Body: European homes and businesses appear to be getting safer.The number of break-ins across the EU has dropped by more than a third in just a decade (35%), falling to 1.2 million from to 2014 to 2024, according to new Eurostat data.These figures cover both residential and business premises, yet despite the good news, Europe continues to be a battleground between intruders and private citizens and business owners, with many countries having a significant rate of burglaries relative to their populations.Austria faces a huge wave of burglaries, with the highest rate in the EU: 700 per 100,000 people reported in 2024, with Sweden (601) and Luxembourg next (568).Which countries enjoy the lowest burglary rate?Intruders are far less prolific in Lithuania. The country reports a 24/100,000 people burglary rate, followed at the bottom of the table by Bulgaria (46) and Slovakia, the only EU countries below 100.Lithuania has also seen the steepest decline in break-ins compared to 2014, down by an impressive 79%, followed by Bulgaria with a 78% decline, and Greece, with burglaries down 71% from its peak in 2015.The picture is less optimistic in Spain. The country saw the smallest fall in burglaries, only down 21% since 2014, according to a Europe in Motion calculation.France is only slightly better, with a 23% decrease. It's also the country most affected by burglaries in general, with more than 300,000, closely followed by Germany, and far below by Spain, which experienced 143,000 burglaries yearly.How are Europeans taking matters into their own hands?European citizens are better equipping themselves against burglary threats, particularly through the purchase of security alarms.Between 2015 and 2025, EU production of security alarms grew from 30.1 million items in 2015 to 68.3 million items in 2025, according to EU Trade Explorer.Ireland is one of the most remarkable examples.The country's Central Statistics Office reported that the use of domestic security technology — such as alarms, CCTV, video intercoms and securised frames and fixtures grew from 17% in 2022 to 30% in 2024.In general, across the EU, the UK, Switzerland and Norway, around 20 million alarm systems for private properties and small businesses are installed, according to consultancy firm Berg Insight, with a global penetration of 8%.However, that's much smaller in comparison with the North American market (US+Canada), where the reported concentration of alarm systems is three times higher (24%).

Headline: 'Enough is enough': EU moves toward restricting social media access for under-15s
Body: The European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced an EU Kids Act proposal restricting minors' access to platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, alongside new safety requirements for online services including video games and AI chatbots.“We do not have to accept addictive features. We do not have to accept children being drawn into ever more extreme content. We do not have to accept that girls have their photos used for AI-generated sexualised images,” von der Leyen said."No personal account under the age of 15. No social media under the age of 13. That means only mini accounts from 13 to under 15, set up and supervised by parents, with limited features and time restrictions," she told the European Parliament during her State of the Union address.France, Greece, Austria, Denmark, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Germany, Poland and the Netherlands are all considering or advancing national legislation on social media bans, piling pressure on Brussels to present an EU-wide measure and avoid fragmentation.In July, a group of experts convened by the EU executive released a series of recommendations on improving child safety online, many of which are reflected in the upcoming draft law.The bill itself is due to be published on Thursday, but a leak obtained by Euronews already shows the details of the upcoming legislative proposal.“Europe has the power to act. It is us who decide our rules, not big tech,” von der Leyen added.ScopeThe scope is broader than originally anticipated: the bill will also cover other online services deemed potentially harmful to minors, notably video games and AI companions – a move Spain and the Netherlands requested only last week.The draft EU Kids Act covers social media, video-sharing platforms and online games, considered to pose "specific design risks for minors," as well as AI-powered chatbots and companions, described as "virtual tools that can give mental health and personal development advice to minors."Services designed and operated for education or by public authorities, as well as AI systems intended for office or industrial use, are excluded from the scope.Age limitationsThe proposal combines safety-by-design requirements for all the digital services concerned with a minimum age requirement that applies only to social media platforms like TikTok and video-sharing platforms like YouTube.The age restrictions apply to all minors under 15, following a graduated approach. Children under three are barred entirely from social media and other high-risk services.From three to 13, children can access child-friendly services under adult supervision. Those aged 13 to 15 would get restricted access to social media and video-sharing platforms, with limited features and under parental control.Safety-by-design rules remain in place for minors aged 15 to 18, even though teenagers in this age group could access the platforms without parental consent.Companies like Meta and Google will have to verify users' age when they open a new account, using an EU-wide age-verification app or other national solutions that check only whether the user is above a certain age.Proportionate verification is required for existing accounts, based for instance on how long the user has subscribed to the service.Safety by designThe draft EU Kids Act includes a list of dos and don'ts that tech companies will have to follow to ensure their digital services provide a safe, age-appropriate experience.In particular, the bill bans design features such as infinite scrolling, artificial notifications and certain reward mechanisms.Recommender systems, the algorithms that choose which content to display, should be designed to avoid so-called "rabbit holes" and other recommendations driven purely by engagement-based signals.Risky settings should be disabled by default, while minors' account content would have to be set to private, with unknown users unable to contact them. Reporting harmful content should be made easy.The bill also envisages offering parents age-appropriate parental control tools."These rules and principles will be complemented by tailored commitments for online games, AI chatbots and companions, offering a co-regulatory approach based on industry-led self-regulation," the document reads.EnforcementBrussels has often been criticised for being too soft in enforcing its digital rules, as the online environment tends to move too fast for public authorities to keep up.As a result, the Commission is proposing to shift the burden onto tech companies to prove they are complying with child-safety rules.Online services already subject to the Digital Services Act's stricter regime, because they are deemed to pose a systemic risk to society, will have to seek authorisation from the Commission before rolling out any new features that could affect children.Tech companies would be charged a supervisory fee to finance enforcement.

Headline: Yemen's Houthis claim they shot down Saudi fighter jet, deny targeting Mecca
Body: Yemen's Houthis on Wednesday said they shot down a Saudi fighter jet, claiming they used munitions made by the group to target the warplane."The Yemeni Armed Forces, with Allah's aid and grace, succeeded in shooting down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet while it was carrying out hostile operations," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on social media, while accusing Saudi Arabia of launching 450 strikes.He said the aircraft had been targeted "using a locally made air-to-air missile".The spokesman also dismissed Saudi claims that the Houthis had targeted Islam's holy city of Mecca."Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites," he said, adding that "fabrications and lies propagated by the criminal al-Saud regime cannot deceive anyone."The Saudi coalition vowed retaliation, warning that the security of holy sites was a "red line"."The security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line, and the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the terrorist Houthi militia," the coalition said in a statement shared by spokesman Turki al-Maliki on X.Saudi Arabia had issued brief alerts on Tuesday over possible attacks in Mecca and across swathes of the kingdom's south, which borders Yemen.The alerts, including the first one issued in Mecca since the Iran war erupted in February, came a day after a wave of ballistic missile and drone attacks launched from Yemen wounded 13 people in the kingdom's south.Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned on Wednesday "in the strongest possible terms the dastardly and heinous" attack on Mecca."The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act," he said on X.The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, a 57-member bloc of Muslim-majority countries, also condemned the "heinous" attack.The Houthis are Zaydi Shia Muslims, a specific branch of Islam historically rooted in northern Yemen that is theologically distinct from both the Twelver Shia Islam dominant in Iran and Saudi Arabia's Wahhabi-influenced Sunni tradition.Mecca is Islam's holiest site, home to the Kaaba — which Muslims worldwide turn toward for prayer — and the destination of the Hajj pilgrimage, one of the faith's Five Pillars or main tenets.Any confirmed attack on the city would put the perpetrators beyond the pale in the eyes of virtually the entire Muslim world, Shia and Sunni alike.Warnings over Bab el-Mandeb spikeFormally known as Ansar Allah, the Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with the internationally recognised government forces since Yemen's civil war reignited in July.The fighting in the Arabian Peninsula's poorest country has forced 82,000 people to flee their homes since the start of September, according to the UN.Yemen's permanent representative at the UN Abdullah al-Saadi said his compatriots were fighting to restore "national institutions across every inch of their land", and called on the international community to take action against the Houthis.The group has also declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and has been targeting its ships in the Red Sea.In a lightning offensive last week, the Houthis seized control of the entirety of Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb strait.One of the world's crucial waterways connecting the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and the main chokehold on the cargo route to the Mediterranean and Europe has become vital to Saudi crude exports as the wider Middle East war chokes the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.The Houthis have insisted that there is no threat to navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb except for Saudi vessels.Any attacks in the waterway are likely to make it less attractive to shippers.Disruption in the strait could also endanger Egypt, as the Red Sea serves as the gateway to the Suez Canal, on which Cairo relies for crucial foreign revenue.Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi called on Tuesday for "ensuring the freedom and security of maritime navigation" through the Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, the Egyptian presidency said.On Tuesday, Qatar warned of dire consequences if Bab el-Mandeb was closed, saying it would be "catastrophic for the entire world".US media reported last week that the Saudi crown prince made a personal request to President Donald Trump for US intervention, but it was turned down. Neither Riyadh nor Washington have issued any statements regarding these reports.However, a US military task force is working to enhance intelligence-sharing and planning assistance for Saudi forces as they face attacks, a US official told AFP on Tuesday.Canal revenues are currently around half of what they were before the Houthis first started attacking Red Sea shipping in 2023, a campaign they said was in solidarity with Palestinians during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza.The Houthis have also targeted oil infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, the world's leading crude exporter, pushing global prices above the $100-a-barrel threshold.The Saudi-led coalition said it would deal with the attacks "firmly to protect the sovereignty of the Kingdom", and would take "all necessary operational measures to deter this ... hostile and extremist approach".The Houthis are tied to Tehran's so-called Axis of Resistance — a loose network of militant groups in several countries in the region including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and militias in Iraq, all backed, trained and equipped by the IRGC to varying degrees.

Headline: At least 60 dead after gold mine collapses in Sudan
Body: At least 60 small-scale miners are dead, with many missing, after the collapse of a gold mine in Sudan's West Kordofan region.The mine reportedly began to collapse on Tuesday after two shafts that had been dug close together began to give way.Survivors say they do not know how many people remain trapped.One surviving miner Khair al-Sayyed Jabara told AFP there had been an overnight rescue operation since the collapse, and that fellow miners were having to dig using the same rudimentary tools they use to mine."Everyone's working very hard to retrieve the bodies or any survivors, but it's difficult. We need heavy machinery to clear the rock and soil."Heavy machinery is often not readily available at small-scale mining sites. Sudan’s gold industry has become increasingly important since the civil war began in April 2023, providing a significant source of revenue in an economy devastated by conflict.The civil war began in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. As a result, the country is facing the world’s largest displacement crisis, with nearly 20 million people experiencing crisis-level hunger.

Headline: Von der Leyen's heatwave plan comes as Europe runs out of time to adapt
Body: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced a "new European heatwave plan" during her inaugural State of the Union speech on Wednesday, after a dramatic summer that saw thousands of hectares burnt and tonnes of crops lost to raging wildfires."We need better early warning systems and better health preparedness. We need urban adaptation and cooling. And we need to support the most vulnerable," von der Leyen told EU lawmakers in Strasbourg.She described the summer as a “summer of truth”, pointing to hundreds of thousands of hectares burned, crop losses and more than 35,000 excess deaths. However, the timing is hard to ignore. The EU needs no further warning that extreme heat is becoming a major climate risk—it has just experienced it, with repeated heatwaves sweeping across Europe this summer.The continent experienced an exceptionally early heatwave in May, with daily average temperatures in parts of western France, England and Wales more than 10°C above normal. June then brought another intense heatwave across much of Europe, while western Europe recorded its second-highest June temperature on record. By the time the Commission unveils its package, much of the emergency work that a heatwave plan is supposed to prepare Europe for will already have happened — or failed to happen.Failed strategies?However, the EU won't start from zero.Its 2021 Adaptation Strategy already set out the goal of making Europe climate-resilient, while the bloc's Mission on Adaptation is supporting regions and communities in building resilience. But heat has largely remained a national and local responsibility, leaving a patchwork of warning systems, cooling measures, building standards, worker protections and emergency responses.The new European Heatwave Plan, unveiled by von der Leyen on 16 September, matters less because Brussels is finally recognising heatwaves as a European-wide problem than because of what it actually requires governments to do.The Commission’s biggest challenge will be deciding whether to establish a coordination framework or step in where national action is proving insufficient.Cooling is an obvious example. A European survey cited by the Commission's Sustainable Energy Week found that 26% of EU households could not keep their homes comfortably cool in 2023, rising to almost 35% among the lowest-income households. That turns extreme heat from a climate issue into a broader challenge spanning energy, housing and social policy. Simply telling Europeans to install air conditioning is not much of a solution if millions simply can't afford it.Urban residents face another challenge. Concrete-dominated cities can remain dangerously hot overnight, while hospitals, schools, care homes and workplaces must be equipped to cope with temperatures that were once considered exceptional.A serious European heatwave strategy would need to link cooling with building renovation, urban greening, water management, electricity demand and social protection, rather than treating extreme heat as a short-term weather emergency. This would require the Commission to adopt a truly holistic approach.Ticking bombMeanwhile, climate projections point towards more frequent and intense heat, while the EU's climate center, Copernicus, estimates that Europe already recorded about 62,800 heat-related deaths in 2024, following roughly 47,700 in 2023 and 61,700 in 2022. "More than 35,000 additional deaths during the heatwaves. Care homes and hospitals dangerously overheated. And all of this is a mere preview. These were the hottest summer months ever — but probably the coolest of the years to come," von der Leyen said.For years, the EU’s climate debate focused largely on how quickly emissions could be cut. Now, the Commission must urgently determine how to adapt to the warming already locked in — a daunting task, as the newly announced plan highlights the gap between Brussels’ climate ambitions and the pace of implementation on the ground.Facing a financial gap amounting to billions of euros, Von der Leyen also announced the setup of a Climate Insurance Alliance, noting that only around 25% of catastrophe losses in Europe are covered by private insurance."This means that, far too often, national budgets become the insurer of last resort. We need to take action to close this gap," the Commission chief said.

Headline: Tajikistan looks to a new chapter after 35 years of independence
Body: As Tajikistan celebrates 35 years of independence, the milestone offers an opportunity to reflect on how far the nation has come while looking towards the years ahead.Thirty-five years into independence, with decades of peace and stability established, Tajikistan turns increasingly outward. The country’s international agenda is now focused on tackling some of the defining challenges of the modern world, from peacebuilding and water security to climate change and digitisation.In an anniversary address in Dushanbe on 8 September, President Emomali Rahmon highlighted Tajikistan’s ongoing commitment to promoting global peace, referencing the nation’s role in advancing the UN resolution for a “Decade for Strengthening Peace for Future Generations,” from 2027.Another proposal by Tajikistan saw the United Nations General Assembly adopt a resolution to establish the International Day of Safe, Secure and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence, to be observed annually on 31 August.Taken together, the two initiatives offer a glimpse of how Tajikistan seeks to frame its next 35 years within a global context, looking outwards to address shared challenges of digital transformation and sustainable development for the health and prosperity of future generations.35 years of independence and peacebuildingTajikistan declared independence on 9 September 1991, following the dissolution of the Soviet Union. The early years were marked by civil conflict, with a peace agreement reached in 1997.President Emomali Rahmon, who has led Tajikistan since the early years of independence, has placed peace, national unity and stability at the centre of the country’s development narrative.Since gaining independence, the country has rebuilt infrastructure, expanded energy and transport networks, and developed education and social services, while strengthening connections with neighbouring countries and the wider world.To celebrate the milestone, anniversary events are taking place across Tajikistan, including cultural performances in Bokhtar and a military parade in the capital of Dushanbe. In his address at the National Theatre, President Rahmon spoke about the country’s progress and his vision for Tajiks to be recognised internationally as a forward-looking society.That ambition is reflected in investments in the skills, digital infrastructure and institutions needed to participate in an increasingly technology-driven global economy. Water, diplomacy and sustainable growth Tajikistan’s mountainous landscape offers a huge clue to one of the nation’s defining priorities.Tajikistan is home to snowfields and glaciers that bring water down from the Pamir and other mountain ranges to feed rivers across the region. It is one of Central Asia’s most important sources of freshwater, with a water security strategy that matters well beyond its borders.Tajikistan has pushed water security and sustainable management higher on the global agenda, contributing to the establishment of the UN’s Water Action Decade (2018-2028) which has created cross-border projects, promotions and partnerships in efforts to avert a global water crisis.In line with national energy strategy, Tajikistan seeks to further harness its significant hydropower potential, with large-scale renewable energy projects such as the World Bank-funded Rogun Hydropower Plant playing a central role in its plans to improve domestic energy security and strengthen regional connectivity.All this spills over into another of Tajikistan’s priorities: technology. In May 2026, Tajikistan and the United Nations convened a ‘Water and AI: A Two-Way Nexus’ forum in Dushanbe, examining how artificial intelligence could support more sustainable water management while considering the water demands of AI itself.All this illustrates how Tajikistan’s priorities are evolving beyond its own borders, looking to shared technologies and regional cooperation in its strategy to tackle challenges that will shape the coming decades.Looking beyond 35 yearsTajikistan’s 35th anniversary is both a moment to reflect and to aspire.The country’s journey since independence has included the difficult work of establishing peace and stability, rebuilding after conflict and developing the foundations of a modern economy.The next 35 years will bring a different set of challenges – from managing water resources and adapting to climate change to creating economic opportunities while navigating rapid digitisation.As celebrations take place across the country, Tajikistan is looking towards a future in which it plays a growing role not only in tackling challenges at home, but in bringing them to the international spotlight.

Headline: Fallen firefighter given standing ovation as Von der Leyen promises action on wildfires
Body: Ursula von der Leyen says this summer of extreme heat was a "mere preview" of the high temperatures to come.The President of the European Commission spoke about climate very early in the speech, before mentioning AI or migration.She did not mince her words when she listed the many places around Europe that experienced extreme weather this summer leading, she said, to 35,000 excess deaths.She called the the repeated heatwaves "a summer of truth" in the annual State of the Union speech, in which policy and plans for the year ahead are laid out.In a moving moment, she introduced the family of a firefighter who died fighting flames. The parliament gave a prolonged standing ovation in honour of the fallen hero.What action will EU take after summer of extreme heat?Von der Leyen said Europe "can, must and will stay the course of our climate targets".She said mitigation, adaptation and preparedness must lie at the heart of Europe's approach to tackling extreme weather.Von der Leyen announced a European Heatwave Plan, saying "there can be no repeat of this summer.""We need better early warning systems and better health preparedness. We need urban adaptation and cooling. And we need to support the most vulnerable," von der Leyen said. The most common type of cooling - air conditioning - was the subject of intense debate around Europe this summer, as many questioned whether they should install it int he face of unprecedented temperatures.'We will identify 100 of the most vulnerable territories in Europe'Von der Leyen recognises that climate adaptation is becoming an immediate economic and public policy challenge rather than a long-term environmental issue, reports Euronews' Marta Pacheco, who is based in Brussels."We will present a new framework for climate resilience next month. We will identify 100 of the most vulnerable territories in Europe. And we will assess the risks — and at which level they should be managed," the Commission chief recalled as 660,000 hectares were burnt to the ground and roughly 12 million tonnes of crops were lost.Von der Leyen also announced a new Climate Insurance Alliance."Today, only around 25 per cent of catastrophe losses in Europe are covered by private insurance. This means that, far too often, national budgets become the insurer of last resort. We need to take action to close this gap," the Commission chief told MEPs in Strasbourg.

Headline: The 50 Best Hotels 2026: Rosewood Hong Kong named No.1 as 21 European hotels included in ranking
Body: Europe has once again dominated The 50 Best Hotels list, with 21 properties on the continent making the cut for 2026.Asia came in a close second, with 18 hotels, followed by North America with six, South America and Africa with two apiece, and one in Oceania.The World’s Best Hotel gong went to Rosewood Hong Kong, which first took the title last year, having been placed third in 2024. The ranking is now in its fourth edition.The 413-key skyscraper property above Victoria Harbour was praised for its foodie credentials, with 11 restaurants and bars across the 65 storeys, as well as its wellness offering, with the multi-level Asaya spa and a 25-metre-long infinity pool.“Rosewood Hong Kong retaining its No.1 position for a second consecutive year underlines Asia’s continued influence at the very highest level, while Europe’s strong representation and this year’s 10 new entries point to a dynamic, diverse and competitive global hotel landscape,” Faye Huggett, director of community for The 50 Best Hotels, said.“As The 50 evolves, our ambition is to continue to champion the people, places and ideas setting the agenda for the future of hospitality.”The best hotels in EuropeRanked in top spot in 2023, Lake Como’s Passalacqua is the highest-ranked European hotel for the second year in a row, coming in fifth, one place lower than in 2025.The 18th-century property has just 24 rooms, and was also handed the Best Boutique Hotel Award for the third consecutive year.Four Seasons Firenze was the next best-ranked European property, coming in 12th.Both Italy and France have six hotels on the list. The remaining four in Italy are Casa Maria Luigia in Modena (18th), Bulgari Roma (32nd), Portrait Milano (39th) and San Domenico Palace in Taormina (50th).Casa Maria Luigia was the highest new entry on the list, while you’ll likely recognise San Domenico Palace as being the setting for the second season of The White Lotus.In France, four of the top-ranked hotels are in Paris – Hôtel de Crillon (14th), Le Bristol (19th), Cheval Blanc Paris (20th) and Plaza Athénée (41st). Hôtel du Couvent in Nice ranked in 38th place while winning the Johnnie Walker Art of Design Award, while Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc placed 44th.Across the Channel, four hotels in the UK made the 50 Best, including three in London: Claridge’s (13th), Raffles London at The OWO (28th), and The Connaught (49th). Estelle Manor in Witney was the exception outside of the UK capital, claiming number 43.The other European entries on the list are as follows: Four Seasons Astir Palace in Greece (27th), The Peninsula Istanbul in Türkiye (31st), Badrutt's Palace in Switzerland (36th), Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo in Monaco (40th), and Hotel Sacher Vienna in Austria (42nd).The top 20 hotels in the worldRosewood Hong KongCapella Bangkok, ThailandFour Seasons Bangkok at Chao Phraya River, BangkokAtlantis The Royal, Dubai, UAEPassalacqua, Lake Como, ItalyRosewood São Paulo, BrazilMandarin Oriental Qianmen, Beijing, ChinaUpper House Hong KongChablé Yucatán, Chocholá, MexicoMandarin Oriental Bangkok, ThailandAman Tokyo, JapanFour Seasons Firenze, Florence, ItalyClaridge’s, London, UKHôtel de Crillon, Paris, FranceJumeirah Marsa Al Arab, Dubai, UAECapella Sydney, AustraliaRaffles SingaporeCasa Maria Luigia, Modena, ItalyLe Bristol, Paris, FranceCheval Blanc Paris, FranceHow the rankings are decidedThe 50 Best Hotels list is decided by an 800-strong academy. There are 13 academy chairs split across 13 geographical regions who create their voting panel, which consists of hoteliers, travel journalists, hotel educators, business travellers and consumer travel aficionados.Academy members cast seven votes for any hotel they have stayed in around the world (no matter which region they live in) in order of preference. Headline: Five killed in Russian drone strike on bus in southern Ukraine
Body: Five people have been killed and at least seven are injured after a Russian drone strike hit a bus carrying passengers near the frontline in southern Ukraine.The bus was travelling on a known route in the Nikopol district. In a post on Telegram, the regional governor of Dnipropetrovsk, Oleksandr Ganzha said: "Five people have been killed and at least seven wounded as a result of an enemy strike on a minibus in the Nikopol district. The Russians hit the bus with a drone,".Photos provided by the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration show a white minibus with windows blown out and blood streaming down one side of the vehicle.Nikopol is on the opposite bank of the Dnieper river, across from the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, which has been occupied by Russian troops since the start of the invasion in 2022.

Headline: EU digital wallet: 24 of 27 members will miss the deadline
Body: The EU is asking countries to offer at least one certified digital wallet by the end of 2026. Before the deadline, EU-funded pilot projects with 350 organisations issued over 1,500 digital credentials and completed more than 8,000 cross-border transactions.The free wallet can hold national IDs, driving licences, diplomas, health insurance, and bank details. It uses three safeguards: selective disclosure, unlikability, and issuer-blindness. Using the wallet is optional, and paper documents are still valid.The rollout is uneven across countries. Italy leads with almost 8 million monthly users. Germany plans to launch in January 2027, while the Netherlands postponed its rollout to late 2027 after a pilot had only 57 users. Bulgaria is still working on legislation.Businesses must accept the wallet by December 24, 2027, but banks need to comply earlier, starting in July 2027, because of anti-money-laundering rules. The digital rights group EDRi has raised concerns about draft rules that would require facial recognition and reduce privacy protections.

Headline: Belarus launches drills near Suwalki Gap on Polish and Lithuanian borders
Body: Belarus has begun four-day military exercises near its borders with Poland and Lithuania, as Ukraine reported that Russia was using Belarusian relay stations to guide drone attacks on targets in western Ukraine.The drills involve mechanised and tank battalions training in border protection, "counter-sabotage operations" and defence against drone and light aircraft attacks, the Belarusian defence ministry said, according to Radio Svaboda, the Belarusian service of Radio Free Europe.The exercises are taking place partly near the Suwałki Gap, a 104-kilometre stretch of the Polish-Lithuanian border that serves as the only land link between the Baltic states and the rest of NATO, and separates Belarus from Russia's Kaliningrad exclave.Locations include the Hoża training ground on the Lithuanian border and the Brzeski and Różański ranges, approximately 15 and 60 kilometres from the Polish border respectively.The Belarusian defence ministry described the exercises as "purely defensive" and said the number of troops and equipment involved did not exceed the thresholds set by the 2011 Vienna Document, which would require prior notification of other states. No figure has been given for the number of soldiers taking part.Belarus' autocrat leader Aliaksandr Lukashenka visited the Obuz-Lesnowski training ground near Baranavichy on 11 September, saying he wanted to assess the state of the entire national security apparatus.Belarus has held exercises near NATO borders for years, frequently involving Russian forces. The Slavic Brotherhood manoeuvres took place in the Brest area in 2020, followed by the Zapad 21 exercises in 2021.In February 2022, Minsk allowed Russian forces to use Belarusian territory and infrastructure to launch its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.Belarusian forces have not taken part in direct combat on Ukrainian territory, and under humanitarian law criteria cited by Radio Svaboda, Belarus is not considered a party to the war.The logistical and military support it has provided to Russia has drawn sustained international criticism and triggered successive rounds of Western sanctions.The EU expanded its Belarus sanctions regime in March 2022 specifically in response to Minsk allowing Russian forces to attack Ukraine from its territory, adding trade restrictions affecting 70% of Belarusian import volumes and targeting military sector officials.Further rounds followed in 2023 and 2024, progressively aligning Belarus sanctions with those imposed on Russia and introducing export bans on sensitive technologies, firearms and aviation equipment. The US and UK imposed parallel measures.The EU also introduced tariffs on Belarusian agricultural goods and fertilisers, which took effect in July 2025.

Headline: EU's von der Leyen calls for pacing frontier AI models
Body: The EU will support industry efforts to slow the development of more disruptive AI technologies and will collaborate with partners such as Canada and the UK on AI safety, the Commission chief said on Wednesday.In her annual State of the Union address to the European Parliament, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen hailed AI's potential to benefit humanity, provided its risks and opportunities are properly balanced.She singled out the growing risks posed by so-called frontier AI models, those pushing the boundaries of the technology."As the frontier models become more capable, these risks have come sharper into focus. Models being developed will allow hacking on a level we never thought possible. And they will soon be in the hands of adversaries who see the world very differently to us," she said.The Commission President referred to recent incidents in which AI agents escaped their testing environments and independently hacked other systems, as occurred in the OpenAI-Hugging Face breach in July."CEOs of the most advanced companies tell us that it is time to slow down on the self-recursive models. To pace the frontier. If the people developing the technology are clear, then we should be too," von der Leyen continued.The EU already has one of the world's most comprehensive laws on artificial intelligence, the AI Act, which gives the Commission oversight of risk-mitigation measures for the most advanced models."We will step up together with our like-minded partners like Canada, the UK and others. We want to team up on model evaluation, verification, early-warning, AI security and much more," she added.The Commission chief also announced she will convene a discussion with leading AI labs on how public authorities can support industry efforts to pace the frontier of this disruptive technology.

Headline: Iran war has cost the US more than $38 billion so far, says Congressional Budget Office
Body: The US had spent more than $38 billion (€33 billion) on its war with Iran by the beginning of August, according to the country's Congressional Budget Office (CBO).The estimate covers costs incurred by the US Department of Defence from the start of the conflict on 28 February to 1 August, just over five months later.The Defence Department did not provide information to the CBO for its assessment, which instead relied on government databases and publicly available reports. The CBO said its estimates were therefore subject to “considerable uncertainty”.Nevertheless, the figure broadly aligns with an estimate given by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth in July, when he said the war had cost $37.5 billion.The largest proportion of the cost is reportedly the $21.7 billion that has been spent on replacing munitions.The CBO also warned about the depletion of missile-defence interceptors. It estimates the US has probably used between half and two-thirds of its inventory of those weapons since June 2025, leaving stocks depleted for several years.On Monday, a Pentagon inspector general report warned that the US-led military campaign against Iran, known as Operation Epic Fury, had resulted in “strategic inventory shortfalls”.The CBO also warned that the conflict is having a wider impact on the US economy, largely because disruption to oil and gas shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and Red Sea has pushed up energy costs.The estimate was prepared in response to a request for information from Representative Brendan Boyle, the top Democrat on the House Budget committee.Boyle criticised the amount spent: “this nonpartisan CBO report makes clear that the war has also cost American taxpayers tens of billions of dollars and counting, while continuing to drive up costs.”“Donald Trump and Republicans have spent years telling Americans that we cannot afford to help families here at home,” Boyle said in a statement, "but apparently they can find tens of billions of dollars, and potentially much more, for a reckless war that is leaving Americans to pay the price.”In June, the White House requested an additional $87.6 billion (€76 billion) in supplemental funding, much of it for the war effort. Congress has not approved the request.

Headline: US plans to send bombs to Israel in $2.8 billion weapons deal
Body: The US is planning to deliver a package of 40,000 powerful bombs to Israel as part of an upcoming arms deal. The $2.8 billion (€2.42 billion) deal includes 2,000-pound (900 kg) Mk84 and BLU-117 aircraft bombs, according to two US officials and a person familiar with the plan who spoke on condition of anonymity.The same weapons prompted concerns about the possibility of mass casualties in Gaza, and their delivery was put on hold by the the Biden administration two years ago. Trump lifted that hold when he took office again.Congress has been informally notified about the pending deal, most of which is to be paid for with foreign military financing — in which US taxpayer dollars are given to Israel to turn around and buy the weapons from the United States.The proposed deal is just the latest in a series of Trump administration steps to improve Israel's military capacity. The conflict in Gaza has left tens of thousands of Palestinians dead and has decimated the enclave. The US had brokered a fragile ceasefire, but violence has continued.The package, which was reported earlier by The Washington Post, comes as Israel has faced increasing international isolation over its war in Gaza in response to the deadly attacks by Hamas on 7 October 2023.The sale signals that while the relationship between President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is reportedly strained, the US-Israel military relationship has not significantly weakened.The two countries launched the war against Iran in February. Trump had expressed frustration with Netanyahu tied to the Iran conflict before their latest meeting in July at the White House.Last year, the Trump administration bypassed a normal congressional review process and approved a nearly $3 billion sale to Israel that included more than 35,500 of the bombs. The administration then approved a new series of arms sales to Israel totalling $6.67 billion in January.

Headline: Ed Sheeran's support acts quit US tour after Macklemore dropped for pro-Palestinian comments
Body: The US tour of British pop singer Ed Sheeran has been thrown into jeopardy after all support acts quit in response to the rapper Macklemore being dropped from the line-up for making pro-Palestinian comments on stage.The move came hours after Sheeran took to social media to explain his views about Macklemore's ouster, attributing the decision to the tour's promoters, Messina Touring Group.“Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine,” Sheeran wrote on Instagram on Tuesday. “I would never let down the fans who had made plans, nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living."“I respect Macklemore’s strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes," Sheeran added. "However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: peace. I choose to use my fame and platform to be a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open, not closed.”But his words have seemingly failed to placate his support acts with Irish artists Aaron Rowe and Beoga, the Danish band Lukas Graham and Billie Eilish's brother Finneas all making their feelings clear on Instagram.“Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” Finneas said on Instagram. “I have decided to withdraw from my upcoming tour dates with Ed Sheeran. I stand with Palestine and its people.”Rowe and Beoga each cited their country’s history in their statements explaining their decision. “We are Irish people who understand colonialism. As founding members of the Irish Artists for Palestine movement, we are committed activists for justice and will continue to be,” Beoga said.Rowe called Sheeran a friend and said the British singer-songwriter changed his life. “But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation,” he said, adding that he couldn't “stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up.”Mixing pop and politicsEarlier this month, Macklemore posted a clip on social media of his perfomance at New Jersey's MetLife Stadium where he repeated "Free Palestine!" while introducing his protest song 'Hind's Hall.'“To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters, criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, it in no way is criticism of you,” he said during the concert.Macklemore said Monday on Instagram that several US venues told the promoter they would prohibit him from performing as Sheeran’s opening act, rallied by American billionaire Robert Kraft, owner of NFL’s New England Patriots. His Kraft Group also owns Gillette Stadium, where the Patriots play.In a statement Monday, Kraft said the decision to cancel Macklemore was a result of his recent comments “and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community.”Meanwhile, old pictures have emerged of Macklemore wearing a fake hooked nose and wig for which he has apologised.The moves by his fellow artists have put enormous pressure on Sheeran, who has tried to avoid politics and taking a side in the Gaza conflict, arguing that his fans don't come to his shows to hear politics.

Headline: The 'silent waste' of Greek seas: Thousands of concrete blocks lifted from seabed
Body: More than 6,000 concrete blocks and thousands of synthetic ropes, which are used illegally by traditional Mediterranean fishing vessels and then abandoned at sea, have been recovered from Greek waters in recent years.Abandoned fishing gear makes up a significant share of the waste that ends up on the seabed. Its removal is at the heart of the Fishing For Litter programme, run by the Athanasios C. Laskaridis Public Benefit Foundation, in partnership with the environmental organisation iSea.According to iSea's Communications Manager, Anastasia Charitou, since 2019, when the programme began, 6,278 concrete blocks and around 11,700 ropes linked to fishing boat activity have been recovered and recorded."The biggest problem is found in the Euboean Gulf, followed by the Thracian Sea and the Thermaic Gulf," says Charitou.Since 2019, fishers taking part in the programme have removed more than 360 tonnes of waste from deep waters. Over 83 per cent of it is plastic, while 34 per cent consists of abandoned fishing gear.The programme is continuing this year across Greece, with the participation of 67 fishing vessels and an expanded geographical reach.How do concrete blocks end up on the seabed?The problem is linked, among other things, to a practice used during night-time fishing with gri-gri, traditional Mediterranean fishing boats.After the fish have been located, fish-aggregating light devices known as 'robots' are deployed. These are small floating boats equipped with lamps, which are lowered into the water near the fishing vessel in order to attract and concentrate the shoals.As iSea notes in its report titled 'The silent waste of fishing – How synthetic ropes and concrete blocks pollute the seas', the fish are attracted by the light source, which simulates moonlight.To keep the light devices stable, they need to be anchored. The General Port Regulations stipulate that 'robots' must be deployed with appropriate anchors and lifted out of the water once the fishing activity is finished.In theory, special small anchors are connected to the devices by chains. At the end of the process, the 'lampsman', the crew member who monitors the fish around the lights, gradually hauls in the equipment, steering the shoal towards the main vessel at the same time.However, according to iSea, because the prescribed procedure is more time-consuming, in some cases it is replaced by an improvised and illegal practice.Instead of anchors, concrete blocks are used, usually two for each light device, which are attached with polypropylene ropes, the so-called 'gri-gri ropes'.When the time comes to recover the light devices, the ropes are cut. The 'robots' quickly return to the vessel, but the concrete blocks and severed ropes remain on the seabed.In this way, a practice that saves time for the crew turns into a permanent source of waste on the sea floor.Thousands of kilos of solid waste on the seabed"The concrete blocks are passively fished by the fishers. They get tangled in their nets and are thus removed from great depths. Those that are recovered and recorded in the programme weigh around four to five kilos each," Charitou explains.On the basis of the 6,278 concrete blocks recorded to date alone, this amounts to dozens of tonnes of solid material that had been abandoned at sea.The problem, however, is not limited to the volume of waste.Synthetic ropes and concrete blocks accumulate on the seabed and put pressure on benthic ecosystems, affecting organisms and habitats that are in direct contact with the sea floor.At the same time, polypropylene ropes, because of their low weight, can hang in the water column and wrap around the propellers of other vessels, causing mechanical damage, as well as entangling marine life and breaking down into toxic microplastics that fish ingest.Similarly, when concrete blocks get caught in fishing nets, they can damage the equipment and destroy part of the catch.Impacts on biodiversity and fishingFor iSea, this practice is not simply a matter of marine pollution. Leaving these materials on the seabed harms ecosystems, creates risks for other vessels and adds yet another stress factor in marine areas that are already under pressure from overfishing and the accumulation of waste.The organisation stresses that tackling the phenomenon requires stricter and more systematic inspections to ensure the existing legislation is applied, as well as the imposition of the penalties provided for.Among the measures proposed are beefing up on-the-spot checks at sea, and inspections when fishing vessels leave and return to port.At the same time, according to iSea, a clearer description of the gri-gri fishing gear in legislation is needed, especially with regard to the auxiliary fish-aggregating light devices and their anchoring equipment.The aim is to fully clarify what constitutes the correct and lawful way of using them, so that a practice which today leaves thousands of "silent waste" items on the seabed can be effectively curbed.

Headline: Fishing waste from as far away as US and Canada washes up on Portuguese beaches
Body: Since 2010, researchers at the University of the Azores have been monitoring waste brought in from the sea, until they began noticing the same objects appearing again and again."We started to realise that these items, which at first we did not know where they came from, had certain numbers on them. And when we started to find quite a lot, we began trying to look up what they actually meant," explains Christopher Pham, researcher and head of the marine litter research group at the University of the Azores.It turned out that the objects were coming from the lobster fishery, a sector with significant economic weight along the North American Atlantic coast. They also realised that the numbers printed on some of these plastics were mandatory tags that make it possible to identify their origin and date.That is how a study involving scientists and volunteers began."We asked local people and colleagues that if they went to the beach and managed to find these items, they should bring them back," says Christopher Pham. "We had at least ten people who were very interested and kept sending us material every month."Between 2017 and 2025, they found more than 1,500 items on the beaches of Faial and Pico.These two islands are part of the Portuguese archipelago of the Azores, located in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, about 1,600 km from mainland Europe.Waste travels more than 3,000 kmThese items are objects or fragments of objects that are placed in the sea to catch lobster, such as corners and clips from the pots (cage-like traps), funnels or tags.The tags with legible inscriptions had their origin in the United States (63%) and Canada (37%). Within the United States, the tags referred mainly to the state of Maine (80%) and Massachusetts (11%). The tags from Canada refer to the province of Newfoundland and Labrador.The study, published this summer, says it is an example 'of how an isolated oceanic archipelago is directly exposed to plastic waste from a coastal fishery that operates more than 3,000 km away'.For waste to make the journey across the ocean from the North American coast to these Atlantic islands is not exactly a surprise to the researchers; it is more a confirmation. This movement of debris had already been suggested by models showing the behaviour of currents, winds and waves."We know there is that direct link and it was to be expected that we would receive particles from this part of the Atlantic, because the currents really circulate clockwise, from west to east," says Christopher Pham, explaining that this study validates those models.And although this study is limited to the islands of Pico and Faial, this waste can travel much further, even all the way to mainland Europe."These lobster-fishing items are also quite frequent along the Portuguese coast and even in England and Ireland," adds the researcher.More than 40 years in natureThe researchers were also able to determine the age of part of this waste because among it there are tags stamped with the year of registration.Most of the tags are between 7 and 13 years old. The most recent dates from 2023 and the oldest from 1983, meaning it was put into the sea more than 40 years ago. This shows that these plastics can reach the Azores in just two years and then remain in the environment for many decades without breaking up."Most of the items entered the sea many years ago. That is also significant because it shows that plastic has enormous persistence in the environment", says Pham."It is very likely that, if we keep looking, we will find things that are perhaps even older. Because these tags are made from very high-quality plastic."Access to this information was possible because this industry in North America requires this material to be tagged, even though the rules differ between the United States and Canada, for example in terms of the information provided and how long the tags remain valid.More waste on Azores beachesLobster fishing is the most economically important fishing activity in the United States and Canada. In 2020, lobster exports from the two countries were worth around 1.74 billion euros.Estimates suggest that every year three million pots (traps) are deployed off the coast of the United States and two million off Canada to catch these crustaceans.But lobster fishing is not the only source of pollution on Azores beaches. There is other fishing-related waste on these beaches in the middle of the Atlantic, but it is less common and cannot be traced back to its source."We found trawl nets, but a trawl net can be used in Greenland or in Brazil. In those cases we no longer know where it comes from," explains Cristopher Pham."Sometimes we manage to find some pots that are typical of octopus fishing, but these traps are used from Spain all the way to Morocco; they are not as specific as in the case of lobster."Other types of waste also wash up on these beaches, and they can come from anywhere."We almost never know the precise geographic location. Sometimes we have Chinese bottles, but we do not know if they come from China. They probably come from a Chinese ship that was offshore and threw the bottle into the sea," says Christopher.Besides bottles, there are also cigarette butts, shoe soles and lighters. But the most common waste consists of small pieces of plastic, "a 2-centimetre white piece of plastic", fragments of an unrecognisable object."All these towns that are dumping huge amounts of plastic into streams," says Christopher Pham. "With sunlight and the action of the sea, it starts to fragment and then you get that soup of fragments that entered the sea many years ago but are no longer recognisable in their original form."Tackling the problem at sourceOnly by knowing where these objects come from can we take measures at the source to solve the problem. That is why labelling fishing gear, as happens in the lobster industry, is so important.The Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations (FAO) has issued recommendations that gear used in fishing should be identifiable. The scientists at the University of the Azores stress how important it is to adopt this practice.The team behind this study also has specific recommendations for the fishing industry in North America. These include better management of gear, incentives to hand in old material and the creation of collection points.For these researchers, the next step is to carry out a more systematic analysis, in terms of the density and volume of waste from lobster fishing."To try to understand whether this is increasing or decreasing and what proportion it represents in the overall picture of plastic pollution – what contribution these items make," explains Christopher Pham.But they believe the most important work has already been done: alerting the authorities in the United States and Canada, so that they act."It is important that you take action to reduce this flow of plastic into the sea, because people who have nothing to do with the pollution are becoming victims," Christopher Pham concludes.

Headline: Strasbourg stage set for von der Leyen’s big moment
Body: There is a saying in Brussels: in a legislative term, you spend the first year thinking about what you want to do, the second year announcing it, and the third to fifth years actually doing it.By that logic, this is von der Leyen's last real window to unveil big initiatives she might still see through before she leaves office. So, what made the cut, and what won't? Let's dive in.Three tipping points are shaping von der Leyen's speech: climate change turning from forecast to lived reality after devastating wildfires and heatwaves, AI technology moving faster than anticipated, and the industrial competitiveness drive intertwined with relations with China.On climate, von der Leyen will have to walk a tightrope between conservative lawmakers pushing for adaptation – with improved preparedness for natural disasters and closing the insurance gap – and progressive MEPs demanding she stay true to the mitigation drive of the Green Deal with an eye for international climate diplomacy.On artificial intelligence, she will need to balance the risks of frontier AI models progressing at neck-breaking speed – like job losses, cybersecurity, and loss of control – against the potential benefits of wider technological uptake.On the economy, beyond the usual nods to competitiveness, expect references to cutting dependence on energy imports and boosting the EU's clean tech sector, as the war in Iran pushes energy prices higher.On China, with an October deadline looming for Beijing to make trade concessions in talks with Brussels, von der Leyen is unlikely to pre-empt the negotiations, but could send a strong signal about what happens if they collapse.Ukraine will also feature prominently, with the Commission bracing for Kyiv to endure a brutal winter as Russia intensifies its campaign of ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones against civilian infrastructure.More broadly, Russia's ongoing campaign of sabotage and drone incursions across Europe — the attempted attack in Leipzig its most prominent example — is set to draw strong condemnation, as hybrid threats tip into kinetic reality.On sanctions against Moscow, a 22nd package is in the works but unlikely to be ready for announcement. Instead, expect von der Leyen to double down on enforcement, pointing to ways of shutting down circumvention.She'll also give an extensive preview of an upcoming proposal, due on Thursday and leaked for you by yours truly, to restrict under-15s' access to social media and video-sharing platforms.Canada will be the elephant in the room: Mark Carney's arrival in Strasbourg could steal von der Leyen's thunder when he addresses the Parliament on Thursday. Expect some opening remarks on bringing Canada as close to the EU as possible, short of full membership that is prevented by the treaties.Finally, on migration, von der Leyen will focus on implementation of the new migration pact, touting the recent drop in EU asylum applications, while pledging to ramp up the bloc's crisis management capacity — incidentally, EU border agency Frontex is due for a review later this year.Migration remains a raw nerve for von der Leyen's centrist coalition in the aftermath of the Ceuta crisis, after a plenary debate on Tuesday turned into a shouting match between right-wing and left-leaning MEPs.In this climate, references to the controversial proposal to finance return hubs in third countries with EU money are unlikely to feature, given that member states are already entangled in a complex negotiation on the bloc’s next long-term budget.Still, expect the unexpected. Von der Leyen likes to drop a surprise or two, jealously guarded until the very last moment — case in point, nobody saw last year's proposal to suspend the EU-Israel Association Agreement coming.NATO 'committed and ready' after shooting down drone over LithuaniaNATO stands "vigilant, committed, and ready," Lithuania's foreign minister said Tuesday, after an allied fighter jet destroyed a drone that crossed into the country's airspace from Belarus — the latest in a string of aerial incursions testing the alliance's eastern border with Russia.Kestutis Budrys credited the interception to the strength of collective defence, thanking the allies whose air presence, he said, protects Baltic skies and reinforces regional security.But the message lands beyond Vilnius: as Russia's war on Ukraine grinds on, the alliance's eastern members are increasingly treating airspace violations — deliberate or not — as tests of NATO's resolve, and Tuesday's response was framed as proof the system works.Simon Ormiston has more.More from our newsroomsECB staff raise stability concerns about rumours of Lagarde's early departure. In a letter seen by Euronews, European Central Bank staff members have questioned the institution’s stability in the face of rumours of the early departures of its president, Christine Lagarde, and board member Isabel Schnabel. Eleonora Vasques has more.US threatens EU with retaliation over European preference in EU budget. In a document sent to EU legislators and seen by Euronews, the US has threatened the EU with retaliation if it does not scrap European preference provisions in its multiannual budget, Peggy Corlin reports.Belarus concentrates forces near border with Poland and Lithuania in military drill. Belarus has begun four-day military exercises near its borders with Poland and Lithuania, the Belarusian service of Radio Free Europe reported, citing the defence ministry in Minsk. Mateusz Jaronski has the details.We're also keeping an eye onEuropean Council President António Costa meets the President of the European Investment Bank (EIB) Nadia CalviñoMembers of the European Parliament (MEPs) debate the need for the EU to support Ukraine against Russia’s escalationThat’s it for today. Luca Bertuzzi, Vincenzo Genovese, Sasha Vakulina and Jorge Liboreiro contributed to this newsletter.

Headline: Trump threatens to keep Kennedy Centre closed over name change row
Body: Most of the Kennedy Centre in Washington, DC will close for repairs following a board vote Tuesday, hours after a federal judge again blocked the landmark venue from being renamed after President Donald Trump.“Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” US District Judge Christopher Cooper said in the latest ruling Tuesday.Trump, in response to the ruling, said the $257 million (€223 million) allocated by Congress for the repairs would only be released if renaming was permitted. Federal courts have twice ruled cannot be met without Congressional approval.Judge Cooper ruled in May that the Kennedy Center illegally added Trump’s name to the building, ordering it removed. The institution’s leaders complied in June but left a tarp and scaffolding in place where Trump’s name was once displayed.The Justice Department has appealed the latest ruling.Trump, who was named the Kennedy Centre’s chairman last year by loyalists on the board, participated in the virtual board meeting and said on social media he’d given $17 million to an endowment intended to support the institution.The meeting included testy exchanges at points between Trump and Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat who has led the campaign to block efforts to memorialise the president at the Kennedy Centre.Fans worry about possible demolitionThe developments have thrown into limbo the fate of one of the US's most prominent cultural institutions, a place where presidents, lawmakers and celebrities of all political ideologies have gathered for decades to recognise and celebrate the best in American arts and culture.The venue’s leaders have long argued that the building, which began construction in 1965, was in dire need of renovations. A partial ceiling collapse in the building’s main hallway earlier this month intensified the calls for renovations.“The building is not currently built to last; the chairman knows that because he is among the best builders in the world,” Brian Ballard, Kennedy Centre board member, said in a statement.But Trump’s insistence on a physical recognition of his work, reminiscent of his tendency to add his name to buildings as a real estate developer, has been a persistent sticking point.It's the latest setback in Trump’s second-term bid to dramatically remake the US capital in his gilded tastes. He’s demolished the East Wing of the White House and is replacing it with a ballroom and plans to build a triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery. He’s also eyeing a golf course renovation along the Potomac River.The Kennedy Centre board voted in August to inscribe his name on the Kennedy Centre’s facade so it would read “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump.” If the Trump Kennedy Centre Fund reached $100 million, (approximately €86.66 million), another inscription would be added reading “Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.”The plaza in front of the Kennedy Centre would also be renamed in Trump’s honour.There are concerns that the administration may seek to demolish the Kennedy Center. According to a filing last month, administration lawyers told the court that absent recognition of the president, the Kennedy Center would struggle to raise money for renovations.Without that money, they suggested, the building may need to be demolished.

Headline: Spain sets out 2030 sustainable tourism strategy – with residents a ‘core’ focus
Body: Spain is on course to welcome 100 million international visitors this year, but amid concerns over mass tourism, the country is rethinking how it manages continued growth.In a presentation at Arabian Travel Market in Dubai, Carlos Ruiz González, director of the Spanish Tourist Office for the Gulf region at Turespaña, outlined how Spain’s Tourism 2030 plan will put people and sustainability at the centre of its next phase of growth – with residents and lesser-visited destinations a key focus. Developed in consultation with more than 200 tourism experts, businesses, government bodies and other organisations, the plan recognises that destinations across Spain face very different challenges. These range from mature coastal resorts and heavily visited cities such as Barcelona to rural and inland areas looking to attract more tourists. Spain, the world’s second-most visited country, welcomed 96.8 million international tourists in 2025, while tourism accounts for 12.6% of the country’s GDP and supports around three million jobs. Visitor numbers are continuing to rise in 2026, but the government is increasingly looking beyond arrivals as it considers how to manage growth and reduce pressure on destinations facing overcrowding. “For the last few years, our government has been thinking about what we should do to manage this success,” Ruiz González said. “We have some destinations that are dying of success, I would say. Well, we have a big country, a diverse country. “So, the government of Spain decided this has to be a full government policy, a country policy, and not just tourism. All the ministries, all the sectors in Spain are aligned.”How does Spain plan to make tourism more sustainable? Devised with a three-phase roadmap, which will be delivered through a series of two-year action plans, Spain Tourism 2030 is a government-wide policy covering economic, social and environmental sustainability. According to Ruiz González, the main challenges range from climate change and employment to housing pressures, overcrowding and regional depopulation. Recognised as a “core audience”, but “not a side effect of it”, residents are one of five groups at the centre of the new strategy, alongside destinations, businesses, tourism workers, and visitors. “We want the residents also to be part of the system,” Ruiz González said. “Tourists go where people live, so people need to keep living and be able to afford to buy a house or buy an apartment or just walk in and out without problems.”Part of the strategy will focus on spreading visitors more widely across Spain, while encouraging slower trips and longer stays.Where should tourists go to in Spain? While Spain is not looking to discourage tourists from its most popular destinations, Turespaña wants travellers to explore rural and lesser-visited parts of the country. “Some destinations don't need much promotion – they are very well known,” Ruiz González said. “Basically, we want people to go more inland in Spain. We also want people to travel slow, to stay as long as possible.”For travellers interested in nature and hiking, he highlighted the Pyrenees and Picos de Europa, as well as the Sierra de Guadarrama mountain range, a national park within easy reach of the capital, Madrid. Ruiz González also highlighted the historic cities and smaller towns of Castilla, while Spain’s extensive high-speed rail network is helping make destinations beyond the established tourism hotspots easier to reach. “We want all our destinations to be part of the solution,” he said.
