Headline: Supermarket deliveries: Lidl tests autonomous electric lorry
Body: Since this week, a lorry without a cab and without a driver has been on the road in public traffic in Edermünde in the German state of Hesse, near Kassel. Lidl says it is the first food retailer in Germany to deploy a cabless electric HGV with autonomous driving capability in live operations. Its partner is Swedish technology company Einride.What the lorry can doThe vehicle operates at SAE Level 4, the second-highest of six automation levels (0 to 5). Under the definition used by the German Federal Motor Transport Authority, the system permanently assumes full control within a clearly defined operating area. A human does not need to intervene or monitor what is happening.If the vehicle detects it is reaching the limits of its operating domain or encounters a malfunction, it brings itself into a safe state on its own. Unlike Level 5, however, this only applies on predefined routes, not everywhere and under all conditions. For the deployment in Edermünde, the Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) has granted an official approval, according to Lidl.Control is provided by sensors, cameras and a control system rather than by a traditional cab, which it does not have at all. The rigid vehicle's loading area can accommodate 15 Euro pallets. Up to three times a day, the electric lorry shuttles between the administration and distribution centre in Edermünde and a nearby store, covering all dry-goods deliveries there. More than 3,000 pallets are to be transported during the four-month test phase.Einride CEO Roozbeh Charli says in the press release (source in German) from Lidl: "The German approval process is among the toughest in the world. Clearing that hurdle there sets the course for scaling up decisively."Einride is already carrying out autonomous deliveries with real volumes for customers in the United States and Europe, Charli adds. Germany, as the "largest European market for road freight transport", is of strategic importance.What advantages Lidl is hoping forFor Lidl (part of the Schwarz Group), the core issue is a logistics challenge: moving huge volumes of goods reliably at a time when drivers are in short supply. According to the press release, the project is designed specifically to address highly complex supply chains and the shortage of skilled workers. Thomas Dangelmayer, head of operational logistics at Lidl in Germany, says: "Intelligence creates efficiency, and that is the backbone of reliably ensuring product availability over the long term. We make sure that products are always in the right place at the right time and in the right quality for our customers."With 39 distribution centres and more than 3,250 stores, Lidl has a tightly scheduled logistics network in Germany. If the first route proves successful, the next step will be a "milk run" model with multiple stops at another location.Berlin is also giving its backing. Christian Hirte, Parliamentary State Secretary to the Federal Transport Minister, described the launch as a signal for Germany as a hub of innovation: "Autonomous and zero-emission driving is no longer some vision of the future; it is becoming a reality on our roads." The project has been supported, among others, by the Mobility Data Space.Not an isolated case in EuropeAutonomous lorry deliveries in Europe are not entirely new, however. Back in 2019, Einride operated its first cabless electric lorry in test service in Sweden, using the "T-Pod" to run between two warehouses belonging to logistics company DB Schenker.According to the company, it now operates around 250 lorries for more than 30 customers in seven countries, including Amazon, Heineken and PepsiCo. In Antwerp-Bruges, Einride tested a fully autonomous lorry in port operations for the first time in September 2025, the specialist portal Electrive reported.Competition is growing internationally. According to a report by news agency Reuters, Chinese provider Pony.ai already has several hundred Level 4 lorries in operation in China and is now looking to enter the European market, with initial tests under way in countries including Croatia.Regulation could slow things downHow quickly autonomous lorries gain ground beyond pilot routes will depend heavily on regulation. Germany and 16 other EU member states want to coordinate the development of automated vehicles more closely in future so that they no longer have to stop at national borders, the specialist site Eurotransport.de reports. The aim is to establish common standards so that an autonomous lorry approved in Germany can also operate in countries such as France or the Netherlands.The economic potential is substantial. According to a McKinsey analysis prepared for the IAA Transportation trade fair, autonomous road freight could generate revenue potential of 80 to 120 billion euros in Europe alone by 2035.At the same time, the study says, European commercial vehicle manufacturers are under pressure from Chinese rivals, which enjoy cost advantages of 30 to 40 percent and shorter development cycles.

Headline: Billions risk being locked out of the AI revolution due to smartphone costs
Body: Global telecoms industry body GSMA is calling for urgent action to make smartphones more affordable for people living in low- and middle-income countries so that everyone can “benefit from the AI revolution”.The call to action comes as the organisation launches its State of Mobile Internet Connectivity Report 2026, an annual study of global mobile connectivity.The report found that while 4.8 billion people now use mobile internet on their own device, 3.4 billion do not, despite 90% of them living within mobile broadband coverage. GSMA refers to this as the “usage gap”.Growth in the world’s digital population is also slowing, with roughly 160 million new users coming online in 2025, compared with 190 million in 2024.Commenting on the report, GSMA Director General Vivek Badrinath said: “Artificial intelligence has the potential to improve lives on an unprecedented scale, but AI is meaningless if people cannot get online in the first place.”“The greatest risk is not simply an AI divide between countries, but between people who can afford to participate in the digital economy and those who cannot.”GSMA says it is important to “avoid a large portion of the population in emerging economies being completely left out of the digital economy” and is calling for a number of actions.A growing usage gapA key factor behind growing global digital inequality, according to the report, is the “sharp increase in the cost of smartphone memory and chipsets, driven by global demand for AI infrastructure and data centres”.Memory prices have skyrocketed recently, more than doubling between the third quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of 2026, followed by a further 80-90% increase during the second quarter of 2026.These rising component costs are then passed on to consumers, with prices for entry-level smartphones becoming unaffordable for many people around the world. This dynamic, GSMA says, threatens to undo the “years of progress made on closing the mobile usage gap”.“Unless we protect the affordability of entry-level smartphones, billions of people risk being excluded from the next generation of digital services before they have even had the opportunity to experience the internet,” said Badrinath.This year’s report found that, by the end of 2025, entry-level smartphones cost the poorest 20% of people in low- and middle-income countries up to 44% of their average monthly income and up to 76% in sub-Saharan Africa, with prices expected to continue rising.GSMA believes the sharp rise in smartphone prices will translate into the “largest annual decline on record” in smartphone shipments globally, with emerging markets the most vulnerable.Bridging the digital divideTo address the world’s growing digital inequality, the organisation is calling for manufacturers to reduce the price of entry-level smartphones to $30, arguing that this could “make devices affordable for almost 1.6 billion people” while a $20 price point could make them affordable for around 2.2 billion people currently living within mobile broadband coverage.The telecoms organisation is also calling on chipset and memory manufacturers to “take meaningful steps to increase availability of affordable components for entry-level handsets," arguing that this would help smartphone manufacturers make their entry-level devices more affordable.GSMA also recommends addressing “other key barriers to digital inclusion" such as “low literacy and digital skills, safety and security concerns, and availability of relevant content and services”.

Headline: 'A wake-up call': California music festival cancelled after El Niño-linked hurricane erodes beach
Body: A music festival in the US has been cancelled after a hurricane eroded the beach where it was due to be held.The two-day Ocean Way Festival was scheduled for later this month in Santa Monica, California. But 4.5 metre-high waves and storm runoff have left the beach near Los Angeles badly degraded, forcing local officials to cancel the event."Storm surf generated by Hurricane Marie and runoff from a storm drain outfall eroded a large portion of the festival site," said a statement from the city of Santa Monica.The Killers, Olivia Dean and Jack White were due to play at the inaugural Ocean Way Festival, which was promoted by Coachella organisers Goldenvoice.Hurricane Marie, spurred by the ‘Super’ El Niño weather pattern resulting from warming waters in the eastern Pacific Ocean, severely damaged coastal areas from Malibu to Long Beach and Dana Point.‘The surf took the beach’The storm, which churned the waters of the Pacific over the last week, stripped sand off the beach meaning that it wouldn’t be safe to hold the festival there, the city said."The surf took the beach we planned this on, and we cannot put tens of thousands of festival-goers on that sand until it's safe," said Mayor Caroline Torosis.The coastal city of Santa Monica - the official end point of Route 66 - has a wide stretch of golden sand and a large wooden pier that features frequently in American television shows and films.Non-profit Ocean Conservancy’s Oscar Negroni, a resident of Los Angeles and veteran of the entertainment industry, said in response to the cancellation: “The ocean is the beating heart of our blue planet and its health touches us all, from our coasts to the center of our country.""When climate change makes headlines because it disrupts the music we listen to, the sports we play and the communities we live in, it should be a wake-up call. Whether you’re an athlete, an entertainer or a fan, we all have a stake in protecting the cherished spaces that bring us together. Building a safe, more resilient future won’t be possible if we don’t protect our ocean.”News of the festival cancellation came days after the pounding surf opened a massive sinkhole on the driveway of a beachfront home belonging to Oscar-winning US actor Nicolas Cage. Officials in Malibu, which sits just north of Santa Monica, have ordered the evacuation of 31 homes because of the danger posed by the hole.Further south, at least seven homes in Dana Point were declared uninhabitable after the coast on which they sit rapidly eroded, with one house collapsing into the sea.A similar problem has occurred in nearby Laguna Beach.El Niño blamed for worse stormsThe waters of the Pacific Ocean have been unsettled in recent weeks by a series of tropical storms, with some of them developing into hurricanes.Scientists say a near-record strength El Niño is warming the ocean's waters and creating extra volatility.While the phenomenon is part of a natural cycle, human-caused climate change is thought to be super-charging the heating and exacerbating its effects.Ocean Way is not the first festival to be affected by climate change. Bonnaroo, in Tennessee in the US, announced last month that the festival would take 2027 off to repair the grounds, after heavy storms canceled sets and prompted evacuations this year. Stagecoach, the country music festival on the same site as Coachella, also temporarily shut down this year due to strong winds.

Headline: NBC news helicopter crash kills at least three in Los Angeles while reporters covered car accident
Body: An NBC news television helicopter crashed into a car park in Los Angeles on Tuesday, killing at least three people.The helicopter crashed near a storage building in the neighbourhood of Chatsworth in the San Fernando Valley, as news crews were covering the bus crash that left at least two people dead and six others injured, according to the Los Angeles Fire Department. A fourth person was taken to hospital, though their condition was unknown.Colleen Williams, an NBC4 Los Angeles anchor, confirmed during a live broadcast that the station’s chopper went down just before 7 pm.“We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that and process it,” she said, her voice shaking with emotion. Moments later, coverage was abruptly cut off.The Los Angeles Fire Department said it was still working to determine how many of the victims had been on board the aircraft.At least one person killed was on the ground outside, spokesperson Captain Branden Silverman told reporters."We're trying to determine how many patients were inside the helicopter," Silverman said.The crash occurred near the scene of a separate deadly bus accident, though the connection between the two incidents, if any, was not immediately clear.Photos and videos online showed around half of an SUV lodged into the side of an MTA bus and a large group of fire crew working around the crash.Two people were reportedly killed and six others were injured after an SUV crashed into a city bus in Los Angeles, officials said.According to the fire department, more than 50 firefighters responded to the helicopter crash. The fire had damaged four vehicles and two storage containers but was out by Tuesday evening, according to officials.Silverman described the helicopter as “pretty well destroyed” and said they’re going to have to go through the rubble to see how many victims were on board.According to media reports, the helicopter came down into a park serving a large single-storey building, striking or landing near several parked vehicles.The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration will be handling the investigation.

Headline: Increase in air pollution takes a toll on your sleep
Body: Even in cities where local pollution levels were below the World Health Organization’s recommended daily exposure limit, a new study has found that bad air quality can lead to respiratory symptoms at lower exposure levels than previously thought. That’s due to the human respiratory system being extremely sensitive to short-term fine particulate matter fluctuations even in relatively clean urban environments.Researchers from the University of Cambridge in the United Kingdom, Tsinghua University in China and the sleep technology company Sleep Cycle found that when pollution levels increased by 10 micrograms of particulate matter per cubic metre (μg/m³), there was a 2.4% rise in coughing levels over the next five days.They analysed coughing sounds from around 100,000 users of the Sleep Cycle app across 32 cities in 12 countries over 500 days.“This suggests that there may be no such thing as a safe threshold for exposure to air pollution, although our research is purely observational,” said Cecilia Mascolo, who led the research at Cambridge. “However, people may wish to consider how they might mitigate their own exposure to air pollution, by using masks or air filters, for example.”In addition to immediate respiratory irritation, night-time coughing also disrupts sleep, which could link acute air pollution exposure to broader systemic consequences, including cardiometabolic dysfunction, impaired cognitive performance, and neurodegenerative risks linked to poor-quality rest. Researchers also looked at the case of Los Angeles in 2025, where the city suffered its worst wildfire season in years. They found that a 10-microgram-per-cubic-metre increase in particulate matter produced a 10% surge in nocturnal coughing, suggesting that extreme air pollution episodes trigger immediate, disproportionately large spikes in acute respiratory symptoms.The researchers also accounted for external factors that could contribute to a rise in coughing levels, such as weather conditions or influenza levels — yet, the pattern caused by air pollution remained. What are the air quality levels in Europe? Across the 13 European cities included in the study, average daily fine particulate matter concentrations ranged from a low of 5.47 μg/m³ in Uppsala, Sweden, to a high of 14.70 μg/m³ in Bergamo, Italy. The mean level across all 13 European cities was approximately 10.58 μg/m³. The World Health Organization recommends that daily exposure should not exceed 15 μg/m³ for a 24-hour average more than 3 to 4 days per year. Overall, European cities in the study exhibited low-to-moderate baseline pollution levels compared to the most polluted cities in the broader global dataset, such as Beijing at 40.97μg/m³ or Shanghai at 33.48 μg/m³. Broader health consequences Beyond the irritation of coughing and a sore throat, such symptoms can be a sign of latent conditions, the authors warned.  “Everyone coughs from time to time, but coughing, whether it’s a one-off or more persistent, is a sign of irritation or inflammation in the lungs,” said lead author Tong Xia from Tsinghua University. “A cough could be a sign of something that hasn’t become chronic yet, but might in future.”

Headline: Why is European money financing the American AI boom?
Body: European savings are increasingly exposed to—and helping finance—the expansion of artificial intelligence in the United States.Eurozone households hold around €440 billion in US technology companies, including Nvidia and Alphabet, according to European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde.Speaking in Vienna on Monday, Lagarde warned that European savings risk paying for the US AI boom without Europe receiving a comparable share of the economic benefits.“The companies are being built elsewhere,” she said. “Last year the United States produced 59 notable AI models, and China produced 35. France and the United Kingdom produced one each.”Europe does not lack money. The problem is getting more of it to companies that can grow.Eurozone households held nearly €10 trillion in bank deposits as of May 2026, according to a new ECB analysis published on Tuesday. They keep around one-third of their financial assets in deposits, compared with 11% among US households. Around 80% of eurozone households own no shares, bonds or investment funds.The ECB found that limited resources, knowledge gaps, low levels of trust and concerns about risk discourage many Europeans from investing. More than 60% of eurozone households held most of their wealth in property, while around a quarter relied mainly on bank deposits. About 10% invested indirectly through pension and insurance products, while just 4% held a substantial share of their wealth directly in financial markets.Those in Europe who want exposure to AI frequently invest in American technology companies, often through investment funds and pensions.Is investing in US technology necessarily a problem?Jeremie Peloso, chief strategist for Europe at BCA Research, told Euronews Business that investing in US technology was not necessarily a problem for European households. “US tech has been outperforming European indices for the past 10 years,” he said, adding that international investments can help savers spread their risks.He also said that a weaker euro has sometimes increased the returns made by euro-based investors on dollar-denominated assets, he added.However, he warned that the US technology sector had become highly concentrated, leaving investors exposed to a relatively small group of companies affected by many of the same market forces.Ben Barringer, head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said European capital had moved abroad because many of the world’s leading technology companies had been built and expanded outside Europe, offering stronger growth prospects and investment returns.How does European money finance US AI?Buying an existing US technology share does not provide fresh money to the company. However, strong investor demand can support its valuation and make it easier to raise capital by issuing new shares.When European retail investors buy newly issued shares, as happened when SpaceX invited them to participate in its IPO in June, they provide money that the company can use for investment.But IPOs alone are unlikely to provide enough capital to sustain the breakneck pace of investment by AI hyperscalers. The largest technology companies have therefore also been borrowing heavily through the bond market.Major hyperscalers are expected to spend more than $1 trillion (€870bn) on capital investment by 2028, according to an ECB analysis. This includes spending on data centres, advanced chips, electricity supplies and network infrastructure.Lagarde said major US hyperscalers issued more than $100bn (€87bn) in bonds last year and now account for close to one-tenth of new euro-denominated bond issuance by non-financial companies.Five large US hyperscalers have around €40 billion in euro-denominated bonds outstanding, according to the ECB. European funds, insurers and pension schemes that buy these bonds are directly lending money to American technology companies.This borrowing can also have wider consequences. Heavy US bond issuance can contribute to higher global yields, while long-term interest rates in the eurozone often move alongside US rates.“Europe will bear part of the price of this boom in its own borrowing costs,” Lagarde said. “The question is whether it will also get the growth that goes with it.”Europe’s AI investment gapRapid AI adoption could raise eurozone productivity by as much as 4% over a decade, according to ECB estimates.But Europe remains far behind the US in the infrastructure needed to develop and run AI. Lagarde said the United States hosts around 75% of global AI computing capacity, compared with approximately 5% in Europe.The European Commission estimates that the gap between demand for data-centre capacity and available supply in the EU could reach 19 gigawatts by 2036. Closing it could cost as much as €600 billion.Eurozone companies are expected to devote around 10% of their investment to AI in 2026, while AI-related borrowing accounted for approximately one-quarter of the first-quarter increase in credit to companies, according to ECB estimates.Europe has promising private AI companies, but ordinary investors have much easier access to America’s listed technology giants.“There is no shortage of capital in Europe, simply a problem of channelling funds,” Peloso said.He added that Europe also had a considerable number of technology companies, but relatively few were publicly traded. This leaves retail investors—and funds restricted to public markets—with a limited choice of European technology investments.Mistral illustrates both Europe’s potential and its investment problem. The French AI company raised €3 billion last week in the largest equity fundraising by a European technology company, but ordinary savers could not participate directly because its shares are not publicly traded.Barringer said simply encouraging investors to direct more money towards European AI would treat the symptom rather than the underlying cause.“The challenge is not simply a lack of available capital, but creating the conditions for more world-class European companies to emerge and compete globally,” he said.That would require deeper venture-capital markets, greater willingness to finance higher-risk businesses and rules that support innovation while maintaining appropriate oversight.“Ultimately, investment will follow opportunity,” Barringer added.Can Europe redirect more of its savings?The EU’s main response is the Savings and Investments Union. It is intended to make it easier for households to invest and for European companies to obtain funding across national borders.Proposed measures include simpler, potentially tax-advantaged investment accounts, changes to supplementary pensions and efforts to reduce the cost of operating across different European financial markets.The EU has also introduced its Listing Act, which is designed to make it cheaper and easier for companies to go public. It includes simpler listing documents and rules allowing founders to retain greater control after their companies enter the stock market.These reforms could help more European technology companies grow and eventually become accessible to ordinary investors. But they cannot guarantee that European households will choose them over American companies offering stronger prospects.Peloso said channelling more savings into businesses would be a multi-year process requiring easier regulation, a more favourable environment for start-ups, deeper venture-capital and private-equity markets, and stronger incentives for households to invest.Barringer similarly argued that policy should focus on building stronger companies rather than simply directing savings towards a preferred sector.“If the underlying foundations are not strong enough to support innovation, simply directing more savings towards the sector is unlikely to solve the problem,” he said.Europe therefore appears to have the capital—and a growing number of promising technology companies. Its challenge is to help those businesses expand, become publicly accessible and offer investors opportunities compelling enough to compete with America’s technology giants.

Headline: Think you’re the same person when on holiday? Plenty of travellers say otherwise
Body: Travel has a funny way of changing the way we live our lives. Away from the routines and responsibilities of home, travellers may feel freer to stay out late, spend a little more cash or say yes to something they’d normally turn down – even as the pressure to make the most of every minute ramps up.New research suggests this isn’t just holiday abandon. Many travellers are consciously giving themselves permission to behave differently while they’re away, with some even returning home surprised by their own choices.Hint App, which offers advice based on birth charts, surveyed travellers to see how they behave away from home.It questioned some 14,673 adults across the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, European Union, Australia and Latin America and found that a surprising 61% deliberately behave differently while travelling than they would at home.That’s despite respondents describing themselves as generally predictable or routine-driven in everyday life when out of office isn’t on. Here’s what else the survey revealed. How travel changes the way we behaveWhile some of us would never dream of doing something out of the ordinary while abroad, 47% of those surveyed actually said they had knowingly done something while away because it felt appropriate during a trip.They added that they did it in spite of likely rejected the same choice at home, which suggests a temporary change in the standards people use to evaluate their own decisions when not at home.That attitude shift can relate to countless different activities we all do when on holiday.For instance, respondents said purchases are often easier to justify when they’re attached to a place they’ll likely never visit again. The data found that 38% admitted they’d chosen to buy something they’d typically consider to be unnecessary because it was inextricably linked to the memory of the trip.Similarly, a late evening out can feel more valuable because the number of evenings available on a trip is limited. In fact, 42% said they had stayed out later than they actually wanted to because they did not want to “waste” a holiday evening. The survey also showed that although travellers do behave in unusual ways, they’re actually often replacing one set of expectations with another, making sure they can justify to themselves the time, money, and effort invested in the trip.A shift in behaviour isn’t always easy to recognise while actually in the middle of it, with 35% of respondents saying they arrived home surprised by something they had done or agreed to while away. Ultimately, though, the survey can’t tell us whether our holiday behaviour is a truer reflection of who we are. What it does suggest is that the routines we stick to at home may be more flexible than we realise.For the 61% who knowingly change their behaviour while travelling, a holiday creates a temporary excuse to rewrite the rulebook – whether that means splashing out on something unnecessary, squeezing one more drink into the evening or saying yes to an experience they’d usually turn down.

Headline: Maduro ally Alex Saab pleads guilty to money laundering in US court
Body: Alex Saab, a close ally of ousted Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, pleaded guilty on Tuesday to a money-laundering charge linked to an alleged bribery scheme to secure lucrative public contracts in Venezuela.As part of the plea agreement, Saab agreed to cooperate with ongoing federal investigations in the United States and to hand over 195 million dollars (some €168.9 million) derived from the corruption scheme.Saab, 54, was deported to the United States in May by Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez. US authorities have been investigating the Colombia-born businessman for more than a decade.The money-laundering charge carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. However, prosecutors have agreed to recommend a term at the lower end of the guideline range and to seek further reductions if his cooperation proves useful, including assistance in investigations targeting four co-defendants whose names have not been disclosed.Saab was arrested in 2020 and later pardoned by BidenSaab had already been charged in 2019, during Donald Trump's first administration. He was arrested in 2020 during a refuelling stop in Cape Verde, in what the Venezuelan government claimed at the time was a high-level humanitarian mission bound for Iran.During his court appearance on Tuesday, Saab told Judge Kathleen Williams that he takes the antidepressant Zoloft every day along with other medication for what he described as "post-traumatic stress disorder" following his 2020 arrest.The then president Joe Biden pardoned Saab in 2023 in exchange for the release of several US citizens imprisoned in Venezuela. The deal was part of a failed attempt by Biden's White House to persuade Maduro to hold free presidential elections.The decision was sharply criticised by Republicans and by senior federal law-enforcement officials, who immediately opened new investigations into Saab over other alleged offences not covered by the pardon, whose scope was limited.US long regarded Saab as Maduro's 'front man'US authorities have for years described Saab as Maduro's 'bag man', a term used to refer to someone tasked with handling or moving money for another person. They could now call him to testify about the character of the former Venezuelan president, who is awaiting trial in Manhattan on drug-related charges after being captured in January during a US military operation.The new legal proceedings against Saab and Maduro come as the Trump administration reshapes the United States' relations with Venezuela and focuses on tapping the country's vast oil reserves.This month, Trump announced a partnership with Venezuelan oil tycoon Alejandro Betancourt under which the US government will secure a stake and access to cost-price crude shipments from fields with an estimated production potential of 65 billion barrels.

Headline: Where Europe spends its money: A look at public spending across the continent
Body: Citizens pay taxes, and tax revenues make up a significant share of public revenues across Europe. They are crucial for governments to fund public services such as education, healthcare and social protection.But where does public spending actually go across Europe? What do governments spend money on? And how is government spending allocated?In 2024, tax revenues accounted for 40.3% of gross domestic product (GDP) in the EU, according to Eurostat. General government total expenditure exceeded this rate in the EU, reaching 49.6% of GDP in that year. Two in five euros go to social protectionAs government spending as a percentage of GDP varies significantly across European countries, looking at how total spending is distributed provides a clearer comparison.For example, in the EU, 19.6% of GDP was spent on social protection, which accounts for 40% of total government spending. That means two in every five euros of general government spending in the EU go to social protection.Social protection is designed to protect people against the risks associated with unemployment, parental responsibilities, sickness/health care and disability, the loss of a spouse or parent, old age, housing and social exclusion.  Pensions are the largest component of social protection benefits, making up almost half of the total. Social protection also covers sickness, disability and unemployment benefits.Among 31 countries, including the EU, the UK, Norway, Switzerland and Iceland, social protection accounts for the largest share of government spending in every country, ranging from 26% in Hungary to 45.9% in Finland.The share of social protection is above the EU average, meaning above 40%, in Luxembourg (42.5%), Italy (42.2%), Denmark (41.5%), France (41.5%), Austria (41.3%), Germany (41.3%), Spain (41%) and Portugal (40.4%).The EU’s ‘Big Four’ economies are all above 40%, while the share is 34.5% in the UK. The UK figure is from the OECD.A European Central Bank report prepared by Marta Rodríguez-Vives and Linda Kezbere underlines that there is no “one-size-fits-all optimal level of social spending” as a share of the economy.“The set-up of pension systems varies significantly across euro area countries,” it says. Rankings by spending share and actual amounts may differThis wide gap between countries shows how governments prioritise their policies and spending. However, as GDP and total government expenditure in nominal terms vary widely, the share of spending and the actual amounts spent can look considerably different.Therefore, looking at social protection spending per person, both in euros and in purchasing power terms, can provide a more meaningful country-level comparison.Health is second-largest, but not in all countriesHealth is the second-largest spending category in the EU on average, with a 15% share. This is also the case in the majority of countries, but other categories rank second in nine countries. They include Italy, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Greece, Malta, Luxembourg, Latvia and Switzerland. The share of health spending ranges from 6.7% in Switzerland and 10% in Hungary to 24.3% in Ireland. The UK allocates a comparatively larger share of government spending to health, at 19%, than major EU economies such as France (15.6%) and Germany (15.4%).The ECB report points out that differences in healthcare financing models affect government health spending as healthcare costs are shared between governments and households in different proportions.Social protection and health account for more than halfThe combined share of social protection and health exceeds 50% in two-thirds of countries, while together they account for 55% of government spending in the EU.The EU’s ‘Big Four’ are all above the EU average, and all five Nordic countries also exceed 50%.Hungary (36%) and Malta (39.5%) are outliers with shares below 40%, while Ireland and Finland exceed 59%.The shares of three categories — general public services (12.4%), economic affairs (10.8%) and education (9.7%) — are close to each other at around 10% in the EU. However, there are significant differences across countries.General public services cover the basic running of government, including government administration, parliament, public finances, foreign affairs, public debt and transfers between different levels of government. Their share differs significantly across countries, from 7.5% in Bulgaria to 21.2% in Hungary.General public services also account for the second-largest share of government spending in Hungary, Greece (17.1%) and Italy (15.4%) after social protection.Economic affairs are the second-largest spending category in Malta, Latvia, Romania, Bulgaria and Luxembourg. The share ranges from 6.5% in Denmark to 20.3% in Malta.It covers government spending on the economy, including jobs and business, agriculture, energy, industry, transport, communications and economic research.Education: Switzerland has the highest spending shareEducation has the second-highest share of government spending only in Switzerland, at 16.3%. Remarkably, the share of spending on education is below the EU average in all four of the EU’s largest economies, with Italy having the lowest at 8%.These five categories make up between 80 and 92% of government spending across the countries, with the EU average at 87.9%. Defence is the sixth-largest spending category in the EU at 3.5%. The UK allocates a comparatively higher share of government spending to defence at 4.9%, than some of the EU’s largest economies, such as France (3.2%) and Germany (2.7%).Government spending on recreation, culture and religion, environmental protection, and housing and community amenities is very limited. Together, these three categories account for just 5.6% of total government spending in the EU.

Headline: US to divert $52 million in military aid from Europe and Middle East to Trump-friendly nations in Americas
Body: The Trump administration is redirecting $52 million in military aid from countries in Europe and the Middle East to help back US-aligned governments in the Americas.The US State Department notified Congress on Tuesday that it would divert the funds from Iraq, Tunisia and NATO members Slovakia and North Macedonia to Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Panama.The US State Department said the funding would go towards combatting "narcoterrorism in our backyard" and helping "continue to secure the Panama Canal," adding that it would "prevent adversaries from establishing strategic footholds in our hemisphere."The impacted countries are still expected to receive some assistance despite the change, although the exact amount is unclear.Trump has increasingly turned his attention to the Americas since his return to the White House in January 2025, carrying out strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats coming from the region and launching an operation to capture former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. He has also sought to gain access to Venezuela's oil industry - striking a major oil deal with Caracas in August.But Trump has also worked to deepen relations with governments he considers aligned to his goals as he looks to build the US' presence in the region.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio made a trip to South America last week as part of this push, meeting with the conservative leaders of Peru, Colombia and Ecuador to pledge further support and cooperation.In Europe, however, Trump has made no secret of his wish to reduce the US' role, repeatedly hitting out at European NATO allies over their defence spending and threatening to withdraw American forces from the continent.In August, the State Department said it also planned to announce a $1 billion security package for new Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella's right-wing administration.The office of the spokesperson for the department said the package aimed to help Washington and Bogotá achieve "our shared goals."Trump has long been complimentary of de la Espriella, calling him a "smart, strong, and tough leader" and promising the "total support and strength of the United States behind him."

Headline: At least five killed and more than a dozen injured in Russian attacks on Ukraine
Body: At least five people have been killed and more than a dozen have been injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the last 24 hours.The mayor of Kyiv, Vitali Klitschko, said on Tuesday afternoon that at least 12 people had been injured in strikes on the Ukrainian capital since the morning, with one critically injured person dying in hospital.Kyiv police said warehouses, a business center and a fast-food restaurant were damaged in attacks on the city, with Ukrainian media reporting that the restaurant was a McDonald's.In the southern city of Kherson, a 74-year-old woman was killed by a Russian drone strike, Oleksandr Prokudin, the head of the Kherson Region Military Administration, announced on Telegram.Two men, aged 38 and 60, were also wounded in a drone attack on the Kherson region on Tuesday morning, per local authorities.In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, the acting head of the Zaporizhzhia Oblast Military Administration, Mykhailo Semkin, said early on Tuesday that another man was killed and a woman was injured after an attack that reportedly targeted the power grid.Two others were killed and one person was injured in strikes on Sloviansk in the eastern Donetsk Oblast, authorities said.Moscow launched 200 drones overnight at Ukraine as it continued its attacks on the country, with 187 intercepted, Ukraine's armed forces said.Russian oil refinery struckFor its part, the Ukrainian military reported attacks on Russia's Syzran oil refinery, as well as on the Atlant Aero facility in the city of Taganrog, which reportedly specialises in the making of unmanned aerial vehicles and components.In an operation carried out by Ukraine's Special Operations Forces, including its deep strike units, the Syzran refinery's primary crude oil distillation unit and tank farm were hit, the Ukrainian General Staff said.Ukraine launches counteroffensiveIt comes as a Ukrainian unit's commander announced that it had launched counteroffensive against Russian forces near the eastern Ukrainian city of Lyman.The city of Lyman remains one of the few in the region of Donetsk not to have been occupied by Russian forces since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but Russian forces have been making efforts to encircle it for months.Military analysts say that its occupation could facilitate Russia's advance towards taking the Ukrainian strongholds of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.But the commander of Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps, Andrii Biletskyi, said in a video on Telegram that the unit had launched an "offensive operation" and that Ukrainian forces had cleared an area of around 75 sq km.

Headline: French police take to streets in mass protest over pay, staffing and resources
Body: Thousands of French police officers took to the streets of Paris to protest against their working conditions on Tuesday. The protest — led by the Alliance Police Nationale union — began at the Champs-Élysées and culminated at the National Assembly.After the march, union representatives headed to the Interior Ministry to share their grievances — they subsequently told reporters that the meeting showed positive signs authorities were taking their grievances into account.Mounting anger among police officers has been fuelled by a range of issues: including discontent around the special police duty allowance (ISSP), their "risk bonus", which has not gone up since 2019.Alongside side this, the Alliance Police Nationale union is also calling for an increase in resources for administrative, technical and scientific staff, as well as action on career progression and staffing levels. The union estimates it requires an additional 300 to 500 million euros a year to meet its needs.Ahead of the protest, one officer working in Rennes described a situation, which he qualified as "alarming". He condemned staff shortages, equipment problems and the lack of decent pay: "we need equipment, we need manpower, we need recognition in our pay," he said, arguing that working conditions "are getting worse and worse".Longterm discussionsOn 4 September, major police unions — Alliance, Unité and UNSA Police unions — were received by Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. After the meeting, the unions complained that there had been no meaningful progress on their budget demands.But on Tuesday, they appeared to reach a turning point.After his meeting with France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, Fabien Vanhemelryck, secretary-general of the Alliance union said authorities had been open-minded and took note of the gravity of the situation for officers.“The only thing we can be satisfied with is that there is an open-mindedness and an awareness of the situation", he said.Vanhemelryck told reporters that Nuñez asked officers for a "few days", as he was working on a "plan."At the start of the summer, Alliance launched a "zero initiative" campaign, soon joined by Un1té. The union set 15 September as the next step in its mobilisation, speaking at the time of a possible large-scale "social rentrée" for police officers.Tuesday's mobilisation comes just a few months before professional elections within the national police, scheduled for December, which is adding to the pressure from the unions.

Headline: Nearly $12bn project pipeline gives new weight to Seoul –Tashkent ties in minerals, AI and transport
Body: Nearly $12bn (€10.4bn) in prospective projects is giving new economic weight to ties between Uzbekistan and South Korea, a relationship Seoul already classifies as a Special Strategic Partnership, its only one with a Central Asian country.Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev is in Seoul ahead of Wednesday’s first C5+Korea leaders’ summit, with bilateral talks focused on investment, technology and industrial cooperation.The latest discussions have also produced a new $8bn (€6.9bn) cooperation programme with Korea Eximbank, while agreements signed or exchanged during the visit cover critical minerals, AI in manufacturing, transport, healthcare and other sectors.The economic agreements were accompanied by a broader political push during Mirziyoyev’s summit with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.Lee called Uzbekistan a “precious friend and a key partner” while Mirziyoyev noted that the relationship had proved resilient over time.“Our bilateral ties do not falter with political changes,” he said, while reaffirming Uzbekistan’s support for Seoul’s efforts to promote peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula.The talks also covered deeper military-technical cooperation, including training and closer contacts between the two countries’ defence institutions.Mirziyoyev also met Prime Minister Han Seong-sook on Tuesday, with talks covering trade, investment, the digital economy and cybersecurity. They also discussed processing critical minerals using Korean technology and Uzbekistan’s raw-material base, as well as cooperation on transport and railway infrastructure.Critical minerals move to the centreCritical minerals are one of the clearest strategic areas of cooperation.Uzbekistan plans 120 projects worth more than $4bn (€3.5bn) in the sector in the coming years. But Tashkent’s pitch is not simply about giving Korean companies access to new deposits.President Mirziyoyev said at a business forum that the priority was not simply to export raw materials, outlining plans to build full production chains inside Uzbekistan, from deep processing to finished high-tech products.South Korea has its own strategic interest: its automotive, electronics and battery industries depend on secure supplies of critical materials.The two countries now plan to expand cooperation through their existing Korea-Uzbekistan Rare Metals Center, a joint project developing technology for refining and processing high-purity metals. Seoul says cooperation will cover the full chain from exploration and development to processing.A joint fund for strategic critical-mineral projects has also been launched, while the two sides are considering a centre to develop and test semiconductors and new materials.For Uzbekistan, the aim is to keep more of the value generated from its resources at home. For South Korea, the partnership offers another route to diversify critical-mineral supply chains.Korean finance targets strategic sectorsUzbek President Mirziyoyev also met Korea Eximbank chairman Hwang Ki-yeon in Seoul, with financing for critical minerals, digital technologies, transport and healthcare among the projects discussed.Under a financing framework agreed with Uzbekistan’s investment ministry, Korea Eximbank will help identify prospective projects and assess financing options in six priority areas, including critical minerals, AI and data centres, smart cities, an industrial zone for Korean companies, pharmaceuticals and biotechnology.The mechanism is intended to help move projects from the planning stage towards financing and implementation.From assembly to local productionShavkat Mirziyoyev used a series of meetings with senior Korean executives to push for more production to move inside Uzbekistan.He met Kim Seong, Hyundai Motor Group’s president for strategy, and Kia Motors senior vice-president Cho Sang-woon to discuss expanding the automotive cluster in Jizzakh, increasing local production of components, introducing new Kia models and exploring the assembly of electric and hybrid vehicles.He described the broader objective at the business forum as a shift from assembly operations towards full-cycle industrial clusters.Korean companies were also invited into copper processing, electrical equipment, robotics, automation, battery storage and grid modernisation.Uzbekistan wants its electrical engineering industry to reach $11bn by 2030, with exports reaching $5bn.Trains and airportsTransport infrastructure was another focus of Mirziyoyev’s meetings with Korean companies.He met Hyundai Rotem chairman Lee Yong-bae to discuss further rail cooperation, including a service centre in Uzbekistan, localisation of railway components and production of magnets for electric motors.The two governments signed a memorandum for a South Korean-funded feasibility study on the possible acquisition of up to eight additional high-speed trainsets.Possible Korean participation in a new Tashkent-Samarkand railway is also under discussion.In aviation, Mirziyoyev met representatives of Incheon International Airport Corporation, which is involved in plans to modernise Urgench airport and develop a new international airport for Tashkent. The company also plans to establish a representative office in the Uzbek capital.Beyond business and politicsPresident Mirziyoyev also met members of the Uzbek community living and working in South Korea, including entrepreneurs, academics and specialists.The visit also highlighted the cultural ties between the two countries. During his summit with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, Mirziyoyev described Uzbekistan’s ethnic Korean community as a “spiritual bridge” between the two countries. The two leaders also agreed to designate 2027 as a Year of Culture and Exchanges.The visit is also being accompanied by Days of Uzbek Culture in Seoul and other South Korean cities, adding a cultural dimension to the political and economic programme.

Headline: Carney bound for Europe as Ottawa seeks closer ties with EU
Body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to travel to Europe on Tuesday as Ottawa pushes for deeper ties with Europe amid frosty relations with Washington.Carney is scheduled to visit Strasbourg in eastern France and Liverpool in the UK's northwest during his trip to the continent.In Strasbourg, the Canadian leader will give a speech at the European Parliament (EP) and meet with EP members to "strengthen Canada’s ties with the EU in trade, investment, and security." He will also attend European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the European Union address on Wednesday.Carney is expected to use the trip to seek a new arrangement with the EU that could allow Canadians to live and work across the bloc without visa restrictions, a senior Canadian official familiar with the talks told the Associated Press.According to the official, the Canadian government is not looking for a Norway or Switzerland-style deal with the EU and has not proposed "associate membership" of the bloc.Ottawa is instead looking for a bespoke arrangement aligned with its priorities and centring on investment, per the report.Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Carney clarified that Canada was not looking to become a member of the EU but that the country had its sights on forming what he called a "unique alliance" with the bloc.Canada has been increasingly looking to Europe amid an ongoing trade spat with Washington that reignited last month after talks over a deal to avoid hefty duties on some Canadian goods fell apart.Following the breakdown in negotiations, 50% US duties impacting around C$28 billion worth of Canadian goods came into effect in late August, prompting Ottawa to announce counter-tariffs of up to 15, 25 or 50% on roughly C$27.6 billion in imports from the US.Carney nevertheless told an audience at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Tuesday that Canada "will continue to be the US's most important partner in many key areas.""Even at times of disagreement over our long-shared history, we have always maintained deep ties," Carney said at the event, which saw global investors come together with Canadian executives and representatives from the public sector amid a push to attract more investment into Canada.In the UK leg of his trip, Carney is due to meet his British counterpart Andy Burnham for the first time, with the pair lined up to go over issues including defence and security, artificial intelligence, energy and critical minerals.

Headline: South Korea and Kazakhstan sign agreements worth €16.5 billion
Body: President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, during his official visit to South Korea on Tuesday, said that the countries should double their trade turnover, which last year amounted to €2.6 billion.“To achieve this, it is important not only to increase volumes, but also to qualitatively transform the structure of trade and expand the range of high-value-added goods,” Tokayev said during his meeting with Prime Minister Han Seongsook.He welcomed the development of the Comprehensive Program for Trade, Economic, and Investment Cooperation between Kazakhstan and Korea for 2027–2030 and offered to prepare a roadmap for industrial cooperation.In a meeting with Korean President Lee Jae Myung, Tokayev highlighted the productive nature of the visit, which resulted in signed commercial agreements worth €16.5 billion."We are firmly committed to taking our cooperation to a qualitatively new level and comprehensively strengthening the bonds of friendship and partnership," said the Kazakh president.The heads of state also agreed to elevate bilateral relations to a Future-Oriented Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.Oil, critical materials, and carsAs part of the visit, President Tokayev met with a number of heads of Korean companies and spoke at the Kazakhstan-South Korea Business Roundtable.He noted that foreign direct investments from South Korea to Kazakhstan over the years of cooperation came to €10.4 billion, while over 1,000 Korean companies work in Kazakhstan. Tokayev offered to expand this relationship and indicated a number of areas where South Korean and Kazakhstani companies could work together.For South Korea, the main point of interest was raw and critical materials.President Lee Jae Myung welcomed the signing of the Framework Agreement on Crude Oil Cooperation, which established details of the decision to import 18 million barrels of crude oil from Kazakhstan. The country decided to make this purchase in April to mitigate the effects of the Middle East instability on oil supplies.Lee also welcomed the establishment of a the Rare Metals Technology Cooperation Center in Almaty. In this regard, Kazakhstan vouched to increase the supply of materials and components for microelectronics and semiconductor manufacturing necessary for the production of all appliances.For Kazakhstan, South Korea is a source of technological advancement and capital. The negotiations spanned construction, car manufacturing, oil and gas processing, digital technologies, food processing and logistics."We believe the time has come to expand South Korea's participation in the development of the Middle Corridor," said Tokayev, proposing joint ventures and logistics projects, such as logistics centers and multimodal terminals established by CJ Logistics and LX Pantos, which will ensure the seamless transit of Korean cargo through Kazakhstan to Europe.Hyundai Engineering is already taking part in the construction of the Karachaganak gas processing plant and Tokayev invited more Korean companies to establish their presence in gas processing, petrochemicals, and energy infrastructure.The two countries also have a long-standing relationship in car manufacturing with Hyundai factory working in Kazakhstan for six years and Kia opening a factory last year.In a meeting with Hyundai Motor Group President for Strategic Planning Sung Kim, the Kazakh president outlined the country's desire to become a regional car production and export hub. The parties agreed to deepen localisation, expanding the production of automotive components, and boosting the industry's export potential.Hyundai Motor Company and Astana Motors also exchanged the agreement on production of new Hyundai Tucson in Kazakhstan.One other venture the Kazakh president tried to attract partners to was the construction of the Alatau Smart City near Almaty.Korea Overseas Infrastructure & Urban Development Corporation (KIND) is already taking part in the creation of the city master plan and the development of residential areas. Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology (KAIST) is planning to build its branch in the city, while Lotte plans a hotel and residential complexes.

Headline: Canada still a crucial partner for US in 'many key areas,' PM Carney says
Body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has reassured the US that Canada will remain a key partner despite an ongoing trade war that has seen relations between Ottawa and Washington unravel.Speaking at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Tuesday, Carney said: "To our American friends, let me say this. We will always be neighbors, and Canada will continue to be the US's most important partner in many key areas.""Even at times of disagreement over our long-shared history, we have always maintained deep ties," Carney went on, while pledging that Canada would be an "even better partner" when future "opportunities return.""Stronger, more resilient, more independent, ready to advance our mutual, economic, and security interests," he told the audience.The two-day Investment Summit, billed as a "first-of-its-kind gathering" in Canada, brought together global investors, Canadian executives and representatives from the public sector as Ottawa seeks to diversify and bring new investment into the country.The goal, the government says, is to attract C$1 trillion in investment over the next five years.In a statement later on Tuesday, Carney's office said the summit had resulted in nearly C$500 billion in new investment commitments, including almost C$100 billion in new capital for Canadian assets from pension funds, insurers, and institutional investors, C$325 billion in new financing for Canadian businesses and infrastructure from banks, and over C$14 billion in capital to grow Canadian businesses, infrastructure, and "strategic sectors" from investment funds.It comes amid a growing trade dispute between the US and Canada that came to a head last month after negotiations over a deal to avoid hefty duties on some Canadian goods fell apart.Following the breakdown in talks, 50% US duties impacting around C$28 billion worth of Canadian goods came into effect in late August, prompting Ottawa to announce counter-tariffs of up to 15, 25 or 50% on roughly C$27.6 billion in imports from the US.

Headline: Astana Arena in the capital of Kazakhstan selected to host 2028 UEFA Super Cup
Body: The decision was made and officially announced by the UEFA Executive Committee.Since 2013, the Super Cup venue has changed every year, moving to a new location each time. Kazakhstan has obtained the chance to host such a major match, marking a historic first for the country. For the uninitiated, the UEFA Super Cup is a single-match curtain-raiser where the Champions League and Europa League winners meet.Beyond the Super Cup, the Thessaloniki meeting produced several other key venue decisions. The 2028 UEFA Champions League final will take place in Munich, while Camp Nou in Barcelona was picked for the 2029 edition.The Astana Arena sports complex seats 30,000 spectators. The venue has also hosted high-profile tournaments, including the Champions League and the Europa League matches.It is worth recalling that the reigning UEFA Super Cup champions are PSG, who defeated Aston Villa 2–1, thanks to goals from Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and Desire Doue.

Headline: ECB staff raise stability concerns about rumours of Lagarde's early departure
Body: In a letter seen by Euronews, European Central Bank staff members have questioned the institution’s stability in the face of rumours of the early departures of its president, Christine Lagarde, and board member Isabel Schnabel.The staff calls the board to provide "appropriate clarity regarding potential leadership transitions", as discussions of major departures can affect both monetary policy and ECB internal reforms."We do not take a position on the accuracy of these reports, nor do we question the right of any individual to consider future professional or public responsibilities," the staff members write, referring to press coverage of the rumours. "However, when such possibilities concern members of the Executive Board, and specifically the ECB President, they inevitably raise institutional questions."In early February, the Financial Times, which also first reported on the letter, spread the news about a possible early departure by Lagarde before the end of her mandate in October 2027.What she would like to do next is not certain, but she has floated some options herself, telling Euronews that she would like to play a role in French presidential election campaign – albeit not by standing as a candidate.Another possibility is her taking the helm of the World Economic Forum, which the Wall Street Journal first reported in February.Another board member, Isabel Schnabel, might depart before the end of her term, as she is in negotiation to take a senior role at the International Monetary Fund, the German outlet Handelsblatt reported in early September.These rumours are circulating just as other ECB leaders prepare to depart on schedule. Among them is Chief Economist Philip Lane, whose mandate ends in May 2027."Prolonged uncertainty regarding the future of the institution's senior leadership can therefore affect trust in the ECB's communications, create concern among staff and stakeholders, and complicate the orderly planning of leadership succession and strategic priorities," the letter says.The potential reshuffle also comes in a moment of high uncertainty for the eurozone.The volatility of energy prices due to the ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine are making the job hard for the ECB to keep inflation low. Last week, Lagarde announced an interest rate hike to keep inflation low, that the ECB's 2% inflation target will not be met by the end of 2027.

Headline: Spain's Supreme Court refuses to apply amnesty to Catalan leader Puigdemont
Body: Spain's Supreme Court has refused to apply amnesty to Puigdemont for the alleged offence of embezzlement in the "procés" case — Catalonia's independence movement, which peaked in the 2017 referendum and unilateral declaration of independence. The court is also keeping in force the national arrest warrant for Catalonia's former president.Investigating judge Pablo Llarena, who is leading the case, has dismissed the request filed by Carles Puigdemont following the ruling by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) on 16 July.The court agreed with the Socialist-led government's argument that the 2024 amnesty law for Catalan separatists complies with EU legislation.But Puigdemont, who headed Catalonia's regional government when it held a banned independence referendum and attempted to secede from Spain, was excluded on two grounds: that Puigdemont had intended to obtain personal financial gain, and that the events had harmed the EU's financial interests.The EU court said granting amnesty for the misuse of funds did not undermine the bloc's financial interests.However, Llarena maintains that the European ruling doesn't affect his other ground for excluding the amnesty: the alleged intent to obtain personal financial gain.The ruling stresses that the new request isn't being rejected because the CJEU's interpretation is irrelevant, but because that interpretation doesn't reach the second argument underpinning his refusal to apply the amnesty.Llarena also notes that Spain's Constitutional Court has not yet ruled on how the Amnesty Law should apply specifically in this case. Those rulings, he says, have neither overturned nor specifically endorsed his finding of personal financial gain — and he adds that he cannot predict the outcome of the appeals still pending before that court.Puigdemont's arrest warrant remains in forceThe defence had asked for the national arrest warrant to be withdrawn on the grounds that the case might be closed, that the amnesty should apply, or that pursuing the men twice for the same acts would be unlawful.Having rejected all three grounds, Llarena finds no basis to lift the warrant either. He notes, though, that this doesn't rule out reviewing the measure in future if circumstances change, nor does refusing the amnesty by itself justify any tighter restriction.Because the warrant is national in scope, Puigdemont and Comín can be arrested only if they enter Spanish territory.Supreme Court refuses to transfer the caseLlarena also rejects requests to transfer the case to the High Court of Justice of Catalonia (Catalonia's own regional high court) or to courts in Barcelona.He likewise dismisses the request to close the case on grounds of "non bis in idem" — the legal principle barring double punishment for the same act — which the defence argued applied because an accounting-liability case is already underway at Spain's Court of Audit.As a result, Llarena maintains that the CJEU's ruling doesn't touch the argument he says still blocks the Amnesty Law from covering the embezzlement charges against them.

Headline: Two years after COP29, Azerbaijan turns climate commitments into investment
Body: Azerbaijan has committed up to 1 billion manat (€540 million) to climate-resilient irrigation infrastructure under its 2026-2030 state programme, as the country hosted a regional climate week two years after staging COP29 in Baku.The figure, announced by Agriculture Minister Majnun Mammadov at Baku Climate Action Week, represents nearly 40% of the state agricultural budget earmarked for climate adaptation.The funding will support modern irrigation systems across the South Caucasus, where water shortages, shifting growing seasons and soil degradation are accelerating.The government also launched an AI-based farmer scoring system this year, developed in partnership with the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO).First piloted in 2024 and tested in 2025, the digital platform distributes advance subsidy payments to smallholder farmers managing between five and 100 hectares.Mammadov said eligibility is assessed across three criteria: adoption of modern farming practices, the economic value of the chosen crop, and whether the farmer uses water-saving or soil-regenerating techniques."The scoring system evaluates three fundamental pillars," Mammadov told Euronews. "First, the adoption of modern agricultural practices, second, the economic value and profitability of the crop for the farmer and the wider economy.""And third, ecological impact. How the selected crop interacts with soil health and whether the farmer utilises climate-supporting subsidies like soil-regenerating or water-saving techniques."Smallholder farmers are the most exposed to climate volatility across the Caucasus, where minor shifts in temperature or water availability can destroy yields.Mammadov said international investors in local farming infrastructure would receive the same subsidy access as domestic operators."Agriculture is in a very unique position, it is causing climate change, and it is being affected by climate change," FAO Representative in Azerbaijan Nasar Hayat said.'Opportunity to build'Separately, the UN Industrial Development Organisation urged Azerbaijan to prioritise domestic industrial use of green hydrogen before pursuing European export ambitions.Petra Schwager, chief of UNIDO's climate and technology partnership division, said pipeline exports to Europe would take years because the infrastructure does not yet exist.In the short term, she said, green hydrogen derivatives such as green ammonia could be used in domestic fertiliser manufacturing and shipping fuels."The true benchmark of success for industrial decarbonisation is not policy pledges or technology partnerships, but verifiable CO2 emission reductions," Schwager said.On financing, Turkey announced two new mechanisms ahead of COP31 in Antalya: BRIDGE, a technical support platform for developing countries to structure investment-ready projects, built alongside the UN Development Programme, and SURF, which adapts a Turkish municipal lending model to scale low-cost credit lines to cities across developing nations.Fatma Varank, CEO of COP31 and Deputy Minister of Turkey's Ministry of Environment, Urbanisation and Climate Change, pointed to the long-term cooperation between host nations. "Along our shared journey from Baku to Antalya, we have an opportunity to build on this foundation and achieve stronger outcomes by sharing experiences, deepening partnerships and channelling climate finance towards tangible implementation," Varank said.Azerbaijan's Deputy Foreign Minister Yalchin Rafiyev confirmed that a Black Sea subsea cable project to carry renewable electricity from Azerbaijan and Central Asia to European markets remains a priority."Continuity between the COPs is extremely important in order to keep the legacy for the host country, but at the same time, globally it is very important," Rafiyev told Euronews. He said COP29's legacy had brought Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan forward with specific green grid proposals.At COP29 in 2024, wealthier nations agreed to provide at least $300 billion (€258 billion) per year by 2035 to help developing countries cut emissions and manage climate impacts.UN Secretary-General António Guterres said at the time the deal provided "a base on which to build" but fell short of what the crisis required.According to Jens Nielsen, Founder and CEO of the World Climate Foundation, global climate diplomacy is undergoing a structural evolution, which is “changing from the politics of climate change to the economics of climate change."  "We need to move beyond commitments and action straight into bankable financial transactions," Nielsen told Euronews.  Baku Climate Action Week was held in parallel with the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change regional climate week for Eastern Europe, the Caucasus and Central Asia.

Headline: US threatens EU with retaliation over European preference in EU budget
Body: In a document sent to EU legislators and seen by Euronews, the US has threatened the EU with retaliation if it does not scrap European preference provisions in its multiannual budget.EU member states are currently discussing the EU’s long-term budget (2028-2034), which includes a €402 billion fund dedicated to competitiveness that favours the production of key goods within the EU, including in defence.The measure would potentially exclude foreign firms from EU financing to protect strategic and economic security interests.“With further expansion of European preference measures in EU defence funds, the United States will review all potential response measures, including a rollback of the existing 'Buy American' blanket waivers and exceptions associated with the RDPAs [Reciprocal Defence Procurement Agreements] with 19 of the 27 member states,” the non-paper reads.The Buy American Act requires the US government, including the US Department of Defence, to give preference to products manufactured in the US for certain public procurements, with some exceptions being granted in defence for some EU countries.The non-paper adds that the European preference would impede "partnership” and “collaboration” with the US, and calls on the EU to introduce a “made with Europe” system – or, in the specific area of defence, a “made in NATO”.Trade tensionsThe US's latest warning comes after the creation of the Security Action for Europe programme in 2025, already sparked trade tensions between Washington and Brussels over a European preference for joint purchases of arms and military equipment.The “made in Europe” approach is also pushed by France and the European Commission in several pieces of legislation over the last year designed to boost EU industry, with foreign countries lobbying hard against being excluded from the EU market.The US and EU have been at loggerheads over trade since the start of the second Trump administration, amid repeated tariff threats and disputes over environmental and digital regulations which the White House deems to be non-tariff barriers.The Commission hoped that the conclusion of a trade agreement in July 2025 would be a step towards a more stable transatlantic relationship.

Headline: Trump blasts Supreme Court over mail-in ballot ruling
Body: US President Donald Trump has lashed out at the Supreme Court after it rejected his request to lift an order halting his planned limits to mail-in voting."Republicans just got another bad decision from the United States Supreme Court," he wrote in a lengthy post on his Truth Social account on Tuesday, calling it a "horrible, highly political" ruling."Certain Justices are petrified of these crazed and depraved Democrats, and are totally unable to show the courage necessary to save our America," he added.Trump had sought to limit mail-in voting ahead of November's key midterm elections, which will determine the makeup of Congress for his final two years in office, arguing without evidence that the system is susceptible to fraud.In March, he issued an executive order directing the United States Postal Service to develop new rules that would prevent it from delivering mail-in or absentee ballots to voters unless they were on state-specific lists. The order prompted 23 states to file a lawsuit against the Trump administration seeking to block the move, which they called "as unprecedented as it is unconstitutional."The Supreme Court on Monday denied Trump's request to lift an order halting his plan. In a concurring opinion, Justice Brett Kavanaugh said there was "at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service’s statutory authority" but that "state and local election officials do not have sufficient time to reasonably implement the rule before the elections."Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented.Civil rights groups such as the NAACP have welcomed the decision."Big win for voters ahead of the midterm elections," the organisation wrote in a post on X. "Our country works best when every eligible voter can make their voice heard".Despite his opposition, Trump himself used a mail-in ballot to vote in an election in Florida earlier this year.Explaining his decision to reporters at the time, he said: "Because of the fact I'm president of the United States, I did a mail-in ballot for elections that took place in Florida.""I decided that I was going to vote by mail-in ballot because I couldn't be there, because I had a lot of different things," he added.
