Headline: ‘Do you know where Ceuta is?’: EU Parliament erupts over migration
Body: A European Parliament debate on the situation in Ceuta on Tuesday descended into a bitter internal clash between the political groups backing European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, just one day before her landmark State of the Union address.The two main groups underpinning the centrist majority — the European People’s Party (EPP) and the Socialists and Democrats (S&D) — clashed over the aftermath of the mass influx of migrants into the Spanish exclave on 30-31 July, when around 80,000 people crossed the border irregularly and more than 150 people died.“The EPP has been exploiting Ceuta for more than a month with the sole aim of attacking the Spanish government,” Socialist leader Iratxe García Pérez said in a direct attack on the centre-right group.S&D MEPs rallied behind Sánchez’s government while criticising other EU countries for what they described as a failure to show solidarity with Spain.Some lawmakers targeted the Italian government, which came under fire for extending by another 15 days its reintroduction of checks at air and maritime borders with Spain.“Meloni asked for solidarity for Lampedusa and denies it for Ceuta,” Italian Socialist MEP Sandro Ruotolo said, accusing Rome of applying a double standard on migration.EPP lawmakers, meanwhile, largely used their interventions to criticise Sánchez, accusing his government of allowing an “invasion” of European territory by failing to prevent the mass influx.Earlier this month, a leaked Spanish police report suggested that Moroccan forces had played a role in pushing migrants towards Ceuta, adding pressure on Madrid and fuelling criticism from the EPP.“The police warned him. The intelligence services sent reports. [...] Sánchez knew it and went on vacation for 25 days,” Spanish MEP Dolors Montserrat said.Centre-right lawmakers also used the debate to attack the Spanish government’s broader migration policy, including its plan to regularise thousands of undocumented migrants, although the measure is not directly linked to the Ceuta crisis.“Sánchez asked for solidarity after resisting common tools needed to prevent crises and initiated mass regularisation even though there was no agreement on this in Europe,” Dutch EPP MEP Jeroen Lenaers said.A resolution on the issue is due to be put to a vote next Thursday, with a political battle over amendments expected to determine its final wording and expose further divisions between the two main centrist groups.The EPP is expected to push for critical references to Spain’s handling of the crisis, while the Socialists are likely to seek to soften the language of the accusations.Migration is also expected to feature in the State of the Union address, where von der Leyen is likely to propose further restricting measures on asylum rights and a boost to the EU border agency Frontex.Far-right and left clashed in chaotic debateBeyond the EPP-S&D clash, several MEPs from the far right and radical left also took the floor with provocative remarks and counter-accusations, sparking heated exchanges.Podemos MEP Isabel Serra Sánchez accused far-right colleagues of turning Ceuta into a “hate laboratory” by calling for migrants to be “hunted”, which she said had contributed to attacks against migrants in the exclave.Diego Solier, of the Spanish nationalist party The Party Is Over, challenged her, asking whether she cared about women who had allegedly been sexually assaulted by migrants in the autonomous city.Vox MEP Jorge Buxadé Villalba shouted during an intervention by Green MEP Jaume Asens, while non-attached MEP Alvise Pérez claimed he had been insulted by left-wing colleagues. Pérez was then reprimanded for having previously insulted The Left’s Irene Montero, prompting an unusual exchange with Parliament Vice-President Younous Omarjee.After a passionate speech warning of an “invasion” of Europe by irregular migrants, League MEP Susanna Ceccardi was challenged by Swedish liberal MEP Abir Al-Sahlani, who hit back with a pointed question: “Do you know where Ceuta is?”

Headline: How can Europe decarbonise without sacrificing economic development? New study offers roadmap
Body: Europe wants to clean up its heavy industries without sacrificing jobs or economic growth. A new study suggests that may be possible – but it will require compromises.Researchers from the Euro-Mediterranean Center on Climate Change (CMCC Foundation), Politecnico di Milano and Technische Universität Berlin say that Europe could cut industrial emissions dramatically without hollowing out its manufacturing base.The cheapest path to doing that, however, could require importing some of the materials that require the most energy to produce, and then using them to make higher-value goods in European factories. How can Europe cut industrial emissions?To find out how Europe could do this, the researchers modelled steel, cement and chemical production through 2050.Steel and chemicals could be made using far fewer fossil fuels, the study found.Under the strictest emissions targets studied, which requires a 90 per cent cut in greenhouse gas emissions by 2040, most steel, ammonia and methanol would be produced using green hydrogen – hydrogen made using renewable electricity instead of fossil fuels. Steelmakers, meanwhile, would also use recycled scrap metal and power more of their work with electricity rather than coal or gas.Cement is more complicated. The process of making it releases carbon dioxide, even if the energy used to produce it comes from environmentally friendly sources. The study found that capturing emissions at cement plants could reduce the amount that gets released into the atmosphere, though critics say this technology remains unproven at scale.But green production comes at a price.The transition would be most expensive around 2040, when European industry would need major investments in infrastructure and equipment. Costs would fall by 2050, but Europe would remain at a disadvantage to places with cheaper renewable energy.Could moving factories closer to renewables cut costs? One solution is to put factories where renewable electricity costs less.In the model, when companies were allowed to relocate, they sent their production to Spain, the Nordic countries and the UK, where cheaper, abundant renewable power lowered electricity costs.But the savings come with a catch: the calculations left out the cost of relocating factories, building new infrastructure, finding workers and untangling existing supply chains.The authors stress that the exercise was a benchmark for potential savings, however, and not a forecast of Europe’s future industrial map.Green imports could keep manufacturing in EuropeThey did find one cheaper alternative.Importing some of the most energy-intensive materials – such as ammonia, methanol and hot-briquetted iron (HBI) – produced bigger savings than moving production within Europe. It would also allow companies to keep the later stages of manufacturing in their existing European factories.HBI is a form of iron used to make steel. The researchers say it could be made in countries with cheaper renewable electricity and shipped to Europe for the final stages of production.By 2050, almost all ammonia and methanol could be imported under this scenario as well. Europe would need to produce around 25 per cent less green hydrogen as a result.Would importing green materials just create a new dependency?But relying on imports carries its own risks. The study doesn’t account for wars, pandemics or other seismic events that could disrupt international supply chains.Europe has already seen how vulnerable some of them can be.This year, conflict in the Middle East interrupted shipments of oil, gas and fertiliser through the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Russia’s cuts to gas supplies after its invasion of Ukraine sent energy prices soaring, forcing some European factories to cut production.The researchers argue that fossil fuels come from a handful of suppliers through fixed infrastructure like pipelines, whereas green iron, ammonia and methanol, “can be shipped from any region with cheap renewables”.There’s also a difference in what the supply chain can become, they say. A fossil fuel supply chain “is emitting by construction”, whereas an iron or ammonia supply chain “can be progressively decarbonised” – which is what the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is designed to encourage.And the alternative isn't really independence, they add. Producing everything at home is what pushes subsidy costs above €200 billion a year. A dependence “avoided only through permanent state aid isn’t obviously more secure”.What would it cost to keep more production in Europe?Trying to grow European industry without imports could be pricey, though.In the most expensive scenario the researchers modelled, Europe would increase its industrial production and continue making the most energy-intensive materials needed to do so at home. Governments would need to spend around €235 billion a year to cover the difference between European production costs and import prices.“Europe should be practical about its capacity to expand its heavy industry,” says Massimo Tavoni, co-author of the study and institute director at the CMCC Foundation. “It should prioritise decarbonisation and the retention of existing industrial capacity, supported by targeted, time-limited public support and smart use of green imports.”

Headline: EU unveils digital platform to ease recognition of social security and professional qualifications
Body: In a proposal put forward on Tuesday, the European Commission has set out plans for a digital European platform that citizens can use to get their working documents recognised across the bloc.The aim of the platform, which will be known as the "European Social Security Pass", is to overcome delays that cross-border workers face when they need to receive working documents or get them recognised in member states other than their home countries. Those delays often result in basic rights being violated.With the new package, workers will be able to more easily claim their social security and health insurance benefits, as well as have their professional qualifications recognised in other EU countries without unnecessary red tape.The proposals also aim to protect mobile workers and to address challenges faced by companies when recruiting talent from abroad within the EU."The single market must also become a genuine skills market with more opportunities for workers and businesses," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press statement.Commission data from 2024 showed that around 14 million Europeans lived in EU countries other than those they were born in; 10 million of them were of working age. A recent Eurobarometer survey, meanwhile, found that 18% of Europeans want to move abroad.European Commission Vice-President for Social Rights Roxana Mînzatu told Euronews that a new EU platform will save “talented" people from “wasting their skills” when they move across EU borders.The Commission estimates that the platform could deliver as much as €6 billion in benefits by 2040."Over 12 years, digitisation could save up to €64 million for businesses, €69 million for healthcare providers, and €72 million for labour inspectors through faster cross-border verification. Digital signatures could avoid up to €277 million in fraud over the same period," the Commission said in a statement.

Headline: Russia, Venezuela and Trump’s oil push: the EU's awkward G20 energy summit
Body: European Union Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen will join this week’s G20 energy meeting in Houston, Texas, alongside unexpected Russian and Venezuelan officials, exposing an increasingly uncomfortable rift between Brussels and Washington over what energy security actually means — and who should be responsible for delivering it.The G20 energy ministerial meeting, hosted by the US administration from 14–16 September under the banner of “energy abundance,” reflects Washington’s push for a model centered on expanding oil and gas production, increasing electricity supply and rolling back environmental regulations viewed as obstacles to energy investment.The approach stands in sharp contrast to the EU’s focus on climate policy and the clean energy transition.Though the EU, the US and Russia are all full G20 members, Jørgensen will have to navigate Russia’s presence at the meeting, despite Moscow’s war against Ukraine and the EU’s efforts to end its remaining reliance on Russian fossil fuels. Venezuela will also be at the table as a controversial guest, bringing a major oil producer into the mix.“For sure it’s a very uncomfortable situation, but he (Commissioner Jørgensen) will pass the EU’s message," a Commission official who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, told Euronews. The official added that "Russia is part of the G20 and the ongoing Presidency was responsible" for whoever attends these meetings.Washington used the G20 gathering to promote its own energy agenda, announcing plans to roll back US carbon-emissions limits on coal-and gas-fired power plants. Arriving in the US to represent the EU’s climate-focused approach, Jørgensen is likely to find himself in an increasingly uncomfortable position.The EU’s energy strategy is increasingly focused on reducing Europe’s dependence on imported fossil fuels by accelerating electrification, expanding renewables, upgrading grids, improving energy efficiency and developing other domestic energy sources. Jørgensen has repeatedly framed energy independence as a strategic and security imperative, while arguing for a more electrified European economy. For Washington, energy security comes from abundant production — particularly US oil, gas and electricity — while Brussels argues that dependence on volatile global fossil-fuel markets is a security vulnerability.That message, however, may fall on deaf ears as US Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who is attending the G20 in Houston, snubbed previous G20 ministerial meetings on energy, saying they were all about "climate extremism" and "how to stop energy production"."If you want to talk about affordability, this is actually a conference where we’re talking about increasing supply and increasing security," Burgum told reporters.A Russian in the roomThe setting makes the clash even more politically charged, with a Russian official seated at the same table as Jørgensen.The White House made the announcement recently but has not identified the Russian official. However, the representative is likely to be Energy Minister Sergey Tsivilyov.It remains unclear whether the EU was informed about the last-minute participation. The European Commission has so far not responded to Euronews’ request for comment.Russia’s participation is particularly striking given Moscow’s ongoing war against Ukraine and the EU’s efforts to end its remaining reliance on Russian fossil fuels.The participation of Venezuela comes as Washington moves to deepen its energy relationship with Caracas and encourage a revival of Venezuelan oil production after ousting former President Nicolas Maduro.However, the guest list risks turning the energy ministerial into something more than a discussion of supply and prices. It places the EU alongside the US, which is determined to expand fossil-fuel production, while also putting it in an awkward position between Washington and two countries whose oil and gas sectors are deeply entangled in broader geopolitical power struggles."The G20 is an opportunity for leading economies to align on pragmatic principles like these (deregulation, permitting reform) which will unlock energy abundance and strengthen global resilience," reads the official G20 page.If Washington uses its G20 presidency to build a coalition around a pro-production message, Brussels risks being cast as the outlier, with the bloc arguing that the answer to an energy crisis is to accelerate the transition away from the fuels at the centre of the crisis.EU lawmaker Virgil-Daniel Popescu (Romania/EPP) urged Commissioner Jørgensen not to get into a dispute with Washington over the meeting’s name, which the Trump administration has rebranded as the “Energy Abundance Working Group”."The useful line is a shared one: more energy, more security, more production at home. Nuclear and renewables belong together. Gas that replaces a risky import is a security project, not a fight against the transition," Popescu told Euronews."The test in Houston is whether we can talk abundance without amnesia — without forgetting Ukraine, and without forgetting that dependence, on fuel or on technology, is still the strategic risk."Decarbonisation vs abundant energyIn Houston, Jørgensen will be challenged to defend the EU's own definition of energy security without appearing disconnected from the immediate problem confronting governments: high and volatile energy prices and fears over physical supply.European gas prices climbed to around €75/MWh on 9 September, rising further above €83/MWh on 14 September, compared to pre-conflict levels of around €31/MWh before the US and Israel war against Iran. The spike in prices has prompted the European Central Bank to warn that gas prices were becoming an inflation problem.Brent crude oil has also risen to over $100 per barrel amid escalation in the Middle East, with pump prices likely to rise again.Brussels is likely expecting Washington to point to the US’s vast domestic energy resources and argue that expanding oil and gas production is the fastest way to shield consumers and industry from geopolitical shocks.However, the EU's longer-term answer of decarbonisation and electrification won't be a quick fix for the soaring energy bills, exposing the EU's fragility and giving political traction to the energy abundance concept.EU lawmaker Roman Haider (Austria/Patriots of Europe) described the European energy policy as a "failure" and blamed it on the "ongoing industrial exodus"."The American approach of making energy as cheap and reliably available as possible is the order of the day. Exactly that should be the central task of the Commissioner, not moral grandstanding about who sits next to whom, where and when. That has its place in kindergarten," Haider told Euronews.

Headline: European telecoms execs push back against planned Huawei crackdown
Body: Leading telecoms executives across Europe have raised the alarm over EU plans to ban Chinese equipment makers such as Huawei and ZTE from the bloc's networks, warning the move would drive up costs at a time when operators are already stretched.Under its Digital Networks Act, unveiled in January, the European Union is proposing to ban suppliers classified as "high risk" on cybersecurity grounds.The Act avoids naming Chinese companies directly, but once a supplier is designated as high-risk, telecoms operators would have a three-year window to remove its equipment from their networks.The plan is the latest in a string of measures reflecting cooling trade ties between Brussels and Beijing.In an open letter, the Connect Europe lobby group — representing telecoms operators — argued that the Cybersecurity Act "risks draining the sector of the very capital needed for fibre, 5G and 6G" infrastructure.The letter was signed by 17 senior executives, among them the chief executives of Orange (France), Deutsche Telekom (Germany) and Telefónica (Spain).While also stopping short of naming China specifically, the signatories estimated that a blanket ban on suppliers from outside the EU could saddle the industry with as much as €40 billion in replacement costs.The proposal is now being thrashed out between the European Parliament and the governments of the EU's 27 member states.It follows a 2023 push by the European Commission urging countries to strip Huawei and ZTE from their mobile networks over security concerns — an appeal that yielded only patchy results.Where Europe stands on HuaweiProgress among EU and wider European countries has been uneven. As of a few years ago, just 10 countries in the bloc had excluded Chinese hardware makers from their networks following the Commission's recommendation, even though almost all member states had put a regulatory framework in place, with only a handful, such as Sweden and Latvia, actually enforcing restrictions.Sweden was among the earliest and firmest movers, with its telecoms regulator banning the use of Huawei and ZTE equipment in its 5G network ahead of a spectrum auction, a decision later upheld by an appeals court.France took a softer, phased approach, declining to renew operators' licences for Huawei gear as they expire, effectively easing the company out over time, while Romania and Estonia passed legislation in 2021 that in practice barred Chinese vendors from their networks.Outside the EU, the United Kingdom went further, ordering Huawei equipment to be purged from its 5G network entirely. Denmark also introduced investment-screening powers partly in response to security concerns over a Huawei bid.Germany, the bloc's largest economy, has moved more cautiously, agreeing with its major operators to remove Huawei and ZTE components from 5G core networks by the end of 2026, with broader access and transport-network components to follow by 2029 — a timeline critics say still leaves the country exposed for years to come.

Headline: Losing access to Bab el-Mandeb would be 'catastrophic for the entire world,' Qatar warns
Body: Qatar has called for international efforts to keep Bab el-Mandeb open, warning that losing another major shipping route while the Strait of Hormuz remains blocked would be "catastrophic".Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi, director of media and communication at Qatar’s foreign ministry, told Tuesday’s briefing in Doha that closing the entrance to the Red Sea would worsen the disruption already caused by the Hormuz blockade.“The world is suffering enough with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, so we cannot also afford to add the Bab al-Mandeb into that equation,” said Al Hashmi.“The whole world is going to suffer and it’s going to be catastrophic for the entire world,” he said.He said the blocking of international waterways could not become the “new normal” and urged countries to work together to prevent it.Houthis in controlThe warning comes after the Iran-backed Houthis seized more islands in the southern Red Sea, strengthening their position in and near Bab el-Mandeb.Internationally-recognised government and Houthi officials both said on Monday that the group had captured the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands following the withdrawal of government-allied forces. The Houthis had already taken the coastal port of Mokha and Perim Island at the very entrance to the strait.Saudi Arabia backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, whose forces have been trying to regroup after the losses. The Houthis have also launched multiple attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and ships in the Red Sea, after announcing a blockade on Saudi shipping in July.Those attacks have placed further pressure on energy supplies during the Iran war. On the other side of the Arabian Peninsula, US and Iranian blockades have already disrupted shipping through Hormuz.Why Bab el-Mandeb mattersBab el-Mandeb, whose name in Arabic means "Gate of Tears," links the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea, meaning vessels travelling between Asia and Europe through the Suez Canal must pass through it.Earlier Houthi attacks forced many vessels to sail around southern Africa instead, adding time and expense to their journeys, according to the US Energy Information Administration.Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline allows it to bypass Hormuz by moving oil to Red Sea ports — but tankers sailing south from those ports still need to pass through Bab el-Mandeb.Al Hashmi said Qatar was working with regional and international partners to support talks on freedom of navigation through Hormuz, and urged diplomacy to resolve the conflicts.“It is not an impossible task because at the end of the day, the only solution will be through the negotiation table and that’s what we are working diligently on,” he said.

Headline: Living in deprived areas linked to poorer brain health
Body: Where people live may leave a measurable imprint on their brains, according to new research published in Radiology, the journal of the Radiological Society of North America.Researchers analysed nearly 3,000 brain MRI scans from patients aged between 18 and 96. They compared brain measures with an Area Deprivation Index (ADI) score, a neighbourhood-level measure of socioeconomic disadvantage based on factors including income, education, employment and housing. The index describes the conditions of a place rather than the circumstances of any individual resident.People living in the most disadvantaged neighbourhoods had a higher “brain age” and lower total brain volume than those living in less deprived areas.“Where you live leaves a measurable imprint on your brain,” said John-Paul J. Yu, one of the researchers. An individual’s environment, he said, has “clear, quantifiable implications for brain age, and, by proxy, brain health”.The findings add to evidence that the conditions in which people are born, live, work and age can shape long-term neurological health.The researchers also found higher volumes of white matter hyperintensities — bright spots visible on MRI scans that are associated with damage to small blood vessels in the brain — among people living in the most disadvantaged neighbourhoods.“White matter hyperintensities are essentially the footprints of cardiovascular damage in the brain,” Yu said, pointing to factors such as high blood pressure, poor sleep and chronic stress that can affect blood flow to the brain over time.Higher volumes of white matter hyperintensities have been associated with an increased risk of memory loss, cognitive problems and dementia.Yu said neighbourhood disadvantage should therefore be considered when designing health interventions and public policy.“Neighbourhood disadvantage, quantified by indices such as the ADI, is an important determinant because it reflects accumulated structural inequities extending beyond individual behaviours that contribute to disparities in clinical outcomes,” he said.

Headline: Azerbaijan offers F1 fans visas on arrival for Baku Grand Prix
Body: Azerbaijan will grant visas on arrival to Formula 1 ticket holders and accredited racing personnel ahead of next weekend's Grand Prix, as Baku looks to boost attendance and extend the race's economic reach beyond the circuit.Fans with confirmed race tickets — physical or electronic — or valid accreditation from Formula One Management Limited, the FIA, or the Baku City Circuit Operations Company can collect visas at the airport on arrival.Travellers without tickets must use the electronic ASAN visa system or apply through an Azerbaijani embassy or consulate.The facilitation window runs until 30 September, four days after race day on Saturday 26 September. This is the first time in Baku's F1 history that the race falls on a Saturday, moved from Sunday to respect Azerbaijan's National Remembrance Day on 27 September.International visitors accounted for more than 80% of spectators at the 2024 Azerbaijan Grand Prix, according to official figures.Foreign attendees spent an average of more than $2,200 (€2,000) during the race weekend, and 72% said they intended to return within two years, according to Formula 1 data.Florian Sengstschmid, chief executive of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board, said motorsport fans' late-booking habits made arrival-based visas particularly useful."Formula 1 fans tend to decide late, and a visa issued on arrival against a ticket or accreditation means that spontaneous decision can become a weekend in Baku," Sengstschmid told Euronews.Sengstschmid said the post-race extension was intended to encourage visitors to travel beyond Baku to destinations including Gabala, Shaki and the Absheron peninsula."That is where the lasting value lies for us: turning a three-day motorsport trip into a week in Azerbaijan, and a first-time visitor into a returning one," he said.Several other major sporting hosts have introduced similar measures. Brazil waived visa fees for World Cup ticket holders in 2014, and Qatar used the Hayya Card as a universal entry permit for the 2022 tournament.

Headline: Eurostar’s new trains will have two-storey cocktail bars – but you’ll have to wait until 2031
Body: We love a good train story here at Euronews Travel. We’re fans of fast trains and slow trains, new trains and vintage trains, sleeper trains… book us a ticket, we’ll ride ‘em all.But if there’s one kind of train I personally adore, it's the double decker ones. Likely because I grew up in the UK where there aren’t any, the novelty of stepping aboard one on the continent still hasn’t worn off.So the announcement late last year that the Eurostar will start running double-decker trains across its network from 2031 was big news for myself and other double-decker enjoyers not of the chocolate kind.But now, there’s even bigger news for those of us who are also fans of train tinnies: Eurostar’s new trains will have double-decker bars on board.Open to everyone on board, the two-storey bars are meant to be the “star attraction” of the Celestia trains.A Eurostar spokesperson told Euronews Travel: “The name Celestia means ‘heavenly’, reflecting the idea behind the double-decker bar: to create a travel experience beyond the ordinary.”We’re convinced already.What else to know about the new Eurostar trainsEurostar has ordered 30 Celestia trains, with the first due to welcome passengers from May 2031. At that time, six will be in operation across all of Eurostar’s current destinations, as well as Geneva and Frankfurt.Following record-breaking heatwaves across Europe this summer, Eurostar also announced that its new trains will have air conditioning that can operate in temperatures of up to 55°C.“These trains will enter service in 2031 and run into the 2060s, so it’s essential to be prepared for the future,” a Eurostar spokesperson said.

Headline: The history of Ceuta and Melilla and why they are Spanish territory
Body: "Ceuta and Melilla are not just Spanish, they are quintessentially Spanish and untouchable", said Spain's Defence Minister Margarita Robles, speaking days after the surge of irregular migrants from Morocco who stormed the Spanish border last July.The sovereignty of Ceuta and Melilla regularly returns to public debate, fuelled by Rabat's claims and by renewed migratory tensions on the North African border. After the migration crisis that unfolded in Ceuta, several Moroccan politicians seized the moment to call for both Spanish autonomous cities to become part of Morocco.The narrative that both cities are "colonial remnants" is often deployed as a political argument, but history, international law and the United Nations (UN) itself contradict this premise.Since when have Ceuta and Melilla been Spanish?To understand the special status of both enclaves, it is necessary to go back to the 15th and 16th centuries, a time when the concept of "colonialism" did not yet exist in the modern terms we understand today.Melilla was incorporated into the Crown of Castile on 17 September 1497 by an expedition led by Pedro de Estopiñán and authorised by the all-powerful Catholic Monarchs, Isabella and Ferdinand. The capture served a strictly defensive objective: to secure the Strait and protect the peninsular coasts from Barbary piracy.Ceuta was initially conquered by Portugal in 1415 and came under Spanish sovereignty in 1580 following the dynastic union under Philip II, after he inherited the Portuguese throne. When Portugal regained its independence in 1640, Ceuta freely chose to remain linked to the Spanish monarchy, a decision legally ratified in the Treaty of Lisbon of 1668.Both cities have spent between 358 and 529 years without interruption under Spanish sovereignty and have never belonged to the Kingdom of Morocco.Did Morocco exist when they were incorporated into Spain?Not in the form of a contemporary unified state. The Alaouite dynasty, which currently rules the country under Mohammed VI, began its reign in 1666.This means that Melilla, for example, had already been part of the Castilian Crown for more than 160 years before the founding of the dynasty that underpins modern Morocco.The nuance between 19th-century expansions and the ProtectorateTo carry out a rigorous analysis, it is necessary to consider a nuance highlighted by various historians: around 90% of the current urban area of both cities stems from territorial extensions carried out throughout the 19th century and the early 20th century. This coincided with the era of European expansion in Africa and with the establishment of the Spanish Protectorate in Morocco (1912-1956).The size of the cities grew through border treaties, but their sovereignty was already established 300 years earlier and they were never managed as a temporary colony, but as national territory.However, there is an underlying legal distinction:- The legal title to sovereignty over the original territory is several centuries older than Moroccan independence.- Neither Ceuta nor Melilla ever formed part of the Protectorate. While Moroccan territory was under temporary administration, the two enclaves retained without interruption their status as national territory under full Spanish sovereignty.The key position of the UN and the international communityThe ultimate legal backing for Spain's position comes from the multilateral arena.In 1975, the Moroccan government formally asked the UN to add Ceuta and Melilla to the list of "territories pending decolonisation" (which does include Western Sahara, occupied by Morocco and whose citizens Spain intends to grant nationality to). The UN rejected the request.To this day, the United Nations does not consider them colonies or include them in any list of territories to be decolonised. Strategic allies such as the United States, despite its current closeness to the Moroccan regime, formally recognise both cities as part of Spain's sovereign territory.Furthermore, with the entry into force of their Statutes of Autonomy in 1995, they were consolidated as Autonomous Cities, fully integrated into the European Union and represented in the Spanish Congress and Senate.Claims about the alleged "colonial" nature of Ceuta and Melilla may reflect Rabat's short-term geopolitical strategies, but they do not stand up to historical scrutiny or to the legal framework of international law.

Headline: United States Space Force says US has weapons in orbit
Body: The United States Space Force confirmed on Monday that the US has deployed weapons into orbit."The US has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action," a spokesperson for the force said in a statement."Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain -- employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities," the statement continued.It added that "these capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes.”Responding to the US announcement, a spokesperson for China's Foreign Ministry urged the US to halt its "military buildup" in space and said China "opposes any arms race in outer space or any attempt to weaponize it and turn it into a warzone."The Kremlin has also called for space to be kept "free of any weapons.""We are counting on broad international consolidation to continue working toward the complete demilitarisation of space," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said.'Strategic competitors'The space domain has become increasingly viewed as a critical component of national security, with much of the world economy relying on space infrastructure such as satellites.Once a hunting ground for Cold War bragging rights, space has now evolved into a key strategic arena, as states jostle for a military and technological edge.The US moved to better position itself in 2019, establishing the Space Force to address what the military calls the "growing threat posed by strategic competitors."Washington is particularly wary of potential threats posed by China and Russia in space.The Space Force says Beijing and Moscow are developing a range of new systems designed to boost military effectiveness and "end any reliance on U.S. space services," while also "testing and fielding sophisticated counterspace capabilities."The Chinese military, the force says, believes space will have an important role in future conflicts, "enabling long-range precision strikes and denying other militaries the use of space-based information."It adds that China has also been developing and operating space and counterspace capabilities as part of a push to modernise its military.For its part, Russia runs one of the world's largest space programs, and while it has been hampered by funding issues and international isolation, it is still a "capable space actor," the Space Force says."Russia views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts," it adds.

Headline: Europe’s fake pesticide crisis: inside a $20 billion illegal trade
Body: Up to 14% of Europe's pesticide market may be counterfeit or illegal, rising to 25% in parts of Greece.Farmers in Serres say the appeal is purely financial: illegal products can cost a sixth of the approved price. But scientists warn these unregulated substances, often smuggled from Turkey, contain carcinogenic chemicals banned across the EU.Police describe organised international networks moving products by car, truck and even tourist bus. Since 2020, authorities have seized nearly 8,700 tonnes of banned pesticides, part of a trade worth an estimated $20 billion globally each year, according to TRACIT.

Headline: Inside an Uzbek wedding: traditions, family and the start of married life
Body: In Uzbekistan, a wedding is a major family occasion, bringing relatives, friends and several generations together. Before the celebrations begin, however, the couple first make their marriage official at the civil registry. Traditional customs can start earlier, with families gathering for meals, blessings and ceremonies that prepare the couple for their wedding day.From the registry office to the wedding tableOn the wedding day, preparations take place separately in the two families’ homes. The groom gets ready with relatives and friends, while the bride prepares at her family home.The groom later arrives with his friends as part of ‘Kuyov Navkar’, a traditional procession or gathering accompanying the groom to the bride’s home.Food is central to the celebrations. At the bride’s home, guests gather around a table for wedding plov, Uzbekistan’s signature rice dish, typically cooked with meat, carrots and onions.Before leaving for the main wedding reception, the bride and groom receive blessings from their parents and older relatives.For the groom, Abbos Sabitov, the day marks a new stage in his life.“Seeing all my loved ones together in one place is a great happiness for me. I'm starting a new chapter in my life. I feel a great sense of responsibility, and I'm fully aware of everything that comes with it.”The gathering then moves into the main celebration, where music, dancing and food bring the two families together.A celebration for two familiesFlowers are exchanged between the newly joined families as relatives and friends take part in the festivities. For Feruza Avazova, the groom's sister, these gatherings provide an opportunity for relatives to meet, share a meal and offer their wishes to the newlyweds.Uzbek weddings can involve hundreds of guests, with friends and relatives taking part in dances, games and other activities during the reception.The celebrations also extend beyond the wedding day. Avazova mentions Challar, a post-wedding gathering hosted by the bride’s family for the newlyweds and the groom’s relatives, as well as Beshik Toy, a later celebration held after the birth of a child.At the end of the wedding, the couple's mothers come forward to offer their blessings. For many families, this is one of the most emotional moments of the celebration.Welcoming the bride into a new familyThe celebrations continue at the groom's home, where his mother welcomes the bride and wishes the couple a happy life together.For Dildora Adilova, the groom's mother, modern family life also comes with changing expectations.“I think modern brides should be well-rounded in every way. She should be able to manage the household, have a career and continue her education.”One of the most recognisable customs that follows is Kelin Salom, a formal greeting performed by the bride as she meets members of her new family.For Muslima Sabitova, the bride, the ceremony carries a personal meaning.“Performing the Kelin Salom and meeting the members of my new family gave me a different kind of emotion. I expect love and kindness from my new family, and that they will treat me like their own daughter.”Wedding customs in SamarkandWedding traditions vary between regions. In Samarkand, some ceremonies take place before the main celebration and are closely connected with the first moments of married life.One such custom is chimildiq, a private space prepared for the bride and groom in the bride's home. Among the rituals associated with it, the couple look at themselves in a mirror and feed each other honey, symbolising wishes for a sweet married life.After these intimate customs, the wedding becomes public again, with photographs, music, food and gatherings involving both families.Samarkand's historic architecture provides a backdrop for wedding photographs, with couples often visiting landmarks and studios as part of the day's preparations.The groom's friend Bobojon Ergashev describes his own role as part of the wedding party.“My role here is to take care of any problems or issues the groom might have during the wedding, to make sure everything runs smoothly.”Traditions that begin long before the weddingFor the families involved, preparing for a wedding can take years. Relatives plan the ceremonies, organise meals, prepare clothing and coordinate gatherings involving large numbers of guests.The customs may differ between families and regions, but many centre on the same elements: family participation, blessings from elders, shared meals and the formal welcome of a new member into the family.By the time the celebrations end, the wedding has marked more than a single ceremony. It has brought two families together and set the couple on the next stage of their life together.

Headline: 'Is this sport?': Sydney Sweeney faces backlash from female athletes over nude advert
Body: It seems that whenever American actress Sydney Sweeney signs on for an ad campaign, the internet ends up losing its mind.Following her hugely controversial American Eagle publicity campaign, which some perceived as promoting White supremacism and eugenics, her latest stunt has sparked fresh backlash. This time, Sweeney has managed to exasperate female athletes and Olympians, who have labelled the advertisement as "infuriating" and "a kick in the face to every woman."The source of fresh division comes down to Sweeney featuring in a commercial for Novig, the American sports trading app. Read: gambling firm.In the NSFW advert, the Euphoria actress poses with little-to-no clothing and pieces of sporting equipment. Very little is left to the imagination."Novig is just sports," she says, strategically covering her bathykolpian figure with footballs - followed by a baseball bat, a hockey stick, a tennis racket..."Sports... Sports... Sports..." she repeats, before adding: “No betting on wars or deaths, and no politics. Just you and your takes on sports.”“The campaign was about embracing a fun idea,” said Sweeney, who is also a Novig strategic partner and equity holder. “The concept is simple: cut through the noise and put the focus entirely on sports. The campaign brings that idea to life with confidence, humour and a playful edge.”No one bought it, as the focus was less on sports and clearly on appealing to those... titillated by her Sweeneys.Of course, social media went into overdrive. The ad clearly worked for some and enraged others, who saw it as a shameless way of treating people like idiots."Sydney Sweeney is single handedly setting feminism 1000 years back and you can't convince me otherwise," wrote one social media user, while another added: "It's basically soft-core porn.""Stop sexualizing women's sports," another wrote. "In WHAT world do you need to be butt ass naked for a SPORTS COMMERCIAL?!"Beyond the usual bile-filled back-and-forths on X, the advert has raised concern among female athletes, who have argued that Sweeney's ad shamefully sexualises women's sports and is "demeaning".“I can’t describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this,” Ariarne Titmus, a four-time Olympic gold medalist for Australia, wrote on Instagram. “Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity."She added: “How do we live in a world where monetising a woman’s body and sexualising women’s sport is still a thing?”Australian World champion boxer Skye Nicolson said it was about making a “mockery” of women in sport. “There’s a big difference between looking ‘sexy’ because you do sport compared to using sex to sell ‘sport’,” she wrote in an Instagram story. “There is nothing wrong with looking good and doing sport and there’s nothing wrong with embracing your femininity while also being a badass athlete.”As for Canadian skier Cassidy Gray, who competed at the 2026 Winter Olympics, she took to TikTok to respond to Sweeney's ad, noting how female athletes face being sexualised, not being taken seriously and not given the same opportunities as men. Gray went on to describe Sweeney's actions as "idiotic" and "senseless" in a video that now gone viral.Meanwhile, in a post liked by several celebrities, including actress Florence Pugh, UK athlete Lucy Davis wrote: “I don’t know wtf Sydney Sweeney was doing, but it’s 2026. Stop sexualizing women in sport.”British sprinter Amy Hunt used a BBC interview to call out the actress. “Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like,” she said after racing at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship. “Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears. This is a beautiful evening.”Elsewhere, the Female Athlete Project, which fosters a community for women in sports, posted the following statement: "We're not entirely sure if Novig or Sydney Sweeney and her PR team have ever watched sports. But honestly, wow. It's incredible they could fit so much misogyny in 40 seconds. Sports has long treated women's bodies as commodities, and this objectification does nothing to support real women in sport."Naturally, this statement also prompted some backlash, featuring a few less than erudite comments and even some support for Sweeney."Why don't we blame / name the ad company instead of the actress? I'm sure if she declined the offer someone else would have done it. I don't think it's right to blame her," wrote one user on Instagram. Another commented: "This is so dramatic. It’s a sports betting ad. It doesn’t have anything to do with women in sports. It’s meant to draw in silly men to spend money on sports.""Sooo guess it’s body positivity if they’re overweight?" queried another, adding: "Pretty sure she never said anything specific about women in sports. Women have been used in sports ads for forever. What if Sydney Sweeney was fat? I’m sure everyone would praise her? What if it was Taylor Swift in the ad? I’m sure everyone would praise her. “Support other women”… unless it’s Sydney Sweeney???"Sweeney has seemingly responded to the backlash by taking to her Instagram Story to post various covers from ESPN Magazine's The Body Issue from over the years which show nude sports photos featuring athletes including Serena Williams, Ronda Rousey and Megan Rapinoe.Still, that hasn't stopped more than 200,000 of her followers from smashing the “unfollow” button on her account...Role playThe ad has left many wondering what Sweeney is playing at. Provocation for the sake of it? Inviting objectification of her own body and accepting the pornification of whatever big companies want in exchange for a big fat paycheck? Or just doing ads for the love of reminding horny viewers that spherical sports equipment can be reminiscent of breasts?Whatever it is, sadly, it's working – as her recent stunt has already achieved infamy. But beyond the nose-bleedingly tacky nature of it all – as well as the predictably misogynistic "hot takes" online reminding everyone that X gathers the binjuice of humanity - one aforementioned British athlete raises an important question.Amy Hunt doubled down on her criticism by warning that the Novig advert risks becoming a "barrier" to young girls wanting to take part in sport.Speaking on ITV's Good Morning Britain, she said: "I think when we’re trying to provide role models for young people and young women in sport, we really want to show that it’s about what your body can do, not so much what it looks like.""I think when we see the the stats of 64 per cent of young girls drop out of exercise and sport before they reach the age of 16, we don’t need to place any kind of barrier whatsoever in their way in terms of providing the opportunity and the empowerment for them to still exercise, whatever that looks like, professional or kind of just going to do a ParkRun with your friends. So it’s about empowering young girls and young women and young people to show that you really can just get out there and you don’t have to worry what you look like, you don’t have to worry about what you’re wearing."She added: "Sport, it’s not pretty, and I think that’s the thing to get to the level that we’re at. It’s shown to people that being aspirational and trying to be elite is something amazing, and you should really want to be the best version of yourself you can be. And that doesn’t always look attractive, and that doesn’t always look nice. Sometimes it looks like throwing up in the corner of the track, or I’ve had sessions this year where I’ve been crying afterwards."Will Novig and Sweeney take notice or think again in the future? Probably not. They're doubtlessly rubbing their hands at yet another viral Sweeney moment and fooling themselves into thinking they're getting away with the "put the focus entirely on sports" line. Shame, as maybe people would muster more goodwill towards the ad if the makers openly acknowledged that the only thing sex sells is sex itself. Not sport.

Headline: Catherine Ringer, iconic singer of French rockers Les Rita Mitsouko, dies aged 68
Body: A voice, a style, an energy and a freedom that left their mark on several generations. Catherine Ringer, singer and co-founder of French pop rock group Les Rita Mitsouko, has died at the age of 68.Her children announced her death to AFP, saying she had been taken by "a fast-acting cancer" on 14 September 2026.Ringer was born in Suresnes in 1957. Her father, Sam Ringer, an Ashkenazi Jew born in Poland, had been deported to several concentration camps. Catherine Ringer recounted his story in the song 'C'était un homme', on the album 'Cool Frénésie'.In 1979, she met Fred Chichin, and from their artistic and personal encounter came one of the most original duos in French music. Les Rita Mitsouko would quickly create a world apart, blending rock, pop, funk, electro and chanson.Critical and commercial success arrived in the mid-1980s with the song 'Marcia Baïla', which became emblematic of the French scene. The band then reeled off a string of hits, including 'Andy', 'C'est comme ça' and 'Les Histoires d'A'.Their music, their videos and their offbeat aesthetic turned Les Rita Mitsouko into a phenomenon that far exceeded the usual boundaries of rock.In November 2007, the death of Fred Chichin, also taken by cancer at just 53, could have brought the adventure to an end. Instead, Catherine Ringer chose to keep their repertoire alive. She pursued a solo career and regularly returned to the stage with the songs of Les Rita Mitsouko.Still active in 2026, she had notably performed in Paris last February. She was due to continue championing on stage the body of work born from her collaboration with Fred Chichin.With her death, French music loses a unique figure. Catherine Ringer remains inseparable from Les Rita Mitsouko, but also from her very own way of taking to the stage: free, provocative, original and widely loved by audiences.

Headline: Escalation is 'on the way' but region must keep calm, Syria's al-Sharaa tells Euronews
Body: "It looks like escalation is on the way” in the region gripped by the Iran war, and “with all the tensions, nobody can predict” what will happen, but the hope is that the situation “remains stable," Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said on Tuesday.In an answer to a Euronews question at the Arab Media Summit in Dubai, al-Sharaa urged the region’s countries to “keep calm” and “work together to alleviate the problems that come” with conflict, which is vital to Syria’s new beginning “after 60 years of destruction and 17 years of war”.The Arab Media Summit kicked off on Tuesday with a wide array of regional leaders, officials, media executives, analysts, writers and influencers, bringing together eight specialised forums, including Euronews’ Forum on Wednesday, and welcoming some 10,000 participants.As the headline speaker at the summit opening, Al-Sharaa said, “Syria is being transformed into a story being told across the world,” after overcoming all the obstacles of its past tragic decades and marking “a new beginning” which “could be a big opportunity.”Syria’s president outlined how his country took the initiative to turn the Iran war-generated crises into opportunities.“People are talking about Syria as a pathway, as security and supply chains can link the West and the East,” giving the UAE as an example of “targeting the right opportunities” with its moves to bypass the Strait of Hormuz closure.“Syria has always been a trade pathway as being traders and negotiators has been in our DNA,” al-Sharaa told the summit, adding that with transparency and honesty, “Syria is increasing its credibility,” as “it is not affiliated towards any direction”.From the podium in Dubai, he said, “We rely on our dear brothers and sisters in the Arab world and learn from them, so we don’t try to reinvent the wheel.He said Syria is in “a transformational phase” towards a democracy, after being plagued by sanctions that Trump “has been helping to lift,” which led to “breaking the chain” of the past.“We are expecting some shocks and we need to move into a quieter stage,” and that Damascus “need to give it time” for the reforms and transformations to make their mark.He further outlined food security and supplies as important targets for the region, where Syria has many opportunities that European investors and neighbouring countries with investments from the Gulf are interested in.Al-Sharaa told the summit that he hopes the region remains stable and that Syria “tries to find ways to mitigate the damage of war,” and to work together with the Arab world “to spread peace in the region which will help economic growth.”As a keynote speaker at the Arab Media Summit, Al-Sharaa said, “It is a heavy burden to work in the media, to fact-check and to stay away from politicising.”“People’s lives are in the hands of the media, as they need to keep up with the Arab societies to be aware of the actual facts of what is happening: authenticate information with channels and people and the messages of media,” the Syrian president concluded.

Headline: Prominent Greek neo-Nazi exits prison and says he will return to politics
Body: A former leading member of the Greek neo-Nazi party Golden Dawn, Ilias Kasidiaris, has been released from prison and vowed a return to politics.Kasidiaris was convicted and imprisoned in 2020 as a leading member of the criminal organisation, which for years had been linked to violent attacks on migrants and political opponents, as well as to the murder of anti-fascist musician Pavlos Fyssas in 2013. He served only part of his 13-year sentence.Leaving prison on Monday, Kasidiaris announced a return to Greek politics, vowing to start a new political movement on Monday.Dozens of his supporters had gathered outside Domokos prison in central Greece, some were holding Greek flags. The crowd chanted slogans in his favour, including "Ilias, we are with you".Kasidiaris addressed supporters upon his release: "I had given you my word that as soon as I passed through this gate I would return to the front line of the national struggle. I see that I am not alone, but that alongside me stands a major national party, like those that dominate in Europe.My aim is for the country to be rid of the most corrupt government of the post-junta era. In these past days I see the politicians whining and conspiring, saying they will not allow me to return to parliament. But in a democracy there is only one judge, the sovereign Greek people."Political careerKasidiaris became Golden Dawn’s press spokesman in 2012 and later served as an MP for the party until 2019. Golden Dawn caused a political earthquake in Greece in 2012, when it managed to enter parliament amid intense social and economic upheaval brought on by the financial crisis, the erosion of trust in institutions and the discrediting of traditional political parties.Despite being behind bars, he did not give up political activity. He continued to intervene via social media, mainly through his YouTube channel, which has around 162,000 subscribers.Before he was imprisoned, in October 2020 Kasidiaris had founded a new political formation, "Greeks", and even from prison tried to take part in the 2023 parliamentary elections. However, the Supreme Court (Areios Pagos) banned his party from standing in the elections.In 2023, the far-right "Spartans" party won more than 240,000 votes with Kasidiaris’s public backing.In July this year he found himself in the spotlight after billionaire Elon Musk called the continuation of Kasidiaris's detention was "confusing" or "wrong", triggering fresh reactions to the case. Kasidiaris has described Musk as "the most prominent personality in the world".Violent pastKasidiaris has appeared in the headlines over the years after a number of violent incidents. He has been photographed with a swastika tattoo on his left arm and is known for a series of aggressive behaviours.In 2012, live on television, he slapped Communist Party MP Liana Kanelli and threw a glass of water at an MP from a left-wing party.He has also been recorded verbally and physically attacking television crews. In a discussion with Golden Dawn supporters in November 2012 he claimed that party members entering parliament were allowed to "carry legally licensed weapons".Political futureLegal experts say he is still barred from running for office until 2033, although the Supreme Court would rule on his eligibility at election time. Greece’s next elections are due in 2027.His release comes at a time when the far right is gaining ground in several European countries. In Germany the far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD) has made significant progress in the polls, including a recent victory in a regional election contest, for the first time since the Second World War.

Headline: Poké Ball-shaped hotel opens in Japan to mark 30th anniversary of Pokémon
Body: A lot of people on the internet point to 2016 as both the moment where Everything Went Wrong, but also the last time the world felt truly united.I won’t get into the former, but the latter is tied to one thing: The release of Pokémon Go. It was a summer of fun, of running around with strangers, of embracing nostalgia.While it currently feels as though we’ll never reach those highs collectively again, there is still some whimsy in the world – and Pokémon-related whimsy to boot.That’s because NOT A HOTEL has teamed up with the sleep game app Pokémon Sleep to create a Poké Ball-shaped hotel.Located in Tomakomai City, Hokkaido, the hotel pod is three metres across, with a round bed under a curved acrylic window letting you enjoy the lakeside views while relaxing in the Poké Ball.There are plenty of nods to the beloved anime throughout, including tiles inspired by Snorlax's colors in the bathroom area next to the hotel. You can even pick your favourite Pokémon on an iPad in the room, which will transform the lighting to match your selection.Can you stay there?Bad news, I’m afraid.The hotel concept was created to celebrate both the 30th anniversary of Pokémon and the third anniversary of Pokémon Sleep, but only Japanese residents using the latter will be able to enter a competition for a stay.Users will be able to enter through X, formerly known as Twitter. If you are lucky enough to be eligible to apply, all the details can be found here.Those chosen will get a free one-night stay between 8 and 18 October.

Headline: ECB invites Europeans to vote on future banknote designs as deadline approaches
Body: Birds, rivers and figures from European culture, including composers, are among the design choices the ECB is asking people to consider for future euro banknotes. More than 9 million people have already voted, but the ECB is encouraging more people to share their opinions before the survey closes next Monday.The ECB has previously consulted Europeans about the redesign, but this is the first time it has launched a survey asking them to assess the ten shortlisted designs. The proposed designs also differ markedly from those on existing banknotes.In an increasingly cashless world, the ECB is sending a message to Europeans: cash is here to stay, and they can help choose what it will look like."Cash is not simply a legacy of the past. It is part of daily life for millions of Europeans," ECB Executive Board member Piero Cipollone said during an event on euro banknotes in Brussels on Monday.The survey covers ten shortlisted designs under two possible themes: “European culture” and “Rivers and birds”. The results will inform, but not determine, the ECB Governing Council’s final decision, which is expected around the end of 2026. The new banknotes will then take several years to develop and are expected to enter circulation gradually from 2029."More than 31 billion euro banknotes, worth over €1.6 trillion, are in circulation, with an annual growth of around 3%. There are also more than 150 billion euro coins in circulation," Cipollone said. He also noted that cash still plays a role when other payment methods are disrupted, for example during power or internet outages.The role of cash could be further reinforced by proposed EU legislation known as the Single Currency Package. The package, which is under negotiation in Brussels, includes measures intended to strengthen the legal-tender status of cash and its mandatory acceptance."Cash provides something that is difficult to replace: a tangible anchor of stability and trust. Cash also fosters financial inclusion. It is simple and intuitive. It protects privacy. And, perhaps most importantly, it safeguards freedom of choice," Cipollone said during his speech.According to a 2024 ECB survey, a growing majority of Europeans think that retaining cash as a payment option is important."Cash is the only form of money that every citizen can hold directly. Once you have cash, you don’t need any intermediaries or devices to use it," Cipollone said.Digital and physical euroIn its payment strategy, the ECB is investing not only in the redesign of banknotes but also in the creation of the digital euro, an electronic form of central bank money that would complement cash. The ECB says its support for cash is intrinsically linked to this new electronic means of payment, which is intended to enable both offline and online transactions with a high degree of privacy.The digital euro could be issued for the first time in 2029 if negotiations in Brussels are concluded by the end of 2026."We are investing in both euro cash and the digital euro. Together, they will ensure that Europeans have access to central bank money in both physical and digital form for day-to-day transactions," Cipollone said.Together, the two forms of central bank money could ensure that a "European solution is available for all types of payment, at all times, throughout the euro area," he said.One reason the ECB has developed a new payments strategy is the need for strategic autonomy amid significant geopolitical uncertainty and the EU's heavy reliance on US payment infrastructure.Visa and Mastercard, both American, account for 61% of card payments in the eurozone and nearly all cross-border card transactions, according to 2025 ECB data.

Headline: Danish PM condemns Russian flare attack on helicopter as 'reckless'
Body: A Russian warship has fired two emergency flares at a helicopter in the Baltic Sea, with the Russian ambassador summoned over the incident, Danish officials reported."One of the air force's Fennec helicopters was today fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate, which was located in international waters off Gedser," Danish armed forces said in a statement.The frigate had fired "two flares towards the helicopter. One of the flares passed at close range to the helicopter."Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen condemned the incident as "reckless"."Reckless action from Russia towards Danish military during a routine overflight yesterday. Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed. We will not waver," Frederiksen said in a statement on X.Danish foreign minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said "Russia is gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour," he warned."That is something we cannot accept," he said."Russia's ambassador has therefore been summoned for a discussion about the incident."Moscow blames Danish pilotsHowever, Vladimir Barbin, the Russian ambassador to Denmark, responded blaming the helicopter pilots."The Danish side's attempts to explain the helicopter's provocative actions against the Russian frigate as 'routine practice' give rise to serious concern about the possible consequences of such recklessness," Barbin said in written statement to AFP."The Russian side will thoroughly investigate all the circumstances of the incident," Barbin said while adding that "this is not the first time that Danish Air Force helicopters have carried out dangerous manoeuvres near Russian warships, when they were at sea and outside Denmark's territorial waters."The ambassador claimed last year he informed the Danish foreign ministry of "dangerous flyovers and low-altitude hovering" by a Danish Air Force helicopter over a large anti-submarine vessel.The incident coincides with Lithuania's foreign minister confirming an allied fighter jet destroyed a drone that crossed into the country's airspace from Belarus on Tuesday.
