Headline: Thirty years on, what is left of the French Touch?
Body: Will the 21st century be the era of the "great transfer"? This notion, which first emerged in Anglo-Saxon private finance under the name "Great Wealth Transfer" before being taken up in economic and sociological research, refers to the transfer of wealth linked to the gradual disappearance of the baby-boomer generation.In France, experts estimate that several trillion euros could change hands over the coming decades.Culture is also a matter of transmission, and economic stakes are never far away. Can a music scene become part of our heritage? Musical cycles move much faster than generations: in the space of around twenty years, a movement can go from marginal to a point of reference, and from a reference to part of the cultural canon.Feeding into a national narrativeThe French Touch is a good way to measure that journey. This tricolour musical movement, which propelled France onto the international stage in the 1990s and 2000s, has, after the pioneers, seen its own heirs emerge. Now an object of memory, it has gradually been woven into the national story – to the point where it is today claimed both by institutions and by political leaders.The shift is now official: French electronic music has been added to the National Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage. The Culture Ministry’s dossier, drawn up when Rachida Dati held the portfolio, pays tribute to figures such as Daft Punk, AIR and Laurent Garnier, who in the 1990s helped "establish French electronic music as an international benchmark"."Today these genres are diverse and experienced collectively across all regions," the ministry stated, adding that they are "anchored in French society, bringing together different audiences, fostering social and cultural mixing, and encouraging experimentation, collaboration and free expression."French Touch had already been given front stage at the Paris 2024 Summer Olympics. Two years later, a tragic event in turn underlined the place it now holds: the death of Kavinsky and the wave of tributes that followed.The French producer and DJ, whose real name was Vincent Belorgey, was found dead at his home on 28 July 2026, at the age of 50. He is believed to have died of a stroke."Kavinsky, French pride for ever," Emmanuel Macron said simply on Instagram in a post (source in French). The statement (source in French) from the Elysée Palace was less laconic, describing him as a "towering figure of electronic music and the French Touch, a distinctive voice who made people dance and dream", before recalling: "Invited to perform at the Fête de la Musique at the Elysée in 2018, in 2024 he brought his emblematic track 'Nightcall' to the closing ceremony of the Paris Olympic Games, alongside Angèle and the band Phoenix. That night, French electronic music rang out before the whole world.""At once danceable and nostalgic, his music will continue to transcend generations and borders," the new culture minister Catherine Pégard felt moved to add on X."Bourgeois, or the children of bourgeois"Political interest in this legacy does not, however, date from Emmanuel Macron’s time in office.Speaking to Euronews, Stéphane Jourdain, a journalist at France Inter and co-author of the podcast "Histoire secrète de la French Touch" (source in French), who also wrote the book "French Touch, 1995–2015: une épopée électro" (source in French), recalls the controversy that followed the decision by Renaud Donnedieu de Vabres, Jacques Chirac’s culture minister, to make the duo AIR, Philippe "Zdar" Cerboneschi (half of Cassius) and Dimitri From Paris knights of the Order of Arts and Letters."Awarding them an official decoration of the Republic caused a stir, it sparked debate in the scene: Daft Punk refused the honour. Laurent Garnier did too.""Zdar told me: when somebody offers me a decoration, I accept it – my mother is going to be so proud. He brushed the criticism aside," says Stéphane Jourdain, who wonders: "Are DJs compatible with this kind of institutionalisation and political recognition?"In his view, electronic music is a "space where minorities can express themselves", notably sexual minorities. "It’s something that lives outside these types of recognition," he says, all the more so as free parties have been "hunted down by the authorities for 30 to 40 years."That said, he does qualify his comments: "Kavinsky, AIR… We’re talking about the 18th arrondissement of Paris, about people who are mostly bourgeois, or the children of bourgeois."He also notes that the music championed by the leading names of French Touch falls under a "broad" definition of techno, "whether we like it or not". For him, there is a "continuum" leading up to the emergence of French Touch. "It is still part of the same family.""There is something paradoxical about a president of the Republic paying tribute to a DJ while his Interior Ministry is clamping down on rave parties," says Stéphane Jourdain, while acknowledging that Emmanuel Macron is "from the same generation" as Kavinsky and that "the tributes paid by our representatives should not be limited to Léo Ferré."Since the RIPOST law – short for "Réponses Immédiates aux Phénomènes troublant l’Ordre public, la Sécurité et la Tranquillité" (Immediate Responses to Phenomena Disturbing Public Order, Security and Tranquillity) – came into force last August, both organising and taking part in an undeclared music gathering have constituted criminal offences punishable by prison sentences.This weekend, for the first time since the reform, several hundred revellers defied a prefectural ban to attend a music gathering near Caen in Normandy, exposing themselves to heavy penalties.French Touch: Still going strong?In June 2025, when he pushed for French Touch to be added to UNESCO’s list of Intangible Cultural Heritage, Emmanuel Macron drew a parallel with the recognition granted to Berlin techno.For Stéphane Jourdain, this is about "window dressing" and "popol" – slang for "politique politicienne", or party politics – which, he says, "changes nothing". He notes that in Germany it is not techno as such that is protected, but the clubs that keep it alive. "Because they are under threat, (…) because some of them have closed, because property developers are trying to grab those spaces.""There, there is a genuine movement of resistance built around this club culture, which is very particular," he continues. By contrast, he believes that "French Touch does not need that: it has no clubs, it has no venues. French Touch is everywhere."And there is no shortage of signs that it remains vibrant. "David Guetta is one of the guys racking up the most streams right now. Bob Sinclar is still around. Records are still selling." He cites in particular the song 'Lady' (source in French) by Modjo, which is expected soon to join the select club of tracks that have surpassed one billion streams on Spotify. "Every time Bangalter does something, it creates a buzz. People wonder whether Guy-Man (Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo), the other half of Daft Punk, is going to release a solo album."For Stéphane Jourdain, it is hard to interpret all this any other way: French Touch "is in rude health; it doesn’t need to be protected.""Little moments of music"Sven Løve is a DJ who has changed his life. Now a doctor of French literature at a Spanish university, he was one of the driving forces behind Parisian garage house in the 1990s. Co-organiser of the Cheers parties, his journey is largely told in the film Eden, directed by his sister Mia Hansen-Løve.He does not see himself as part of French Touch; the music he championed at the time drew mainly on house from New York and Chicago."I was a bit in my own niche," he tells Euronews, acknowledging that there were many "connections" – meetings, friendships with Alain Braxe just as he was meeting Daft Punk and Benjamin Diamond for the 'Stardust' project."Of course I could see that [French Touch] was a global success – I had a ringside seat," he says."Back then, the organisers of the Respect (is Burning) parties, which were very French-Touch oriented, would invite us along too, me and my partner at the decks, Greg Gauthier. They had a fairly wide musical spectrum, even if the main movement was French Touch. That created a big gap between them and us, because we didn’t play the same music at all. The success was attractive – we’d have liked it, sure (laughs) – but not enough to change our style."The pioneers of French Touch stood out for their use of very short sampled loops, drawn mainly from disco and soul. They turned them into "something more personal and specific," Sven Løve recalls. "Little moments of music brought to the fore.""We’ve exhausted the subject""This musical movement became huge, its success feeding off itself until it was almost mainstream. And then, inevitably, things calmed down a bit, without completely dying out," analyses Sven Løve, before adding a nuance: "The leading figures of French Touch were smart enough to find ways of keeping their activities going, one way or another."As early as 2005, Le Monde was already talking about the "new generation", the "heirs to this electronic movement" who wanted to "escape its flagging momentum and the clichés, just as the culture minister was consecrating the genre by decorating some of its inventors."Kavinsky was among that second wave, as were the Ed Banger Records crew, including Justice and the much-missed DJ Mehdi, whose fans marked the 15th anniversary of his death on 13 September.According to Stéphane Jourdain, even if the core of the movement is confined to a particular period, those who came later, such as Thylacine or Petit Biscuit, "still benefited from what had happened.""And there is still a musical lineage, with a slightly polished, effective kind of electro that makes people dance.""The typical French Touch sound still exists, but it no longer has that sense of newness," says Sven Løve. "Yet pop music runs on the principle of novelty. It is no longer what young people listen to now. (…) In any case, pop music is bound to renew itself and head off in other directions – that’s perfectly normal.""That is the story of music," agrees Stéphane Jourdain. "What was done with those samples, those filtered funk basslines, that very accessible music, was linked to the arrival of certain machines; there is no reason to go on doing exactly the same thing.""They did it, and did it well, and I think, musically, we have now exhausted the subject."The curse of French TouchMusical movements, explains Sven Løve, often "play out over 20 or 30 years": there are "revivals or re-celebrations" of a scene that was strong two decades earlier.For the former DJ, the "tragic side" surrounding French Touch heightens fans’ emotion, with the early deaths of DJ Mehdi and Philippe Zdar, both after accidental falls. Then came Kavinsky’s death, two years after the triumph of the Olympic Games. "All of that lends itself to storytelling and, through those stories, that era is brought back to life a little."Noah, 20, likes and shares several Instagram posts commemorating DJ Mehdi on the anniversary of his death. "French Touch, for me, was my first way into music – to the point where I had it tattooed on my forearm," he tells Euronews. Just a few centimetres from his Diesel watch, the Ed Banger logo appears on his skin: a cross between a musical note and a pencil-like shape."That movement of the 1990s and 2000s embodies the pride and talent of young French musicians who embraced a kind of 'corniness' and ended up on top of the world," he says.Even if the music "is no longer centre stage," Sven Løve believes the story of French Touch continues to feed a certain sense of national pride. "Suddenly France had become the centre – there is a sort of pride there, which is why we keep talking about it," he notes. Is that pride justified? He says he can understand it, while sometimes finding it "a little excessive.""There is a curiosity among 20-year-olds about all this. But does that mean we are seeing a genuine mass movement? No, I don’t think so.""French Touch is in their blood"Then there are the heirs, in the literal sense – those who grew up in the families of the people who embodied it.In February 2026, during a back-to-back (B2B) set by Fred again.. and former Daft Punk member Thomas Bangalter at London’s Alexandra Palace, his son Roxan Bangalter was standing at the side of the stage among a handful of guests. He had no idea what was about to happen. Without telling him, Thomas Bangalter slipped into his set the vocal of 'Never The End', a track his son had composed under the alias Roxb at the age of 12 years old.He blended that vocal with the classic 'Can’t Do Without You' by Caribou, who was also on stage. The footage (source in French), filmed from the crowd, shows Roxan’s emotion as he is overwhelmed to see his father play his own creation in front of thousands of people. In his own way, and in his first performance in the UK for almost 18 years, Thomas Bangalter was giving a platform to the next generation.While Thomas Bangalter’s son remains relatively discreet, the children of Bob Sinclar – Paloma and Raphaël Le Friant – and David Guetta’s son Elvis are now themselves trying their hand at DJing.This summer, all three racked up dozens of dates: Paris, London, Ibiza, Mykonos and, of course, the Côte d’Azur.JC Murray, founder of the Isabelle festival on the heights above Saint-Tropez, says he wants to "bring back the very best of what I see around the world, in terms of both music and production, and showcase it in a place that means so much to me and my family.""When an artist moves me, I immediately picture them playing in the Citadel," he tells Euronews.For its third edition, last July, Elvis Guetta and Raphaël Le Friant opened the festival’s second day. Speaking of their family ties, JC talks about "a new generation, clearly, but one that embraces its heritage without being trapped by it.""That said, French Touch is in their blood: their fathers belong to that story," he adds. As for why he booked them, JC explains that it is first and foremost because he heard them play: "They work incredibly hard. (…) That’s what convinced me, not their surname."As for family, they were joined for a B3B by Jean-Marc Murray, the organiser’s younger cousin, the first of the three to start mixing, at around the age of 13. They are "close friends, lifelong friends". Their getting together on stage this year was something he felt "particularly strongly about.""But if they’re on the bill, it is above all for what they are in the process of becoming."

Headline: Analogue avenger: Film director Isabel Coixet defends the past in time capsule for future
Body: A cassette with 18 songs in which Camarón, Lucho Gatica and, very significantly, the Catalan rumba of "La lista de la compra" by La Cabra Mecánica and María Jiménez all rub shoulders. A personal collage, with a distinctly Lynchian feel, intentionally devoid of any explicit meaning. And a letter written with a Bic biro, with which Isabel Coixet underlines the handmade nature of her gesture and, in passing, pays tribute to torrijas, clay water jugs and open-air summer cinemas.The filmmaker (Sant Adrià del Besós, 1960) nostalgically champions, in short, a present that is on the verge of extinction, which may have vanished altogether by 2076. That is the year when box 1586 at the Instituto Cervantes will be opened, where the honouree has deposited these objects as part of her legacy to the public institution devoted to promoting the Spanish language."Understanding makes the mind lazy," says Florence Green in "The Bookshop". Coixet (historian, publicist, screenwriter and standard-bearer of the third wave of Spanish women directors) quoted her in her speech to explain why she chose not to assign any meaning to the collage in her Cervantes legacy, created on the cover of an abandoned 1913 book."I am writing this with a Bic biro, my favourite. I wonder if they still exist. You, whoever you are, do not be taken in by treatises on the wonders of the world. The Bic biro is one of humanity's great inventions," she writes in her letter, which was read out during the ceremony at the Institute. Not everything is a rallying cry: Coixet also takes the opportunity to rail against speciality coffee chains. "I hope," she wishes her anonymous reader, "that you never have the misfortune of coming across them."Perhaps for that reason, among the selection of songs Coixet is sending into the future, she has chosen to highlight "La lista de la compra". "It seems to me that in 50 years' time all the things that song talks about - the kitchen table covered in crumbs, those unbearable mixed plates, sweat, scrubbing, scouring - may well be a thing of the past."The Catalan director, who is to receive the Antonio de Sancha Award 2026 from the Madrid Publishers' Association ("for her outstanding work in bringing literature closer to the general public and for her defence of bookshops as spaces of cultural resistance"), has immersed herself in the world of film adaptations in her penultimate creative phase. In the aforementioned "The Bookshop", in a kind of metafiction, the protagonist defends her new business in rural England as both an exercise and a weapon of liberation.The event continued with a conversation between Coixet and the former president of the Association of Women Filmmakers and Audiovisual Media, Cristina Andreu, in which the two looked back over their prolific careers. Earlier, the director of the Cervantes, Luis García Montero, had also dedicated a brief speech to her: "Her films have travelled far and wide, but it would be a mistake to confuse that international trajectory with simple geography, because she has turned freedom and travel into a way of working her way towards the heart of things."The filmmaker has been nominated four times for the Golden Bear at the Berlin Film Festival, and once (for Map of the Sounds of Tokyo) for the Palme d'Or in Cannes. Over the course of her career she has also won eight Goya Awards, as a director, screenwriter and documentarian. Since 2015 she has been a Chevalier of the Order of Arts and Letters in France, and she has received Spain's National Film Award as well as the Gold Medal of Fine Arts in 2009.The Caja de las Letras at the Institute stores almost 1,800 tributes in the vault at its Madrid headquarters, a tradition that began in 2007 for all kinds of figures - individuals and institutions, living or dead - from the Spanish-speaking cultural world.

Headline: How did Greece end up borrowing more cheaply than France?
Body: In March 2012 the Greek state had to pay a market yield of close to 40% on its outstanding ten-year bonds, effectively shutting it out of normal market borrowing. Even at that price, it found few takers.That same month, France raised ten-year money at under 3%. Fourteen years later the two have swapped places.France's 10-year yield, the rate Paris pays to borrow for a decade, is trading near 4.50%. Athens pays about 4.28%.Investors are now demanding more interest to lend money to Paris than to Athens. The gap is small. What it says is not.Greece still owes more relative to the size of its economy than almost any country in Europe, while the French economy is more than ten times larger, richer and far more diversified.On paper the pricing makes no sense. It makes sense once you accept that bond investors have stopped treating the size of a debt pile as the whole story.What they weigh now is the direction it is moving, how often it has to be refinanced, and whether a government has the political room to stop adding to it.On all three, Greece and France are pulling apart.Greece owes more, but the pile is shrinkingAt the end of the first quarter, Greek public debt stood at 143.5% of annual output, against 117.6% in France.Those are the numbers that flatter Paris, and they are the only ones that do.Over the previous twelve months Greece's debt-to-GDP ratio fell by 9.4 percentage points. France's rose by about four.The European Commission expects Greece to keep falling, from 146.1% in 2025 to 134.4% by 2027. It expects France to climb above 120% over the same period.The budget picture is starker still.Greece closed last year with a surplus worth 1.7% of GDP and is forecast to stay in the black through 2027. France ran a deficit of 5.1%, one of the widest in the European Union, and this year's is getting away from it.And the French number is getting worse, not better.On 11 September, Finance Minister Roland Lescure halved the government's 2026 growth forecast to 0.5% and abandoned the 5% deficit target the budget had been built on."Five percent is no longer an option," he told reporters, declining to put a new figure in its place.The statistics office INSEE is gloomier still at 0.4%, and calls France the only large advanced economy expected to slow this year. Greece is growing at close to 2%.Why Greece’s enormous debt is less dangerous than it looksNot all debt behaves the same way, and Greece's behaves unusually well.Most of it was created by the bailouts, which means it is owed to European public institutions rather than to fund managers who can sell at the first bad headline.The loans run for decades at concessional rates. Greece's Public Debt Management Agency puts the average maturity above 18 years and the annual cost of servicing the stock at 1.94% as of the end of June.Almost the whole Greek debt is fixed-rate.Picture a household that fixed a very long mortgage when money was cheap. Rates can climb all they like; the monthly payment does not move.France does not have anything like that duration of fixed-rate protection.Bonds sold in the era of near-zero rates keep maturing and keep being replaced at today's cost. Interest payments are on course for €65 billion this year, some €4.5 billion above budget, which makes debt service the single biggest item of state spending.The Cour des Comptes, the public audit body, has warned the bill could approach €100 billion by 2029.Economists call the mechanism a snowball.Once borrowing costs rise faster than the economy grows, debt climbs on its own unless the state runs a surplus before interest, and the OECD has warned that without policy changes French debt could reach about 200% of GDP by 2050.One country sells €8 billion of bonds. The other sells €310 billion.Then there is supply. France plans to issue €310 billion of medium and long-term bonds in 2026, net of buybacks.Greece plans to issue only about €8 billion of bonds this year. It is also repaying roughly €13 billion early, helped by cash reserves of close to €40 billion.A bigger economy naturally borrows bigger sums, but the market still has to absorb them auction after auction, and a market that has to absorb can name its price.Political risk has changed addressThe ratings capture the reversal.Greece, which spent much of the previous decade below investment grade, is now investment grade at every major agency. S&P Global and Fitch rate it BBB, while Moody's rates it Baa3. All three have stable outlooks, while several smaller agencies have positive outlooks.France remains more highly rated. But the direction has changed there as well. S&P and Fitch currently rate France A+. Moody's rating is Aa3, with a negative outlook.Ratings agencies are not suggesting France is close to default. The concern is more mundane: repeated large deficits, slow growth and limited political agreement over how to reduce spending or raise revenue.France's fragmented parliament has made that task harder. The presidential election next spring adds another layer of uncertainty.None of this makes France the new GreeceNobody is pricing a French default. Paris commands deep markets, a large domestic savings base and a tax capacity Athens could only envy in 2012, and its credit standing remains several notches higher.What the crossover marks is a change in what investors reward. Falling debt, budget surpluses and a quiet refinancing calendar now buy a discount. Rising deficits, heavy issuance and a deadlocked parliament carry an additional charge on interest rates.In 2012, investors were pricing in the possibility that Greece would still be using the euro by Christmas. In 2026, the more immediate question is how much further Athens can reduce its debt.France faces almost the opposite one: how long can debt keep rising before investors demand an even higher price to finance it?

Headline: Doomers vs boosters: Who's who in the global fight over the risks of AI
Body: The furious debate over artificial intelligence has hardened into warring camps, with a cautious middle caught between them.Here is a look at the battle lines in the war over a technology that is now the backbone of the economy and could decide the future of the planet.Both terms grew out of online AI debates on X and internet forums rather than formal usage, borrowing the slang habit of tech and crypto communities that coin shorthand for opposing camps.'Doomer' describes those forecasting catastrophe, while 'booster,' sometimes used interchangeably with 'accelerationist,' describes those pushing for AI's rapid, unrestrained development.The doomersFear of technology's dangerous consequences for society goes back far in history.OpenAI was founded in part because its backers, including first investor Elon Musk, feared that AI's development would end up in the hands of Google, which they believed could not be trusted with the technology.Today, most of the doomers warning against the impact of artificial intelligence come from inside the companies themselves, from academia, or both.Those inside the industry are best represented by Dario Amodei, who co-founded Anthropic, now a major AI giant heading toward a historic IPO.He left OpenAI because he felt the Sam Altman-led company was not taking the technology's potential and dangers seriously enough.His stance is decried as hypocritical, coming from a company that is itself pushing out cutting-edge technology.Former Google researcher Geoffrey Hinton and fellow computer scientist Yoshua Bengio led the warnings about AI's threats in the months after the release of ChatGPT in 2022, which kickstarted the latest AI frenzy.MIT physicist Max Tegmark, who heads the Future of Life Institute, organised the open letter in 2023 that called for a six-month pause in the development of the most advanced AI systems, drawing thousands of signatures, including Musk's.Further outside the industry is Eliezer Yudkowsky, a self-taught theorist who has spent two decades arguing that a sufficiently powerful AI would wipe out humanity.Build, build, buildDiametrically opposed to the doomers are the accelerationists, who believe in technology's advancement, its inevitability and its fundamental benefit for society, and who also make their fortunes on its success.The ethos is widespread in Silicon Valley, but it is best represented by venture capital figures with considerable sway in the White House, such as Marc Andreessen, the influential head of venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, and David Sacks, the former White House AI czar.Personally and philosophically aligned with tech figure Peter Thiel, the group is fundamentally opposed to regulation and battles behind the scenes and on X against what it calls a well-financed doomsday "cult."They accuse doomers of being a front for companies seeking to use regulation to crush rivals.Garry Tan, who runs the startup incubator Y Combinator, is among the loudest of those voices, casting safety-driven regulation as a threat to the small companies that cannot absorb its costs.Andreessen and his allies lavishly fund political action committees that donate to Republican and Democratic lawmakers promoting AI growth, with Anthropic now leading an effort to match that spending through its own fundraising.In the same go-faster camp is Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, whose chips are the bricks and mortar of the AI revolution, housed in the gargantuan data centres now meeting opposition across the United States.Huang dismisses talk of AI-driven extinction as "complete nonsense," though he has broken from some accelerationists in calling for a unified federal AI framework and industry-run peer review, rather than no regulation at all.Also worth noting is Yann LeCun, who shared the Turing Award with Hinton and Bengio and has spent years dismissing their warnings of existential danger as overblown.Proceeding with cautionMany big tech companies try to proceed carefully, in a positioning more typical of large corporations that do not want to be caught on the wrong side of a political fight.At its founding in 2015, OpenAI was structured to ensure that researchers, and not investors, would have the final say on how the technology was deployed, with safety for humanity the guiding philosophy.But under Altman, who survived an in-house coup in 2023 led by safety-focused colleagues, the company now toes a more complicated line, speaking to AI's dangers while still accelerating and cozying up to a no-holds-barred White House.Google, Microsoft and Amazon are veterans of talking about safety in tech while navigating Washington successfully to keep regulation to a minimum.With AI, they are still walking that fine line.

Headline: How Belarus helps Russia and its drone arsenal target Ukraine and threaten NATO
Body: The drone shot down by NATO over Lithuania overnight on Tuesday had entered the country’s airspace from neighbouring Belarus, Vilnius said.The drone flew over Lentvaris close to the Lithuanian capital before being brought down near the village of Pratkūnai, according to Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre.It was the first time a drone was shot down over Lithuanian territory.The incident puts Minsk back in focus not only for helping Russia carry out drone attacks against Ukraine, but now also as a source of drone threats to NATO territory.The incursion came just a day after Ukrainian officials said Russia was using Belarusian mobile networks and signal repeaters to support Shahed-type drones during attacks on western Ukraine.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's advisor Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said the flight paths of Russian drones during a mass attack on Saturday suggested they were making use of mobile networks across the border.“If we look at the movement of jet-powered and conventional ‘Shaheds,’ they stay close to the border with Belarus," Beskrestnov said.Beskrestnov said he believed the drones probably had access to Belarusian commercial LTE networks.On Monday Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service separately said recent Russian attacks on the western regions of Rivne, Volyn and Lviv had been supported by communications infrastructure located inside Belarus.“The air assets launched by Russia were fed with a signal through repeaters that were also located precisely on the territory of this country,” border guard spokesperson Andrii Demchenko said.The claims suggest Russia is again making use of communications infrastructure inside Belarus to support its drone campaign against Ukraine, months after Kyiv demanded that the equipment be shut down.Ukraine’s military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko said last week that Kyiv had identified six repeater stations in Belarus used by Russian forces to relay video streams from strike drones, and that some of the equipment had resumed operating.The equipment has been a source of tension between Kyiv and Minsk since June, when Zelenskyy gave Belarus a week to dismantle or switch off the Russian-installed repeaters, warning that Ukraine would otherwise act itself.Days later, Zelenskyy said the repeaters had stopped operating on 22 June, although it remained unclear whether they had actually been removed.The shutdown did not last long. By the end of June Ukrainian military officials said the equipment had not been dismantled and that at least one repeater had been switched back on.Their apparent return gives Russia another means of maintaining communications with strike drones operating close to Ukraine’s northern and western borders, including areas close to NATO territory.Russia has increasingly used a mixture of mobile networks and radio technology to maintain links with its long-range strike drones and overcome Ukrainian electronic warfare.

Headline: Suspected sabotage brings Dutch rail network to a standstill on Budget Day
Body: Rail travel across large parts of the Netherlands ground to a halt on Tuesday after authorities discovered tubes tied to tracks at roughly 20 locations, in what officials are treating as coordinated sabotage.Rail infrastructure operator ProRail said deliberately placed objects had triggered widespread track-circuit failures."Materials were found at multiple locations on the track that were deliberately placed there," said ProRail in a statement."This causes section malfunctions. Sabotage appears to be involved," added the operator.The devices caused signalling systems to read affected sections as occupied, halting all trains through them regardless of whether one was actually present.The disruption began around 5:30am (CET) and hit the Amersfoort–Zwolle, Utrecht–Arnhem, Arnhem–Zutphen and Zwolle–Leeuwarden routes hardest, with national operator NS reporting severe knock-on delays around Zwolle, Deventer and Amersfoort during the morning commuter hours.One train struck a tube near Steenwijk, in Overijssel and ProRail confirmed no one was injured.Timing of disruption linked to Budget DayMalfunctioning level crossings also disrupted road traffic in affected areas.The disruption occurred on the same day as Prinsjesdag, the Netherlands' annual Budget Day, when the King traditionally processes through The Hague before large crowds.Authorities have not said whether the two are connected.State Secretary for Infrastructure and Water Management Annet Bertram said she was "deeply concerned" and called for a thorough investigation.The National Police are leading that inquiry. No group has claimed responsibility, and ProRail says it does not yet know who was behind the attack or why.

Headline: UN urges full access for investigators as Gaza death toll mounts
Body: The United Nations has called on Israel to grant international investigators access to every part of Gaza, as the recovery of human remains from the territory's ruins continues nearly three years after the war began.The UN's human rights office said gathering evidence at destroyed sites was essential, urging that "international investigators be allowed into all parts of Gaza to assist with evidence-gathering."Most of the dead being recovered are reported to be women and children, a detail the UN says points to the likelihood that war crimes were committed during the campaign."The remains of what appears to be entire families are now being unearthed at locations that were pulverised by Israeli attacks," UN rights chief Volker Turk pointed out in a statement."I worry the remains recovered so far may only be the tip of the iceberg," he said, pointing to how "much of Gaza has been flattened by Israeli bombing or demolition and clearing by heavy machinery and explosives"."Today, many areas in Gaza where the Israeli military is deployed continue to be levelled by bulldozers with no respect for the dead under the rubble," he said.According to the Palestinian Civil Defence, more than 630 bodies and other remains have been pulled from beneath collapsed buildings across Gaza since last November alone.The UN's rights office cited an estimate that over 8,000 people remain missing under the rubble — a figure that underscores how much of the territory's devastation has yet to be fully accounted for.Turk insisted that "every feasible effort must be taken to document and identify these victims, preserve forensic information and biological samples, record their burial locations and inform their families"."The discovery of extensive remains under the rubble in Gaza City resurfaces (the) concerns of war crimes and other atrocity crimes," he warned.The war began after Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which killed at least 1,195 people according to official Israeli data. Israel's subsequent bombing campaign and ground invasion left much of Gaza in ruins.Gaza's health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority, says the offensive has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in total, including over 1,350 since a ceasefire was signed last October.For European governments navigating the diplomatic fallout of the conflict, the UN's call adds pressure on Israel to open Gaza to independent scrutiny at a moment when the scale of civilian loss is still being uncovered.

Headline: FLEX satellite in orbit: studying plant responses to climate change from space
Body: The Vega-C rocket has placed the FLEX and Sentinel-3C satellites in orbit from French Guiana, enabling scientists to study the state of vegetation and obtain new data on the oceans, land, ice and the atmosphere.Since Tuesday, Europe has had two new satellites to observe Earth from space. The Vega-C rocket lifted off from the European spaceport in Kourou, in French Guiana, at 22:21 on Monday carrying the FLEX and Sentinel-3C satellites.The mission, known as VV30, will help expand the information available on the state of the planet and the effects of climate change.The main goal of FLEX is to gain a better understanding of how plants function and how they respond to situations such as extreme heat or a lack of water.The satellite is equipped with an instrument capable of detecting a faint light that plants emit when they carry out photosynthesis. This signal cannot be seen with the naked eye, but it contains information about the state of vegetation and makes it possible to detect when plants are suffering because of environmental conditions.FLEX will be able to produce maps of vegetation activity with a resolution of around 300 metres by 300 metres. The mission is designed to operate for at least three and a half years.The mission also has significant Spanish involvement. Scientist José Moreno, a professor at the University of Valencia and principal investigator for FLEX, is leading the mission's scientific team. Spain's Ministry of Science itself has underlined the country's role in this European Space Agency project.Travelling alongside FLEX is Sentinel-3C, the third satellite in the Sentinel-3 mission under the European Copernicus programme. Its job will be to continuously monitor the oceans, land surface, ice and atmosphere. Its data are used, among other things, to improve weather forecasting and to study how the climate and the environment are evolving.Sentinel-3C will join a mission that already includes the Sentinel-3A and Sentinel-3B satellites. The new spacecraft will replace Sentinel-3A, which has been in operation since 2016.Although FLEX and Sentinel-3C travelled into space together, they will not initially remain in the same orbit. This will allow data from both missions to be combined to gain a better understanding of how vegetation responds to environmental conditions.

Headline: Trillions sitting idle: Here's how much money Europeans are losing on savings
Body: Doing nothing with your savings has a price, and new figures put a number on it.Revolut published its European Wealth Drain Index last week, combining a survey of 20,007 adults across 20 member states with official deposit and inflation data, and the picture it paints is of a continent whose households are quietly getting poorer while sitting on their money.In 12 of the 20 markets included in the study, average one-year deposit rates fail to keep pace with inflation.Across the sample, deposits pay an average of 2.76% against inflation of 2.94%, meaning even savers who lock their money away are losing ground in real terms.Inertia, confusion and app fatigueThe opportunity cost is larger than the inflation loss.Benchmarked against the MSCI Europe ETF's ten-year annualised return of 9.06%, Revolut calculates households forgo an average of €638 per €10,000 each year by staying in cash.Scaled across the €6.3 trillion, that amounts to €422 billion a year in growth capital not reaching European businesses.Why savers stay put comes down to three things.Two-thirds have never switched banks for a better rate, with 26% saying they simply prefer their existing bank, 18% considering the difference negligible and 15% not knowing where to look.Nearly half, 46%, misjudge their inflation-adjusted returns, and 19% are unaware inflation affects their cash at all. Over half use multiple financial apps, and among those, 45% say the fragmentation actively hinders investing.To make matters worse, one in five Europeans has no savings at all.If inertia runs that deep, the obvious question is whether better products can overcome it or whether something more forceful is needed, such as the automatic enrolment used to lift pension participation.Rolandas Juteika, Revolut's head of wealth and trading, rejects that approach.However, his company, which has more than 80 million customers, has a clear commercial interest in the answer as it sells the investment products the research says Europeans should be using, and reports that active EU retail investors on its platform grew 56% year on year.Among those who do not invest, the survey found perceived risk was the main barrier for 29% and a lack of knowledge for 27%."Forced enrolment doesn't tackle the root causes of inertia: perceived risk (29%) and a lack of knowledge (27%)," Juteika told Euronews, adding that "with our median first-time EU investment at just €18, we see firsthand that lowering the barrier to €1 naturally empowers consumers to act."Asked whether folding banking, savings and investing into a single app genuinely reduces fragmentation or simply moves it somewhere else, Juteika argued the difference is structural.Consolidating those functions "removes the administrative wall between a person's salary, savings and capital markets," he said.A continent divided three waysThe regional patterns are stark.Central and eastern Europe faces the widest gaps between inflation and deposit rates, led by Bulgaria at 2.3% , Slovakia at 1.7% and Lithuania at 1.3%. Yet, appetite for investing small sums is highest there, with 51% in both Bulgaria and Romania willing to start.Western and southern Europe holds the largest piles of idle cash, with Germany at €1.9 trillion and France at €588 billion, and faces an opportunity gap of 6% to 7%.Northern Europe has deposit rates that broadly match inflation but the weakest awareness, with fewer than 40% of respondents in Denmark and Sweden understanding how inflation affects long-term wealth.Brussels wants the same money movedThe findings land in the middle of a live political argument.Addressing French business leaders in Paris last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen made almost identical points, framing idle deposits as a problem of European competitiveness rather than personal finance."In Europe, there is no shortage of technology or savings," von der Leyen declared, adding that "there is still a shortage of capacity to scale up Europe's businesses."Companies that start in Europe too often leave to find funding, she added, shifting their centre of gravity or being bought outright."Europe has savings. And unfortunately, those savings are sitting idle," she continued."Today, €10 trillion in household savings are kept in bank accounts. And a large share of Europe's savings is invested outside our continent. Europe now needs to put these savings to work for its companies. This is the goal of the Savings and Investments Union."The Commission's €10 trillion and Revolut's €6.3 trillion measure different things.The Commission figure covers household savings held in bank accounts across the whole EU, while Revolut counts only liquid deposits in the 20 markets it surveyed, which excludes seven member states.The arithmetic behind Brussels' interest is straightforward.The Draghi report put Europe's additional investment needs at €750 billion to €800 billion a year by 2030 to fund digitalisation, energy, defence and infrastructure, a sum member states cannot raise through borrowing.Public debt stood at 82.9% of EU GDP in the first quarter of this year and 88.9% across the eurozone, according to Eurostat. If the money is not going to come from governments, it has to come from somewhere else.The Savings and Investments Union, adopted as a strategy in March 2025 and overseen by Financial Services Commissioner Maria Luís Albuquerque, is the vehicle.It is not a mechanism for touching anyone's deposits, and confers no power to do so.Instead it works through incentives and plumbing with a recommendation on savings and investment accounts giving retail savers a simple route into capital markets, a review of the pan-European pension product on which the Council agreed a position in June, rules on securitisation, changes to how banks and insurers can invest, and deeper supervision."Together, these measures could unlock up to €470 billion in additional investment," von der Leyen said.Juteika supports the effort but sees a missing piece."It's important that the EU can rely on a unified single market driven by open banking and open finance principles, allowing citizens to see their full financial picture, benefit from innovation, and move capital seamlessly," he told Euronews, adding that "while policy catches up, we're already bridging this gap across all 27 member states."Not everyone is comfortable. Critics argue that a Commission facing this scale of funding gap has an obvious interest in influencing where household money ends up, and that harmonised supervision concentrates authority in Brussels over decisions previously left to national regulators and individual savers.The timetable is tight, and von der Leyen has already signalled she will not wait for everyone."We now need to reach an agreement, before the end of the year, ideally with all 27 Member States. But if that doesn't work, if necessary we will do it with those that are ready," she declared.

Headline: Iran's new ayatollah is a Nolan fan interested in start-ups, in-laws say
Body: Six months into his tenure as Iran's ayatollah, Mojtaba Khamenei has given no public interviews and appeared in no new photographs, yet his late wife's family is now depicting him as a movie buff with a keen interest in start-ups.Farideddin Haddad Adel, the brother of Zahra Haddad-Adel — killed alongside Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in the 28 February US-Israel strike on the supreme leader's compound — has described his brother-in-law in interviews republished by state-aligned Iranian media.He portrayed Mojtaba Khamenei as someone with broad interests spanning technology, start-ups, psychology, cognitive sciences and film, and said he is familiar with the work of British director Christopher Nolan."Unlike His Eminence (Ali Khamenei), he is not into literature, but he watches a lot of films," Haddad Adel said.Tayyebeh Mahrouzadeh, Zahra's mother, said in comments republished by Iranian media in June that before asking for her daughter's hand, Mojtaba Khamenei had obtained a TOEFL English-language certificate and was diligent in learning foreign languages.Living simply, dressing plainlyHaddad Adel also said his brother-in-law spent some 25 years working in security, military and political roles alongside Ali Khamenei.He dates it back to May 1997, when reformist candidate Mohammad Khatami won the presidential election against the candidate backed by the ayatollah's office, in what became known in Iran as the start of the reform era.Ali Khamenei and institutions under his control subsequently worked to obstruct the reformist government's legislative agenda — Khatami later said his administration faced a crisis every nine days.The family also describes Mojtaba Khamenei as living simply, dressing plainly and sleeping little. The details are not independently verifiable.Presenting a simple lifestyle was a recurring feature of pro-regime media coverage of Ali Khamenei throughout his decades in power, used to distance the leadership from corruption allegations and signal loyalty to the values of the 1979 revolution.Now, Mojtaba Khamenei is intentionally presented as a cleric rooted in religious and security structures while staying in touch with modern culture — someone familiar with English, Hollywood cinema, and technology, yet not at odds with the Islamic Republic's political order.Mojtaba Khamenei, 56, was appointed ayatollah by the Assembly of Experts on 8 March, nine days after surviving the strike that killed his father and wife. He had married Zahra Haddad-Adel in 1999.Her father, Gholam-Ali Haddad-Adel, is a prominent conservative politician who served as speaker of parliament and adviser to Ali Khamenei.

Headline: China's retail sales slow again as Beijing struggles to revive consumer spending
Body: Chinese shoppers are barely spending more than they were a year ago, and the gap between what the country makes and what it buys is widening.Figures published by China's National Bureau of Statistics on Tuesday showed year-on-year retail sales growth of just 0.4%, falling short of the 0.8% economists had forecast and slowing from 0.6% in July and 1% in June.However, the number is at least positive.Retail sales shrank 0.6% in May, so August represents an improvement on the low point, but it leaves consumption close to flat at a time when the Chinese government has made reviving it a priority.Domestic spending has been sluggish since the end of the Covid-19 pandemic, dragging on economic growth even as exports have boomed.Factories up, investment downThe rest of the data pulls in opposite directions.Industrial production expanded 5.2% in August, a jump from July's 4.5% and comfortably ahead of the 4.8% forecast. Fixed-asset investment, by contrast, contracted 7.2% year on year in the first eight months of 2026, in line with forecasts.The statistics bureau said the economy "operated steadily" last month while conceding that "adverse external factors are intensifying."It went further in describing the underlying problem by stating that "the domestic imbalance between strong supply and weak demand remains pronounced, some firms face operational difficulties, and the foundation for steady economic improvement requires consolidation."Analysts read the same split."China's economy continues to show diverging signals, as consumption and investment remain weak while industrial production maintains the momentum," wrote Zhiwei Zhang, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management.Beijing is targeting economic growth of between 4.5% and 5.0% for this year, its lowest goal in decades.Money already committedThe figures land days after Beijing moved to shore up its financial system.Announced the previous Sunday, the finance ministry is leading a 360 billion yuan (€46.1bn) capital injection into eight state-owned banks and insurers, with around 290 billion yuan (€37.2bn) going to banks specifically to preserve their capacity to keep lending as the government presses them to support and stimulate economic activity.Whether that filters through to household spending remains a question.Zhang expects continued weakness in the near term precisely because fiscal support takes time to reach the economy."The economy faces downside risk in [the third quarter] as the fiscal support takes time to be implemented and transmitted to the economy," he wrote.That leaves Beijing leaning on the one part of the economy still performing, with industrial output expanding and exports remaining strong.The next move is diplomatic.Xi Jinping is expected to travel to Washington on 24 September and is reportedly preparing to bring a large delegation of Chinese business executives — a departure for a leader who rarely travels with corporate figures and has not done so on this scale since 2015.Many of those executives lost standing during the regulatory crackdowns on technology, education and property that began in 2020.Bringing them to meet US President Donald Trump would signal a willingness to invest and trade, though expectations for the summit remain modest, with the two sides still divided over which products should count as non-sensitive under existing trade arrangements.

Headline: France ties EU sanctions renewal to prisoner release
Body: But first, a scoop: The European Commission is set to propose restricting children’s access to social media such as Instagram, TikTok and YouTube while introducing safety requirements for online services like video games and AI chatbots, my colleague Luca Bertuzzi reports.Under the proposal, due to be unveiled Thursday, minors under 15 years old would not be able to create their accounts on social media or video sharing platforms without their parents’ approval, while tech companies would have to make their digital services safe by design, according to a confidential document obtained by Luca. The bill is set to feature in European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s annual State of the Union address to the European Parliament tomorrow, and follows similar moves by several EU member states to tighten restrictions on children’s access to social media.EU sanctions deadlock: In other news, France is pressing for Russian-Uzbek businessman Alisher Usmanov to be removed from the EU sanctions list in an effort to secure the release of an unspecified number of French nationals detained in Azerbaijan, according to several officials and diplomats familiar with the negotiations who spoke to Euronews last night.France’s demand – also backed by Slovakia, a rare joint effort that has baffled Brussels – forced EU ambassadors to agree to extend the existing sanctions for just one week until 22 September to give themselves more time to find a solution that has so far proven stubbornly elusive, my colleague Jorge Liboreiro writes in to report.The renewal of the sanctions relates to as many as 3,000 Russian individuals accused of supporting Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "France isn't for budging, but it would send the absolute wrong message at the wrong time," one official said, speaking on condition of anonymity. "I'm not sure what will change in a week."Most member states remain opposed to removing names from the sanctions list while Russia continues its war in Ukraine and amid concerns over hybrid attacks in Europe.‘National security’: However, some officials acknowledge that France has cited national security concerns, a principle applied to critical issues. The French government declined to comment. "Everything has an explanation," one diplomat said."Consultations will continue, and further discussions are expected to be held in due course," a spokesperson for Ireland's EU Council presidency said."Renewal of the listings is essential to continue undermining Russia's war machine, and keeping the pressure on those individuals and entities supporting, enabling and benefitting from it. This is a priority for the Presidency."State of the Union countdown: Expectations are running high ahead of tomorrow’s State of the Union speech by Ursula von der Leyen, and my colleagues Vincenzo Genovese and Luca Bertuzzi, currently en route to Strasbourg, have dug into the main topics set to feature.The annual address is known for its breadth and length, covering issues ranging from defence readiness to natural disasters while setting the agenda for the next legislative cycle through new policies, strategies, initiatives and action plans.Yet the sheer number of promises means some inevitably go unfulfilled, while others are quietly dropped or simply fall apart. Our team parsed over last year’s speech to assess von der Leyen’s performance. The results are defintely a mixed bag.VDL’s U-turn: A spokesperson for the European Commission confirmed last night that von der Leyen will attend the plenary on Thursday when Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, the guest of honour at this plenary session, delivers his much-anticipated speech. That’s despite the Commission initially saying the president would skip Carney’s speech, despite the Canadian premier attending hers tomorrow. Von der Leyen’s agenda was re-arranged to “make it possible”, the spokesperson said.EU-Canada renewal: Von der Leyen could flesh out in her speech her vision for a deeper relationship with Canada, EU officials say, after Carney publicly made the case for building a “unique alliance” between Brussels and Ottawa. Yet experts tell me that the revamped relationship is likely to be symbolic above all else, with deeper integration on trade and economics likely to require pain-staking negotiations.In other news this morning: The European Commission Vice-President for social rights, Roxana Mînzatu, has told Europe Today that a new EU platform on labour mobility set to be presented today will avoid “talented” people “wasting their skills” when they move across EU borders.The Commission will later today unveil a new European platform designed to make it easier for Europeans to request, receive, and verify social security documents online. The aim is to address the difficulties Europeans face when their documents need to be recognised across borders, ensuring that their social security rights are fully upheld. Watch the full interview.Ukraine’s prosecutor general suspended after leaving country amid corruption scandalUkrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy suspended Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko on Monday, hours after it emerged that he had left the country after resigning amid a major corruption probe that had reached his own office, Sasha Vakulina reports.Kravchenko crossed the border overnight, according to Ukrainian media citing law-enforcement sources, and later released a video saying he had signed a notice of suspicion against Semen Kryvonos, director of Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU), whom he alleged had forged official documents to obtain an unlawful benefit.Kryvonos rejected the allegation and told reporters later on Monday that he had neither seen the notice nor been formally served with one.NABU and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) described Kravchenko’s actions as part of what they called a “systematic attack” on Ukraine’s independent anti-corruption institutions.Zelenskyy intervened later on Monday, signing a decree suspending Kravchenko and asking parliament to dismiss him. “This prosecutor general has only one path ahead: dismissal from office,” Zelenskyy said, urging lawmakers to act without delay. Lawmakers expected to vote on Kravchenko’s dismissal on Tuesday.Read the full story.More from our newsroomsParliament pushes tougher energy permit deadlines, setting up clash with EU countries. MEPs are pushing for tougher EU-wide deadlines and automatic approvals to speed up energy infrastructure, setting the stage for a clash with EU countries seeking more flexibility over how their national permitting systems work, according to an internal document seen by Euronews’ Marta Pacheco. More.EU trade chief to visit Manila to finalise Philippines trade deal. EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič will visit Manila next week to finalise a trade agreement with the Philippines, the European Commission confirmed to Euronews’ Peggy Corlin on Monday.US Supreme Court rejects Trump mail ballot restrictions ahead of midterm election. US President Donald Trump's attempt to limit mail-in ballots for the midterm elections was denied by the US Supreme Court on Monday, ending a flurry of last-minute legal action with voting already under way, Jeremy Fisayo-Bambi reports.We're also keeping an eye onEuropean Council President Antonio Costa continues his whirlwind European tour; meets Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker in Vienna, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in Rome and French President Emmanuel Macron in Paris.The European Parliament plenary session continues in Strasbourg. MEPs debate the recent mass entry of migrants into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at 13.00 CET, and the pompous funeral given to war criminal Ratko Mladić in Belgrade at 14.00 CET.European Commissioner for Energy Dan Jørgensen participates in the G20 Ministerial Meeting on Energy in Houston, the US.That’s it for today. Jorge Liboreiro, Sasha Vakulina, Shona Murray, Eleonora Vasques and Vincenzo Genovese, contributed to this newsletter.

Headline: Microsoft introduces AI guardrails for US schools amid growing backlash
Body: Microsoft is introducing guardrails and privacy standards for its AI in schools in the United States, as negotiated with the country’s second-largest teachers' union, amid a growing backlash against AI and screen time.The agreement, signed last week, prohibits the use of AI companions or features “designed to foster emotional attachment or dependency” or designed to keep students engaged for longer than a learning task requires.The standards are legally binding and require third-party audits to check compliance.As part of the wide-ranging agreement, Microsoft says it will not use student or educator data to train AI systems, apart from a narrow exception for data that could help protect students. It says the data it collects cannot be sold, used for advertising or used for product development.It also includes audit and transparency measures requiring the company to explain to families in plain language how its tools work and what data they collect.“This standard sets a high bar for child privacy and AI safety, and we’ll extend this agreement to every school district across the country,” said Brad Smith, Microsoft's vice chair and president, in a statement.The standards will apply to Microsoft school contracts across the US from November 1, according to the company.Is an AI brake needed in European classrooms?AI is already making its way into European classrooms and young people are also increasingly turning to chatbots beyond schoolwork.A European Commission study of early adopters in secondary schools in Finland, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg and Spain found students were using generative AI to explain difficult topics, practise skills and prepare for exams.Meanwhile, a separate 2026 Austrian study found that 60% of 11- to 17-year-olds surveyed had sought advice from AI chatbots about issues such as stress, conflicts or heartbreak, while 30% had discussed worries or feelings with them.Some European governments are already drawing limits around younger pupils' use.Norway said this year that children aged roughly six to 12 should generally not use generative AI themselves for schoolwork, while those aged around 13 to 15 can begin experimenting with it cautiously.France allows pupils to learn about AI at primary-school age but says they should not directly use generative AI. Supervised classroom use can begin from around age 13 or 14.A document seen by Euronews suggests that the European Commission will propose barring under-15s from risky online services like AI chatbots in a legislative proposal that will be published on Thursday.OpenAI and Anthropic in talks over similar safeguards While experts say the safety provisions in the US agreement are meaningful, some warn that stronger safeguards should not automatically be interpreted as an endorsement of greater AI use in schools.“I worry that a high-profile framework like this will be misunderstood and schools will think, ‘If they’re doing a good job on data privacy and safety, then that means we should be using the tool,’” said Josh Golin, executive director of US online safety nonprofit Fairplay.Golin says the standards will only be effective if other major AI companies also sign on.“Is Google going to embrace this framework? That is a huge question,” he said.Google faced criticism in the US after expanding Gemini-powered tools in Google Classroom in August to school-issued accounts used by students under 18.Critics have described the expansion as another step in the competition between tech giants to establish their AI products in schools and reach younger users. Google says Classroom is used by more than 150 million teachers and students worldwide.The US teachers union is also in talks with OpenAI and Anthropic, which both publicly welcomed the Microsoft agreement.OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, called it an “important milestone for AI safety and privacy in schools.” The company said it had been working with the teachers' union and expected to finalise its own agreement.Anthropic, the maker of Claude, said it also supported efforts to promote responsible AI use in education and was working with the union on safety and privacy standards.

Headline: EU institutions face budget cuts as member states scramble for money
Body: Most European Union capitals want to cut the money allocated to the bloc's civil service, as part of a deal on the EU's next long-term budget, a document seen by Euronews reveals.Member states are currently weighing how to cut costs as part of a wider agreement, under which the European Commission, European Parliament and Council of the EU could all see their budgets shrink.EU countries are locked in intense negotiations on the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), the budget for 2028-2034. On Wednesday, ambassadors will discuss potential landing zones for the total volume, originally set at around €2 trillion."A majority of member states saw Heading 4 [European Public Administration] as an area where reductions could be made," reads a note circulated ahead of a discussion at EU ambassador level on Wednesday and seen by Euronews.According to the document, many European governments questioned "the justification of the proposed increase in staff levels contained in the Commission proposal while many member states are constraining expenditure and headcount in their own national civil services".How high Brussels should set the bar for the next budget remains a point of contention between member states, split into a camp calling for a more ambitious budget led by France and Spain, and the so-called "frugals," like Germany and the Netherlands, who want to reduce it by "several hundred billion euros."In June, the Cypriot rotating presidency of the EU Council presented a compromise proposal reducing the overall size by 2%, with the heftiest cuts falling on the Competitiveness Fund, for defence and industry investments, and the Global Europe Fund, the development aid pot.The current Irish presidency is now working on a new compromise, expected in early October, ahead of a fresh discussion at the European Council summit on 15-16 October."What is your view on the volume of expenditure proposed by the current Negotiating Box and what do you see as the potential landing zone for these discussions?" the Irish government asked EU ambassadors in the note.On funding for National and Regional Partnership Plans, which cover EU support for poorer regions, agriculture and fisheries, the note states that it "is the most important priority for the majority of member states".On the Competitiveness Fund, the presidency acknowledges broad support for its objectives of boosting Europe's research and defence industries, but notes "there is a degree of openness by some to more moderated increases".Enlargement support, particularly for Ukraine, is also seen as a priority within the international aid programme.In other words, the area of broadest consensus, according to the presidency note, is the budget allocated to the EU institutions themselves. Many European capitals are already tightening their belts, squeezed by ballooning defence spending, rising energy costs and aid to Ukraine.The European Commission is already undergoing a review expected to lead to an internal reorganisation. Those plans could be coupled with a proposal on how to make a union of 30 or more member states work in practice, expected at the end of the month.The European External Action Service is also under pressure to reform and become more effective, with the latest German-led proposal suggesting the EU's diplomatic service could be placed directly under the Commission's remit, with a significant presence of seconded national diplomats.The discussion on the bloc's budget will continue at a meeting of the General Affairs Council next week.
